Googlebook review: Android on a laptop is still Android

Ars Technica Long form October 16, 2026

Android laptops are here, but Google has a lot of work ahead to make them good.

Android was designed for phones, but that hasn’t stopped Google from trying to adapt the OS and its apps to larger machines over the years. Googlebooks are just the latest attempt after tablets, Chromebooks, and foldables induced little change in how people interact with Android software. These new Android-powered laptops are designed to pick up where the web-focused ChromeOS left off, offering premium hardware and native support for Android apps.

Google sees Googlebooks as an alternative to Windows and macOS, but these platforms are entrenched with decades of software and UI conventions that keep users locked in. Googlebooks have to offer something very special to steal users away from either of the dominant operating systems.

For devoted Android phone users, there are some cool things in Googlebook OS, but the Android roots of these machines are impossible to miss. Sometimes it feels like using a Chromebook, and sometimes it feels like using a giant phone. It almost never feels like using a premium laptop, and that’s the problem.

While there were a few premium Chromebooks, the platform was really only successful in the budget segment. With Googlebooks, the company is almost conspicuously ignoring lower-cost options. And as most of the lineup clocks in at well over a thousand dollars, Googlebooks are not just a new take on budget-oriented Chromebooks.

All of the launch Googlebooks have excellent touchscreen displays, aluminum and magnesium bodies, biometric unlock (fingerprint or face), and big trackpads. There’s also the Glowbar, which doesn’t do very much right now. It lights up in Google colors when Gemini is activated with the wake word and during boot-up. It also shows the battery level when you plug in a Googlebook. The latter is modestly useful, but it’s not really a selling point.

There’s something in the lineup for most premium laptop buyers. If you want a convertible, there’s the Acer machine. Sleek and spendy? Asus and HP have you covered. Want something a little bigger? Lenovo has a 15.3-inch model with an HDMI port and USB-A.

The least-spendy model, the Acer Googlebook 14, starts at $899, and that’s a limited-time deal. Even this one gets a lot of the hardware right. It has a vibrant OLED screen, a metal chassis, and three USB-C ports (all of which can charge the laptop). However, you won’t get a haptic trackpad, just the old-fashioned kind that physically clicks. The supposedly DTS-tuned speakers also don’t sound great. Still, the hardware is at least as nice as any $900 Windows laptop. Acer hasn’t decided when the price will change or what it will be, but it’s at $899 for the rest of the year at least.

The next step up from that is the Dell XPS Googlebook at $999, but this model has an LCD instead of OLED. If you want the most capable Google laptops with OLED and haptic trackpads, you’re looking at spending at least $1,100 for the Lenovo version. This machine is solid, and the larger footprint allows for vents in the hinge instead of on the bottom. But I don’t love the slightly wobbly feel of the keys or the flex in the middle of the keyboard. The HP Googlebook 14 has a much nicer keyboard, a better overall look, and a Snapdragon X Elite chip inside. However, it’s also $1,300.

I appreciate that Google is pushing for things like haptic trackpads and high-resolution OLED screens, but the more expensive Googlebooks suffer from the same issue as premium Windows laptops—they don’t exist in a vacuum. If you’re spending $1,300 on a laptop, the entry-level MacBook Air is probably a better overall option for most people.

All of the launch Googlebooks have the same keyboard layout, which is a bit different from what you get on other laptops. There’s a G button that works similarly to the Windows button, and the top F-row has been revamped. You get the usual Windows staples like brightness and volume control, but there are also Android navigation buttons and a voice input key that activates the AI-powered Rambler.

Probably the best change to the Googlebook keyboard is ‘quick insert’ in place of ‘caps lock’ (you can still get caps lock with the Fn toggle). Just press this key to add emoji, recent screenshots, clipboard contents, recently visited URLs, and more. Admittedly, I don’t mind using function layers on a keyboard, so the extra step to access caps isn’t a concern. You may feel differently, and that’s okay.

Googlebooks come in both Intel and Snapdragon variants. I’ve been using both, and general performance feels about the same. There have been some reports of app issues with Intel-powered Googlebooks, but I haven’t run into any apps that will only run on Snapdragon.

The Snapdragon model (HP) seems to have a higher performance ceiling, if you can find a way to reach it. Gaming performance also appears better on Snapdragon, but even the heaviest Android games seem fine on the Intel models (Lenovo and Acer). It can be hard to push these machines when you’re relying on software that was originally designed to run on phones. Unsurprisingly, software proves to be the biggest hurdle for Googlebooks.

Google has flirted with Android on larger screens on a few occasions, mostly with tablets and tablets that impersonate laptops. This is the first time it has totally revamped the OS for a laptop, but it’s still Android under the hood. Sometimes that’s good, and other times not so much.

Setting up a Googlebook is a snap for Android users. Just like configuring a new phone, you can scan a QR code with your current phone to copy your accounts, data, and apps over automatically. You can be up and running in minutes, and your phone will integrate deeply with the OS. Well, provided it runs Android 17. That’s going to be a sticking point, since most phones don’t have that update yet.

With Google’s “Better Together” services, a Googlebook can access files on your Android 17 phone, sync notifications, remember where you left off in apps, and even mirror apps from your phone. This all sounds great, and when it works, the experience can be good. However, there are various limitations and bugs that get in the way.

To remain in contact, the phone and Googlebook need to be on the same Wi-Fi network, and switching to other networks can break the connection in annoying ways. Even when the devices appear to have a solid connection, I have rarely seen any hint of Google’s Continue On feature, which is supposed to let you pick up where you left off in a phone app. Mirroring phone apps on your laptop can also be handy, but the performance is varying degrees of bad, and apps with system-level security features won’t work at all. You are also limited to one app at a time, and they won’t stay open in the background.

Accessing the files on your phone from the laptop is a good idea, but the transfer speed is often sluggish. More annoyingly, the connection only goes one way—the Files app on the Googlebook can see your phone, but the Google Files app on a phone can’t see the Googlebook. Speaking of the Files app, this is emblematic of how far behind Google is with desktop software. The app lacks basic things like tabs and support for network shares. It’s nice that it can access my phone, but it feels very restrictive if you’re used to Finder or Windows Explorer.

Google has at least done a good job of making Android look like a desktop OS. There’s a proper desktop that you can fill with app shortcuts, folders, widgets, and files. There’s a folder in the storage tree where you can manage that content, or you can simply drag things onto it from a file manager. You also get ChromeOS-style split-screen support and multiple desktops. These features work, but they’re not as intuitive or capable as what you get on either macOS or Windows.

AI is a big part of the Googlebook experience. Google talks a lot about Magic Pointer, which you can activate by wiggling the cursor. This allows you to hand any content on your screen over to Gemini, but calling it magic is a little silly. You can have it translate text, make images, create calendar appointments, and so on. You’re basically feeding Gemini screenshots and asking it to do things.

Magic Pointer can be useful sometimes, but it’s hardly revolutionary to streamline the process of feeding screen content into an AI by attaching it to the mouse. You still have to contend with the inaccuracy of Gemini. Even adding calendar appointments can fail, which means you have to double-check almost everything the AI does.

Magic Pointer is an optional feature, and you can adjust the sensitivity of the gesture. However, I never found a level that I was entirely happy to use. Too much sensitivity, and the gesture triggers when you don’t intend it. Too little, and you have to shake the mouse so hard that the cursor is probably going to be nowhere near what you wanted to highlight.

Rambler, which debuted on the Pixel 11 lineup, is included with all Googlebooks. This AI-powered voice input feature works in any text field on the laptop, which is handy if you want to add a lot of text without typing and don’t mind sounding like a robot. This has been popular on phones, and most people using it on a Googlebook will probably be impressed.

Create My Widget is another head-scratcher, though. The pitch is that you can simply describe the widget you want, and the AI will place it on your desktop. It sounds cool, but in reality, the content you can rope in is so limited as to make the feature largely useless. If you want calendar countdowns and sports scores, great. If you want system info or app content, you’re out of luck.

Googlebooks come with the Play Store, which is crammed full of all the Android apps you could ever want. But desktop apps? Google says it has worked with devs to optimize apps for Googlebooks, and some software has been newly built from the ground up for a desktop experience. For example, Chrome on Googlebooks is a mostly desktop-class experience. It’s missing a few niche features like split windows, tab groups, and multiple profiles, but it will work with all of your extensions.

On other platforms, I’ve routinely used desktop clients for Dropbox and Drive to sync files. I had hoped something similar would be possible on these Android laptops, but no such luck. Dropbox runs on a Googlebook, but it’s not optimized. The UI is clunky, and even if you save a folder offline, it only updates when you refresh the app manually (just like a phone running the app).

Meanwhile, the Drive app isn’t even an Android app—it’s a progressive web app (PWA). So you can’t set it up to sync a folder to the device. All you have is the option to make individual files in Drive available offline. Without a real desktop app experience here, you actually get a lot more functionality out of Google’s cloud storage system on Windows and macOS.

Drive isn’t the only Google web app masquerading as a native app. Gmail and Calendar are also PWAs on the Googlebook, offering the same experience you’d get opening them in a browser tab. Gmail exists as an Android app with a large screen format. Why not adapt that for Googlebooks? Real operating systems have email apps. If you’re just going to end up in a web app, why not buy a Chromebook for a third of the price?

The Play Store uses labels to let you know which apps are best on a laptop, but most apps in the Play Store are very obviously built around a phone experience. Google is in a tough spot here. Developers only build for what people use, and so far, no one has been demanding desktop-style Android apps. As you peruse the Play Store, you’ll see a few of those “optimized” labels, but there are many more “Compatible with desktop” tags, which means you can expect only nominal support for a keyboard and mouse.

The most problematic apps are flagged in the Play Store as “Built for mobile” or even “Better on the website.” Some popular apps fall into these categories. For example, team chat app Slack is an abysmal experience on anything other than a phone. The app runs on Googlebooks, but the web UI is much more desktop-friendly. You are supposed to be able to install Slack as a progressive web app, essentially what Google is doing with Gmail, Drive, and other apps. However, this doesn’t work currently for unknown reasons. Again, you could just use a Chromebook if you wanted everything in a browser tab.

Even apps that have been optimized for desktop can be frustrating on a Googlebook. These apps are aware you have a keyboard, but they can respond to button presses in ways you don’t expect. Photoshop is a major offender here. The app has a poorly scaled mobile UI shifted into landscape, and there are only a few keyboard shortcuts. Sometimes, you’ll see a UI element that looks like it should be controllable with the arrows or enter key, but you just end up moving the cursor around and selecting the wrong thing. In fairness, Android’s Photoshop app is free, whereas the real Adobe suite on other platforms costs money. But calling this a desktop app is a stretch.

You’ll find lots of phone-first apps that don’t fully understand that you have a trackpad, ignoring hover interactions and right-clicks. Many apps also expect you to frequently trigger the Android back gesture to navigate the UI. On that last count, Google has a solution. Googlebooks have Back, Home, and Multitasking buttons on F1-F3. So you can make phone apps work, but reaching up to mash F1 constantly is annoying.

The Android lineage of Googlebook OS also means that even apps built for desktop may not operate the way you’d expect on a desktop PC. Android was designed for a memory-constrained environment, so the system closes apps in the background whenever it needs to free up RAM. It’s common to come back to an app you left in the background to find that it has lost your place and has to reload. This is a phone-like experience that doesn’t really fit with a real computer.

Google is aware that Googlebook apps may not fulfill all needs. One possible solution to that, say reps, is to simply make what you need with Antigravity. The new Android version of Google’s AI-centric development app is included on every Googlebook, giving you the option to vibe code apps for your laptop. The AI can generate plans, mockups, and line after line of code to bring your idea to life.

Antigravity can autonomously download all the Android developer tools it needs and builds APKs ready for installation on your device. Installing your apps is technically sideloading, as they’re not hosted in the Play Store, but Google gives these special treatment. They get scanned by Play Protect, but you don’t have to enable unknown sources in the settings. Google also confirms these apps won’t be affected by developer verification when that rolls out on Googlebooks next year.

After struggling with the Files app for a few days, I decided the lack of network shares was a deal-breaker. I keep most of my files on a NAS so I can access them from any device, and Googlebooks were cramping my style. I first tried to find an alternative in the Play Store, but the apps with sufficient features were totally unoptimized for a laptop, so I decided to test Antigravity on Googlebooks by making one.

Using Google’s default Gemini Flash model, I was able to get a functional but very buggy file manager installed in a few minutes. Making it work reliably and support all the features I needed took several hours of prompting over a few days, but the result is something I like using more than Google’s default Files app.

My custom file manager is essentially Windows Explorer on Android. While I did not set out with that intent, that’s where I ended up. The app has a desktop-friendly UI, tabs, network share support, expandable file trees, file previews, and more buttons. It has more features than Google’s default app, although it lacks the deep phone and system integration of the default file manager.

On one hand, it’s cool that you can create your own apps with the included Antigravity software. However, you’ll need to pay someone (probably Google) for enough AI compute to get the job done. It took a lot of iterations and bug hunting with Gemini 3.8 Flash to get my app where I needed it to be, and lighter models will struggle to produce something functional. It’s also not ideal to expect people buying a laptop to spend hours chatting with a robot to make it do basic laptop things. It should do those things out of the box.

I keep coming back to one inescapable question that hangs over everything Google is doing with these new laptops: Do Googlebooks need to exist? This seems like a lot of effort just to deliver deeper Android phone integration and more AI features when Chromebooks are already established in the market. True, that’s not a premium part of the market, but going after premium laptops means you need a premium experience, and currently, Googlebooks don’t offer that.

The hardware is solid—it’s smart that Google is pushing for things like OLED and haptic trackpads on Googlebooks. Its OEM partners have made some very nice-feeling laptops for Google’s software, but the OS isn’t doing its part. I just don’t feel more productive on a Googlebook than I do on a Chromebook.

I’ve been using Android since the beginning—this should be a good laptop for someone like me. However, the rough edges of the Googlebook experience are still wearing me down. It’s great that it talks to my phone, but that conversation is too often one-sided and buggy. It’s good, in theory, that Googlebooks have a deep software library with the Play Store, but too few apps are actually good on a laptop. And it’s cool that Googlebooks have such nice hardware, but they’re too expensive for what you get.

Maybe Google can fix this—ChromeOS looked a lot different a year or two after its consumer launch, after all. But Google has a lot of work ahead to make the Googlebook experience what it needs to be, and in the meantime, it’s not a viable alternative to macOS and Windows. Does Google have the patience to spend years doing this work? The company’s recent history leaves me feeling skeptical, and that makes it difficult to recommend a Googlebook to even the most ardent Google customers.

It’s a weird time to buy a laptop, but the new MacBook Pro doesn’t skimp on quality

Ars Technica Long form November 06, 2026

It has the best laptop screen we’ve used, but there may be reasons to wait.

Apple’s new MacBook Pro is expensive as hell.

Let’s get that out there right away, because for a lot of people, it will be the only thing that matters. As with so many things in life, though, you get what you pay for. There’s no questioning the quality of the laptop’s display or most of its other hardware components.

But should you buy it? Well, that’s a complicated question in 2026.

We’re in a time of great uncertainty when it comes to buying a computer. Prices are at levels we’ve not seen in recent history, and they may well keep climbing. Meanwhile, users paying close attention to the early developments in both local and agentic artificial intelligence are asking an important question: “What will computing even look like in a few years, and what does that mean for the computer I should buy today?”

Apple’s new MacBook Pro sits at the intersection of all of this uncertainty. In multiple ways, it’s also straddling different worlds.

It arrives amid a changing of the guard in Apple’s leadership, potentially raising questions about the future direction of Apple’s ecosystem. It’s a mass-market consumer product, but configuring it with enough RAM and storage to make it feel future-proof pushes its price into territory mostly only well-funded businesses can afford. It’s firmly rooted in the computing paradigms of the past 20 years, but it shows early signs of flirtation with new AI workflows. It’s a conventional Apple laptop in most ways, but it also has a touchscreen—something that would never have happened in a prior Apple era.

It’s an outstanding, high-quality product, but whether it’s something you should buy depends on you—what you’re doing right now, what you’ll be doing in the future, and what you value.

For most of the specs we look at, Apple isn’t claiming any difference here. The new MacBook Pro promises 24 hours of battery life (though you’d have to use it in a conservative way to achieve that), it has the same ports (three Thunderbolt, one HDMI, one SDXC, and MagSafe), and it has the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity.

And like its immediate predecessor, it offers the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options. Running synthetic benchmarks, we found no meaningful difference at all compared to when we ran the same tests on the previous model, so we won’t spend time discussing their performance today. We’ve covered both thoroughly in prior reviews, and you can read up there if you’d like.

The chips are more than fast enough for normal workflows for the foreseeable future, including most 3D work. AI inference is the main area where they may be less future-proof. To be clear, they’re strong enough for now, but the field is evolving rapidly, and there’s reason to expect significant improvements in future chips on this front.

According to Bloomberg, Apple is skipping Pro and Max versions of the M6 chip that was introduced earlier this year to focus its attention on a significant rework for the M7 due in 2027. “The M7 line is designed primarily around major advancements to on-device AI processing,” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote. The line would emphasize memory bandwidth, which matters for fast, efficient AI inference.

Even without Bloomberg’s report, I’d expect Apple to prioritize those areas in its next high-end chip refresh. That’s partly because there’s another tea leaf to read here: Apple made just such an update with the A20 Pro, which debuted in its latest iPhones several weeks ago. That update brought a substantially improved Neural Engine and a significant increase in memory bandwidth. We also found that the A20 Pro delivered improved 3D graphics performance in some cases.

Similar improvements could come to Macs, meaning it might be worth waiting another year if you’re focused on AI workflows or even 3D applications—especially given the high cost of these machines. That’s part of what makes this such an uncertain time to buy a laptop. We’re in a moment when these companies are revisiting the architecture of these chips because of these new workflows, and we don’t know what the end result is yet.

Here’s one thing that’s not at all uncertain: The display on the MacBook Pro is the best I have ever used in a laptop. If the display is your primary concern, this is a big moment.

Apple calls it a “tandem OLED display,” meaning a panel with two emissive layers. This approach helps achieve a higher peak brightness, but perhaps more importantly, it can reduce the risk of burn-in. Most of the time, the display won’t need both layers running at full power. Instead, they can share the load and run at a reduced current, helping extend the panel’s lifespan.

The new display can achieve up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness on HDR highlights, but it’s rated for 1,000 nits of sustained brightness. In general, I like the way Apple handles HDR for this at the OS level, too.

The brightness matters for HDR content, sure, but what really makes OLED stand out is per-pixel illumination—meaning each pixel can turn on or off independently. That allows for absolute black levels and very strong contrast. The MiniLED display in the previous MacBook Pro offered good contrast for an LCD display, but OLED has a fundamental advantage here, and it shows.

As you’d expect, the screen offers native support for both P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts. It also has a variable refresh rate from 10 to 120 Hz, just like many of Apple’s other products. As before, the MacBook Pro comes in roughly 14-inch (3,024×1,986 pixels) and 16-inch (3,472×2,226 pixels) variants. There’s also a nano-texture glass option to fight glare, though that will set you back another $150.

It’s one of the most impressive displays I’ve used in any device, and it’s certainly the best I’ve ever used on a laptop. The colors are vibrant, the contrast is outstanding, the blacks are inky, and it can get very bright when it needs to—not just with highlights but full-screen brightness as well. And on the whole, it’s extremely precise. Uniformity appears basically flawless. It’s what you’d expect from an ultra-high-end TV or reference monitor, not a laptop or computer screen, and it’s genuinely striking.

We’ll see about longevity, but OLED has come a long way in recent years, and my first impressions are that Apple has made all the right choices here.

I find myself trying to find something negative to say about the MacBook Pro’s screen to avoid sounding too effusive, but I can’t think of anything substantive. The best I can do is complain that Apple’s proprietary “PROLED XDR” label is silly and eye-roll-inducing.

Branding aside, the screen is the main reason to pay extra for this model.

With its lid closed, the new MacBook Pro looks identical to its predecessor. The dimensions are largely the same. It’s slightly thinner, but you’d have to check the spec sheet or handle them side by side to notice.

Pick it up, though, and you’ll find that it’s noticeably lighter than the last model, by about half a pound. It’s not in a totally different weight class, but you can notice the change, and it’s a nice improvement. The reduction is partly due to the display technology switch; it’s easier to make a light OLED screen than a light MiniLED one.

Open the MacBook Pro and turn it on, and you’ll see one of a few other notable differences, depending on whether you’re behind or in front of it. From behind, you’ll see the Apple logo on the lid now lights up, as it did on MacBooks of yore. It’s arguably a little tacky, but it’s also neat and nostalgic. I don’t hate it.

From the front, you might notice that the already barely there bezels are even more barely there, though that’s subtle. More likely, you’ll see that the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by a cutout just like the Dynamic Island Apple introduced on the iPhone.

When I reviewed the first iPhone with a Dynamic Island, I was largely positive about it. No, it’s not ideal to have a cutout on the screen, but Apple has handled it as intelligently as possible, and I would even go so far as to say it has turned what should be an albatross into an attractive feature.

Thanks to the OLED display, it’s possible to make any of the pixels around the camera cutout just as black as it is. Apple has designed live activities, the volume bar, and more to appear as if they are expanding out of and around, and contracting back into, this little dot. It remains ingenious.

When the Dynamic Island first arrived on the iPhone, it helped unify several previously disparate approaches to displaying notifications in iOS, making it especially useful. This time, it doesn’t solve as many problems, but it’s an improvement over the dead weight of the notch. It also helps that the MacBook Pro’s much larger screen means the cutout takes up a small share of the screen’s real estate.

The Dynamic Island works the same with full-screen apps as the notch did. By default, the top of the viewport ends just below the Dynamic Island, so it just looks like there’s a taller top bezel, and it doesn’t cut into the application interface. The menu bar, clock, and other system elements still occupy the space above the application (set against a totally black background) when you move the cursor up there.

I tested a few fullscreen games with it, like World of Warcraft and Cyberpunk 2077. Some behaved by default like the default fullscreen app behavior I just described, but others tried to occupy the whole thing, making the cutout visible. Vitally, every video app I tried avoided the cutout in fullscreen.

This isn’t something to upgrade for, of course. But on the whole, I think it’s an improvement over what we had before.

Apple has finally added a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. I say “finally” because the possibility has floated around for about two decades. Steve Jobs was famously opposed to the idea; there’s even video of him explaining why he thought it would make for a poor user experience.

A couple of years ago, reliable reports emerged that Apple was moving forward with the idea regardless. When I first heard about it, I imagined what could be a really exciting implementation: a convertible laptop that would let you use it in a tablet-like mode, with Apple Pencil support for drawing and writing.

As a game developer, I imagined quickly sketching 2D game maps with an Apple Pencil, using a local AI model to convert them into 3D geometry, and then switching to a laptop configuration to start testing and coding. I also imagined using it like an iPad to more comfortably watch movies on a flight.

That’s not what we got, though. The laptop has the same form factor as the previous MacBook Pro model—no tablet mode or Pencil support. Instead, it just lets you reach up from the keyboard and trackpad to touch the screen. That feels like a missed opportunity.

Some creative apps have implemented touch features that might justify the touchscreen functionality if you use them a lot. For example, you can play the on-screen virtual piano keys on Logic Pro with multiple fingers, which could be nicer than clicking on them. I imagine many people already have workflows built around other approaches, though.

If you were specifically waiting for a touchscreen on your MacBook Pro, this seems like as good an implementation as you could hope for without turning the laptop into a convertible. Apple has put real care into it. For example, it has re-engineered the hinge so the screen is not particularly wobbly when you touch it. It’s fast, accurate, and responsive. It supports multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom or swiping with three fingers to switch desktop spaces.

There’s one use case I find compelling as a developer. Testing iPhone and iPad apps in the Simulator has always been a minor hassle because of the difference in input methods. You either have to approximate only a subset of the interactions available to users with a trackpad and mouse or connect an iPhone or iPad to test them that way. A touchscreen could provide a more elegant way to test such apps in Xcode, Unity, or whatever else you might use.

Unfortunately, some of the UI elements in macOS are too small for my large fingers, so I have to tap very carefully. I also keep forgetting the touchscreen is even there for hours at a time and go back to my normal habits, partly because there’s nothing you can do at the OS level that you can’t do just as easily with trackpad gestures. And as Jobs predicted all those years ago, my arm got tired while I was using it.

For me, it feels faster, easier, more comfortable, and more natural to use the keyboard and trackpad 100 percent of the time, but I admittedly have decades of muscle memory and habits built around them. There’s apparently a generation coming up with the same kind of familiarity with touch interfaces, so this feature may appeal to them. Plus, touchscreen laptops have been a thing on Windows forever, and some people seem to want to buy them, though I never quite got why without an added tablet configuration.

It’s unlikely to account for a big portion of the device’s cost compared with the rest of the OLED panel, memory, storage, and so on. So, my own bafflement aside, I’m not unhappy it’s here. I imagine it will serve those who want it well enough.

As noted earlier, whether this laptop is worthy of a recommendation depends on you and how you use your machine. That’s always been the case, but it seems more so here.

If you’re a creative professional or a display enthusiast who wants the best laptop screen you’ve likely ever seen, you won’t be disappointed if you shell out for it. And hey, maybe you can show me your workflow and prove me wrong about the touchscreen!

If you’re just looking for a great laptop with strong performance for everyday use, consider the non-OLED, non-touchscreen model that’s still in Apple’s lineup—or even a MacBook Air, which compromises relatively little for most users. And there is, of course, the entire world of Windows and Linux laptops.

If you’re a developer—especially one working at the frontier of AI workflows—well, that’s where things get tricky. Will waiting be worthwhile? So much about how those workflows will evolve and what they’ll demand from your hardware is still so up in the air that I can’t make a confident recommendation. (For what it’s worth, I fit best in this category, and I’m still holding onto my M1 Max machine, though my resolve is wavering.)

All that said, in most ways, this is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve reviewed again and again for the past few years. Touch adds a feature aimed at a particular niche, or perhaps it’s there to roll out the welcome mat for a newer generation. The display is a more substantial update and makes a compelling case for upgrading, especially if you’re coming from an older, pre-MiniLED laptop.

But this is an expensive machine. The configuration I reviewed here (16-inch, M5 Max, 128 GB of RAM, 2 TB SSD) retails for a whopping $7,399, though you could at least shave $1,600 off that by going to a more typical-for-most-people 64 GB. (The cheapest configuration starts at $2,899.)

For the vast majority of buyers, the pre-OLED version that’s still in Apple’s lineup or another MacBook altogether will offer more bang for your buck. If you’re the kind of person who wants OLED or a touchscreen, though, you probably know that already. Based on my time with the new MacBook Pro, both features deliver on their promises, even if the latter isn’t as ambitious as some of us had hoped.

Clashes erupt in Barcelona as thousands join Spain general strike

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 20:52:52 GMT

Clashes have broken out between groups of protesters and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living.

Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas.

Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption.

Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.

The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."

There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields.

Some of the disturbances took place in the Passeig de Gràcia, close to the iconic Plaça de Catalunya in the centre of the city.

Small fires burned in the middle of the streets where the disturbances took place. Local media reported that a group of people fired fireworks towards police and looted shops including the Lego store. Protesters were also seen trying to enter the Apple Store.

Earlier in the day there was major disruption around Madrid and Barcelona, with traffic halted on several main roads.

The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.

"We've completely brought the city to a standstill.," a protester in Madrid told Reuters news agency, adding there was widespread support for the general strike. "Everyone's out there, despite the rainy weather; everyone's out on the streets."

Another protester, 37-year-old teacher Olga Domingo, said she was protesting because the government "keep making cuts" and "the housing situation is outrageous. The current cost of living compared to wages is completely unsustainable".

The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.

Rental prices in the capital have risen in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50 sq m apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 ($1,300; £1,000) in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460.

That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform.

Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes.

And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing.

"Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes.

The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain.

PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election.

Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike."

Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.

Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.

The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.

Álvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.

He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay €1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.

"It's absolutely crazy… with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."

He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."

With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".

However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.

"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.

Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.

Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.

Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

Author says there were 'real concerns' about David Walliams within publishing industry

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 20:40:47 GMT

Author Chloe Combi has said she had heard rumours that there were "real concerns" about David Walliams's behaviour within the publishing industry more than a decade ago.

Combi told BBC News she had heard there were allegations about his "behaviour around young female staff" and says she was told in 2015 to warn schools that he was "not an appropriate booking".

An investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that Walliams has been accused by several women of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behaviour and abusing his position, which he denies.

HarperCollins, which published Walliams's best-selling children's books, dropped Walliams last year after an investigation into his behaviour.

In response to the Guardian and ITV report, a spokesperson for HarperCollins said the company had decided not to publish any new titles by Walliams and that it took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously".

Walliams told ITV News and the Guardian that he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a scheme to bring "high-profile and inspiring writers and speakers" to talk in schools.

At an event in 2015, Combi said she got speaking to someone "quite senior" in publishing, who warned her about Walliams.

"We were talking about [the scheme] and possible writers who might be good for the project to work well with teenagers," Combi said.

"She gave me some great recommendations and said to me: 'Whatever you do, don't invite David Walliams, and FYI if you are speaking to head teachers or teachers, please inform them that he's not a good booking, not an appropriate booking for a school'."

Combi continued: "I obviously asked why, and to be honest I had already heard quite a lot of rumours because those worlds are quite small and contained.

"One of the things she said was that there had been real concerns about his behaviour around young female staff."

Asked whether concerns about his behaviour was an open secret, Combi replied: "Yes definitely... and I'd heard it from people who worked in publishing, fellow writers, people kind of in celebrity and TV circles."

Combi said she never met Walliams herself, and said her information had come from "a number of people I was speaking to".

HarperCollins in September announced it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.

The allegations against Walliams include:

In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Contains sexual content.

Earlier on Wednesday, media minister Ian Murray said there is a "cultural problem" in the industry that needs to be "stamped out".

Giving evidence to the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, Murray said he was "deeply saddened and also angry" to see the prevalence of abuse by men in the media industry.

Meanwhile, Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson paid tribute to the "bravery" of victims who have shared their experiences in recent days.

Speaking in the Commons, she said: "Women and girls should never have to shrink our lives or ambitions because of outdated, misogynistic attitudes, and the appalling testimonies we have heard in recent days underline how much further we have to go."

Phillipson later said the government would "go further" on restricting the use of non-disclosure agreements, telling Sky News: "We cannot have a system where rich and powerful individuals, rich and powerful men, are able to silence women, buy their silence and stop things coming to light."

She said that she believed injunctions were being misused, and that her colleagues at the Ministry of Justice were looking at how the government can intervene to ensure this did not happen.

Comedian and podcaster Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women are "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.

She told the programme that perpetrators understand consent but they just enjoy the power that comes with ignoring it, adding: "The thrill is in the contravention of consent."

Asked whether she recognised the picture Russell Brand's conviction and allegations against Walliams had painted of the comedy industry, she said: "Yes, entirely."

She described an industry where she was asked to meet male producers in darkly lit rooms "walking a tightrope", having to make them feel attractive and avoid being assaulted as they influenced future employment opportunities.

She said these events are "definitely still going on" and that she is in a WhatsApp group with female comedians who share their experiences with each other.

Comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News that she was one of the people who spoke to the Guardian about allegations raised with her about Walliams.

Beaumont said she had been approached by a young TV worker who alleged inappropriate behaviour while working with Walliams on another show.

"This young person's job was to take young girls - he didn't think that they were children... he definitely knew that they were over 16 - he had to take them to Walliams's dressing room," she alleged.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday, Labour MP Jess Phillips said the behaviour alleged "needs to be stopped".

"What is described in the David Walliams story is an absolute modus operandi, a target group of women of a certain age, the kind of women who don't have the same amount of power as if you were doing this to a 35-year-old woman who might have a bit more about herself in the world," she said.

'Not the answer': Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:15:45 GMT

Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments.

There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective".

But in a sign of the division within the party, about a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns about approving it during a Westminster Hall debate in Parliament.

Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support.

One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate".

"The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said.

Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer.

Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test.

"It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices."

Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise."

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh. She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance.

Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields".

Licences for both Jackdaw and Rosebank were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 respectively.

But the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approvals unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a fresh decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch sought to tease at Labour divisions on the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday.

During the debate, Labour MP Anna Gelderd said: "We live in an unprecedented era where our energy security is more vital than ever, in which jobs and wealth must be protected and economic opportunities seized - on both of these points, Rosebank fails."

Labour MP Julia Buckley said she had received opposition to Rosebank from her constituents in "regularly flooded Shrewsbury" and said fossil fuels "belong in the past, not the future".

She urged Fahnbulleh to "reject the oil licence in favour of renewables", adding: "Please don't add further to our climate emergency."

Other Labour MPs expressed their support, including recently departed veterans minister Al Carns, who warned that Britain would continue to need fossil fuels for decades and importing more would be a mistake.

"Refusing to produce it here does nothing on its own to eliminate that demand - it simply increases our reliance on imports which can carry their own environmental cost," he added.

Those representing communities with ties to the oil and gas industry, including Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, stressed the benefits of approving Rosebank for British jobs.

Energy minister Michael Shanks told the debate the government would take a "pragmatic approach" to a clean energy transition, stressing it was "not a turn off the taps government, but nor can we justifiably be a drill every last drop government either".

"This government will not make decisions for this country which are not compatible with our climate obligations," he added.

Police believed train attacker had schizophrenia, jury told

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:03:40 GMT

Police dealing with a man accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train noted he had schizophrenia following his arrest, a court has been told.

Anthony Williams denies attempting to murder passengers and staff on a London-bound train, which made an emergency stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November last year.

Cambridge Crown Court heard PC Caitlin Brown, who was involved in transporting Williams to hospital then to the police station, said he "appeared to be talking to himself" and spoke about the devil.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, also denies four other counts of attempted murder related to earlier attacks in Peterborough and London.

Jurors were shown footage of Williams' arrest in the car park of Huntingdon railway station, and the court heard a Taser and a baton gun - which fires less lethal objects - were used against the defendant.

In a statement read to court, the arresting officer said Williams had said something along the lines of "kill me, kill me".

PC Matt Panks, another officer involved in transporting Williams, said in his statement he saw the suspect "acting strangely, appeared completely unphased by what had occurred... he was rocking and laughing".

Contains some upsetting scenes.

He said he heard Williams state, "Do you reckon it was worth it?", and he repeated it again, before reminding him he was under caution.

Sgt James Cox, who was custody sergeant at Parkside police station in Cambridge when Williams was arrested, gave evidence in person to the jury.

The court heard Williams was "treated as a vulnerable adult" and he authorised him to be supported by an appropriate adult.

Jurors heard Williams had officers constantly on watch.

Running Sgt Cox through the detention log, Gillian Jones KC, representing Williams, said: "It was reported to you that [Williams] suffers from psychosis, wasn't it."

Cox replied: "I believe so, yes."

The barrister said: "It was reported to you that he took medication."

Cox again replied: "I believe so, yes."

He said it was his assessment Williams "didn't appear to be intoxicated", and the court heard he was informed by escorting officers "Mr Williams suffered from schizophrenia".

The court heard it was determined the detainee was not fit to be interviewed.

Jones said a note from a healthcare worker in custody logs read that Williams "appeared to be responding to voices".

She told the court it said Williams "laughed", agreed when asked if he was hearing any voices, and when asked what the voices were saying, "he smiled and said 'lots of things'".

Jurors have also seen CCTV footage of Williams punching an officer in the face in the early hours of 2 November, and heard he was observed to be "climbing on his toilet several times and stroking the air vent".

The following afternoon, a forensic psychiatrist advised he observed "active psychotic symptoms".

The court heard Williams was never interviewed about the allegations.

As well as arguing Williams was attempting to murder the 10 people on the train, prosecutors allege that on 31 October he tried to kill three people in Peterborough.

He is also charged with attempting to murder a teenager in the early hours of 1 November on a DLR train in east London.

Whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question - the court has been told - but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill.

The trial continues.

Scottish DJ, 32, confirmed as victim of Krakow shooting

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:53:57 GMT

A 32-year-old Scottish man has been confirmed as one of the victims of a mass shooting in Poland that left six people dead.

The man, who is understood to be James Thomas Campbell from Prestwick in South Ayrshire, died when a lone gunman opened fire in central Krakow on Saturday.

Campbell worked as a DJ in Ayrshire. Police Scotland confirmed it was providing specialist support to the victim's family, but formal identification is yet to be carried out.

The 24-year-old attacker, named as Michal Oksinski by local media, died in hospital on Monday, having also fatally shot four Polish citizens and an Austrian woman with a further 15 people, including two police officers, injured.

Det Ch Insp David McAlinden, senior investigating officer from Police Scotland's Counter Terrorism Policing unit, said the force was "aware of the tragic death of a Scottish man in Krakow".

He added: "Working in conjunction with COPFS (the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service), Police Scotland is supporting the UK counter-terrorism policing network and the Polish authorities.

"The immediate shared priority is to ensure that identification is properly established for the family, so that repatriation can take place as quickly as possible.

"The family has asked for their privacy to be respected. Our thoughts are with them and everyone impacted by this incident."

Mark Jewell, a close friend of Campbell's who regularly DJ'd with him, described him as "a quiet, kind and soft-hearted person, who wouldn't have harmed a fly".

He added: "It's just so tragic that he had to be in the wrong place at the wrong time.

"I had been speaking with him when he was headed over to Poland and I messaged him as soon as I heard about the terrible attack, to ask if he was safe - not for one minute expecting that he would have been caught up in it all.

"I was fully expecting a funny message back from him, saying not to worry. I can't quite get my head round it all."

The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, a popular tourist spot.

Police said the gunman drove into the square before beginning to fire at random people from his car.

Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the man, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning.

In addition to the six people killed in central Krakow, police later found the bodies of the gunman's parents and sister at his address on Saturday.

Earlier this week two friends from Aberdeen described how they ran for their lives as the shooting started.

Ciaran McMenemy, 26, and Charlie Hutchison, 27, said they had just sat down for a drink when the gunfire began. They quickly fled and took shelter.

Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:48:19 GMT

Poundland and its 11,000 employees are hopeful that the retailer's impending collapse can be delayed to allow time for a last-minute rescue deal.

The discount chain has been edging towards administration after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation have told the BBC that they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of £10m in funding.

A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers, Poundland's US owners, on Wednesday following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm has denied the claims.

But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

However, sources close to the matter told the BBC on Tuesday that a release of £10m by its owners, while "small in the scale of things" could help at least postpone the chain's collapse while a longer term solution was explored.

Following the behind-closed-doors meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chair Liam Byrne said he was "deeply concerned" that firm's behaviour "may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain's high streets".

"Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a 'knife edge'," he posted on social media.

"Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there's concerning signs it's been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run up to Christmas."

He claimed that Gordon Brothers refused to say it would prioritise saving jobs "over and above its own financial returns", but added the prospect of a good outcome for the business was "now higher thanks to the focus on the business of the last week".

He called on Gordon Brothers "to do the right thing" and give Poundland access to its own funds and work to protect the maximum number of jobs.

The 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires on Thursday, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.

Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners.

Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.

He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m.

However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up and sold off in chunks.

The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain.

Famed ship SS United States to be sunk off coast of Florida

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:42:27 GMT

A ship that was once the fastest in the world and measures longer than the Titanic will be sunk off the coast of Florida and turned into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.

The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will soon become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for sea enthusiasts.

Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.

Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it will be added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, as a land-based museum detailing the ship's history is also planned.

Before its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities from the US the Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969.

A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.

The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work. On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will be sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives.

Stars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing tenure.

Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed.

Instead, the famed ship sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out.

The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.

Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped designed the SS United States - said she was glad that the story of the ship would live on.

An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.

Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.

The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.

The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.

Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.

The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.

Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.

Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.

He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.

Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".

"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.

He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.

"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.

Of the parents relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.

Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.

"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

Raducanu to return at January's United Cup after injury lay-off

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:05:25 GMT

Emma Raducanu missed Wimbledon and the US Open through injury

Emma Raducanu will make her return to tennis in the United Cup team competition in Australia in the first week of 2027.

Britain's 2021 US Open champion has not played since June because of a stress fracture of the shin.

Raducanu was beaten by Croatia’s Donna Vekic in her first grass-court final at Queen's Club on 14 June, but had to pull out of Wimbledon on the eve of her opening match just 14 days later.

The 23-year-old contemplated playing a couple of events in Asia this autumn but, by delaying her return until January, she will be able to use a special ranking of 38 to enter tournaments.

A special ranking is available to players who have been out with injury for at least six months. In Raducanu's case, it reflects her position in the world rankings after Wimbledon, as she received some prize money despite not playing a match there.

The current British number five will be able to use a special ranking to enter eight events next year, including two Grand Slams and five WTA 1000 tournaments.

Her actual ranking of 107 would likely be too low to make the main draw of January's Australian Open and most other WTA Tour events.

But with a special ranking, Raducanu will not only be assured of playing in Melbourne but also at the WTA 1000 events in Doha, Dubai, Indian Wells and Miami which follow in February and March.

The entry deadline for the United Cup passed on Monday, shortly after Raducanu had her application for a special ranking approved.

A ranking of 38 will make her the British number one for the purposes of this event, giving her the chance to play alongside Arthur Fery in a competition featuring 18 national teams.

Francesca Jones, Jan Choinski and doubles players Neal Skupski and Olivia Nicholls complete the British team for the tournament, which takes place from 1-10 January.

Britain will play Australia and France in their group matches in Sydney, and Raducanu can expect to be face current top-40 players Talia Gibson and Diane Parry.

'I don't fear for my safety from online abuse - because we're so used to it'

Raducanu made a gradual return to training in early September - and four months is a long time to train without any competitive action.

She may also not play any exhibitions between now and the end of the year but a spell of warm weather training is anticipated, with the Middle East a popular destination for players in the run-up to the Australian Open.

Recent practice sessions in London with head coach Andrew Richardson and LTA national coach Alex Ward have been increasing in intensity, according to observers.

But by the time Raducanu returns, she will have been on the sidelines for over six months. Playing a few tournaments in Asia would have helped her regain some match sharpness, and perhaps allowed for a faster start to 2027.

Her fellow Briton Sonay Kartal is a fine example, having enjoyed considerable success since returning from six months out with a stress fracture of the back in September.

After reaching the third round of the China Open in her first WTA Tour event back, she beat world number six Elina Svitolina and then world number 12 Belinda Bencic on her way to the Wuhan Open final.

Kartal says there were a "lot of conversations" about where she should make a return.

"I think I wanted to just go straight in. I trusted that I would be able to get my level back, I just didn't know how quickly," the 25-year-old said.

"But I still think there is a long way to go. I can produce the level, but can I sustain it?

"Rehab is draining, and the body is not used to a lot of matches on the tour, so I do feel the aches and the pains from that."

There will only be 24 candles on Raducanu’s birthday cake later this week, but there is no escaping the amount of time she has missed since her stunning New York victory as a teenage qualifier.

She has averaged just 31 matches a season in the five years since that triumph. Players with aspirations to be inside the world's top 20 would hope to play around twice that number.

Elena Rybakina, for example, played 68 matches across 20 tournaments this year as she rose to the top of the world rankings for the first time.

By contrast, Raducanu played just 21 matches, losing in the second round of the Australian Open and the first round at Roland Garros.

Last year, Raducanu contested a career-best 50 matches, and earlier this year rose to 23 in the rankings shortly after reaching the final in the Romanian city of Cluj.

But her early preparation was affected by bone bruising of the foot, and she did not play for two months between March and May because of a post-viral illness picked up in Cluj.

Raducanu said a stress fracture of the shin was only confirmed after a final scan on the night before Wimbledon. But in her desperation to play, she had continued to train at times in the run-up to the championships, when medical advice had suggested that might be unwise.

Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:04:58 GMT

Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.

Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.

However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.

Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."

"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.

Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.

After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.

The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.

For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.

For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.

Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.

That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.

Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.

Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.

Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.

Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.

There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.

Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.

Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.

Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.

Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.

Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again.

"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."
