What is the state of our grooming laws?

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:45:41 GMT

Time and again since the international explosion of the "Me Too" movement in 2017 against sexual violence against women and girls, politicians have been pushed on whether we in the UK have an adequate list of crimes in place to deal with all manner of incidents.

Those demands for reviews and rethinks have come back again with the conviction of one comedian Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault - and separate accusations of sexual misconduct against another one, David Walliams. He denies being a sexual predator and is not facing a criminal investigation.

The modern landscape of sexual offences in England and Wales is complicated - but it is far more nuanced than it once was because of major changes over the last two decades.

There is some confusion in public debate over what counts as grooming - but in general it's understood in the criminal courts to refer to situations where a predator builds a relationship of trust with a child target in order to prepare the ground for sexual activity. Given the end goal, that relationship will often involve a great deal of manipulation - usually emotional, often subtle and regularly coercive.

Since 2003 it has been an offence for an adult to meet a child "following sexual grooming" and the maximum sentence is 10 years.

The crime is committed when an adult has met or communicated with someone under 16-years-old on at least one occasion and then intentionally meets them, or travels to meet them, with the intention of committing a sexual offence.

There are other offences which generally cover some of the ground of grooming: arranging and facilitating a child sex offence, sexual communications with a child, causing a child to watch a sexual act or inciting an under 13-year-old to take part in one.

The offence gets little media attention, but analysis from the Centre of Expertise on Child Sexual Abuse, an independent body funded by the government to provide insights, shows that grooming offences are regularly turned to by the police and prosecutors.

Its latest report on crime statistics shows that 7,197 sexual grooming offences were recorded by the police across England and Wales in 2024/25.

Nearly a third of those ended up in a charge - and in 2024 just over 2,000 defendants were convicted. The rate of prosecuting suspects for grooming has more than doubled in seven years.

One final offence to highlight is the crime of abusing a position of trust for a sexual purpose with a child. This covers young people up to the age of 18 because the abuse may be taking place in a care environment.

Since June, grooming has been a specific element of sentencing law. Judges who are deciding a sentence for a child sex offender to consider how the contact came about - and if there was evidence of grooming, that becomes a factor to increase the length of the sentence.

So does that mean that the law is entirely settled and accepted? Well not quite.

Some campaigners have been calling for the law to clearly define what grooming means.

ThirtyOne:Eight, a charity consultancy that works on improving safeguarding in religious settings, said last year that its work had led it to conclude that the intention to groom - whether or not sexual abuse takes place - should become a self-standing crime.

And Baroness Louise Casey, who carried out a national audit of grooming gang abuse, highlighted another issue.

Sexual offences law includes a subtle exception for teenagers who have not yet reached the legal age of consent at 16 but who are in a relationship with each other. That nuance is designed to avoid needlessly criminalising 13 to 15-year-olds who seemingly know what they are doing.

But, says Casey in her report, there were "examples of perpetrators being charged with the lesser offence of 'sexual activity with a child', rather than rape, because of a belief that the child involved had 'consented' to having sex."

Speaking to the BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, she said that it was "staggering" that adults who have sex children aged 13, 14, and 15 are not automatically charged with rape, as is the case in France.

She has asked for that gap to be closed and told the BBC she had received an assurance from ministers this it would happen.

"The recommendations from the grooming gang audit that I did last year are works in progress," she said. "They're not completed yet, and obviously, I would like the government to press on with those."

The Ministry of Justice has been contacted for comment.

All of that is aimed at dealing with crimes against children and young teenagers. So is there space for changes elsewhere?

Some argue that the UK should have a "staggered" age of consent.

This became a talking point in 2023 after allegations against Russell Brand exploded over the media.

One of his alleged victims told BBC's Woman's Hour at the time that we should consider changing the law so that people over 18 would not be allowed to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds.

"There's a reasonable argument [that] individuals between the ages of 16 and 18 can have relations with people within that same age bracket," she said. "You're allowed to make mistakes as a teenager, they should be with other people your own age."

The counter-argument to that is once someone is over the age of consent, the law already makes clear that they have the maturity to consent to sex. And if they have not given it, the law is clear: the act is not one of love, but rape.

Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 16:59:34 GMT

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris. Some of the incidents were said to be directed by the men over FaceTime.

The DOJ said they acted in the name of the group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI).

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

The DOJ said that most recently, al-Hassani "orchestrated a terrorist plot" at RAF Fairford - where on 27 September a major incident was declared after suspicious vans were reported near the base.

Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident at RAF Fairford.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement.

Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were allegedly both in Iran at the time of the incident, the indictment claims.

Meanwhile, al-Saadi was coordinating with the pair through third parties from a prison in New York, where he is awaiting trial on previous charges after being arrested in August, it adds.

US court records show that al-Saadi is due in court on 19 November, though it is not clear whether this status conference - which is usually a routine scheduled appearance - relates to the new charges or the previous ones. The BBC has asked the Southern District of New York for comment.

Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources told the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The BBC has asked the DOJ for comment on the suspected whereabouts of the two men not in US custody.

In the DOJ's statement detailing the indictments, it said: "Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK."

It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".

Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.

The indictment also details an arson attack on a Jewish charity in London on 17 April, which allegedly saw al-Hassani "directing" an individual over FaceTime.

On 17 April , a building previously used by Jewish Futures, an educational charity, was set alight in Hendon, north-west London.

The following day, the DOJ said al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London.

On 18 April, Kenton United Synagogue in Harrow was targeted in an arson attack. A 17-year-old boy pleaded guilty to the incident earlier this year.

The indictment also claims the three were involved in attacks on the Bank of New York Mellon building in Amsterdam on 15 March and on the Bank of America building in Paris on 28 March.

It added that the trio tried to carry out attacks on "Jewish institutions in the US", including attempting to target a synagogue in Manhattan, New York in March or April.

"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.

He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.

Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.

A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.

No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".

On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.

In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.

According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".

The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated.

"On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."

The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive.

"At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.

It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.

The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot.

The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason.

RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

This video can not be played

Kane explains how his game has evolved

Long before Kane made his first senior appearance for his country in a 4-0 Euro 2016 qualifying win over Lithuania at Wembley, he was an England fan.

Aged 12, he remembers the heartache of going out on penalties to Portugal in the quarter-finals of the 2006 World Cup under Sven-Goran Eriksson and failing to qualify for Euro 2008 under Steve McClaren.

"During most major tournaments we would go to the pub to watch England, with the beer garden and the screen," said Kane.

"We loved England, we loved watching England and we were big England fans. I remember many tears being shed after we went out on penalties and things like that."

Kane fell in love with football from an early age.

Aged five, he wrote about his ambition to become a footballer in a school project.

Weekends and holidays were spent playing football in his local Ridgeway Park with his dad Patrick and brother Charlie.

They would use trees as goalposts, with the two brothers taking turns to shoot while Patrick was in goal.

At the age of five, Kane wrote "I want to play football" in a school project

At Larkswood Primary School, Kane and his friends would play football in the playground - where they were only allowed to use tennis balls.

By then, the future England captain was playing for Sunday league team Ridgeway Rovers - whose former players included David Beckham, Kane's idol growing up.

Former Manchester United midfielder Beckham, who won 115 England caps between 1996 and 2009, was playing for Real Madrid when Kane was at Chingford Foundation School.

"He had sent a Real Madrid shirt back to our secondary school," added Kane.

"Seeing Beckham's shirt hanging there growing up and knowing he grew up in the same surroundings as I did was a source of great motivation."

2015: Celebrating his first goal on his senior England debut against Lithuania aged 21

2017: First game as England captain - a 2-2 World Cup qualifying draw against Scotland at Hampden Park

2018: First England hat-trick against Panama at the 2018 World Cup in Russia

2023: Celebrating becoming England men's record goalscorer after scoring against Italy in a Euro 2024 qualifier in Naples

2024: Receiving a 'golden' cap to mark his 100th England appearance in a Nations League game against Finland at Wembley

1 of 5

Wayne Rooney was England captain and Joe Hart was goalkeeper when Kane came on to make his Three Lions debut 11 years ago.

"My reaction when he first came into the England squad was: 'Alright, who is this guy?'" Hart told BBC Sport of the young Tottenham striker called up after scoring 26 goals in 42 league and cup games in 2014-15.

"Then I was like: 'Oh OK, he's good! Then he kept coming back [into the England squad] and my reaction was: 'Flipping heck, he's getting better!'

"I went to Tottenham during Covid and it got to the point in training where he was that good that I wasn't even diving for his shots. I was thinking: 'I adore you, but you are frustrating the life out of me.'"

Kane has served five different England managers.

As well as Hodgson and current boss Tuchel, Kane won 81 of his 125 caps under Gareth Southgate, played for Lee Carsley when he was interim boss in 2024, and appeared in Sam Allardyce's sole match in charge in 2016.

It was Southgate who recognised Kane's leadership skills and handed him the England captaincy for the first time in 2017, even though Kane was not captain of Tottenham at the time.

"I want people with leadership qualities who are respected by the group, and capable of stepping forward at the right moments and handling responsibility," said Southgate.

When he has started, Kane has captained the Three Lions 97 times - more than anyone else.

This video can not be played

"Amazing" Kane targets 100 international goals

How long will Kane carry on playing for England? More worryingly, who will lead the attack when he retires?

Despite individual awards and back-to-back Bundesliga titles with Bayern Munich, Kane has yet to inspire his country to a major trophy.

He will be approaching 35 when England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland co-host Euro 2028.

"He aged, but he got better too, like red wine," Lothar Matthaus, West Germany's 1990 World Cup-winning captain, told BBC Sport.

Kane, who has had to adapt his game to stay at the top level, is certainly not ready to talk publicly about retirement dates while he is still only 33.

"From a physical point of view, I feel great," he told BBC Sport recently.

"My numbers are as high as ever, and I've recently reached a new top speed in a game against Borussia Dortmund. I'm going to keep pushing and see what else is possible."

A Madame Tussauds figure of Harry Kane with Peter Shilton and players from Ridgeway Rovers - the club Kane played for as a boy

Kane's former Tottenham and England team-mate Hart added: "He's never particularly relied on pace. It's all about his thought process and his brain and how he calculates the game."

The Three Lions have won 83, drawn 22 and lost 20 of the 125 games Kane has appeared in.

His 91 goals for his country include 58 with his right foot, 15 with the left and 18 headers, with three from outside the box. Twenty-six have come from the penalty spot.

This video can not be played

"I'm speechless" - Kane reacts to England's victory over Mexico

Kane's rise from Leyton Orient loan signing to Ballon d'Or winner is well-documented.

His story - the model student and family man who married his childhood sweetheart and became an England great - serves as a reminder to pupils at his old school to never give up on their dreams.

He has not forgotten his roots - or the clubs that helped him on his pathway.

In 2020, Kane sponsored Leyton Orient's shirt. The club's home strip carried a message of thanks to frontline workers tackling the coronavirus pandemic.

Mental health charity Mind and Haven House Children's Hospice also had their logos on Orient's two change shirts as part of the deal.

"I was born and brought up only a couple of miles from Orient's stadium and I'm really happy to have the opportunity to give back to the club that gave me my first professional start," said Kane at the time.

"It also gives me a platform to say a big thank you to the many frontline heroes and charities out there who provide care and support during these challenging times."

Matthaus, who has witnessed Kane's impact at Bayern Munich, added: "He is a good person, a good ambassador, the captain of the English national team playing at a German club."

On Thursday, England's players and fans will salute Kane for breaking another record and making it 126 not out.

"He is superhuman," added Hart.

Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Carrick

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 16:03:02 GMT

Michael Carrick is set to depart as Manchester United manager, with Mauricio Pochettino in talks to replace him

Mauricio Pochettino is ready to accept an offer from Manchester United to become their next head coach.

United have opened talks with the Argentine about him potentially replacing Michael Carrick, who is expected to be relieved of his duties in the next 48 hours.

Once Carrick's future is clarified, sources have told BBC Sport that USA manager Pochettino wants to take the job.

US Soccer officials are expecting an official approach from United - and sources have told BBC Sport they have a contingency plan for their manager leaving, which includes a succession plan.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino wants to remain respectful to the US Soccer Federation and will wait for United to make their approach.

The Red Devils would be required to pay $10m (£7.5m) to release Pochettino from his contract, which he only signed in August.

The USA have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week.

With confidence over a succession plan, it raises the possibility that Pochettino may not take charge of those games.

On Thursday, US Soccer cancelled planned media with players citing a clash with Veterans Day, though some reports claimed it was to stop the squad being asked about their manager.

Pochettino, 54, is understood to view the prospect of managing United as a serious opportunity, with the expectation being he would accept the job were it formally offered.

United have spoken to the ex-Argentina defender about their managerial position on three previous occasions - when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, then in 2022 before the club appointed Erik ten Hag and again when the Dutchman was sacked in 2024.

Carrick's future at United will be decided at a meeting in Monaco on Wednesday that will be attended by chief executive Omar Berrada, director of football Jason Wilcox and co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Is Pochettino the right man for United?

Berrada and Wilcox have flown to Monaco for one of their regular, planned meetings to discuss strategy around the football club.

On this occasion, the main issue to be decided is Carrick's future and what should happen next.

It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go.

Carrick, 45, was pictured arriving at the club's Carrington training base on Wednesday.

United are 18th in the Premier League - inside the relegation zone - after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August.

It is the club's lowest position at this stage of a top-flight season since 1986-87, when they were 20th.

Pochettino's first job in the Premier League was at Southampton from January 2013, before a five-year stint at Tottenham from 2014 that included a Champions League final appearance.

He managed Paris St-Germain from January 2021 to July 2022 before spending the 2023-24 season in charge of Chelsea.

Pochettino moved into international football by taking the USA job in September 2024, and led the co-hosts to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup.

This video can not be played

How close is Carrick to Man United exit?

While it may seem a touch immoral for Manchester United to be talking to a potential new manager before they have decided if their current one is staying or not, this kind of situation is not uncommon in football.

Jose Mourinho had agreed a contract with United in 2016 before Louis van Gaal was sacked, which is how stories - including from BBC Sport - came out that the Dutchman would be dismissed as he was celebrating the FA Cup final triumph over Crystal Palace.

Going further back, Mark Hughes was replaced immediately by Roberto Mancini at Manchester City in 2009. Hughes' imminent dismissal was reported on the morning of his final game in charge.

It is impossible to reach that situation without talks taking place beforehand, and it would be naive to think they do not go on in a world in which agents are pushing clients for jobs that either do, or do not, exist or clubs are trying to gauge interest before making a decision.

I have been told by one source the Pochettino terms to join United are more or less agreed. I have also been told if they decide to push on, United can decide whether the former Spurs and Chelsea boss remains with the USA team for their matches against Haiti.

If he did stay, it would mean a sharp turnaround from a Tuesday night match - which finishes in the early hours of Wednesday - to be at Carrington for preparations before United's game against Liverpool at Anfield on 22 November.

There are a lot of gaps to fill in yet, not least whether Carrick will be dismissed or not.

But it seems more likely there will be clarity on that on Wednesday, and from that the rest of the jigsaw pieces should start to slot into place.

Japan want 'the sky to fall in' at Twickenham - Jones

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:57:42 GMT

Eddie Jones (left) and Steve Borthwick have worked together with Japan and England in the past

Head coach Eddie Jones says Japan are drawing inspiration from Italy, who beat England for the first time in March, as the Brave Blossoms attempt to heap pressure back on Steve Borthwick with their own landmark win on Saturday.

Jones was sacked by England in December 2022 after a miserable autumn which ended in a 27-13 Twickenham defeat by South Africa and jeers from the home fans.

The Australian, 66, hopes to cause similar unrest on his return to Allianz Stadium this weekend.

"We're massive underdogs," Jones told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We've got to find a way to disrupt an England side that's looking at New Zealand next week [England play the All Blacks on 21 November] and sometimes may be a little bit distracted.

"Our opportunity is to get in there, cause some havoc, cause some chaos, put off their game, get the crowd booing. Then the sky starts to come in on Twickenham and you never know what can happen.

"We've seen it happen with Italy and other countries."

Japan have lost all six of their previous Test meetings with England, most recently going down 54-19 on their autumn visit two years ago.

However Italy, who won for the first time in 33 attempts earlier this year, and Fiji, who broke their duck with a 30-22 success in 2023, have both secured maiden victories over England during Borthwick's reign.

Jones believes England's players are uniquely susceptible to pressure, given a level of scrutiny which is unprecedented in the rest of the global game.

This video can not be played

Steve Borthwick is 'an outstanding coach': Eddie Jones

A run of five successive defeats earlier this year, combined with reports of a rift between players and coaches, raised the stakes for England before Sunday's meeting with Australia.

However, Borthwick's players, who had insisted that the squad remains united, delivered an impressive 45-22 victory to vindicate their coach.

"The noise does get to the team and it can be pretty loud in England," said Jones, for whom Borthwick worked as an assistant during a previous stint with Japan and then with England.

"You've got a lot of newspapers, a lot of media, probably more than any other country in the world. Sometimes that can weigh down on the players and it's the job of the leadership to get the players thinking straight.

"Steve's an outstanding coach and a very intelligent man, and a really good coach. So I've got the highest respect for him."

This video can not be played

England ease pressure on Borthwick after big win over Australia

England back row Henry Pollock scored two tries after replacing the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso on the wing at half-time against Australia, and has been tipped to make only his second start for his country on Saturday.

Having also scored a hat-trick off the bench against Fiji in July, Pollock is averaging a try every 22 minutes in the Nations Championship.

However, Jones believes the 21-year-old's sky-high strike-rate is not the best measure of him as a player.

"I wouldn't look too much into it," he said of Pollock's two scores against Australia.

"Everyone was licking the ice cream on Sunday. They were on the front foot, everyone's lining up to run the ball, there's no pressure in the game.

"He's a fast back rower, he got the ball in space and he's a talented player, there's no doubt about it, but you couldn't read into it any more than that."

Jones is missing his own young star.

Fly-half Ryunosuke Ito was plucked from university rugby by Jones, and made his debut against Italy in July without having ever played a professional match.

Ito scored his own solo try against Australia in August, neatly stepping through the Wallabies defence., external

Ito's Test career has been stalled while he completes his obligations to his university team

However the 21-year-old fourth-year student, who has established himself as Jones' first-choice fly-half, is required by Meiji University for a collegiate competition, meaning he is missing the northern hemisphere leg of Japan's Nations Championship campaign.

Ito will join top-flight Tokyo side Suntory Sungoliath next season, who have former New Zealand captain Sam Cane and Ireland and British and Irish Lions wing James Lowe in their squad.

"That's the uniqueness of Japanese rugby," added Jones.

Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserves better

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:58:17 GMT

Mauricio Pochettino has been in charge of the USA since September 2024

When the expected formalities of Michael Carrick's dismissal as Manchester United manager are completed after a summit meeting in Monaco, Mauricio Pochettino looks set to turn a decade-long courtship with Old Trafford into a full-blown relationship.

Pochettino and United go back a long way, with the Argentine's name associated with the club since he was spotted leaving a lunch appointment at Scott's restaurant in Mayfair with Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016.

Ferguson was three years into his retirement, while Pochettino was building his reputation at Tottenham, where he fashioned an intense, all-out-attacking team that the great Scot admired.

Pochettino called it "a meeting in London between colleagues, between a genius and an apprentice".

In that moment, a link was forged.

Pochettino was mentioned as a contender to succeed Louis van Gaal when he was sacked by United in May 2016, then when Jose Mourinho suffered the same fate in December 2018.

Pochettino was the other name on United's shortlist when Erik ten Hag was appointed in April 2022, then again when the Dutchman was shown the door in October 2024.

Finally, as Carrick awaits what looks to be the inevitable, it looks like Pochettino will inherit the Old Trafford empire.

The problem for Pochettino is that the once great footballing empire is crumbling before the eyes, the dysfunctional product of years of poor decision-making and questionable appointments, allied to a Frankenstein's monster of a squad assembled by six managers.

One of Pochettino's quirks is to have a box of lemons in his office, believing they absorb negative energy. He will need several truckloads of the industrial strength variety to suck away the current mood at Old Trafford.

First things first, however, and that means waiting for the official confirmation of Carrick's departure, a long drawn-out affair which does little credit to part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

Carrick, 45, has proved to be out of his depth since being confirmed as permanent head coach following a successful interim spell, but his history of success as a player, his basic decency and his obvious desire to turn United's fortunes around makes the ham-fisted handling of his sacking another uncomfortable episode.

It is an emotion reflected by United's increasingly disaffected fanbase, who have made it clear who they blame for their current place in the Premier League relegation zone.

Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Carrick

The Monaco summit that will decide the future of Carrick and Man Utd

Would Pochettino be the right appointment to replace Carrick? Have your say

Pochettino's appointment would land in the middle ground between the flawed sentimentalism of turning to fan favourites with little or no track record of success, such as Carrick and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, as well as the quick fix of bringing in proven past winners such as Van Gaal and Mourinho.

With his one-time dream of returning to Spurs now seemingly out of reach forever, Pochettino is ready to pick up the reins at the fallen giants that are United, another club he has clearly always had in his sights.

He is currently coach of the USA, whom he led at this summer's World Cup, but even then United were lurking on his agenda.

During the campaign Pochettino held court with invited journalists at the USA team hotel in California.

When mention was made of United, Pochettino turned to his closest confidante and ever-present assistant coach Jesus Perez to say: "One day, your dream comes true. You go to Manchester United."

Perez replied with "United should have got you", promoting the response from a smiling Pochettino: "Future. Future."

Now the future is here.

The big question now is what Pochettino will United be getting?

He remains a beloved figure at Spurs, where he had an outstanding record of consistency following his appointment from Southampton in May 2014.

He never finished lower than fifth - in his first season - in any full campaign in charge, including second place behind Chelsea in 2016-17 and third in 2015-16 and 2017-18.

The one question mark always placed against Pochettino, including when he finished sixth at Chelsea in 2023-24, was an inability to get his teams over the line to tangible success in England.

Pochettino claimed the first trophies of his managerial career with Paris St-Germain after leaving Spurs - the 2021 French Cup and 2022 Ligue 1 title - but the club's hierarchy felt that was the minimum he should achieve given the squad at his disposal, and he did not see out his contract.

In England with Spurs, he was runner-up in the League Cup in 2014-15 and reached the FA Cup semi-finals in 2016-17 and 2017-18. In 2018-19 he reached the Champions League final and the League Cup semis.

In one season at Chelsea - a loveless relationship in which he could never shed his Spurs connections in the eyes of fans - he reached the FA Cup semi-finals and lost the League Cup final.

Pochettino's driven, competitive nature means that is an itch he will want to scratch when his United appointment is confirmed.

While Spurs have always appeared to be his first love, there is also no doubt United occupies a special place in his thoughts.

Spanish football expert Guillem Balague, who worked with Pochettino on his book Brave New World, says: "There is a fit with the people at the club too.

"Omar Berrada is a fan. When Manchester City drew up a shortlist to replace Pep Guardiola, some City supporters, including Omar, argued for Pochettino to be on it.

"There are plenty of clues about his feelings for United in the book. He was at the stadium in 1999 when United won the Champions League.

"Sir Alex Ferguson is mentioned 28 times, more than any other name in the biography.

"Spurs tried to push back and cut those references. Pochettino and I talked it over and decided that none of it would be touched. That shows how much it mattered to him."

Pochettino is a renowned builder, as he proved at Spurs after succeeding the sacked Tim Sherwood, working with Harry Kane to develop the recently crowned Ballon d'Or winner, as well as bringing Son Heung-Min to the club for a bargain £22m from Bayer Leverkusen in 2015.

If Pochettino can repeat that - a tough job in United's circumstances - and reproduce the easy-on-the-eye, attacking football played with relentless energy, then he could finally be the perfect fit Ratcliffe has so far looked in vain to discover.

Pochettino is also his own man, so it will be intriguing to see how he works with Ratcliffe, Berrada and Wilcox.

The road to Pochettino's sacking at Spurs effectively started following a friendly win against Real Madrid only weeks after their Champions League final defeat, when he made it clear he was not having enough influence at the club.

He enjoys warm relationships with his players, with a track record of improvement. It was no co-incidence that Cole Palmer enjoyed his best season working under Pochettino at Chelsea, scoring 25 goals in 45 appearances.

Pochettino, however, is also single-minded and ruthless, as he proved with an emphatic response to criticism for not phoning the players he left out of the USA World Cup squad.

He said: "When I was a player, when I didn't make the roster I didn't want my coach to call me. The players who didn't make the roster, they don't want to hear me say 'I apologise'. What are you going to say? Am I going to lie?"

He will need to call on every one of those qualities if and when he assumes control at United.

Back to that lunch date with Ferguson.

The final word on that day went to Pochettino as the pair argued over who was picking up the tab.

Ferguson said Pochettino could pay if he named an Argentina player who scored in the 1930 World Cup final.

Pochettino, in what he claimed was a moment of inspiration, named Guillermo Stabile.

He won that argument. Now both he and Ferguson will hope Pochettino can produce more moments of inspiration to win something more substantial at United.

What are cold weather payments and who can get them?

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:49:31 GMT

As temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather payments.

This financial help is triggered across hundreds of postcodes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland when there is a prolonged period of below-zero temperatures.

In Scotland, those on low incomes and benefits may receive a separate winter heating payment, which does not depend on how cold it gets.

The cold weather payment is a government benefit top-up to help with fuel bills.

The average temperature in a local area must be recorded as, or forecast to be, 0C or below for seven days in a row.

The temperature is recorded by the relevant weather station for your postcode.

More than 1.4 million cold weather payments were made during winter 2025-26.

To qualify, you must live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland.

Payments are not age-related but you must already be receiving certain benefits, including:

Each cold weather payment is for a seven-day period and is worth £25.

More than one payment will be made during the course of the winter if there are enough periods of cold weather.

The scheme runs between 1 November and 31 March each year.

Hospital stays can affect your entitlement to the payment so you should tell the Pension Service or Jobcentre Plus if you become an inpatient.

You should also update the relevant service if you have a baby, or if a child under five comes to live with you.

In Scotland, the winter heating payment is worth £62, and is paid automatically between December and February.

You do not have to do anything in order to receive cold weather payments.

The money should be paid automatically into the same bank or building society account as your benefits, within two weeks of the qualifying period of cold weather.

If you do not receive a payment, you can contact the Pension Service or Jobcentre Plus.

Cold weather payments do not affect other benefits.

They are separate to the winter fuel payment, which is worth £100 or £300 depending on your individual circumstances.

About nine million pensioners get the Winter Fuel Payment, after a government u-turn over changes to the eligibility rules.

Assessing the reasons for Man City's decline in form under Maresca

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 11:47:09 GMT

The ongoing international break will give Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca much-needed time to fix the growing issues in his squad.

The Italian made a dream start after taking over from Pep Guardiola in the summer, leading the club to a record seven consecutive victories at the beginning of the Premier League season.

But three consecutive defeats have followed as they have fallen six points adrift of league leaders Arsenal, who are looking in imperious form as they aim to retain their title.

In September, it was announced that City had been found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, and matches have continued as the club await the outcome of their appeal.

With possible sanctions hanging over them, is City's recent league form down to psychological issues or are there tactical problems Maresca needs to address?

Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare as title hopes hit

Property, football and politics: The links between Manchester and Abu Dhabi explained

Renowned sports psychologist Dr Paul McCarthy has 25 years' experience working in the industry with top clubs in England, Scotland, Germany and France.

McCarthy works on the personal and professional lives of players and says both contribute to how well they perform on the pitch, with the need to "piece together a jigsaw" when situations become disrupted.

"Players are like everyone else - they talk about what is going on in their own lives and things that are topical, especially about uncertain events," McCarthy tells BBC Sport.

"It generates communication with a lot of stories and rumour and over time if there are enough losses, there often becomes a reduced collective efficacy.

"A collective efficacy is a squad's belief in their ability to do what they need to do [to win] and because of their success in the past, that is often shaken a little by consecutive losses."

This video can not be played

Man City fan addresses club's midfield problem

City were sitting pretty at the top of the table after a flawless start, but have dropped to third - behind Arsenal and Brighton.

After the guilty verdict was announced during the last international break, Maresca's men won their first game back - against 10-man Liverpool at Anfield - then narrowly overcame Ipswich at Etihad Stadium in their following match.

But they have since lost to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest, with defensive issues exposed and individual mistakes proving costly.

In their first seven games of the season, City did not concede any goals because of individual errors - but that has shifted dramatically in the past three matches, with four mistakes from players contributing to goals.

City have conceded 13 goals after 10 league games - their highest total at this stage of a season since 2008-09, when they had let in 16 - and that has prompted questions about their defensive solidity.

Asked if the uncertainty over the ongoing appeal process may affect the focus and attention of players, McCarthy said: "Yeah, that would be a very reasonable human response.

"When people are uncertain about their future, that uncertainty leads to a lack of perceived control, so uncertainty is often more stressful than bad news and the research shows that.

"So while you are waiting and you don't know the outcome, you are uncertain of where you are and there is that lack of control for a lot of people - they come to training, they play their games and it's outside of their responsibility."

Are Manchester City's players being affected by the charges verdict?

While at Chelsea, in a video for NBC Sports, Maresca discussed his tactics - moving counters into a 3-2-2-3 shape before pushing one up to create the 3-1-6 shape.

He explained using six attackers was a tactic he had employed against Inter Milan to outnumber their back five.

This season, he has adopted the 3-1-6 shape more permanently - trading a second holding midfielder for an extra attacking midfielder.

Coaching a team full of quality footballers, there is logic to wanting to play in a more front-footed and imposing manner, but how well tactics are performed depend on the skillset of the players asked to do them.

City's shape in possession this season has often looked like a 3-1-5-1 or 3-1-6 shape, with Anderson typically the holding midfielder

The big questions come in the form of Elliot Anderson and his midfield partners.

Anderson - naturally more of a roaming midfielder - leans on his physical strengths. At Nottingham Forest, he defended intensely, pressed high and wide, and contributed to attacks. This season, Maresca and his staff have looked to mould him into more of a sitting midfielder after the departure of Rodri in the summer.

Learning that role will take time, as it did for Rodri when he first joined.

It is not problematic in its own right to try to coach a player into a key role, but City have looked exposed through the middle of the pitch more often in recent games.

Anderson, who has largely impressed, has played to his habit - stepping out of a holding midfield position to attempt to press or track opposition players, often looking to win the ball back. Clever opponents have used this to drag him out of position before finding players through the middle.

Enzo Le Fee recognises Anderson's willingness to track him and pulls wide

With Anderson vacating the central area, Brian Brobbey is able to drop in and receive the ball directly from his centre-back

With City looking to press high and often in a man-to-man fashion, Anderson has had to cover more space with his partners in midfield lacking the physicality required to support him.

When City are in possession, Enzo Fernandez - often one of City's midfield three - makes frequent attacking runs off the ball into the final third. When this happens, City can find themselves with as few as two or three players behind the ball, giving opponents favourable conditions to counter-attack if they can break the initial press.

Here, City lose the ball. Anderson is drawn out wide whilst Fernandez on the far side remains high and above the line of the ball, leaving City exposed in the middle

For Maresca, the issue is less around the shape, and more around losing the ball in the first instance. After the loss to Forest, he said: "You concede transitions when you lose the ball, and when you don't win duels."

Further concerns arise when assessing the skillset of the players behind Anderson.

Gianluigi Donnarumma is not a goalkeeper renowned for his ball-playing ability. The defensive cohort are serviceable on the ball but have made costly errors under pressure, playing out from the back, this season too.

City have four players near or behind the ball before Josko Gvardiol is dispossessed. Nottingham Forest, with four attackers of their own, score from this turnover

Guardiola's solution to mitigate some of these issues last season came in the form of asking midfielders to shoulder more ball-playing responsibility.

The loss of Rodri and especially Bernardo Silva, who would drop deep and take City from their own goal into midfield alone, have made City's problems more obvious.

As good as Anderson is, he is not a player who can single-handedly resolve build-up play as Bernardo Silva did, but Ayyoub Bouaddi may be somebody that could be used in this manner as we saw him against Brazil's press in the World Cup.

Sherrock, who has been awarded an MBE for her services to darts, made it through an audition process and then had to rely on the public to select her to take on Littler at Manchester Central.

Police have confirmed they helped Jemima Goldsmith to remove ex-boyfriend Russell Brand from her property in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident took place.

Thames Valley Police said officers were contacted by an alleged victim and went to an address in Oxfordshire on 25 July 2014 but no arrests were made.

They listened to her concerns and gave support, and "also ensured the victim's partner left the address, as per the victim's wishes", the police added in a statement on Wednesday.

Goldsmith, who dated Brand for about a year, wrote on X on Monday that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.

Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault on Monday.

In her post, 52-year-old Goldsmith, who wasn't part of the trial, said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".

She wrote: "I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse.

"I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident."

The Press Association reported that Goldsmith had asked for Brand to leave the property, her wish was then communicated to him by police, and he agreed to leave the house.

Goldsmith added: "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children.

"I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."

She also said she had "assisted the journalists who finally exposed him", and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" if they were sued.

TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

The first cold health alerts of the season have been issued for parts of England as a blast of Arctic air is set to sweep into the UK.

From midweek onward, overnight temperatures in many towns and cities will fall below zero, bringing the most widespread frost of the season so far.

Some rural spots could see overnight temperatures as low as minus 5C or lower.

Sleet and snow will be possible in some far northern locations with strong wind gusts causing bitter conditions.

Frosty scenes like this are likely to be widespread

Yellow cold health alerts, issued by UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), cover the West Midlands and the north west of England. , external

They will be in place from 09:00 GMT on Thursday until 12:00 GMT on Saturday.

Cold health alerts are usually issued between 1 November and 30 March.

The UKHSA warns the upcoming cold snap "is likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services" and pose "greater risk to life of vulnerable people".

After the thick fog of recent days, visibility will be better on Wednesday, with crisp sunshine forecast for many parts of the UK.

Low pressure and a weather front will graze southern parts of Britain, bringing outbreaks of rain and slightly milder air with highs reaching 10 to 14C.

Late on Wednesday, cloud will clear ahead of Arctic air surging southwards across the country.

By Wednesday night, a strong to gale force northerly wind will develop over northern and eastern parts of Scotland making it feel especially bitter with gusts exceeding 50mph.

Showers are expected to stream in with sleet and snow possible in Shetland and Orkney as well as northern Scotland.

Over higher ground, snow may settle into Wednesday night. This is not unusual for early November.

Winds will also strengthen along the North Sea coast all the way down to the coast of Norfolk making it feel very cold.

The 'feels like' temperature, which takes into account expected air temperature, relative humidity and wind strength, shows single figure temperatures on Thursday

Winds will remain strong on Thursday across the far north of the UK. However, inland it will be calm as a ridge of high pressure builds.

Widespread frost is expected across the northern half of the UK while the southern half holds on to the somewhat milder morning conditions for a little while longer.

Thursday afternoon is expected to be sunny across much of the country though showers, some of which could be wintry, may still continue in the far north.

While Thursday morning may feel cold across much of the country, daytime highs will still typically reach 7C.

The northerly breeze will make it feel colder in some places.

Thursday night will bring freezing temperatures to most of the UK

On Thursday evening, the weather will be clear and calm across much of the country as temperatures fall rapidly.

Winds will have eased somewhat across Northern Scotland and along the North Sea coast.

Friday will bring frost on grass, pavements and cars in many parts as the air temperature falls below zero from Scotland to Southern England.

Most towns and cities will experience temperatures around zero or just below, while rural spots in Scotland and even southern England chill to minus 5C.

Counties along western and southern western coasts of the UK will not be quite as cold, as the warmer sea and an onshore breeze will prevent frost from forming.

Inland, after a frosty morning, daytime highs will peak at 6 or 7C for most.

Saturday and Sunday night will be cold and frosty in some southern and eastern parts of the country.

By the weekend though, milder weather will already be spreading in from the Atlantic making the cold snap rather brief for most.

London borough is Britain's happiest, survey finds

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 06:15:11 GMT

Richmond upon Thames has been named as the happiest place to live in Britain in an annual survey.

Residents of the south-west London borough have easy access to central London and strolls along the Thames on their doorstep, as well as boutiques, cafes and opportunities to spot roaming deer in their local parks.

Richmond ranked particularly highly across several aspects of local life in Rightmove's "happy at home index", including access to nature and green spaces, essential local services, shops and restaurants, employment opportunities as well as residents' pride in their area.

But, living there comes at a cost, with the average asking price for a home in the borough standing at more than £1m.

Harrogate in North Yorkshire and Cirencester in Gloucestershire came in second and third places respectively in Rightmove's 15th annual "happy at home index".

In Wales, Monmouth was the highest ranked, while Kirkcaldy took the top spot for Scotland.

Richmond returned to number one after previously winning in 2023 and finishing second last year.

Mayor of Richmond upon Thames councillor Nancy Baldwin said: "This recognition is especially meaningful because residents highlighted their pride in the local area, our beautiful parks and green spaces, and the local services they rely on every day.

"Above all, it is our people and communities that make Richmond special."

Second-placed Harrogate also ranked highly for access to nature and green spaces.

Across Britain, four-fifths (81%) of people who took part in the survey said they were happy with where they live.

People took part in the research after being emailed via Rightmove's database, so the survey was self-selecting.

Colleen Babcock, a property expert at Rightmove, said: "Richmond stands out for offering a combination many people value: easy access to nature and green spaces, without having to give up local services, places to eat and shop, or employment opportunities.

"This year's results suggest that the places people rate most highly aren't simply urban or rural, but often bring together some of the best elements of both."

Why is Scotland's housing shortage getting worse?

BBC News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 06:11:51 GMT

It is three years since Scotland's largest cities declared "housing emergencies", followed months later by the nation as a whole.

Since then, homelessness has hit record levels while the cost of renting or buying property has continued to rise.

The solution to this crisis would appear straightforward - build more houses.

But delivering this is more complicated, with responsibility falling to central and local government as well as to private housebuilders.

Scottish ministers claim the country boasts the UK's highest rate of housebuilding but the pace is falling, and there are questions about whether the right homes are being built in the right places.

So far, 13 Scottish councils have declared housing emergencies for a variety of reasons.

They include rising pressure on homelessness services, high levels of people in temporary accommodation and a lack of affordable homes compared to lengthy waiting lists.

Homelessness has increased to a record level, with Scottish government data showing more than 19,000 households in temporary accommodation paid for by councils - a 10% rise on the previous year.

This includes 10,715 children living in temporary accommodation, such as a bedsit.

A total of 35,000 households were assessed as being homeless or threatened with homelessness in 2025-26.

As of March this year, there were more than 140,000 applications on council waiting lists for social housing.

This figure does not include some large authorities like Glasgow which runs its social housing through housing associations, and has more than 6,000 live applications waiting.

The overall social housing stock held by councils and housing associations has been rising since 2017 - the year after the Right to Buy scheme was abolished in Scotland - but has only recovered to its 2004 level.

In March this year, there were 89,000 fewer social homes available than when the Scottish Parliament was reconvened in 1999 - despite a 9% rise in Scotland's population over the same period.

While demand for social and affordable housing has been rising, the total number of homes actually being built has been falling.

The housebuilding sector was only starting to recover from the 2008 financial crash when the Covid pandemic hit.

In the 2025-26 financial year, a total of 17,640 new homes were completed according to Scottish government figures - the third year in a row where the figure had fallen.

There is little prospect for an immediate improvement, as the number of new projects started over the last two years were the lowest since 2012-13.

As to why this is happening, housebuilders point to a range of factors.

The sector faces familiar problems with the cost of doing business, with construction materials particularly vulnerable to inflationary shocks like that which followed the war in Ukraine in 2022.

Industry bodies also complain about a lack of suitable land earmarked for building, and say it takes too long for planning permission to be given to new developments.

Red tape is also a concern. Homes For Scotland - which represents about 200 housebuilding firms - says the "regulatory burden being imposed by government" over recent years has added tens of thousands of pounds to the cost of a new-build home.

They note that Chancellor John Healey promised in his UK budget not to make major changes to building regulations for the rest of the parliamentary term.

Recent examples in Scotland include a levy to address unsafe cladding on tall buildings, new rules requiring "climate-friendly" heat sources and better energy efficiency.

Scottish Housing Secretary Shirley-Anne Somerville told BBC Scotland News that ministers were alive to the concerns of housebuilders, but that these standards helped reduce energy bills and improved housing for disabled people.

There is a notable disparity in rates of building in different parts of Scotland, with construction particularly concentrated in the area around Edinburgh.

In 2025-26, 32% of the new homes completed in Scotland were in the Lothians.

If you add in Fife, which is also a popular area for people commuting to the capital, then this corner of the country accounts for 39% of all new homes built, despite only having 23% of the population.

Look to the west and the figures flip around; Glasgow and the surrounding councils have 32% of the population, but only 26% of the housebuilding.

This is true even in relatively affluent areas with high rates of population growth, like East Renfrewshire - where just 87 new homes were completed last year.

Glasgow has a homelessness problem so acute that the city council is spending almost £70m a year putting people up in hotel rooms.

Along with Edinburgh, the city has been declared to be in a state of "systemic failure" by the Scottish Housing Regulator.

Glasgow faces particular pressure with refugee households seeking support, with 44% of the 8,025 homelessness applications last year from people with refugee status or leave to remain - compared to 16% across Scotland as a whole.

And yet there were fewer new home "starts" there last year than in East Lothian, a more rural area with one sixth the population, with city leaders in Glasgow blaming rising construction costs.

Plans have just been announced for 6,500 new affordable homes to be built on brownfield sites - previously developed land which is currently unused - over the next six years.

The council also says it has identified 59 sites across the city as potential locations for another 12,173 new homes, which could be built by 2032 if funding becomes available. It is also looking at repurposing disused shops for housing.

There has been a historic shift in Scotland's population towards Edinburgh, with the capital's financial and service sector booming while areas in the west struggle to recover from the decline of traditional industries.

Demand for homes around the capital has driven up property prices. Edinburgh, Midlothian and East Lothian all feature in the top four areas in Scotland with the highest house prices, all well above the national average.

This makes it attractive to housebuilders seeking a return on investment - and it also means businesses in the construction trade and related supply chains are more likely to thrive there.

Meanwhile those in the industry say there are fewer small-to-medium sized building firms in more rural areas to take projects forward.

Higher prices in the east of Scotland have meant problems with affordability for some.

A study for Shelter Scotland suggested that 62% of newly-formed households - people entering the housing market for the first time, such as those leaving the parental home - in this area were unable to afford the current market. For Scotland as a whole, the figure was 55%.

That same study suggested an extra 15,693 affordable homes need to be built each year to end the housing emergency.

The Scottish government does not have an overall housebuilding target, but it did set one in 2022 for affordable homes - to complete 110,000 of them by 2032, with at least 70% available for social rent and 10% in island and rural communities.

The latest figures show 36,500 completions towards this target.

The Scottish Parliament Information Centre says that with just over five years left to go, this means on average 15,000 homes need to be delivered each year.

In 2025-26, there were 6,832 completions as part of the Affordable Housing Supply Programme - down from a peak of 10,466 in 2022-23.

So the rate of delivery needs to more than double, and then be sustained at record levels, if the target is to be met.

Ministers say they are committing £4.1bn over the next four years to support the delivery of "around 36,000 affordable homes".

Builders have welcomed the longer-term certainty offered by this funding, but that would still only get half way to the 110,000 target with two years remaining.

Modelling by the Fraser of Allander Institute think tank suggests it is more likely to take until late 2036.

The Scottish government says it "remains focused" on achieving the 110,000 target, while acknowledging that it is "challenging".

Somerville said it could be met through longer-term investment in publicly funded affordable housing schemes - through vehicles like the Scottish National Investment Bank - as well as support for private developers.

The government is also setting up a new national agency next year - More Homes Scotland - which hopes to "remove barriers and accelerate housing delivery".

Blood-thinning drug limits cartilage damage and relieves osteoarthritis pain

New Scientist November 11, 2026

A drug that prevents blood clots reduced pain and improved mobility in mice and monkeys with knee osteoarthritis. The approach seems to partly work by reducing inflammatory signals that degrade cartilage.

Osteoarthritis is caused by the wear and tear of cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, leading to inflammation, pain and stiffness. It affects more than 500 million people worldwide. Painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs can relieve symptoms, but no approved drugs halt or slow worsening of the disease.

“We have nothing to offer our patients apart from suggesting weight loss, or offering drugs that provide pain relief,” says Tonia Vincent at the University of Oxford, who wasn’t involved in the study.

Advertisement

The best non-drug therapies to relieve the pain of knee osteoarthritis

It is widely thought that inflammatory molecules called TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta drive inflammation that worsens osteoarthritis. This has led to clinical trials testing drugs that target either of these molecules. But these have been unsuccessful, potentially because these molecules compensate for each other when one is blocked, according to Chuan-Ju Liu at Yale University and his colleagues.

To explore whether targeting both molecules may be more effective, the researchers surgically removed part of the cartilage in the left knee joints of eight monkeys to mimic wear and tear that triggers osteoarthritis.

A month later, four of the monkeys took a daily dose of a drug called dabigatran, mixed into their food. Dabigatran is commonly used to prevent blood clots in people at increased risk of strokes, but has also been shown to block inflammatory signals via both TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta. The remaining monkeys ate their usual food as a control.

Free newsletter

After seven months, MRI scans revealed that the left-knee cartilage in monkeys on dabigratan was about 60 per cent thicker, on average, compared to the control monkeys. This suggests that the drug reduced cartilage damage, slowing the progression of osteoarthritis, says Liu.

Monkeys on dabigratan also had a roughly 15 per cent greater range of motion in their left knee than the control monkeys. “Monkeys receiving dabigatran showed a more natural walking pattern and a greater range of knee movement,” says Liu. “These improvements are consistent with reduced joint stiffness and discomfort.”

In further experiments, the team confirmed their findings in mice with surgically-induced knee osteoarthritis, which also revealed that dabigratan reduced inflammation in the knee by about 60 per cent.

A drug called pazopanib is known to provide brief relief from arthritis pain – encapsulating it in nanoparticles can make its effects last much longer, research in mice suggests

The findings suggest dabigratan could slow the progression of osteoarthritis in people. “They’ve used the best [animal] models we have of osteoarthritis,” says Vincent. “If the findings can be replicated by another research group, you would certainly consider trying a small clinical trial,” she says.

But it is unclear whether the approach can reverse damage that has already occurred, says Liu. Another limitation is that giving people a drug that reduces blood clotting puts them at greater risk of bleeds, so the researchers are now developing drugs that target TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta without reducing clotting, which they will test in mice before any clinical trials, says Liu.

However, Vincent says prior studies suggest that inhibiting molecules involved in blood clotting may relieve osteoarthritis symptoms, which might mean that some of dabigratan’s benefits are due to its anti-clotting, rather than anti-inflammatory, effect. Further research that compares dabigatran with drugs that target TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta without the clotting effects should help to clarify this, she says.

Science Translational Medicine DOI: 10.1126/scitranslmed. aec8494

Are we outsourcing our thinking to AI – and how much should we worry?

New Scientist November 11, 2026

The CollisionEric C. So, W. W. NortonUS: out now; UK: out 20 November

It was the type of question that Eric C. So had posed to his class for years. As a professor of behavioural economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, So liked to ask his students what impact they believed technology was having on our way of thinking.

But this time, before he could even finish asking the question, a student raised her hand. “I just ChatGPT’d it,” she said, before reading out the answer the AI chatbot had given. When So asked her what she thought, the student seemed genuinely puzzled. ChatGPT’s answer was now what she thought.

Advertisement

“She couldn’t distinguish between her own reasoning and AI-generated reasoning. Or perhaps she could. But she didn’t see why the distinction mattered,” So writes in The Collision: What AI does to us, which explores its impact on our brains.

It is the sort of anecdote people are hearing – and worrying about – around the world. Are we embracing a technology that will see us all become like this student, outsourcing our thinking to AI without even realising?

So certainly seems to think so. The Collision uses research from the fields of behavioural science and neuroscience to argue that AI, especially generative AI tools like chatbots, can cause many of us to suffer from “cognitive atrophy”. This is the claim that intellect is like a muscle, with our brains rewiring neural pathways around our habits and pruning skills we no longer have use for. If we don’t use our independent thinking skills, they will deteriorate, while the “cognitive reflex” to use AI for anything mentally challenging will strengthen, So argues.

Eric C. So proposes the interesting idea that we have evolved over millennia to find the lure of AI irresistible

He points to a study that revealed how people learning to juggle over three months showed visible tissue growth in the regions of the brain designed to track movements, but after three further months of not practising, this brain tissue then regressed. In other words, use it or lose it.

You can see the problems that could cause, especially in children. “When we hand students AI tools before they’ve built their own cognitive foundations, we may be preventing those essential connections from ever forming properly,” So warns. The same risks apply to the skills we usually build up over a career. Within a generation, for example, we could have doctors “whose brains never developed the architecture for independent diagnosis”.

So was inspired to examine what AI was doing to our minds after he found himself asking ChatGPT to finish a simple email he was writing to a colleague and realised “some fundamental relationship between me and my own thinking had shifted”.

The danger of writing a book on such a premise is that it becomes tempting to selectively pick the arguments that support it. So falls into that trap, relying on a few small studies to do the heavy lifting and he doesn’t feature any interviews or case studies. I would have loved to have seen some insight from neuroscientists on the latest thinking around what AI is doing to our brains.

One of the small studies So describes measured the neurological activity of three groups of students writing an essay, with one set allowed to use only their mind, another, search engines and the final group ChatGPT. While completing the task, the unassisted writers’ brains were “alight with widespread, robust connections”, but the brains of the ChatGPT group had “gone quiet”.

Straight after finishing, participants were asked to quote any sentence from their essay. For those who wrote unassisted or used a search engine, recall was nearly flawless. But 83 per cent of the ChatGPT users struggled to recall any direct quote at all.

“The information was never encoded,” So writes. This, he argues, shows how we are in danger of creating a world of “hollow competence”, with a generation that can “produce without comprehending”. But the book doesn’t mention that the study was of just 54 participants, 18 per group, and they were given only 20 minutes to write the essay.

Free newsletter

The Collision never provides quite enough solid scientific evidence to back up its bold claims. Still, it is a well-argued and thought-provoking read. The book points to studies that show how AI can warp our perception of how good we are at something, essentially mistaking its knowledge for our own. Yet because AI makes us feel more capable, we become even more inclined to rely on it, further eroding our thinking skills.

So also proposes the interesting idea that we have evolved over millennia to find the lure of AI almost irresistible, because our brains use up a lot of the body’s energy on thinking and so a preference for “cognitive ease” has become encoded in our very nature. This makes it “extraordinarily difficult for us to resist off-loading our thinking to AI”, So states. “Our biology practically demands it.”

Again though, the author pushes this argument slightly too far by claiming the world is experiencing something he calls “AI gravity” – a force acting on us constantly to use AI as much as possible, unless we actively work against it. That would be an apt description of the smartphone, but it still feels some way off for AI. At times, it felt like this book was written for the small subset of people who are already completely addicted to chatbots. At one point, the author asks: “If AI vanished tomorrow, what would you be capable of doing? Most people don’t know until they try.” Really? I think most people know they would be completely fine.

So posits that the key factor to working with AI successfully is implementing friction into the process. He points to studies that suggest when people have to work through prompts before they get an answer, then AI as a “cognitive partner” can extend our intellectual capabilities.

Otherwise, our intellects could be in trouble, the book warns. “You won’t notice the moment you stop thinking for yourself. No bells will ring, no alarms will sound. The slow surrender will be… almost imperceptible.”

Here’s hoping, for all our brains’ sake, we don’t let that happen.

Artificial Intimacy: Who we become when we talk to machines by Sherry TurkleThis book examines the rise of people using chatbots as a replacement for real human company and shows how that deprives us of personal growth and stunts our emotional development.

As If Human: Ethics and artificial intelligence by Nigel Shadbolt and Roger HampsonA book that explores different schools of philosophical thought to ask what the ethics of AI should be and how humans should treat chatbots, in the hope it can influence how these tools are regulated in the future.

We Are Not Machines: The fight for the future of work by Sarah O’ConnorWritten by the Financial Times‘s associate editor, this book argues that we should fight back against some employers’ expectation that we adjust how we work and live to fit into an AI-led world, rather than the other way around.

Tom Knowles is a technology and business journalist based in London

Blade Runner 2099 is coming. How does Philip K. Dick’s original hold up?

New Scientist November 11, 2026

Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?Philip K. Dick, Gollancz

With the new miniseries Blade Runner 2099 coming out on 25 November, this seems a good moment to return to the source material behind it and the two blockbuster Blade Runner films. That pot-of-sci-fi-gold source material is, of course, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, a shortish novel by renowned sci-fi writer Philip K. Dick, published in 1968.

I read the book as a teenager, but any memory I had of it was then wiped away by the zillion times I watched Blade Runner, the 1982 movie directed by Ridley Scott, and the handful of times I watched Denis Villeneuve’s 2017 follow-up, Blade Runner 2049, which cleaved closely to Scott’s original vision. I returned to the book, therefore, with few preconceptions.

Advertisement

There are a lot of differences between page and screen. Just for starters, the book version of Rick Deckard, the bounty hunter who tracks down rogue Nexus-6 androids that have entered his city illegally from off-world colonies, isn’t quite the super-cool hero that Harrison Ford gives us on screen.

Free newsletter

Book Rick is married to an unhappy woman named Iran, rather than being moodily single in a stunning designer apartment. The couple have a machine that allows them to set their moods every day, but no piano covered in artful photographs. They also have an electric sheep grazing up on the roof where they park their flying car. (The electric sheep, to be clear, isn’t in the movies.) It is a matter of embarrassment to Rick and Iran that they cannot afford a real sheep, when their neighbour has a real horse. In this heavily polluted, post-apocalyptic world, nothing is as precious as a live animal.

You can see why Ridley Scott ditched the pet strand, as well as Rick’s wife, to give us the hero from the films

This matter of the electric sheep sets the scene for an absurdist strand that runs heavy through the whole novel. Book Rick dreams of one potential pet after another, including an ostrich, before finally buying a black Nubian goat. You can see why Scott ditched the whole pet strand (including the goat), as well as Rick’s wife, in order to give us the more sexually available and less ridiculous hero we know from the movies.

Another big difference is that, in the book, a religion called Mercerism is central to the plot. Our characters plug themselves into machines in order to fuse with Mercer, their religious leader. I found this confusing and unnecessary, and I can see why Scott bunged it on the scrap heap.

So, lots of differences. Yet a surprising amount of the novel is rendered very faithfully indeed on the big screen. There’s the whole set-up, of course – a post-fall world, illegal androids, bounty hunters – and the strong connection between Rick and the android Rachael Rosen. (You may choose to ignore his musings on her breasts being too small, this being the work of a male sci-fi writer in 1968.) And then there’s the sympathy that Rachael elicits from both Rick and the reader.

It also preserves the very cool, futuristic vibe that you get from the book, especially when Rachael and Rick are together. The special tests that Rick carries out on suspected androids, with all their weird animal-related questions and focus on pupil reaction, are all essentially lifted from the page.

Would I recommend the book? I think rereading it has given me a deeper understanding of many key elements of the films. The use of animals in the first movie now makes perfect sense, for example. But even if you aren’t a big fan of the films or have never seen them, I would say yes, this is a classic, and well worth tucking into.

FilmBlade Runner (1982)Ridley Scott

I consider this a great work of art… the sets, the music, the everything. There are different cuts available, and all are interesting. By the way, one of the most famous scenes, the “tears in rain” monologue, isn’t in the book and was entirely a creation of the film-makers (and actor Rutger Hauer).

Emily H. Wilson is the author of the Sumerians series (Inanna, Gilgamesh and Ninshubar, all published by Titan) and she is currently working on her first sci-fi novel. She is a former editor of New Scientist and you can follow her on Instagram @emilyhwilson1
