Killer Bigfoot evidence rejected by Bigfoot’s biggest fans

New Scientist November 11, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

One of the defining features of conspiracy theories is that they are “self-sealing”. If you confront a conspiracy theorist with the lack of evidence for their claim, they will turn this back on you and argue that this very lack of evidence is proof of how powerful the conspiracy is.

This is foreshadowing.

Advertisement

Feedback is interested in watching the new documentary Capturing Bigfoot. We can’t, because we live in the UK and it isn’t available here, but if anyone would care to rectify that, we will stick ourselves in front of it immediately.

The film is about the classic footage that purports to show a Bigfoot loping alongside a river in California. Shot by Roger Patterson and Robert Gimlin in 1967, the clip became one of the canonical pieces of evidence for the existence of Bigfoot: a mythical humanoid that supposedly lives in the forests of North America. Bigfoot is one of the icons of cryptozoology, the search for probably-nonexistent creatures. It has hordes of devotees.

In Capturing Bigfoot, film-maker Marq Evans uncovers what really happened in 1967. He speaks to Patterson’s associate Bob Heironimus, who says he wore an ape costume in the footage.

Crucially, Evans also finds a lost piece of 16-millimetre film, shot in 1966, showing a rehearsal for the final Patterson-Gimlin video. A review of the documentary in Variety calls this footage “the smoking gun”. It is, Feedback would suggest, a case no defence lawyer could wriggle out of.

So, the Patterson-Gimlin film purporting to show Bigfoot was fake. Feedback and our editor worried if we were legally safe saying that, but then, as our editor said, “come on”.

It is perhaps telling that, when we mentioned this to Mrs Feedback, her response was “I could have sworn I already knew that”. Indeed, these accusations have been made before, notably in Greg Long’s 2004 book The Making of Bigfoot. The new thing is that rehearsal footage.

Naturally, then, this footage is what the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization pushed back on. Its president is quoted in The Times as saying: “My initial reaction is, how could you believe that in the age of AI?… Even if they found some reel, how would you know whether what they’re showing in the documentary is what’s on the reel?” And thus the foreshadowing pays off.

In late October, a lot of websites suddenly went offline. This was because of a vulnerability in the PHP programming language, which had been known since 2024 but was thought to be too difficult to exploit, until AI tools found how to do it.

Reader Chris Hall had never heard of PHP. This seems to have been a common experience: even the BBC’s cyber correspondent Joe Tidy only learned of the existence of PHP when the story broke. Tidy got a lot of online abuse for this, which Feedback thinks is unfair: his job is to explain things clearly, not to be a walking technical manual. In the interests of solidarity, Feedback will say that we still don’t know what distinguishes a baryon from a boson, and at this point we refuse to find out.

Anyway, Chris looked up PHP and was given “the helpful information” that it stands for “PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor”. “I can understand the ‘H’ and second ‘P’, ” he says, “but what does the first ‘P’ mean?”

Feedback is happy to clarify that PHP originally stood for “personal home page”. When it was upgraded in the late 1990s, the programmers kept the letters and had to think of something new for them to stand for. Hence the recursive backronym that is “PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor”.

Sometimes, scientists fake their results. The problem is spotting the fakery, because it isn’t always obvious. Often, images have been copied from other papers, necessitating systematic searches. Or you have to perform careful statistical analyses on the raw numbers to identify the trends that reveal they have been made up.

Or, sometimes, the authors might just flat-out tell you – leaving you to decide whether or not they mean it.

Nihar Shah is a computer scientist at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania, who mostly studies AI scientists: those systems that can do research and write papers with little or no human intervention. However, he is also the author of the blog Research on Research, about “academia, research, and peer review”, where he writes about some of the weird stuff that finds its way into peer-reviewed journals.

In October, Shah looked at a host of recent scientific studies and found that many of them included variations on the same phrases. These remarks showed up over and over again, in at least 60 papers. Phrases like: “The values in this table are illustrative placeholders for formatting purposes and must be replaced with results obtained from actual experiments”. Or “Planning scenario, not measured results”. Or “note: the values shown are placeholders and should be replaced with your actual experimental results”.

What on Earth is going on? On the face of it, the authors are just admitting that they have made up data. However, Shah says (and Feedback agrees) that there is no reason to assume chicanery. Perhaps all of these papers are built on real results, and the authors just forgot to remove these placeholder texts from early drafts. In other words, this could all be the result of really, really sloppy editing on the part of all concerned. Which is, we guess, reassuring? Um.

Got a story for Feedback?

What is the world actually like, if what we see is just our brain’s interpretations?

New Scientist November 11, 2026

If the world we observe is just our brain’s interpretation of the electrochemical signals it receives from our eyes, what is the world actually like? (continued)

Biram DesaiBrighton, UK

To paraphrase the words of philosopher Alan Watts, a question that is perpetually difficult to answer may indicate that the question needs to be reframed. If indeed there are only relative realities and no objective reality, then the question is only relevant in relation to the observer. So, the world is whatever you perceive it to be!

Advertisement

Brian BalkeVia Facebook

In precise terms, we don’t “see” our brain’s interpretations. We generally see our brain’s expectations. These expectations are categorisations of sensory patterns that prepare downstream networks to initiate muscle and endocrine control.

Tools enhance our power over the world and our understanding of it. As the tools shrink, we build abstract models of their elements, eventually achieving control at scales far below our natural sensory sensitivity. This requires that we develop enhanced sensory tools as well as manipulators.

What this all boils down to is that we don’t just “see” with our senses. We have enhanced our senses using our expectations about the world. Those enhanced senses include ultrasonic imaging, X-ray scanners, particle colliders and pressure sensors. Those enhanced senses, in their agreement with our expectations, confirm that there is a world beyond our perceptions.

Despite this conclusion, we should be aware that there is a great deal in our sensory data that cannot be replicated by artificial sensors. The ability to shift attention to acquire additional detail, the tingle of excitement upon seeing a romantic partner, the disorientation felt during a bout of the flu: these are all subjective experiences that differentiate, in their richness, human consciousness from any form of artificial consciousness built upon linguistic abstractions. That we struggle to convey our subjective experience is also an aspect of the world. It may not be measurable, but I actually kind of like that.

In precise terms, we don’t ‘see’ our brain’s interpretations. We generally see our brain’s expectations

Tony CusanoVia Facebook

The world is actually just like our brain’s interpretation of what we see. But it’s a trick question, because it’s not just “our brain”, but all of our brains linked in a social network.

We can be fooled by randomness, but if the world were purely random, repetitive events would not be as persistently predictable as they are. Unpredictable events becoming predictable with more measurements of more underlying variables also undermines pure randomness.

Thunder and lightning are good examples of events that appeared random for generations, then, with better observations, gradually gained predictability to the point where they can now be prepared for well in advance of them occurring, though not yet with perfect accuracy.

No one brain learned that, but the human social network did.

Julian GoldVia Facebook

All those “brain in a jar” arguments neglect the fact that we are all, in fact, brains in (meat) jars.

Yes, our brains help us approximate the state of the external world. The question as to how close that approximation is depends on a lot of things, but the granularity is extended by our ability to build sensors that augment the range of what we can see, which was originally dictated by the survival needs of 4 billion years of evolution and predation.

Asking what it’s “really” like is meaningless though.

Who will step up to preserve space age artefacts for future generations?

New Scientist November 11, 2026

Around 40,000 years from now, the Voyager 1 probe will pass within astronomical spitting distance of the star Gliese 445. From there, it will continue drifting through the universe on an endless journey that marks humanity’s first attempt to reach the stars.

Voyager 1 – which on 18 November will have travelled one light day from Earth – began its odyssey almost 50 years ago, meaning it has been operating for the majority of the space age. That makes it a rarity: most of our iconic spacecraft ended their lives burned up in Earth’s atmosphere or in bits at the bottom of the ocean. Two of the most important missions still flying today, the Hubble Space Telescope and the International Space Station, look set to share the same fate in the near future, even as scientists call for Hubble to be preserved.

While some craft like the space shuttles are on display in museums, our present space history is, essentially, in its dark ages, with little thought currently given to preserving spacecraft in situ, where our space-travelling descendants may wish to marvel at them. Even the Apollo hardware left behind on the moon has almost no protection in international law.

Advertisement

Perhaps we need an organisation like the UNESCO World Heritage Committee to designate important space artefacts for preservation, and encourage funding from cultural and heritage budgets, not scientific ones, to do this. Of course, with such budgets often under threat and the US set to leave UNESCO at the end of this year, this could introduce new problems.

Private philanthropy is another option. If humanity is to one day take its place among the stars, a fantasy that fuels many a tech billionaire, it would be a great shame to not be able to look back at how we got there. Just as we remember 19th-century captains of industry like Andrew Carnegie and J. P. Morgan for funding great cultural institutions, perhaps we should be lobbying for the creation of a Musk Space Museum or Bezos Orbital Institute.

Why does music evoke emotion, and do people from other cultures feel the same way?

New Scientist November 11, 2026

Why do certain pieces of music evoke emotions such as joy or sadness, and do people from different cultures react in the same way?

Michael EllisonUniversity of Bristol, UK

Happiness and sadness depend largely on whether the harmony and modes involved use natural overtonal intervals or their inversions (with the inversions typically sounding less happy). Of course, nuances and gestures (how one plays) and specific instrument sounds can influence this, but the psychology of music lies in its tuning and harmony.

Advertisement

There is, of course, a lot of difference between musical cultures as to what, by convention, connotes happy and sad. Indeed, those categories themselves seem to derive from a Western common-practice era reduction into two main modes, major and minor, when other cultures may have a lot more modes to choose from.

Even within Western music, major is not always happy (try Ludwig van Beethoven’s String Quartet Op. 59 No. 3), nor minor sad (listen to the song Happy by Pharell Williams, which is in minor!).

A proposed $300 million healthcare precinct in Wānaka has been put on the market, with developers being sought to take over the consented project.

The 1.3ha site, earmarked for a private hospital and other medical facilities, received final resource consent from Queenstown Lakes District Council last year.

Real estate firm Savills New Zealand has been appointed to sell the development opportunity, which includes the land, resource consents and project plans.

Master-planned by Wānaka investment company Roa, the proposed precinct comprises five main buildings with a combined floor area of about 16,000sq m, alongside a parking structure accommodating more than 300 vehicles.

Plans include a private hospital, surgical theatres, emergency care, diagnostic imaging, specialist consulting suites and allied healthcare facilities.

The estimated development cost is $300m.

Savills managing director Ryan Geddes said the project was intended to address gaps in healthcare services across Wānaka and the wider Southern Lakes region.

“The Wānaka Health Precinct is a development born out of necessity.

“But it sits at the heart of what is essentially a healthcare desert. Access to major hospitals is limited, and specialist care is more than three hours away by road.”

Geddes said the concept emerged after a medical emergency involving the developer’s family highlighted difficulties accessing healthcare in the region.

“The vision for this development was actually born from a genuine family medical emergency that the developer experienced.

“They realised that the region’s healthcare infrastructure has not kept pace with wider growth and prosperity, and decided to change that.”

The proposed facility would serve Wānaka, Queenstown, Central Otago and the wider Southern Lakes region, potentially reducing the need for patients to travel elsewhere for specialist treatment.

The sale follows an announcement by Health New Zealand in April that it would evaluate public healthcare options based on projected health needs in the Central Lakes region.

Savills associate director of commercial sales Martin Hebler said population growth and tourism were contributing to demand for healthcare infrastructure.

“Wānaka’s population is growing rapidly, even faster than Queenstown.”

The region’s tourism economy was also expected to increase demand for accessible medical services.

The property is being offered for sale by deadline private treaty, with offers closing at 4pm on December 18, unless sold earlier.

No construction start date or completion timeline has been announced.

Tanya Winter resigns as Ōtorohanga chief executive for Waimate role

New Zealand Herald November 11, 2026

Ōtorohanga Mayor Rodney Dow. Photo / Ōtorohanga District Council

When King Country cartage contractor Rodney Dow became Ōtorohanga’s mayor a year ago, he didn’t foresee that he’d be looking for a new chief executive.

But Tanya Winter has announced her resignation after accepting the chief executive role at Waimate District Council.

Dow said he was sad to see her go and he wished her all the best.

He told Local Democracy Reporting he didn’t realise how big a job it was looking for a new chief executive.

“All this process will cost money you know,” he said.

“It’ll cost us $40-$50k to employ someone.”

South Waikato and Waikato District councils have announced they are looking at a new job-share arrangement.

If approved, South Waikato District chief executive Susan Law would be interim chief executive of Waikato District as well.

The decision comes after Waikato District chief executive Craig Hobbs resigned in October.

According to a statement released by South Waikato District Council, the Western Waikato Unitary Authority proposal was a major factor in making Law interim chief executive of Waikato.

The statement called it an “opportunity to further develop and strengthen working relationships” while saving money.

Ōtorohanga District and Waitomo District also share a few services to reduce costs for their ratepayers.

When Local Democracy Reporting asked Dow if he’d consider a job-share arrangement with Waitomo’s chief executive he said all options were open.

“We’re going to consider all options, but it’s all really new to me.” .

When the same question was floated to Waitomo Mayor John Robertson, he said he didn’t think Ōtorohanga would swing that way.

“We are all waiting for the new government to advise where they want councils to head.

“Sharing CEs is not straightforward.”

Dow told Local Democracy Reporting that as Ōtorohanga mayor he was required to appoint a recruitment company to get a new chief executive.

“But apparently we can just go and ask anyone to be interim CE on a short term,” he said.

“For the formal appointment, there’s a whole process you’ve got to go through, a legal process.”

He acknowledged the process was designed to avoid mistakes, but he wondered if the processes were overkill.

“I’m not fearful of making a mistake, when it’s your own money ... people make mistakes,” he said.

“But you know, when it’s ratepayers’ money, but then [sic] I wonder whether we spend too much money being risk-averse, being too scared to make a mistake and we end up spending more money.”

Winter said it was “an absolute privilege” to serve the Ōtorohanga District. But she couldn’t pass up the opportunity to be closer to whānau in Waimate.

She’ll continue to work for Ōtorohanga until her final day on January 15.

Dow said this about his departing chief:

“She’s done a great job for our district ... she cares deeply about people building strong relationships.”

When asked if the replacement needed to be a dedicated Wahs fan, Dow said he was open to accepting high performers like Nathan Cleary.

Bronson Perich is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist for Taupō and South Waikato based at the Waikato Herald.

With nearly 400,000 special votes still to be counted, a Government to be formed, and a new party poised to enter Parliament for the first time in over a decade, I probably ought to be writing about the election.

But frankly, I've had enough. And I suspect many readers have, too.

I spent Saturday evening at Act's election night celebration in Auckland. There was plenty to cheer about, with the party securing another record result and provisionally returning 13 MPs. Yet, for all the cheering and congratulations, the evening was a bit anticlimactic.

It was a grubby campaign. Researchers at Victoria University of Wellington analysed more than 2200 Facebook posts from political parties and their leaders, finding that 66% of National's and 51% of Labour's were negative.

After months of campaigning, the country had spoken, but as Chris Hipkins noted, we weren't quite sure what it had said. Having spent months anticipating November 7, I found myself impatient for the next political fix, only to discover that it involved more speculation.

Read more of Jonathan Ayling's Premium opinion piece below.

New Zealanders should be able to expect that a political party's share of parliamentary seats will broadly reflect its share of the party vote.

That is the central promise of mixed-member proportional representation, or MMP.

When the rules allow co-ordinated voting tactics to weaken that relationship, criticism is justified.

However, the criticism needs to be precise.

An overhang does not automatically prove manipulation.

Read more of Reynold Macperson's Premium opinion piece below.

National's party vote fell in every electorate seat in the election's preliminary results, compared with 2023.

It's not surprising that it fell in some seats, given National's party vote dropped by about 9 percentage points in the preliminary results compared with 2023.

But to fall in every single electorate across the country is a warning for the party, Victoria University associate professor in politics Dr Lara Greaves says.

"That's a lot of pain for them," she told the Herald, especially when combined with the loss of senior ministers Nicola Willis, Chris Bishop and Paul Goldsmith and Speaker Gerry Brownlee.

"And then also to lose [list candidate and former MP] Nancy Lu, who reached out to important communities. The Chinese community is a huge group, especially among newer migrants that National appeals to.

"They're going to really need to work to make sure they can still appeal to those groups, including in Auckland."

Read more of Derek Cheng's Premium piece below.

Former National Party president Sue Wood has written an open letter to National's caucus, urging them to reconnect with the wider public and take back power over the party's direction following a "lacklustre" campaign.

National's caucus will be entirely made up of electorate MPs, who significantly outperformed the party vote.

Writing in the Post, Wood told the caucus that unlike list MPs, they were not elected by the National Party board, and were not beholden to the board or the leader.

"This makes you the masters of the party's future direction and its level of influence," she wrote.

"While political discipline is important, your decisions must give a voice to your constituents' feedback. Debate those decisions in caucus and find a unified position."

Richard Prebble says Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins are "both losers" and should not be the leaders of their respective parties.

The former Labour Party minister and Act Party leader wrote an op-ed, published in the Herald yesterday, where he called on the National and Labour leaders to stand down.

Speaking on Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast today, Prebble was asked why one should resign if they emerge victorious from the election, to which he replied: "Because they’re both losers."

"Both Christophers have run very bad campaigns, but it's worse than that. You've got to listen to the country, and the country has been telling them for three years that they don't want either of them to be Prime Minister. At some point, you have to listen."

It was not an unfair assessment of Hipkins, despite it being historically difficult to end a government after one term, as the leader should be more popular than their party, he said.

"That means that the leader's capable of attracting other people to come and support the party. Chris Hipkins has never been more popular than Labour. But the same criticism applies to Luxon with knobs on."

Prime Ministers often are supported by over half the country, but Luxon is not backed by a majority of National voters, Prebble said.

Erica Stanford would make a good leader for National and Kieran McAnulty the same for Labour, he said.

Outgoing National MP and Speaker of the House Gerry Brownlee says while he doesn't like negative campaigning, he has great respect for anyone who runs a political campaign.

"They take a lot of responsibility on themselves," he told Ryan Bridge TODAY.

"I know that in the case of of our team, they're not particularly happy with the result, obviously. But you know, you don't want to get into recriminations of any type whatsoever. It doesn't take you anywhere."

Brownlee yesterday told the Spinoff he felt National's campaign specifically was too negative.

Former National Party president Sue Wood has called for the party's electorate MPs to take more power over the party's direction, which Brownlee said was an "interesting proposition".

He didn't believe there should be any massive change but a review was held after every election and that would be the chance for people to have their say.

RNZ’s unlawful overdraft was signed off by the board

New Zealand Herald November 11, 2026

RNZ board chair Brent Impey accepted the organisation had broken the law.

By Mary Argue and Craig McCulloch of RNZ

RNZ has confirmed its request for a $5m overdraft, which breached the Crown Entities Act, was signed off by the board.

The public broadcaster on Monday revealed a shock $12 million budget blowout, after a litany of financial blunders.

Chief executive Paul Thompson took responsibility for the result and said internal reports gave an inaccurate picture of the finances, meaning the scale of the loss only became clear in October.

While carrying out the broadcaster’s annual audit, EY identified a breach of the Crown Entities Act – emphasising it in RNZ’s annual report.

“We draw your attention to Note 12 on page 32 about the Group not complying with sections 160 and 162 of the Crown Entities Act 2004, in that the Group entered into a financing arrangement without the authority of the Minister for Media and Communications and the Minister of Finance.”

The breach concerned a $5m overdraft that was set up without ministerial approval.

RNZ said the $5m overdraft was initiated to provide RNZ with a safety net in the event one of its land sales was delayed, so the company could manage significant one-off costs, but was never used.

By law, RNZ needs sign-off from two ministers to borrow money, which it last received in 2006 for up to $3.5m.

On Checkpoint, RNZ board chair Brent Impey accepted the organisation had broken the law.

“Now, how did that happen? That’s very difficult to explain. That there was a loan with Westpac and again, the Crown Entities Act was breached.”

A RNZ spokesperson said the board approved a temporary $5m overdraft facility on June 9, 2026.

The former chief financial officer, Hilary Parker – who resigned unexpectedly in early October – initiated setting up the overdraft, which RNZ’s executive took to the board, the spokesperson said.

Public law expert and barrister Mai Chen said the fact that ministerial approval wasn’t obtained raises questions.

“You’ve got people in highly paid positions who don’t seem to understand that they’re a Crown entity, they’re subject to the Crown Entities Act,” she said.

“Why did they do it without going through the right process?”

Chen said it was concerning that the board appeared to be unaware of the breach and more broadly in the dark about RNZ’s financial position.

An RNZ spokesperson said the $5m overdraft was set up to provide RNZ with a safety net in the event one of its land sales was delayed, “while the company also managed a significant number of one-off costs”.

They noted the overdraft was undrawn as at June 30, 2026.

Asked if RNZ management was aware of its obligations under the Crown Entities Act, RNZ pointed to section 160 of the Act – that outlines the need for ministerial sign-off – in its borrowing policy.

They said no internal or external legal advice was sought before entering into the overdraft.

“The independent review will establish what happened and why,” the spokesperson said.

A Westpac spokesperson said the bank didn’t comment on specific customers’ banking details.

“However, we can confirm that we have strict approval processes for all lending of this scale. Any questions specifically relating to RNZ’s banking are best directed to RNZ.”

A retail boss says embattled David Jones “lost its magic” when it moved away from a traditional department store layout into a modern store-in-store model.

David Jones is set to close its only New Zealand store, based in Newmarket, by the end of this year.

The store was placed into voluntary administration and receivership last week after a breakdown in discussions between the company and landlords.

First Retail Group managing director Chris Wilkinson described the closure as “sad” on Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast.

“It was such an institution for so many people including for New Zealanders and was a first-stop shop across [the] ditch.”

The 188-year-old business employs more than 6000 staff across its 38 stores in Australia and New Zealand and has been at Newmarket since 2019.

Wilkinson said he believed the issues lay partially with the store layout.

“The big problem is it pulled away from having individual departments ... when it moved to a store-in-store model it lost its magic because it was no different to what you’d find elsewhere.”

He said a carve-up of brands was the most logical move.

“The reality is for a lot of brands in there, there’s a standalone presence.

“Brands can have a second presence online, but the reality of the model was not going to be sustainable.”

David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold said in the initial announcement that the retailer was an iconic company.

“I thank customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support for David Jones through this period,” Berchtold said.

“We have a well-developed plan on how to reset the business for the future and will be working with the administrators, the receivers and our secured lender as we continue to pursue that reset of the business.”

The receivers said they recognised the restructure would have a “material impact” on many members of its team and committed to treating all employees with fairness and respect throughout the process.

A $180 million alpine resort featuring a 136-room hotel and 72 residential properties is being planned for Wānaka, in what would be the town’s first major hotel development in nearly 40 years.

The Mount Iron Wānaka development will occupy 1.87ha at the foot of Mt Iron, combining accommodation, residential living, hospitality and extensive health and wellbeing facilities.

Construction is expected to begin in 2027, with the development anticipated to take about four years to complete.

The project is the brainchild of KR Capital, the development and investment division of nationwide engineering and design consultancy Kirk Roberts.

The resort-style complex will combine a Sudima Hotel with 39 three- and four-bedroom townhouses and 33 apartments, including three penthouses, with residential properties priced from $1.4m.

Owners and guests will share swimming pools, hot pools, saunas, a gym and wellness facilities, alongside sports and recreational spaces, landscaped gardens and relaxation areas.

The full-service hotel will incorporate restaurant and bar facilities, conference and meeting spaces, supported by a pedestrian promenade, hospitality and retail precinct.

An elevated, landscaped walkway known as the Ridgeline will extend 100m through the heart of the development.

Hind Management, the operator behind Sudima Hotels, will manage both the hotel and residential resort operations.

The development comes as the Queenstown-Lakes district experiences significant growth, with tourism activity booming and property values continuing to buck the national trend.

A new privately operated $300m Wānaka Health Precinct is also under development 700m away, within the surrounding Three Parks commercial and retail precinct.

Despite that growth, Wānaka has not had a significant new hotel development since the 106-room Edgewater opened in 1986.

Kirk Roberts chief executive Jade Kirk said the vision was to create something beyond a traditional hotel or residential development.

“We wanted to rethink the traditional resort model and create something genuinely different – bringing together residential living, tourism, hospitality, recreation, and health and wellbeing within one integrated destination,” he said.

“Irrespective of whether people are visiting for a few days or living here all year round, the boundaries between residential living and holidays will appear seamless.

“Everyone gets to enjoy the facilities, experiences and services of a luxury resort.”

Roberts said the project would create employment through construction and ongoing resort operations, support local businesses and introduce new opportunities for hospitality, tourism and retail.

“Our experience designing and developing the five-star Sudima Kaikōura hotel helped shape our approach,” he said.

Sudima Hotels and Hind Management founder and chief executive Sudesh Jhunjhnuwala said the companies had previously partnered on Sudima Kaikōura, which opened in 2022.

“Wānaka has grown significantly, but its hotel offering hasn’t kept pace, and we see a real gap in the market for a high-quality, full-service hotel,” Jhunjhnuwala said.

“Sudima Wānaka will bring conference facilities, dining and wellness amenities to the town, with a strong sense of place.”

New Zealand Sotheby’s International Realty will market and sell the residential properties, with flexible ownership models including private lifestyle and professionally managed rental options.

Local agent Sheryl Alty said the development would appeal to holiday-home buyers, permanent residents and retirees.

“For buyers who divide their time between Wānaka and elsewhere, the option of managed rental arrangements adds another layer of appeal.”

Parliament’s Speaker Gerry Brownlee, who was a casualty of last weekend’s election, talks to Audrey Young about his long career, including that haka, dealing with Winston Peters and what he told his National colleagues at his farewell caucus.

Humour has always been the trademark of outgoing Speaker Gerry Brownlee, from his first speech in Parliament to his parting words to the National caucus this week at the end of a 30-year career.

The former woodwork teacher from Christchurch was explaining to the House in 1997 how politics had been a passion of his since he was a young man, and was acknowledging the support of his wife, Michelle Brownlee.

He recounted how, after she had gone abroad on a working holiday, he realised he wanted to marry her – so he took off after her.

“I particularly remember one morning in the beautiful city of Paris. We were out for a walk. We came to a stop on a bridge over the River Seine. Below us, the riverboats full of people busily made their way up and down the river. In the far distance we could see the top of Notre Dame Cathedral and hear its bells on the gentle breeze.

“In the cafes below, the air was filled with the sound of accordion music and the smell of coffee and croissants. It was a most romantic atmosphere. I thought to myself, ‘This is the moment’. I held Michelle close and said to her: ‘Darling, when we get back to New Zealand, I would very much like to go into politics’.”

It brought the House down, as he has done on so many occasions since, including as Speaker in the past three years.

He has used his humour to defuse situations that could have ignited and to disarm MPs who have taken umbrage at something or other.

So did he have a philosophy to guide him as Speaker?

“Yes, a simple one,” he says. “And that is that the House should manage itself as much as possible. The House belongs to members. The voters elect people to sit in that House, and the conduct of the House is then in the hands of the members.”

He received plenty of correspondence from people saying he should kick out various people from the House – and from people not familiar with the rules who wanted him to kick them out of Parliament altogether.

“The role of the Speaker is to maintain order as much as possible, but in the end, it is up to the members who are in there. And I think most respond appropriately to that.

“The fire-up moments are relatively small inside the whole number of hours that the House sits.”

One of the most infamous moments in the past term was when New Zealand First leader Winston Peters turned on China-born Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan and told him to go back to his own country.

Brownlee describes them as “very unfortunate comments” and says he may have got it wrong by not pulling Peters up on the day it happened.

“But what people don’t also appreciate is Lawrence was sitting in the House,” he says.

“Lawrence is a very robust MP. He’s a very good MP. He’s really taken to Parliament. He knows how it works. He could have taken a point of order and pointed out how he felt about it.

“Any of his party could have, and any other member could have raised the issue, but it wasn’t raised.”

And, he adds, some of the interjections on Peters at the time were quite offensive.

Some had said “sit down, old man”; another had suggested he had been out for a long lunch.

“In the House, you receive the respect that you give.”

Brownlee is sometimes accused of being soft on Peters but he says that Peters, who was first elected in 1978, knows the rules and how far he can push them.

“And he pushes them right to the nth degree.”

The even more infamous incident in his term as Speaker was the haka by Te Pāti Māori MPs during the vote on Act’s Treaty Principles Bill.

“To be clear about the haka, there was nothing actually wrong with the haka itself,” Brownlee says.

But it started while the vote was proceeding.

“That is direct interference in the democratic process that’s just unacceptable.”

Those MPs who left their seats and advanced on the Act Party in a way he said was “by any measure visually quite threatening” was behaviour that could not be accepted in any way, Brownlee said.

“Had they come along to the Speaker’s office beforehand and said, ‘hey, look, at the end of this bill, we want to do a haka’ then I’m sure that in line with business committee decisions, that would have been fine.

“But they didn’t. They had to make that very theatrical statement about the ripping up of the bill and everything else. And that’s just an abuse of Parliament at a high level.”

One of Brownlee’s last actions as Speaker of the 54th Parliament served to remind the public that the punishment dished out to Te Pāti Māori co-leaders, a three-week suspension from the House, was unprecedented (the previous longest suspension was Sir Robert Muldoon for three days).

The standing orders committee that Brownlee chaired recommended that the privileges committee develop a framework for future punishments of MPs being held in contempt of Parliament.

“For the public to have confidence in the House’s disciplinary procedures, it is important to avoid perceptions that they may be arbitrary in their operation,” he said at the time.

He says he had not criticised the privileges committee for its penalty but added: “You’d have to say if three weeks was the most severe penalty that you can get, that leaves a huge amount of scope for a whole lot of bad behaviour before you get to three weeks.”

So what does Brownlee think of where the coalition Government took the country on the Treaty of Waitangi and race relations?

“Backwards,” he says, but he doesn’t think people should get too wound up on the term “race relations” because so many families have Māori connections.

“Over the time that I’ve been in politics, the way in which this country identifies itself increasingly through Māori culture is something that ... no one should be concerned about.

“It is becoming more and more the way in which we recognise ourselves.”

Using Māori names or having two languages for Government agencies should not matter. They were not an issue in places like Wales or in Scotland.

“I just struggle with people who get so particularly wound up about it.

“The really important thing is to look at how does this country present itself to the rest of the world moving forward. And as I say, increasingly, there’ll be an aspect of a strong aspect of Māori culture in that identity.”

Brownlee has held an impressive number of parliamentary and political positions, including deputy leader of the National Party during the turbulent leadership of Don Brash and Judith Collins, 12 years on select committees from 1996 to 2008 and ministerial posts under the Key-English Government: Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, Energy and Resources, Transport, Foreign Affairs, Defence, Civil Defence, Earthquake Commission, and Economic Development.

Of them all, Energy and Resources was his favourite, a role he had to give up when he was made Minister of Canterbury Earthquake Recovery.

The reason was that, despite scepticism from the likes of Treasury, he pushed through reform that had reduced the regular threat of dry years.

“You ended up with three state-owned generators that were more balanced in their capacity across thermal, renewable and fossil fuel. It created a better base for competition and greater encouragement for all those companies to look at their renewable profiles.“

He was the MP for Ilam from 1996 until 2020 when the seat was won by Labour’s Sarah Pallet. In 2023, it was retaken by National’s Hamish Campbell.

Brownlee was a list-only candidate in 2023 and 2026 and no National list candidates were elected in last week’s general election.

All 42 of its seats were electorate seats and the 29.21% it received in the party vote entitles it to 35 seats, meaning it has a seven-seat overhang on provisional figures.

Te Pāti Māori has an overhang of four seats, all of which expands a 120-seat House to 131 MPs.

On election night, Brownlee compared people who had promoted a strategy to engineer an overhang to “children playing with matches”.

“I’ve been fascinated by the people who say any party votes for National this time would have been a wasted vote,” he says.

“Well, you could say that about any vote that was given to any candidate or any party that didn’t end up in Parliament.”

He believes it is hard for the general public to fully understand the mechanics of MMP.

“I’m quite convinced, in fact, that if the public had known that the consequence of vote splitting was a much bigger Parliament, then they might have thought very carefully about whether they participated in that.“

Brownlee won’t get to make a valedictory speech. They are reserved for MPs who are retiring voluntarily. His last speech in Parliament was in the light-hearted adjournment debate during which he revealed that Copperfields cafeteria had sold 166,000 cups of coffee, 18,000 scones, 5690 doughnuts and 12,000 pies.

But Brownlee, aged 70, was farewelled by the National caucus on Tuesday.

“And it’s a tradition of the National Party that you get presented with a silver tray that has your name and the years that you’ve served ... engraved in it.

“When I first came here, those trays were quite large. They were boxed up, blue ribbons on the packaging and they were big enough to carry a decanter and six glasses with a degree of comfort all around them.

“Nowadays, of course, they, they’re significantly smaller, so I can tell you that when I got up to make my final comments, I made reference to that and just said that I was pleased that I was leaving before they turned into tinfoil plates.”

How The Diplomat became TV’s slickest, most addictive thriller

The Diplomat serves up a deliciously fizzy cocktail of ingredients. A dynamic cast generating crackling chemistry. Razor-sharp, briskly delivered dialogue. Robust battles of the sexes. A wild ride through the backroom manoeuvres of global politics executed with the propulsive pace of a thriller. As a bonus, there are the pleasures of what its creator and showrunner Debora Cahn has called “location porn”: a veritable gallery of glamorous settings that provide viewers with access to posh places they could never hope to enter.

The glossy, big-budget political drama’s brand of international diplomacy isn’t about interminable meetings nutting out the minutiae of trade deals in undistinguished conference rooms. It operates in territory closer to the jet-setting realm of James Bond, building its fictional world in English castles, American coastal mansions and Italian villas. When in Paris, it’s a gala function at the Louvre.

This series isn’t concerned with the political ramifications of fuel prices or the cost of living crisis. Focusing on international relations at the top levels of government, it’s high stakes in high style. Aircraft carriers are attacked, NATO is threatened and nuclear weapons are stolen; the Western world seems perpetually on the brink of war. It’s grounded in the real world, but not exactly as we know it.

The Diplomat takes big swings at big subjects, and the skill of the cast and the quality of the writing help to make them work, fuelled by the accelerated pace and omnipresent sense of urgency. As the recent, compelling and cleverly shaped fourth season attests, it continues to fire on all cylinders.

The series began in 2023 with the appointment of Kate Wyler (Keri Russell) to the post of American ambassador to the UK and has subsequently charted her frequently fraught progress, establishing early that she’s a career foreign-service officer more comfortable working in Afghanistan than in London. Kate’s accustomed to, and skilled at, bargaining in basements with warlords, more confident wearing a burqa than a ballgown to do her job.

For her, submitting to interviews with fashion magazines about her life and marriage is torture: she’s comfortable striding around purposefully in a wardrobe of black pantsuits and has to be reminded by her stalwart deputy, Stuart Hayford (Ato Essandoh), to brush her hair. Although extremely cluey in the ways of the world, Kate’s not necessarily suited to the niceties of diplomatic service, and such a high-profile position demands a shift in a range of ways, including learning about English protocols and practices while endeavouring to represent the priorities of her president. Cahn and Russell have both described their title character as “a raw nerve”.

But she’s also a dutiful servant of her country, and advocating for its interests hasn’t been a cakewalk. Through the series, the US hasn’t proven itself to be a reliable or trustworthy force and the recent season has presented particular challenges reflecting intriguing real-world parallels.

Warning: spoilers below, including for the recently released fourth season.

Essentially, there has been ongoing concern about the psychological fitness of the US commander-in-chief. Vice-President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) ascended to the Oval Office following the sudden death of the previous incumbent at the end of the second season. Given Penn’s problematic history when she took the top job, Kate and her equally experienced husband, foreign-service veteran Hal (Rufus Sewell), had doubts about her judgement and capabilities.

From early in the new season, after President Penn is the victim of an assassination attempt, concerns about her state of mind and her behaviour steadily escalate. In the aftermath of the shooting, she becomes more impatient, aggressive and intolerant of objections. She’s increasingly erratic, her temper short and her attitude combative. She jeopardises long-time alliances and steers her country towards conflict.

There are clearly parallels with the current leader of the US – including the shooting – but, given the gender swap, Cahn and her writers also get to play with the idea of an embattled woman digging in and doubling down in the face of uncertainty about her strength and resilience. The troubled and troubling leader is desperate to demonstrate that she’s not weak or unfit for her role. She refuses to acknowledge any chink in her armour that might be exploited by enemies or rivals. And the reliably terrific Janney, who this year won an Emmy for the role, has made a meal of the part.

The Diplomat astutely incorporates attributes of other shows that debut showrunner Cahn has worked on as a writer and producer. It recalls The West Wing’s pace, literate dialogue and passion for the mechanics of politics. (It’s also become a bit of a West Wing reunion, not only with Janney and Bradley Whitford as her husband, but also director Alex Graves – one of West Wing’s best – and writer-producers Peter Noah and Eli Attie.) It has Homeland’s suspense, edgy characterisations and unrelenting sense of threat, as well as Grey’s Anatomy’s affection for attractive, capable professionals and their messy romantic lives.

Front and centre are the Wylers: a pair of talented, knowledgeable and ambitious people navigating a tempestuous, see-sawing marriage. There’s also the wobbly relationship between Stuart and the CIA station chief, Eidra Park (Ali Ahn); and more recently, the increasingly uncomfortable union of the Penns.

Another highlight has been writing and casting of the English prime ministers: initially the cunning, impulsive and explosive Nicol Trowbridge (Rory Kinnear) and, in the new season, a vivid contrast provided by the steely, strategic Bethan Vaughan (Jodie Whittaker).

Given the fourth season’s timely attention to the ructions ignited by a loose-cannon president, it would be fascinating to know what’s happening in The Diplomat‘s writers’ room following the midterm elections. How will they respond to the radically changed landscape in the US? Given a fifth season was recently announced, hopefully we won’t have to wait too long to find out.

The Diplomat is streaming on Netflix.

Suddenly, Pia Miranda is everywhere. The actor who seared herself into the nation’s consciousness as the star of Looking For Alibrandi 26 years ago has over the past year or two cropped up on multiple networks, as an actor, guest and presenter. And always looking as if she can’t quite believe her luck in being there.

She was in Stan’s Invisible Boys, as the mother of one of the young men struggling to come to terms with his sexuality in a remote town in WA. She’s popped up on Luxury Escapes for 10 and Foxtel. She travelled back to her ancestral Sicily with Shaun Micallef for SBS’s Origin Odyssey. She was in Darby and Joan for the ABC, and now she’s co-presenting Recipe of the Year with Adam Liaw for the national broadcaster.

Not bad for someone who as a girl felt there was no place for someone like her on our screens.

“I always wanted to be in movies. I just never thought it was possible because I didn’t see any Italian-Australians in film and TV,” she says.

It was, of course, Alibrandi that changed all that.

She was 25 when she made the film, playing 17-year-old Josie, who starts the film feeling deeply embarrassed of her heritage, trapped by it even, but ends up embracing it. She’d been on Neighbours, but when Melina Marchetti’s script, adapted from her own novel, landed on her desk “I could not believe what I was reading, and I honestly was thinking I have to get this. It was the first time I’d ever imagined I could be in something that meant so much to me.”

As she writes in her rather engaging memoir Finding My Bella Vita (2023), she paid her way to Sydney to audition for the part, and when she landed it, she had to crash with her sister for the three months it took to make it.

The film may have made her famous, but it certainly didn’t make her rich.

“Full disclosure, I wish I’d been paid more and I wish residuals [ongoing royalties] were a thing in Australia because as Australian actors, generally we don’t see a cent after we leave set,” she says. “That’s been something I’ve had to negotiate with my brain, but apart from that, the whole experience has been wonderful.”

She watched the film last year for the first time since its release, with Kick Gurry, the actor who plays her boyfriend in the movie, at her side. “He was crying through the whole thing,” she says, laughing. “I had to look after him. He was crying, holding my hand, going, ‘Look at us!’”

Though it didn’t set her up financially, the movie did yield other fruits; indirectly. It’s how she met her husband, musician Luke Hanigan, whose band Lo-Tel contributed the song Teenager of the Year to the soundtrack.

“I think he has a thing for Italian women,” she says. “I was so scared to take him to Italy the first time because I thought he was going to be like, ‘I didn’t even get a good one’. He saw me on the side of a popcorn box [promoting the film], and he asked me to be in his film clip, and I was just really excited because they were going to pay me $1500.”

Was that more than you got for the film?

“Probably. So we met on that, and we struck up a friendship. We had to do a bit of press together, and one thing led to another. Eventually. He moved slowly. He was a bit shy. I mean, I like shy guys.”

Miranda has worked consistently in the years since, though it’s fair to say nothing made as much of a mark on the public mind as Looking for Alibrandi (it’s amazing what being on the high school curriculum can do for the popularity of a book, and its screen adaptation; plus, it’s a seriously good movie). At least until she won Australian Survivor in 2019.

She came to the show as a hardcore fan, and took the competition seriously, despite having a few blind spots. “I can’t catch a ball. I don’t like heights. I’d never been camping before I went on Survivor, so what was I doing,” she says, laughing. “But I love the game, and I still love the game.”

She approached it, as all winners do, strategically, making alliances (she and Boost Juice founder Janine Allis became, and remain, great friends) and breaking them when needed. It worked, and she walked away with $500,000 in prize money – “financially it absolutely helped me because we went straight into COVID and we were freelancers, so we didn’t get any COVID payments” – but the reactions online were a rude awakening. For perhaps the first time in her professional life, Miranda was not universally adored.

“Some of the online bullying was really embarrassing and hard to deal with,” she says. It was also distinctly gendered.

“I know a lot of female Survivor winners say that the story of when a woman wins is always about how the man loses, and the story of when a man wins is how incredible they are.”

She undertook the move that brought her the most grief, a blindside (elimination), with two male accomplices. As the hate poured in, she checked in with them to ask if they were OK. “And they went, ‘What are you talking about?’ And I’m like, ‘Well, I’m getting 1000 death threats a minute.’”

Awful though it was, Miranda insists there was a positive side to that experience, too, as she became involved in Dolly’s Dream, an organisation dedicated to fighting online bullying. “What was most shocking was a lot of the people who were coming for me were parents of young children, and I thought they’re probably doing this to me and a MAFS contestant and someone else tomorrow. And if we continue to accept it as part of society, how are we going to teach our kids to be better? So that’s something that I take really seriously, and I am hoping that at some point we can make [a] change.”

The Survivor experience gave her another unexpected insight, too. As the competition wore on, something strange began happening to her skin pigmentation. It turned out she had vitiligo, an autoimmune condition that causes the skin to lose pigment related to alopecia (which runs in her family), but of which she had been totally unaware.

“My first thought was, ‘My career is over’,” she says. “They call it a disfigurement; I don’t see it as that because I think people with vitiligo look beautiful, but I started to question the world I was in.

“I’ve spent my whole career trying to fit into this mould and being told things like, ‘You’re not sexy enough, you need to change your body, you need to do this’, where I’ve never questioned being told that, I’ve always just tried to fit in. And I realised that I’m actually part of a really broken system.”

If Miranda has a secret weapon in confronting that, it’s the air of relentless, and the seemingly genuine warmth and positivity she exudes. You can see it in spades on Recipe of the Year, in which she and Liaw shepherd contestants through a CWA-run cooking competition (with nothing more at stake than a ribbon for the winner).

The show is a clear effort on the part of the ABC to fulfil its remit to reach regional Australia. But it’s also illustrative of how much the notion of Australianness has expanded since she got her big break.

“I was brought up in the ’80s as an Italian kid. No one wanted to date me,” she says. “I know that feeling of being called the greasy wog and all those sorts of things. So it’s informed my life, and I really try to make sure that everyone feels included and to speak about that stuff.”

Recipe of the Year airs at 7.30pm on Sundays on the ABC and ABC iview.

‘Nice try, sweetheart’: The red-meat obsessed Aussie BBQ queen showing Texans how it’s done

Sydney Morning Herald November 12, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Barbecues might be as synonymous with Australian food culture as Vegemite, but Melbourne-raised “hardcore carnivore” Jess Pryles, the toast of America’s fire-cooking scene, says you ain’t tasted barbecue until you’ve tasted it in Texas. One bite of smoked beef brisket in a classic barbecue joint over a decade ago, and she was hooked.

The TV host and cookbook author now calls Austin, Texas, home. And she’s happily gnawing her way through her adopted state for her new series showcasing innovative pitmasters, Feast By Fire.

“Brisket’s become quite ubiquitous here,” she says. “When you’ve had one good one, they all end up similarly as good. So I wanted to put the lens on less common or more unusual dishes that set each of these barbecue joints apart.

“And then I took inspiration from those dishes and created a dish that people can make at home, that’s much more accessible, and often much faster as well. Not all of us have a good 16 hours to sit by a smoker.”

Pryles grew up in an enthusiastically meat-eating household, looking forward to steak night. “Dad would cook chicken breasts to the point of being drier than the Sahara, and steaks were usually on the side of well done,” she says. “My mum still loves well-done meat to this day because that’s what she grew up with.”

Then came that “life changing” meal in Texas.

“I wanted to eat more and discover how it was made. And then I got curious to give that a shot,” she says. “And I remember going to my Australian butcher and very confidently saying, ‘Oh, I’ll have a brisket, please’. And they handed me this plastic bag with this piece of meat in it. And I thought, ‘Hang on a second – the thing in Texas that is a brisket is five times the size of that. How can I ask for the same thing and get something different?’ And that moment and that frustration led me down this path to seeking answers.”

Pryles, who worked in communications before getting her break through a blog called Burger Mary, completed a graduate certificate in meat science at Iowa State University, and set about honing her craft from pitmasters across Texas. She also founded competition governing body, the Australasian Barbecue Alliance, and operates an online spice store with her Texan husband, Chris.

Pryles has also built a substantial TV profile both here and in the US, judging Seven’s short-lived reality series Aussie Barbecue Heroes, as well as judging on the Food Network series Pitmasters. She was also invited to barbecue on the front lawn of Parliament House in Canberra by the Red Meat Advisory Council.

“I was one of only less than 10 people who had deep knowledge of Texas-style barbecue, and so I sort of commanded respect from the get-go,” she says. “But it certainly is a male-dominated industry … There’s a certain demographic, particularly Facebook users, who, every now and again, when I get a viral recipe that skips my own fan base and goes large, they’ll be like, ‘Nice try, sweetheart. You belong in the kitchen’. And it’s just hilarious, because I’m making a very nice living off of what I do. And so I just laugh that off … But the men of Texas barbecue are extremely welcoming. There hasn’t been much pushback.”

The first pitmaster Pryles visits in the series is Ali Clem of Michelin-starred restaurant La Barbecue in Austin.

“I think women do have to work a little bit harder than men to get the same recognition,” says Pryles. “So I work my ass off. But Ali and I are in the position we’re in based on our knowledge.

“And, look, people have been cooking over fire for a long time. Back in the hunter-gatherer days, the hunter was traditionally the man, which means the one who was staying home and actually cooking the meat was the woman. So I think that we were barbecuers way back.”

In the series, the pair discusses how to cater for non-meat eaters. Clem is accommodating. Pryles has “no patience for vegans in a barbecue restaurant”.

“I had a cousin who visited Texas who was vegetarian and she went and had all the sides in a barbecue restaurant, to have the experience. And I thought, ‘That’s like going to a bar and just ordering a glass of water, but saying you had this great cocktail experience,’” she says. “I have no problem with vegans and vegetarians. They’re welcome to do what they want as long as they are not being militant about pushing their ideals on other people in a rude, confrontational way.”

Pryles hunts her own meat, visits slaughterhouses to learn about best practice, and admires the pioneering work of ethologist and livestock machinery inventor Temple Grandin.

“I feel it’s a responsibility, if you’re going to be a meat advocate, to understand the full process of it all … It doesn’t put me off at all,” she says. “If you can’t handle what it takes to get the meat to your plate, perhaps you shouldn’t be eating meat. There’s a pitmaster here in Austin who always reminds me that, when you see a pit loaded up with 50 briskets, it’s 25 animals.

“You have to keep it in context that these were once living creatures. Anthony Bourdain also has a great quote about the best part about animal welfare and its relation to the meat industry is that both of those are aiming towards the same thing. To get the best quality meat, it often involves a lot of animal welfare, particularly in the pre-slaughter stages as well. So we all work towards the same goals for that.”

These days, when she visits her family in Melbourne, Pryles is the one in charge of the meat. “We are mutually agreed that I’ll be manning the barbecue!”

She tends to get most homesick around Australia Day.

“Whether or not you want it associated with that day, when that ad comes out in January and talks about lamb uniting everybody, I often wonder if we can’t just all get around the table with some great grilled meats and share a similar feast, share some commonalities.”

In the current heated political climate in the US, she finds people yearning for connection. “I think people are getting by, by just trying to focus on still being respectful to your neighbour and finding things that connect commonly. And honestly, from where I sit, I really don’t see Australia being too much far off, in terms of division at the moment, which is pretty sad.”

For anyone thinking of hosting a barbecue in that spirit, she has some hot tips. “If you don’t have enough heat, you’ll never get the sear that you need. So it’s just not worth messing up your steaks to skimp on the coals.”

And don’t “set and forget”. “We all love beers around a barbie. But unfortunately, you do have to pay attention to what you’re doing. If you prefer not to pay attention, I recommend you buy a smoker where you can sit there for several hours and just wait.”

Feast By Fire airs at 8pm on Mondays on SBS Food and streams on SBS On Demand.

‘What the hell have I done?’: The crisis that inspired Nazeem Hussain’s new comedy

Sydney Morning Herald November 12, 2026

Nazeem Hussain is nervous – and not just because there’s a random white lady standing in what’s usually the men’s section of the prayer hall inside the Albanian Mosque in Melbourne’s inner north. “Oh no, a journalist in the mosque!” he jokes when I meet him during the filming of his new ABC series Separated at Birth. “You’re going to scare all the readers.”

“We’re used to journalists coming in undercover,” he tells me later, laughing. “So the fact that you advertised that you were a journalist is brave.”

In truth, the comedian is nervous because he’s not used to being earnest. And though his new show – and his first time writing a full, scripted narrative series – is a comedy, it’s also a sincere exploration of new parenthood, “dysfunctional” families and the broader community that supports them.

“I’ve been outside my comfort zone since day one on this,” he says of the story, which is based on his life.

“In stand-up and sketch comedy, like Legally Brown and Orange is in New Brown … everything ends in a joke. You’re only sitting in an awkward moment with the intention of breaking it and popping that bubble. But here, there’s no tension to break. You just sit in the sad or the happy [moment].

“This is the hardest thing I’ve ever done: telling a story that is worth telling and worth listening to and investing in.”

That didn’t stop him from breaking the tension on set. As we watch director Nina Buxton (Heartbreak High, Dog Park) diligently set up a scene without him, Hussain mischievously whispers about messing with the “serious actors” where he can. In one scene, where his character shares a picture of his new baby on a phone, he’s been subbing out the image to throw off his co-stars.

“Every take, it would be someone else: Jeffrey Epstein, Bill Cosby, possibly Donald Trump,” Hussain says. “When you see their faces [in the finished series] looking down at that phone – before it cuts away to a sweet baby – just know that they’re looking at Jeffrey Epstein.”

That’s the kind of provocation Hussain is known for. This is the comedian who cut his teeth confronting white Australians on the street for Salam Cafe and Legally Brown. Dressed as Uncle Sam (full name Sameer Iqbal Muhammad Salahhudeen), a caricature of perceived Muslim extremism, Hussain gleefully proposed “making Australia an Islamic state” and told angry bogans to “get out of my country” because they couldn’t pass John Howard’s English language tests for new migrants. Here, Hussain plays a different Sameer: a wayward new dad who is (rightfully) dumped by his wife in the birthing suite after the arrival of their first child. It’s a character that hews much closer to his experiences.

“The idea for this show came from becoming a dad and having this massive identity shift,” he says. “I had a bit of an existential crisis in the birthing suite, holding my [first] kid. I was overcome with all these big emotions and this feeling of responsibility. I was looking at him, thinking, ‘I’m gonna love you, I’m gonna care for you, I’m gonna teach you everything, I’m gonna provide for you … Wait, I have to provide with money I earn from jokes... What the hell have I done with my life? How did I get here? I’ve got to be funny for the next 18 years, minimum.’

“The birth of a child can really test relationships, and it brings to the surface issues that might be dormant … I remember thinking, ‘Oh no, am I going to end up like my own dad who abandoned me? Like, is that in my wiring?’”

Hussain’s eldest son was born in 2018 and the comedian separated from his wife that same year, leaving him to reckon with the prospect of single fatherhood. A year or two later and he was workshopping this TV show (he has since remarried and had three more children). It’s a process that made him reflect on his own flaws and broader family history. “This could have easily been a men’s rights activist series [if written another way],” he says, laughing.

Hussain and his two sisters were raised by their mum after his father returned to Sri Lanka when he was a child. Though the pair were in contact later in life, his father passed away from COVID-19 in 2021 – and that relationship clearly influenced the content of Separated at Birth. The theme of generational trauma looms larger than you might imagine for a half-hour comedy that co-stars Urzila Carlson and has cameos from his other comedy mates including Luke McGregor and Ryan Shelton.

“The way men have received love from their parents and their dad specifically – or how they haven’t – informs how we struggle to do that ourselves,” Hussain says of Sameer but also men more broadly. “We’re trying to figure it out as we go.

“I’ve also found that men often feel their bond with their child is secondary to a mum’s love. It is as a Muslim. We’re taught that the Prophet said, ‘You must love your mother, then your mother, then your mother, and then your father’ … The story of Sameer isn’t that ‘bumbling dad’ thing where he doesn’t know how to change diapers; it’s more of an emotional journey about identifying as a parent and carrying that responsibility properly.”

Sameer is an extreme example of that: a paramedic who we meet while ghosting his wife’s calls for three hours during active labour. (Hussain recalls someone saying this makes the character “c--tish” and he doesn’t disagree, though he’s hoping for some redemption in the back half). But the series also offers meaningful exploration of parental responsibility through its female characters.

Sameer’s ex Aaleyah (Sana’a Shaik) is going on her own journey as a resourceful but overburdened first-time mum. His mother, Husna (Nadee Kammallaweera), who raised Sameer on her own, is trying to guide her son through the crisis while finding a way to help raise her grandson. Aaleyah’s loving but wildly judgmental mum, Sadiah (Leah Vandenberg), who has a longstanding feud with Husna, is also struggling to find her place. And that’s without getting into Carlson’s character, a fiercely independent single woman who is ready to throw blows when Sameer recruits help from their local Dandenong mosque to help renovate her dilapidated new house.

“My family was me, my sisters and my mum, but our extended family was really the Muslim community,” says Hussain, who grew up in Melbourne. And since the inception of the show, he’s felt a responsibility to “maintain authorship” and “depict the community well”.

That includes everything from an initial reluctance to swear or crack jokes about Al Qaeda outside a Carlton mosque (they’re cool with it, he says, “they’re not expecting me to be a sheikh”) to accurately representing elements of Australian-Muslim life.

“I’ve worked on productions before where there are people who have no experience with the world that you’re trying to paint on screen, so then you’re not just the writer or actor, you’re also the set designer, the wardrobe assistant – you’ve got to be across everything.”

Thankfully, that wasn’t the case here. The show canvassed detail and knowledge not just from its cultural consultant, but also the diverse cast and crew – some of whom were young industry professionals taken in as part of a Screen Australia/Vic Screen attachment program. Emerging cinematographer Shaki Prasanna, for instance, ended up filming reference and stock footage for the final episode when he happened to be on holiday to Sri Lanka.

“We had people who hadn’t done these roles before because they’d never been given the opportunity,” Hussain says. “[Princess Pictures] made it a point to hire that way so that we actually got fresh blood – and the industry could change as a result of this show.”

It’s not exactly fresh blood, but Hussain is also proud of another behind-the-scenes detail: the adhan (call to prayer) in the mosque scenes is performed by Yusuf Islam (aka Cat Stevens).

How did that happen? “Muslim community stuff,” he says in disbelief. His mum held the famous singer-songwriter in a “hostage situation” calling Hussain on FaceTime after bumping into him at a function.

“He said yes without really even knowing what the show was about,” Hussain says, laughing. “I hope we’ve done him proud.”

That story won’t surprise anyone who knows Hussain’s mother from his stand-up. This is the same woman storied to have hauled then-premier Jeff Kennett into her kids’ school principal’s office to put a stop to racist bullying.

“Single mums have a resilience about them,” Hussain says. “I could always identify children of single mums or parents because there’s a particular way they viewed life. They had a little more gratitude. They don’t sweat the small stuff as much. Everyone’s carrying a little bit more responsibility on their shoulders.

“I feel like [my kids] have missed out on a lot of that because they’ve got comfort,” he says, laughing. “I hope they don’t end up doing what I do … resolving their trauma via the arts. I hope they get their validation from their dad.”

Separated at Birth premieres at 8.30pm, November 11 on the ABC and ABC iview.

Poundland owner extracted millions when chain was on ‘knife-edge’, MPs say

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:10:26 GMT

Retailer’s management to seek two-week extension of legal protection from creditors in high court

MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal.

The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning.

The budget chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, is under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers. Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.

The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until Thursday morning while a solution to its problems is sought.

Directors of Poundland are now seeking a further 10 working days’ grace, which must be approved by the high court. That comes after Gordon Brothers, which is understood to be supportive of the extension, released £10m more in funds to help Poundland secure new stock and keep trading.

Without the legal protection in place, Poundland is likely to have to call in administrators; the advisory firm Alix Partners is already lined up.

The European head of Gordon Brothers, Mark Newton-Jones, gave evidence in private for almost two hours to the Commons business select committee on Wednesday afternoon after MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the committee, said that after questioning Newton-Jones he was “deeply concerned that Gordon Brothers’ behaviour may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets”. He said: “Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a ‘knife-edge’. “Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there’s concerning signs it’s been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run-up to Christmas. “Worse, Gordon Brothers refused to say it will prioritise saving jobs over and above its own financial returns.”

The committee separately heard from Poundland’s management team, led by Barry Williams, who had been fighting to save the business.

Sources said Poundland continued to trade well, with sales up year on year, despite its problems, but it has only enough cash to support the business for a short period. Gordon Brothers has said Poundland remains “challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading”.

Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with three potential bidders for the entire chain but has indicated it can raise more from a break-up of Poundland, selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers.

The bids are understood to be worth less than the £30m in debts taken on by shareholders when Gordon Brothers bought the chain. It bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025.

Pepco still holds £7.5m of the £30m shareholder debt. It is prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business.

Gordon Brothers is still in talks with Martin Property Group, the Northern Irish family-owned firm supporting a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which includes the Dealz chain in Ireland.

Martin Property Group’s first bid had been rejected by Gordon Brothers as it amounted to no more than half the £30m it wants for Poundland with less than £7m up front.

A little-known finance company, Xyra Group, is thought to have offered about £12m up front and close to £30m in total. However, Xyra has not been involved with retail businesses previously.

Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

British soldier charged with rape of army servicewoman in Cyprus

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:06:48 GMT

L/Cpl Nicholas Horne, from 4th Battalion of Royal Regiment of Scotland, charged with one count of rape on 23 October

A British soldier has been charged with the alleged rape of a UK army servicewoman in Cyprus.

L/Cpl Nicholas Horne, who serves in the 4th Battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland, also known as The Highlanders, was charged with one count of rape on 23 October, the Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) said.

He was arrested on 19 October, two days after the DSCC was informed of the reported rape of a woman serving in British Forces Cyprus.

Horne was remanded in custody pending a court-martial hearing.

The charge comes after an investigation of the DSCC’s major crime team, conducted with service police partners.

A British army spokesperson said: “We can confirm that L/Cpl Nicholas Horne was charged with one count of rape on 23 October 2026, following an investigation by the Defence Serious Crime Command.

“We recognise the great courage it takes to come forward and report an offence. Anyone convicted of a sexual offence will be discharged from the service”

The DSCC, which investigates serious crime committed by military personnel, said anyone affected by sexual offences in the armed forces is encouraged to contact them.

The Ministry of Defence has stepped up efforts to tackle sexual violence and sexual misconduct in recent years.

Last year it announced specialist teams would be deployed at UK military locations in the UK and overseas. The move came after the MoD’s first official survey of sexual harassment across the armed forces found nearly one in 10 women serving full-time in the British military had been subjected to an assault or other non-consensual sexual activity in the previous year.
