England return to site of Ashes angst but Australia gaze stuck on sandpaper

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:00:03 GMT

White-ball tour begins in Perth on Friday but there is only one story in Australian cricket and the tourists are not it

It feels like five minutes since England were last in pristine Perth, preparing – or rather under-preparing – to win back the Ashes, only for their glass jaw to be shattered by the flashing blade of Travis Head and a two-day defeat at Optus Stadium. But 12 months on, the mood is much changed.

Beyond the fact this is merely a white-ball tour – three one-day internationals starting on Friday, followed by five Twenty20s – England’s main character energy has seemingly evaporated. Brendon McCullum is still the head coach in limited-overs cricket but no one is talking about “Bazball” or trying to sell it as some kind of sequel.

Even the West Australian newspaper has struggled to muster the same enthusiasm that had Ben Stokes dubbed a “Cocky Complainer” and Joe Root simply “Average Joe”. Jofra Archer did make its back page this week with a line about the “Poms’ daunting Perth task” – not that the reasons why were explored inside.

The fact is, there is only one story in Australian cricket right now and England are very much not it. To be honest, thanks to Usman Khawaja’s freshly published autobiography Sabr – chiefly the 22 pages that reignited the 2018 sandpaper scandal – Harry Brook’s side are barely second billing.

Aiding this on Wednesday was the decision to put Root up for media duties. Now Root is a star name, clearly, and set to play his 200th ODI this week. But he is also adept at playing the straightest of straight bats. Even when asked about the 2017-18 Ashes tour he captained – a tour that Khawaja has now said featured the hosts ball-tampering – Root calmly replied, “I don’t want to speculate,” before moving on to the cricket ahead.

The only time Root briefly engaged with the hottest of reheated topics was when asked about a common refrain in these parts – a refrain used by Khawaja among others – that every team was doing the same before Australia’s Cape Town comeuppance. “I can only speak from my own experiences,” said Root, with a shrug. “That’s not how I feel.”

But then there is no real imperative for England to wade in when they can simply watch opponents stew in their own juice. Their task is simple: to further the 50-over education of a largely inexperienced side before next year’s World Cup and get back to winning ways after a poor tri-series campaign in Pakistan.

Albeit slightly galling on one level, another difference to a year ago is the fact that England have tuned up with a proper tour match at the Waca. Their backroom staff is no longer deliberately threadbare either, with Kevin Pietersen among a raft of coaches that also features two dog-stick specialists hired from Kolkata Knight Riders.

How long sandpaper will continue to dominate the headlines is anyone’s guess. Cricket Australia has already ruled out reopening an investigation that looked rushed eight years ago and has been confirmed as hugely flawed since. But, even if this holds, the subject feels unlikely to go away any time soon.

Because for all that Khawaja has faced a backlash – some of it nasty and a fair bit misplaced, not least the notion that his wide-ranging book is just a cash grab – he has filled some gaps in the original story and exposed others. While plenty would sooner the topic went away, an appetite for the truth remains. And not least for David Warner, it seems, among the trio slapped with absurdly long bans.

People here also seem very keen to hear from Pat Cummins as the Test captain, despite the fact that he and his fellow quicks Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood are being rested for this series. (As a point of order, the sardine tin schedule is to blame, rather than some cynical move to whip them out of the firing line)

Starc has already spoken this week, in fact, even if his doubling down on the joint statement the bowlers issued in 2021 feels like an increasingly semantic position. Whether Cummins takes the same path, given Khawaja has alleged the use of the sandpaper earlier on that fateful tour, remains to be seen.

Although even as the latest catalyst, Khawaja has already shown how devilishly tricky this whole topic is to navigate, having endured an awkward interview on the ABC’s 7.30 programme on Tuesday night in which he was grilled like a politician and became evasive. (Quite why he’d name names on air, having not done so in print, is another matter)

In that sense Root’s approach was wise, while overall his media conference was another example of how times have changed. Whereas his lack of a Test century on Australian soil was a regular talking point before last year’s Ashes – until he finally ticked that box – no one thought to ask about the fact he is yet to do the same in one-day cricket.

“I don’t think it will ever leave me,” Kane said, when asked whether he continued to have points to prove. “It’s probably part of what makes me push myself to the limits that I do because in football, you’ve never completed it. Kane has been doubted at ­numerous points of his career, ­starting when he was released by Arsenal as an eight-year-old. He had difficult loans from Tottenham to Norwich and Leicester in 2012‑13 and there were the one‑season‑wonder jibes after his breakthrough campaign for Spurs and England in 2014-15.

Kane has been ridiculed for ­setting lofty targets: such as in 2017, when he said he wanted to replicate the numbers of Lionel Messi and ­Cristiano Ronaldo; when he stated his ambition to win the 2018 World Cup Golden Boot. Or when he stood on the verge of his 100th England cap in September 2024 with 66 goals and said he wanted to score 100. There were questions about his place in the team after Euro 2024 when his performances were underwhelming and he was substituted in the final. Every time, he answered back.

“It’s just my mindset,” Kane said. “Because I’ve had to prove people wrong my whole career. From early academy days proving coaches wrong, proving scouts wrong – it has just been instilled in me. If someone tells me I can’t do something it motivates me more to do it.

‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:52:08 GMT

Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms

Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.

Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.

She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.

“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.

“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.

“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”

The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.

António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.

“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”

Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”

Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.

Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.

In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”

Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.

The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.

Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.

Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history, there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.

“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”

Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.

Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”

Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”

Mohammadi said on his Telegram channel that the Americans had proposed a timeframe of about two weeks after which Donald Trump would make a decision on military action. For now, Trump has settled on a strategy of suffocating Iran through economic pressure and tightening the blockade on its oil exports while facilitating those of other Gulf states through Hormuz.

Mohammadi’s assessments suggest some senior Iranians fear Washington’s strategy might work by destabilising the country. The thinking goes that economic turmoil might spark street protests, potentially around the anniversary of nationwide demonstrations that began in late December last year.

On this basis, the Iranian leadership might conclude that the status quo – a “no peace, no war” impasse – was not sustainable and pre-emptive action was required.

Despite Iranian claims that their blockade of the strait is working, there is concern that Brent crude is at a relatively low $93 a barrel, while Saudi oil production is near prewar levels of 9.3m barrels a day. In an attempt to close any loopholes, Iran said it bombed a US radar post on the Omani island of Didamar three days ago.

In another development, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s national security council, said he had told Russia that Iran was not prepared for even a particle of its highly enriched stockpile of uranium to leave the country, saying it might be needed for planned nuclear-powered submarines.

Tehran has been increasingly clear that US bases in Europe will be targeted if fighting resumes. Rezaei said: “If American planes take off from a distant military base and come to this country to bomb Iran, we will also target that base. We are announcing this now so they have no excuse tomorrow.”

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, gave the impression this week that the policy of economic strangulation was sufficient and described Iran’s demands as unrealistic. However, Trump is under pressure to resolve the crisis before the Democrats take charge of Congress on 3 January.

A Reuters Ipsos poll in the US shows 71% of Americans want Congress to pass legislation to end the war in Iran. The overwhelming message from the midterm elections was that the conflict was highly unpopular but the Democrats do not have a strategy to end it and open up the strait of Hormuz. The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:31:34 GMT

PM wrote to transport commissioner to oppose ‘megashed’ in Astley shortly before he entered No 10

Andy Burnham raised safety concerns about dozens of lorries leaving a “monster” warehouse near a primary school because there was “no safe crossing” for children, a public inquiry has heard.

Concerns about the 18-metre-high “megashed” in the village of Astley, Greater Manchester, are being examined by Britain’s office of the transport commissioner.

A deputy transport commissioner, John Baker, launched an environmental public inquiry after significant local opposition to the round-the-clock operation by the logistics company Whistl.

Whistl is asking for a licence to increase its number of HGVs at the site from 40 to 50 and the number of trailers from 60 to 70.

But people living nearby told the inquiry on Wednesday that granting the licence would worsen the “catastrophic” impact on those living nearby, with some left suffering with anxiety, sleep deprivation and depression.

The inquiry also heard that shortly before he became prime minister, Burnham wrote to the transport commissioner’s office to oppose Whistl’s plans.

In the letter sent in February, which was not shown at the inquiry but has been seen by the Guardian, the then Greater Manchester mayor expressed concerns about the route taken by dozens of HGVs to access the 17-acre site near his Makerfield constituency.

Burnham said schoolchildren would be forced to share the road with huge lorries “despite there being no pedestrian crossings, no lollipop service, no traffic calming and sections where the pavement is extremely narrow or ends entirely”.

John Peters, who co-founded the Astley Warehouse Action Group, told the inquiry, at the Brick Community stadium in Wigan, that it was a recipe for disaster, adding: “I hope I never have to say I told you so.”

The Whistl warehouse, which was named Britain’s joint-worst new building this year, was approved by Wigan council in 2024 after a planning application by PLP, a firm part-owned by Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners which is run by the billionaire John Whittaker.

The outcome of the inquiry, expected in early December, is seen as a test case of how local groups could challenge similar large industrial developments across Britain.

The Labour government has relaxed planning rules to allow big logistics projects on previously protected land as the UK strives to compete in the race for AI and the growing e-commerce market, which increasingly relies on next-day deliveries.

Peters, who said he had lived in the village since 1979, was in tears as he likened Whistl’s “megashed” opening in the summer to “a plane crash-landing in that field”.

He said one year ago the only medication he took was a single statin to lower blood cholesterol levels: “I now take high blood pressure [medication], statin, anti-depression and a sleeper. That’s the state I’m in. I know in our group we’re in a truly bad state so I dread to think what would happen [if Whistl’s licence was approved].”

David Gerrard, a builder who lives opposite the site, appeared emotional as he described the effect on his wife and their three daughters.

The Guardian view on welfare reform: time to retire lazy myths and stereotypes

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:30:56 GMT

A speech by the leader of the opposition exemplifies much that is wrong with the way British politics conventionally talks about benefit claimants

There is a big difference between expenditure that is rising and a rise that is “out of control”. The amount Britain spends on social security is in the former category. Too much political rhetoric around the subject assumes that it is in the latter one.

The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts the growth in welfare spending over the next five years at 0.2%-0.5% of gross domestic product, from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032. That money might well be suboptimally deployed. There are rival demands on the state’s resources and a reasonable debate to be had about priorities at the Department for Work and Pensions. But that is not the tone of the debate routinely conducted in Westminster.

The more typical frame is the one adopted by Kemi Badenoch in a speech earlier this week. The Conservative leader characterised the benefits system as a programme of handouts that disincentivises work and encourages the exaggeration of minor physical and mental health problems by undeserving claimants. By way of a moral parable to illustrate the change in attitude that she deems necessary, Mrs Badenoch observed that “double amputees run marathons”.

A moment’s pause would have led a more thoughtful politician to reject that comparison on grounds of both logic and ethics. It makes no sense to extrapolate an argument about what should be normal from a case that is self-evidently exceptional. And it is grossly offensive to people with disabilities to imply that the main barriers to achievement of extraordinary things are an excess of benefits and a lack of motivation.

But Mrs Badenoch is not in the business of serious thought. She has a political strategy that involves casting Labour as a party that only knows how to raise taxes and welfare spending, so she can represent the opposite.

To that end, the Conservatives claim to have identified £36bn in budget cuts, all from working‑age benefits. Pensions, which account for half of all welfare spending, would not be touched. In its verdict on Mrs Badenoch’s plan, the Institute for Fiscal Studies notes that some savings are likely to be available in the areas identified, but the projected amounts are “at the more uncertain end of the spectrum”. That doesn’t stop the Tories promising to spend their hypothetical budget windfall on bolstering defence and a variety of tax cuts.

The government’s approach is more circumspect, partly from political caution. A botched welfare reform last year poisoned relations between Sir Keir Starmer and his backbenchers. But also, Andy Burnham hasn’t wanted to pre-empt the conclusions of commissioned policy reviews – one into youth unemployment, led by Alan Milburn, and another considering the future of personal independence payment, by Stephen Timms. Mr Milburn is due to report next week.

What is known about Mr Burnham’s approach is that he considers investment in skills a more reliable way to help benefit recipients back to work than peremptory withdrawal of support. But while that plausibly leads to savings in the long run, it still involves an upfront cost. How that will be funded in a way that is acceptable to his backbenchers is far from clear. The prime minister might reasonably be accused of lacking precision when it comes to welfare reform. It is a lesser failing than the flight to lazy stereotypes and unserious rhetoric perpetrated by the leader of the opposition.

The Guardian view on Maga after the midterms: doubling down on Trumpism

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:25:56 GMT

Republicans know that the president’s folly and excesses cost them the elections. That doesn’t mean they’re ready to challenge him

Shortly after polls closed last Tuesday, with the scale of the Republican trouncing in the midterms still becoming apparent, Donald Trump briefly adopted an oddly conciliatory tone. He declared that he was “absolutely” willing to accept the results, would look forward to working with Democrats and that deportation policies might have been “too tough”.

It was never going to last. He soon cast doubt on the elections’ legitimacy. On Friday, he replaced his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with her deputy, Stephen Miller – a white nationalist, or “stone-cold racist”, in the words of Hakeem Jeffries, likely to be the next House speaker. Ms Wiles executed the president’s decisions faithfully, but was seen as a somewhat calming if not restraining influence, which may help explain her departure.

Every high-profile woman in the administration has now quit or been ousted, and its machismo has increased. Mr Miller is an ideological extremist and attack dog who has spearheaded the expansion of executive power as well as the draconian immigration excesses that alienated many (particularly Latino) voters. He reportedly wants to wind down the war on Iran, but played a leading role in strikes against alleged drugs boats in the Caribbean – extrajudicial killings.

Happily for Mr Trump, the reshuffle has turned discussion away from lame ducks and the Republican succession. He does not need the mixed martial arts supremo Dana White as his press secretary; he has enough brawlers. On Tuesday, House Republicans picked another aggressive hardliner, Jim Jordan, as minority leader. He has pledged to fight investigations by the new Democratic majority. On the same day, they blocked the attempted impeachment of Pete Hegseth, the self-styled “secretary of war” (with some Democrats also missing the vote). The outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie was pressing the case against him over the Iran war and attacks on drugs boats. Mr Hegseth is manifestly unfit for office. He has shared highly sensitive information on a messaging app and wanted to live stream a military execution. But a case against him might embarrass Mr Trump.

Some still hope that Republicans will have little choice but to hold Mr Trump accountable for last week’s defeat. JD Vance sought to distance himself by criticising the Iran war, and Ron DeSantis declared that there was “no question” that the results were a rebuke of Mr Trump. But GOP politicians either want more Trumpism, or are extremely wary of taking him on, after he torched previous critics. Trump voters are split between the Maga base, which wants to double down (and who turned out last Tuesday) and the rest who want to moderate (and stayed home) – with divisions on everything from datacentres to deportations. The Republicans can’t win in 2028 with Maga votes alone. Yet the GOP regained power in 2016 by becoming more extreme.

The Democrats now have their own challenge. They must use their new congressional power to ensure accountability – including pinning corruption in Mr Trump’s circle to the cost of living crisis – while also trying to deliver for voters who need real improvements in their lives. Republicans will seek to tie them up in fruitless congressional battles.

The Trumpist message is so clear that the outgoing speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, even said it out loud: “The voters made the wrong choice.” The Republicans are promising the electorate more of what they didn’t want. The people have spoken, but the president – and his party – won’t listen.

Richard Lloyd obituary

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:15:29 GMT

American guitarist and songwriter who was a founding member of the punk band Television

When the New York band Television released their debut album Marquee Moon in February 1977, it provoked euphoria among critics, even if they were not quite sure how to describe it – punk, art-rock, new wave, post-punk, progressive or just rock were all terms flung in its direction.

It would frequently be described as an “influence” on countless acts who came after them, but Television’s music was too rare and sophisticated to be easily imitated, made as it was by a unique blend of musical personalities and instrumental skills.

Above all, it was the extraordinary twin-guitar interplay between the band’s frontman, Tom Verlaine, and Richard Lloyd, who has died aged 75 of cancer, that gave the band its inimitable character, along with a collection of songs that seemed both familiar yet mysteriously alien. It was rock’n’roll, but not as we know it.

Nonetheless, it could claim some familiar historical roots. Lloyd would recall how he had been inspired by seeing the Rolling Stones on TV’s Ed Sullivan Show, and the Stones remained a subliminal influence on Television.

“When the band was first formed I was a lead player, and it took a great deal of coaxing from Tom [Verlaine] to get me to play rhythm at all. He’d say stuff like, ‘Well, look at the Stones – Keith [Richards] just plays rhythm, and he’s the backbone of it, and there has to be a backbone.’” Learning how to integrate their contrasting guitar styles and musical roles effortlessly was key to the Lloyd-Verlaine partnership, illustrated perfectly in the title track of Marquee Moon.

The album failed to reach the US Billboard 200 chart, though it peaked at 28 in the UK. But its reputation has far outstripped its initial commercial performance, and it has subsequently appeared in countless “greatest albums of all time” lists.

Television’s second album, Adventure, appeared in 1978, and made the UK Top 10, though still failed to register on the US chart. It was a perfectly decent effort judged by normal standards, but Marquee Moon was the kind of lightning that could not strike twice. The group subsequently disbanded and Lloyd battled a heroin addiction that he eventually overcame in 1984.

In his memoir Everything Is Combustible (2018), the Pittsburgh-born Lloyd revealed that he was the son of John Alt and his wife, Virginia (nee Ewing). John made a living selling wristwatches in a strip club, while Virginia was a “soda jerk”, serving drinks in a restaurant. His parents separated when Richard was young, and Virginia moved to New York with her son. When his mother remarried, Richard adopted the surname of his stepfather, David Lloyd.

He would recall how he first became fascinated with the guitar aged seven. Attending a sleepover at a cousin’s house, he picked one up for the first time, and was so absorbed by the instrument that he shut himself in the bathroom and spent all night experimenting with it. In his teens he dabbled with playing the drums, before experiencing an epiphany-like moment when “an inner voice said, ‘You need to play a melody instrument.’ This was when I switched to electric guitar.”

Soon afterwards, he became good friends with a young musician named Velvert Turner, who was taking guitar lessons with Jimi Hendrix. He would teach Lloyd some of the technical tricks he had learned from Hendrix, and Lloyd met Hendrix a couple of times. When Led Zeppelin were in New York, Lloyd picked up further tips from Jimmy Page’s guitar technician. He expanded his musical education further by seeing concerts by leading bands of the era including the Doors, the Allman Brothers and the Grateful Dead, and he attended the 1969 Woodstock festival in upstate New York.

Determined to become a professional guitarist, he paid less attention to academic achievements, leaving Stuyvesant high school before graduation, then doing the same again at a school in New Jersey after his parents had moved there. Then, as he told ZigZag magazine in 1978, “I went to Boston, I went to Los Angeles, I did the usual sort of vagabond 20-year-old trip around America, and got to New York where I played guitar.”

He initially played a sunburst-coloured Fender Telecaster guitar, then subsequently settled on the Fender Stratocaster as his favoured instrument, the one that he would play on Marquee Moon and subsequently throughout his solo career. As he explained to Guitar Player magazine: “A Strat asks you to play a certain way; it demands a certain grasp. It’s just the way the neck is shaped, I guess. That kind of neck is really conducive to a certain kind of string-bending that you can’t get on most guitars.”

Lloyd had been lured back to the Big Apple by a developing new music scene featuring groups including the New York Dolls and Suicide. He met Tom Verlaine (real name Thomas Miller) and Richard Hell (originally Richard Meyers), who were in a band called the Neon Boys with the drummer Billy Ficca; they invited Lloyd to join and in 1973 the band became Television, achieving its definitive lineup when Hell was replaced on bass by Fred Smith (formerly with Blondie) in 1975.

Regular gigs at CBGB, a club that had previously only hosted bands playing in the country, bluegrass and blues styles that had given it its name, helped to build the band – and the venue – a cult following.

They released the single Little Johnny Jewel in 1975, on their own Ork Records label (named after Terry Ork, who had managed the group and helped support them financially in their early days). Then, after flirtations with Island Records, for whom they recorded demos with the producer Brian Eno, and Arista, Television were signed to Elektra Records in 1976.

After Television, Lloyd pursued a solo career that saw him release nine albums, from Alchemy (1979) to The Countdown (2108). He participated in Television’s reunions in 1992 (which produced their third album, Television) and 2001, but opted out of the 2007 tour marking the 30th anniversary of Marquee Moon.

He also featured as a session musician on albums by Matthew Sweet and John Doe (from the band X), and produced recordings by artists including Rocket from the Tombs and Jim Neversink.

He is survived by his wife, Sheila (nee O’Keefe), his son, Dylan, and brother, Eric.

Richard Lloyd, musician and songwriter, born 25 October 1951; died 7 November 2026

Deep-pocketed windfarm developers shouldn’t need a £1bn state loan

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:15:26 GMT

National wealth fund is to lend £1bn towards the Vanguard projects – but whether the private equity giant needed help is debatable

“This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain,” declared the prime minister.

Andy Burnham is obviously correct that the two Vanguard windfarms off the coast of Norfolk are huge investments. Together, they require almost £13bn of debt financing. But he can’t claim they represent a fresh expression of confidence. The project has been on the runway since the German utility RWE, the developer, was awarded a contract to build the windfarms in January’s renewables auction.

Instead, the new news on Wednesday was how the project will be financed, which is where the story becomes interesting. On the equity front, RWE said it had sold a 50% share in the Vanguard schemes to KKR, the giant US private equity and infrastructure investor. On the debt side, £12.8bn has come from “a consortium of 35 international banks”, including £1bn from the UK’s own national wealth fund (NWF).

It is fair enough, one might say, for the NWF to get involved – directing capital to energy transition projects is, in part, what it was set up to do. But here’s another key aspect of its role: the state-backed body is not meant to be a substitute for private capital; instead, its funding is supposed to be “additional”, in the terminology, to ensure infrastructure is built that might not otherwise be.

Here is how the NWF describes the process: “For each investment we are considering, we test and assess the extent to which impact would not have materialised without us, so we are confident we are delivering financial and non-financial value that would not otherwise be achieved.”

So how does that work with the Vanguard windfarms? Would they have been scrapped if the NWF had not chipped in its £1bn? That seems highly unlikely.

Consider that RWE is one of Europe’s biggest electricity generators and that KKR is a giant among private equity houses. These rich firms are experienced at raising capital. Consider, too, that the main way in which offshore wind projects are de-risked for developers is the auction process that sets a guaranteed inflation-linked price for their electricity for 20 years. In this case, the price is £91.20 a megawatt hour (in 2024 money), or high by historic standards.

If the cost of borrowing has risen post-auction – and it has – that’s unfortunate for RWE and KKR. They might have to pay a bit more for their debt, or pony up more equity, both of which would depress their returns. But that is an everyday risk of commercial life. Why did the NWF, having stayed away from fixed offshore wind until now, think it had to join a lending syndicate on a project where it is a stretch to think its contribution was the make-or-break element?

The NWF’s argument is that its involvement “widens the pool of capital available to offshore wind developers and helps to meet unprecedented liquidity requirements after the success of AR7 [the last auction round]”. In other words, the sector will need so much capital over coming years that the state-backed lender needs to be on standby.

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

It’s a defence, but it will sound very appealing from the point of view of developers. They can bid for an index-linked contract that guarantees revenues for 20 years; then, if borrowing conditions are tight, they are invited to think that the state will lend a hand to try to ease funding pressures. No wonder KKR wanted in. The NWF, note, says it is lending at market rates. Even so, its definition of how it adds “additional” value seems to have become very stretched.

Many of the NWF’s other big loans, such as billions for Sizewell C and £599m for Rolls-Royce’s development of small modular reactors, are far easier to understand. Those projects genuinely might not have happened without state backing. The same applies to the myriad of its smaller investments in battery technology and so forth.

Offshore wind generation, by contrast, is an established market with an effective mechanism – the contract-for-difference – for incentivising developers. The NWF’s pot of capital is not bottomless. Better targets for loans right now might be anything to do with electrification, meaning the take-up of heat pumps and electric vehicles, or storage solutions. As half the energy world is pointing out, it is where the big decarbonisation gains are available.

A bit of state activism to accelerate energy transition is a good thing, many of us would say. But, as argued here previously, more scrutiny of that “additionality” principle is overdue. There is little point replicating what the private sector would do anyway. When a huge private equity firm, KKR, is getting a helping hand because funding conditions are a bit rough, it is fair to ask if the state is achieving the best bang for its finite buck.

Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends?

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:57:16 GMT

After Peta’s call ‘to reject mischaracterisations of chickens’, I wonder what they would make of Polish representations of polecats and Croatian cuckoos

Chickens don’t have it easy. On top of living largely crap, short lives, they endure the ignominy of collectively being a byword for cowardice. The campaign group People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) has written to the Oxford English Dictionary asking for this definition of “chicken” to be changed. Naturally enough, there are those who have been unafraid to holler “Woke nonsense!” as loud as cocks crowing.

For my part, I think Peta is right to stick up for chickens, but I’m not sure removing a definition – assuming definition-removal is a thing – would make any difference. Chicken, in this sense, is in common use as an adjective, a verb and a noun. It’s got deep roots that are going to take some shifting. And any such move could open up a right can of worms (sorry, worms). What about the vulture, rat, shark and sloth lobbies? Not to mention pigs, snakes, weasels, donkeys, sheep, dogs, parrots and all manner of creatures with whom we share this beleaguered planet.

Poor chickens, though. Who knows how they earned this label? They don’t seem particularly cowardly to me. And if they do seem a bit skittish at times, who can blame them, given that they’re at risk of mortal harm from man, fox and others?

If it’s any consolation to chickens, other languages don’t disrespect their courage to quite such an extent. The Spanish at least say hen rather than chicken, and the French, too, although in France to signify cowardice the poor hen needs to have been out in the rain – poule mouillée being a wet hen.

Elsewhere, Russians, Germans, Italians and Turks use hares and rabbits in this way. With other languages it gets more interesting. A Punjabi-speaking friend tells me she has heard jackals’ bravery called into question. Interesting. I’ve always thought of jackals being more on the front foot, as it were – somewhat fierce and snarly. Apparently, in Punjabi folklore, the jackal is the ultimate symbol of fear and timidity, routinely contrasted with the fearless lion or tiger. I’ll fortify myself with that thought next time I go nose to nose with a jackal. I’ll roar like a lion, so I will, and he, indeed a whole pack of them, will surely shrink away with a whimper.

In Polish the story gets even more fascinating. Here it’s tchórz, the polecat, but in this case the belief in the polecat’s cowardice is so deeply held that the word for coward is actually polecat. Again, I must say I didn’t have polecats down as particularly yellow-bellied. (Yellow-bellied!? What’s that all about? Let’s not go there.) This may be because I have in mind Michael Foot’s characterisation of Norman Tebbit as “a semi-house-trained polecat”. The Poles’ view of polecats references the animals’ defensive behaviour if frightened or cornered. At such times they release a foul smell from their anal glands. Depending on your politics, this may or may not be considered unfair on the late Lord Tebbit. The one time I met him, by the way, he was less polecat than pussy cat – until the microphone came on, at which point the polecat in him woke up and the pussy cat was absent until the interview concluded.

In a similar vein, the Welsh have put a couple of words together to make their word for coward: shit and dog, cachgi, invoking perhaps the image of a dog soiling itself in fright. Seems a bit harsh on the coward as well as the dog, to my mind, but each to their own.

I was deep in this rabbit hole (nice to use rabbit there non-pejoratively) before I thought to investigate the language closest to me after English. In Croatian, Serbian and Macedonian, the word for cuckoo – kukavica – is also the word for coward. My mum’s been calling me a kukavica all my life, in a whole variety of contexts. I’d always taken it as a term of endearment more than anything else. Now I know otherwise. I’m just a coward, plain and simple. Still, I’d rather be a cuckoo than a polecat.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Hoax bomb threats made to schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and Italy

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:47:14 GMT

Police assure parents and teachers there is no danger as thousands of schools in Italy and hundreds in the UK affected

Hundreds of schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland were hit by a fresh wave of hoax bomb threats on Wednesday, with some sites evacuated as a precaution.

Police in Scotland said that about 1,000 schools, from Dumfries in the south of Scotland to Aberdeenshire and Orkney in the north, had received the hoax warnings. At least 300 schools were affected in Northern Ireland. Similar claims were sent in a “generic communication” to schools in the Republic of Ireland.

Officials were quick to reassure schools and parents that the threats were bogus, and similar to hoax threats made last month. Earlier on Wednesday, the police had estimated that at least 470 schools were affected in Scotland.

In Italy, an email containing a hoax bomb threat was sent to about 6,000 schools, the education ministry said on Wednesday. Hundreds of schools were reported to have been evacuated.

The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that, based on checks carried out so far, “no element has emerged that would suggest there is a concrete danger”.

Meloni wrote on Facebook: “The reports instead appear to be linked to a strategy aimed at generating alarm and concern, which is currently the subject of all the necessary in-depth investigations.”

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “Our inquiries have established that there is nothing to suggest that they represent a credible threat or that there is any wider threat to the public.

“We understand how distressing messages of this nature can be for pupils, parents, carers and school staff, and the concern they can understandably cause. Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails. They have been sent widely to distribution lists across the UK and Northern Ireland and our assessment remains that they do not represent a credible threat.”

Police Scotland’s cyber and fraud unit is liaising with security and law enforcement bodies in the UK and overseas to try to find who was responsible.

Northern Ireland’s education minister, Paul Givan, said last month’s hoaxes appeared to be “Islamist” and were signed “Allahu Akbar” – Arabic for “God is greater”. However, there was no public confirmation the threats were Islamist in origin.

Schools in Scotland were told to readmit any pupils who had been evacuated and to resume classes. Dumfries and Galloway council confirmed children had been sent home after a majority of schools received messages. Highland council confirmed some of its schools “made the decision to activate their emergency protocols”.

Glasgow council advised parents by email that the claims of devices planted in schools were false, saying: “Our police colleagues have confirmed that this is a hoax and that schools should not be evacuated.”

In Edinburgh, a council spokesperson confirmed schools were “briefly evacuated as a precaution this morning, following receipt of threatening messages”. They added: “[We] understand the impact this can have on families and want to reassure parents and carers that our schools are safe, and there is no need to remove your child.”

In Northern Ireland, education officials advised schools to remain open “unless otherwise advised” by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI).

“We hope that full light will quickly be shed on the origin of these threats and that those responsible will be identified.”

Former NFL coach Rex Ryan charged after allegedly hitting pedestrians with car in Nashville

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:35:54 GMT

Former Jets and Bills coach turned himself in

Ryan faces six misdemeanor charges over incident

Two pedestrians allegedly struck in Nashville

ESPN analyst and former NFL coach Rex Ryan turned himself in to police on Wednesday after allegedly hitting two pedestrians with his car in Nashville and leaving the scene.

Nashville police said on Wednesday that the pedestrians had the right of way while crossing a main street in the city’s downtown last week when Ryan allegedly turned at a red light and drove over their feet.

Ryan was charged with two counts of leaving the scene of an accident, two counts of failing to provide information or render aid and two counts of failing to obey a traffic control signal, according to court records. All six charges are misdemeanors.

Ryan is scheduled to appear in court next month.

Ryan, 63, served as head coach of the New York Jets from 2009 to 2014 and the Buffalo Bills from 2015 to 2016. He led the Jets to consecutive AFC championship games following the 2009 and 2010 seasons.

His father, the late Buddy Ryan, was a celebrated NFL coach who served as defensive coordinator of the 1985 Chicago Bears, whose defense is widely regarded as one of the greatest in league history.

Since leaving coaching, Ryan – who is know for his exuberant personality – has worked as an NFL analyst for ESPN, including on the network’s pregame coverage.

Why does Pete Hegseth call himself secretary of war? ‘Dopey but dangerous’ wouldn’t fit on a badge

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:35:20 GMT

He has survived blame for the US midterms disaster and dodged an impeachment vote, but it will be one battle after another now – and he can’t win them all

Like the brief, wondrous cycle of the mayfly, we may come to look back on the career of Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defence who cheekily rebranded himself secretary of war, as the defining appointment of the Trump era: that is, one in which extraordinary power was handed to a man of cartoonish inappropriateness and which, despite this week’s shelved attempt to impeach him, may still turn out to have been luminously short-lived. In January, the Democrats will assume a majority in both chambers and are likely to have another crack at impeaching Hegseth. In the meantime, we can only look on and wonder at his meaning.

It is quite something, in the context of Trump cabinet appointments that have included Robert F Kennedy Jr and Kristi Noem, to be the most glaringly underqualified person in the West Wing, but since being sworn in almost two years ago, Hegseth has comfortably seen off any rivals to his crown. This week, eight articles of impeachment, or “high crimes and misdemeanours” as the official rubric has it, were levied against him by Thomas Massie, an outgoing Republican congressman from Kentucky, who accused Hegseth of illegal acts including violating the constitution by conducting an unauthorised war with Iran and effecting regime change in Venezuela.

Republicans narrowly saw off the proceedings and, somewhat to the surprise of observers, joined the president in rallying energetically to Hegseth’s defence. This, too, may not last; in the wake of the Republicans’ shellacking in the midterms, speculation as to who would take the fall for Trump’s losses focused on Hegseth, after JD Vance pointed to the Iran war as a root cause of the losses. But perhaps this underestimates Hegseth’s appeal to the president. If Greg Bovino, the former US immigration chief who quit after two people were killed by agents under his command, looked like a textbook psycho in the manner of Sean Penn’s Col Steven J Lockjaw – the screw-loose character from the movie One Battle After Another – Hegseth is a different beast entirely; a Mr Incredible-like figure whose persona is so ridiculous, so dopey, as to distract from his dangerousness.

Such a manoeuvre is, of course, in line both with Trump’s own highly developed ability to marry deadly threat levels with the affect of a buffoon, and a more general tradition in the US of men of war who operate with the affability of the Pillsbury Doughboy. Cast your minds back to Gen “Stormin’” Norman Schwarzkopf, a man shaped like a freestanding wardrobe, who led coalition forces in the first Gulf war, or Colin Powell, his senior at the time who, as chairman of the joint chiefs of staff and despite leading the most powerful military in the world, appeared at briefings with the casual ease and likability of a lounge singer.

Compare this with the way we do things in Britain, where, generally speaking, we like our military men to be slight of form, quiet of voice, thin of moustache and ruthless of execution. As a platonic ideal, if military officers in the US take the shape of comfy old Tom Hanks in Saving Private Ryan, in Britain we’re more partial to Trevor Howard in The Third Man, all twinkly eyes and icy veins, or the unyielding Alec Guinness in The Bridge on the River Kwai, a man who, beneath his quivering, rule-following exterior, is as pitiless as rain and as mad as a snake. Both represent sleights of hand, to some degree. Take your pick.

Hegseth, of course, never led the US army. While serving in the military, he rose to the middling rank of major (it was his service on Fox & Friends that, in all likelihood, made him a four-star general in Trump’s eyes). And US defence secretaries aren’t themselves expected to be especially martial; let’s enjoy a quick drive-by on the memory of Dick Cheney, secretary of defence under George H W Bush, accidentally shooting his own hunting buddy in the face during a quail hunting trip in southern Texas.

But Hegseth looks the part, not just of the genial American warrior, but of the very specific ideal favoured by Trump in which the quiff-wearing, square jaw-rocking secretary of defence embodies the 1950s aesthetic for which the president pines. If Democrats manage to impeach and oust him next year, he may linger in our minds, against stiff competition, as the most hollow, disastrous and surreal piece of casting in Trump’s cabinet of misfits and rogues.

Bridget Phillipson: Kemi Badenoch has ‘no interest in supporting LGBT+ people’

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:26:50 GMT

Exclusive: Equalities minister accuses Tories of ‘chasing Reform into the gutter’ as they drop support for planned law to ban conversion practices

Kemi Badenoch has “no interest in supporting LGBT+ people” or promoting tolerance more widely, a government minister has said, after the Conservatives dropped support for a planned law to ban conversion practices.

The comments by Bridget Phillipson, the equalities minister, come after the Tories removed their previous backing for a law targeting abusive practices that aim to change someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity.

Badenoch’s party say this is because of concerns about the scope of the bill, particularly the way it deals with gender identity.

The draft conversion practices bill, which was published in June and is now open for consultation, sets out potential jail sentences of up to five years for attempts to change someone’s sexuality or gender identity, which are abusive and cause serious harm.

Asked about the bill last week, Badenoch said it would “mean that parents start getting arrested for parenting their children”, agreeing with a question by a journalist who said this could happen if parents refuse to let their child identify as a cat.

Government officials argue that this is not possible, given that the bill sets a high threshold for an offence, involving both abuse and serious harm as well as an attempt to change the person’s sexual orientation or gender identity.

As equalities minister under previous Conservative governments, Badenoch supported the idea of a legal ban on conversion practices, saying in 2021 that she wanted to give people “the freedom to live their life as they see fit without fear or intimidation”.

Phillipson said: “This government is clear: we should live in a society that is tolerant, and that allows people to be their true selves without living in fear. That is the modern Britain I know.

“For almost a decade, there has been political consensus and there has been international consensus that abusing someone to try and change their sexuality should be illegal.

“Until now, that consensus has included Kemi Badenoch and much of the Conservative frontbench, who we now see pledged their support loudly and clearly.

“In chasing Reform into the gutter, Badenoch’s Conservatives have shown their true colours: no interest in supporting LGBT+ people, no interest in calling out abuse of LGBT+ people, and no interest in a tolerant, modern Britain.”

Many of the Conservative objections to the bill were set out in a report by the Policy Exchange thinktank last week, including the idea that protections in the bill for people with non-binary identities could end up being so broad as to include those who are “catgender”, meaning they identify as cats.

Russell Brand’s trial, rape myths and a questionable faith

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:26:36 GMT

Readers respond to reporting on the disgraced actor and comedian’s trial and conviction for rape and sexual assault

You report that in the wake of Russell Brand’s trial, the government pledged “to examine calls to crack down on ‘rape myths’ in trials” (Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women, 6 November). This is not the first time the treatment of women in trials for rape, and the perpetuation of rape myths, has been drawn to the attention of a Labour government.

Sue Lees (1941-2002), a former colleague from the Polytechnic/University of North London conducted research into the reporting of rape in the media and how it was treated within the English legal system in the 1990s.

Sue’s research clearly identified how the legal system systematically enabled rapists to escape justice, while both the judiciary and the media regularly stereotyped women as sexually provocative. Following publication of her book Carnal Knowledge: Rape on Trial in 1996, Sue helped influence members of the 1997 New Labour government to effect change to the legal process by limiting the evidence on a woman’s sexual history in rape trials.

In the 2002 updated edition of Carnal Knowledge, Sue highlighted the continuing problems in our adversarial system. Citing reforms in other countries, she argued the case for further radical reforms to reverse the imbalances of the judicial process and to create a system that would provide justice for victims without jeopardising the rights of defendants.

How disappointing, therefore, over two decades later, to read of the current Labour government’s ambitions to make changes to rape trials so that they “do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court”, as Andy Burnham put it, speaking to Times Radio. What has happened in the intervening years, given the amount of research evidence already available? Where does the blame lie for the continuation of such injustices, misrepresentations and myths? Judy Evans Brighton, East Sussex

Like Lucy Powell MP, we found the rape myths and stereotypes deployed by the defence during Russell Brand’s trial depressing – but sadly not shocking (Police receive further criminal allegations against Russell Brand, 10 November). To think the courts had “long gone past that sort of culture” is wishful thinking at best.

Our research and frontline experience show that rape myths and stereotypes are used in courtrooms across England and Wales, day in, day out – a systemic failing which compounds the trauma for those victim-survivors of sexual violence who have already navigated the difficult journey to trial.

The survivors who courageously came forward in this case had already endured sexual violence. For the defence to then subject them to attempts to blame, shame and discredit them is disgraceful. It also reinforces and amplifies these harmful beliefs in wider society – something that specialist support services like ours have been pushing against for decades.

Words of condemnation aren’t enough. This case must now be a catalyst for meaningful action, so that no other victim-survivor is subjected to this treatment in future. Katie Kempen Chief executive, Victim Support

It is right to question Russell Brand’s Christian faith (‘He’s manipulating its power’: why did Russell Brand convert to Christianity?, 6 November). Conversion is meant to be a renewing of heart, mind and soul. In Brand’s case, the public baptism he sought might have been accompanied by public repentance and a stated intention to make amends or restitution to the women he harmed and whose distress he saw. Perhaps prison will lead him to genuine conversion. Susanna Gridley London

This Christian forgiveness undoubtedly comes from Russell Brand’s participation in the 12-step programme – heavily rooted in Christian terminology, although with its own big book.

My own experience of 15 months in Alcoholics Anonymous and Cocaine Anonymous showed plenty of “reformed” men who had sought sobriety, but also forgiveness for crimes that really should have gone to court – crimes too severe to be washed away by completing the steps and making tea. Deliberately addicting young girls to drugs so they would work as prostitutes was just one I heard that was “forgiven” by the power of God and the 12-step programme. Name and address supplied

Following the jailing of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault, we are being told that the entertainment industry has many attackers lurking in plain sight. While this is probably true, I and other survivors of rape and sexual violence worry that this focus somehow paints a picture that this one industry is an anomaly – that other places don’t suffer from this blight.

In our experience, this is not true. I am part of a panel of survivors convened by Arch Teesside who meet to improve attitudes and practices among service providers through research, presentations, and recommending changes from a survivor’s point of view.

While using the word “rape” fully in the public sphere is a good thing (people often avoid using it), it is unacceptable to portray rape as a result of “stars” exercising their power at work. It happens across the board, as those on our panel know. Managers, CEOs and senior colleagues also have this imbalanced power at their disposal. Please highlight this: rape at work happens everywhere, not just places where celebrities work. Name and address supplied

My only question is why he didn’t do it a few weeks earlier, when the first round of hacked fridges were headline news for several days.

Your article notes that there are millions of devices connected to the internet. This sea of domestic and industrial controllers, known as the “internet of things” in marketing literature and the “internet of shit” by engineers, all have several things in common: their firmware is almost never upgraded, software security features are a fig leaf and the vast majority can run without an internet connection.

For many of these devices, it’s already too late – they are already part of a botnet used to attack other devices on the internet. AI does not bring anything novel, but has massively reduced the time required to find exploits that turn your shiny new toy into part of the problem.

Whether it’s a home security camera, industrial fridge or blast furnace, the advice of this software security specialist with a sideline in industrial controllers is the same: upgrade if you’re confident, unplug if you’re not. Don’t give your oven the wifi password. Name and address supplied

Clearing up confusion over iodine in milk

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:26:21 GMT

Cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow, notes Dale Vince of the Green Britain Foundation

You report that scientists say moving even partly from dairy products to vegan alternatives could lead to deficiencies in iodine and other micronutrients if the substitutes are not fortified (Swapping from dairy to plant-based milk, cheese and yoghurt ‘could lead to micronutrient deficiencies’, 4 November).

To be clear, cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow. As the paper published in the Lancet Planetary Health explains, iodine is in milk because it is added to cattle feed. The vitamin B12 is there because cobalt is added to the feed so the cow’s gut bacteria can make it. Britain has been doing this for decades. If fortification is the answer, and the paper’s authors say it is, then fortify plant milk. It’s better for us and the planet than cow’s milk.

The study assumes that every plant product on the shelf is bought in equal measure, but they’re not, and the most popular brands are fortified with iodine. This means that the study’s deficiency figures are overstated.

Dairy is one of the heaviest climate burdens on our plates, and most of humanity can’t digest it past childhood anyway. Moving away from it is the right direction. The answer to a fortification gap is fortification, not telling teenage girls to put dairy back in the fridge. We need to leave cow’s milk for baby cows. Dale Vince Founder, Green Britain Foundation

I have also faced serious health problems, including cancer, and I remain under specialist hospital care. The uncertainty about our future is causing considerable stress.

We understand that immigration rules can change, but people who have already been granted refugee status should not be left uncertain about promises and expectations they relied on. The hope is that the sectors will strengthen protections voluntarily, but it is understood the government could look to act if ministers believe that efforts to prevent abuse and harassment, and to encourage whistleblowing, are insufficient.

It is not yet known which organisations Nandy will meet, or what the requests might be. One option, if legislation is needed, could be to make it mandatory for companies to sign up to the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA), which tackles bullying and harassment in the sector via confidential whistleblowing.

One government official said the expectation was for voluntary action. “The instinct is that Lisa would like the industries to show they are about to sort this out themselves, but we are not squeamish about stepping in if that does not happen,” they said.

Olivia Bailey, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons women and equalities committee, said in a statement to the Guardian that ministers should give the CIISA proper funding.

She also called for an existing ban on non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) being used to silence employees over harassment or discrimination to be extended to everyone, covering not just freelancers but also volunteers and fans. This should also be the case for other workplace protections against harassment, she said.

It was time to “end the culture of silence”, she said. “Not only do these men seek to hide behind NDAs and injunctions, they rely on a culture of people looking the other way or feeling unable to speak out.”

Speaking to a parliamentary committee on Wednesday, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, said he accepted there was “a lot of concern” about powerful men using the legal system to silence accusers, which could include seeking injunctions, as Walliams did, and NDAs.

There have been widespread calls for action after the publication of an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News setting out accusations that Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and a top-selling children’s author, used his power and status to prey on young women for sex.

Walliams, 55, denies any wrongdoing. The allegations were published after a court rejected an attempt by Walliams to prevent publication.

In a personal letter written to Guardian and ITV News journalists denying the allegations and detailing their impact on his mental health, he wrote: “Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something I never did.

“I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10-20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”

The TV presenter Jonathan Ross said in a statement on Wednesday that he had had no knowledge about the alleged behaviour of Walliams, or the actions of Brand, who was jailed for more than 10 years on Monday for rape and sexual assault.

Ross said that was the case despite the fact he had made a joke about a 15-year-old “going home” with Walliams when he hosted the British comedy awards in 2004.

To laughter from Walliams and others in the audience, Ross said at the event: “The comedy awards is 15 years old – 15 years old! And like most 15-year-olds, it’s drunk, it’s unpredictable and it’s probably going home with David Walliams.”

In his statement, Ross said the joke had been written by the awards’ scriptwriting team, “and I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect”..

Speaking after prime minister’s questions, Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson called the allegations about Walliams “deeply troubling”. “Men in positions of power using their influence to exploit vulnerable young women and girls is evident in this case, and it’s a pattern of behaviour that needs to change,” he said.

“We are clear that every organisation should look hard at whether they are doing enough to keep people safe, and if people can raise concerns knowing that their allegations will be taken seriously.”

Louise Casey, who is separately leading an inquiry into sexual abuse grooming gangs, said many people would be surprised to learn that men who had sex with girls aged 13, 14 or 15 were not automatically charged with rape, saying this should be changed.

She told Sky News: “Those are the sorts of things I think that would really show the country that we are going to protect children … We really need to move mountains, and to move them quickly.”

It is understood, however, that the government has no plans to change the law as Casey suggested.

Later on Wednesday, Norris was asked about the prevalence of high-profile people using the courts to silence accusers. He told the House of Lords justice and home affairs committee: “This has been a source of conversation and engagement in parliament for a long time but brought into relief recently, particularly the way in which powerful men used the system in order to silence people.

“I think there’s a lot of concern in this space and we want to make sure that those things aren’t being used inappropriately and that the legal regime that governs them is robust and finds a fair balance that it ought to.”

Jess Phillips, who until May was the Home Office minister responsible for combating violence against women and girls, told the BBC that the Walliams case was “an outlier” in that an injunction was overturned.

“There are many, many people in this country silenced by injunctions, silenced by non-disclosure agreements,” she said. “That is not new news.”

UK politics live – latest updates

Well, there was one person at least who thought Kemi Badenoch had absolutely nailed it at this week’s prime minister’s questions. And that person was Kemi Badenoch. She could not have been more pleased with herself if she had tried. No one laughed louder and longer at her own jokes than she did. No one admired her laser focus as much as she did. As for the rest of her Tory MPs – aside from Chris Philp, who is basically a parasitic homunculus – they weren’t quite so convinced by Kemi’s performance. She had been so entranced with her one-liners, she had forgotten to ask any serious questions. And never forget how low the gag bar is in the Commons. What passes as a joke at PMQs wouldn’t even register as humour in normal conversation. Wouldn’t even elicit the groan that comes from the recognition of a gag format.

Maybe Kemi was just having a bad day. Had woken up and realised she didn’t have any questions for the prime minister and had decided to busk it instead. Maybe she was so carried away with the excitement of the Tories no longer being in third place in the opinion polls – mainly because Reform have tanked rather than any Conservative surge – that she decided to give herself a day off. Or maybe she’s stalled somewhat. Having found she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, she merely bounces off Andy Burnham’s. Compared with Kemi, Andy looks and sounds like a normal person.

The session began with Kemi trying to make fun of Labour’s as-yet-unpublished – possibly even unwritten – 10-year plan. Where was it, she asked. Burnham had a ready answer. She was sure the 10-year plan had been kicked into the long grass. On Tuesday she had joked it would be a nine-year plan by the time it was published. Now the joke was on her.

Not that she had any real observation to make about it. But she did have a gag and that was all that mattered. It was the “do nothing” budget. Kemi cracked herself up at that. Someone you are inclined to like and trust on sight. The bedside manner of a doctor who can somehow make you feel better about yourself when telling you your illness has become terminal. The sort of person who you feel guilty about for not having responded to treatment.

It’s impeachment season! After the attempt on Pete Hegseth, will Donald Trump be next?

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:00:55 GMT

Trump has already made history as the only president to be impeached twice. After the Republicans’ thrashing in the midterms, could there be a third attempt?

The days are getting shorter, the nights are getting longer and some Republicans are getting nervous. After a long stretch of impunity, it’s impeachment season in the US. While the attempt to impeach the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, failed yesterday, Donald Trump may be worried he’s next.

In January, the president warned Republicans that they had better win the November elections or he would be in big trouble. “If we don’t win the midterms … they’ll find a reason to impeach me,” Trump said. He repeated this plea to voters during an October rally in Oklahoma: “Pretend I’m running, please. Just pretend. ’Cause I am on the ballot. And if we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me.”

I don’t need to tell you what happened with the midterms, do I? The Republicans didn’t just lose – they were given a thrashing so thorough that, for a while, Trump seemed to avoid talking about it. Indeed, in his first public appearance after the election, Trump largely avoided the issue for a full 20 minutes while talking about his beloved White House ballroom project, rhapsodising about its “magnificent” columns. This week, Trump seems to have moved on to another obsession: he is now making baseless claims that the election was rigged. Still, while Trump may be in la-la land half the time, in his moments of lucidity you have to imagine he’s worried a comeuppance is coming.

There are various ways Trump could be held accountable for any alleged crimes, but what he seems most worried about right now is potential impeachment. It’s a multistep process used to charge a public official with serious misconduct and remove them from office. First, articles of impeachment are brought, then the House votes on whether to adopt these articles via a majority vote. If that happens, the person is impeached. But this is where things get tricky. For the official to get removed, the Senate has to hold an impeachment trial and two-thirds of members (67 senators) have to find them guilty; a tough hurdle to clear. There have only been eight cases where this has happened and all the officials removed have been judges.

Trump has already made history by being the only president to have been impeached twice: in 2019 and 2021. In both cases the Senate acquitted him. But now that Democrats have control of government, could Trump become the first president to be removed from office through impeachment?

The short answer is that, while it’s not impossible, it’s unlikely. The Democrats have a majority, but they still only have 54 seats. Attempting to remove Trump would be a gruelling process that many don’t have the appetite for. Kamala Harris said recently: “Going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea … we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations.”

In an interview with NBC News on Sunday, Senator Bernie Sanders went even further. “We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump,” Sanders said. “We have to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.”

Hear me out: how about we do both? And look, if impeachment is unrealistic, we can get a little creative and come up with other ways to give Trump and his lackeys a small taste of the misery they have inflicted on the rest of us. I would suggest exiling the president to an island and forcing him to listen to his incoherent speeches on a nonstop loop, but I suspect he’d quite enjoy that. Although we could fill the place with wind turbines, which enrage him, and make sure the water is filled with sharks. Trump is weirdly obsessed with the fish; according to Stormy Daniels he once said: “I hope all the sharks die.”

Oh dear, I think I’d better stop there before I have the FBI knocking on my door. Forget the sharks, OK? If the legal system fails us, let’s just focus on replacing him at the next election.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Eddie Jones retains his passion and divisive power heading into England reunion

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:00:54 GMT

Japan head coach was criticised for discarding players harshly during his Red Rose tenure but that tough love has paid off for some

To listen to Eddie Jones chewing the fat on assorted podcasts this week is to admire the enduring thickness of his coaching skin. The old crocodile smile is still intact too, along with his sense of humour after an interaction in a lift with a fan after his Japan side’s 28-21 weekend defeat in Cardiff. As Jones later confided: “This Welsh bloke came up to me and said: ‘You almost look human with your glasses on.’”

Next up is a reunion with a few former friends – and foes – at Twickenham. While it is now almost four years since Jones was sacked by the Rugby Football Union, there remain mixed emotions on both sides. Those relieved to see him go in late 2022 will certainly not be too brokenhearted if there is a similar outcome to the last time a Jones-coached Japan came to Allianz Stadium two years ago and lost 59-14.

Yet England under Jones won 59 and drew two of their 81 matches and boasted a 73% winning record, superior to any other head coach before or since, including Sir Clive Woodward. Amid the relentless churn of backroom staff and the Jones regime’s brutal excesses – the former England scrum-half Danny Care compared it to “living in a dictatorship, under a despot who disappeared people” – there were golden days, too.

The question, then and now, is whether the ends justified the means. In his 2024 autobiography, Care wrote: “Did Eddie rule by fear? Of course he did, everyone was bloody terrified of him.” Including a generation of younger players who were thrown in at the deep end before, in many cases, being abruptly jettisoned? In total 112 players were picked for England during the Jones era and many of their Test careers – there were 14 one-cap wonders and a further 18 with two caps – made the lifespan of the average mayfly feel protracted.

In certain cases, though, this “tough love” is belatedly paying dividends long after Jones’s exit. Take Alex Coles, whose first three caps coincided with the Australian’s farewell campaign in charge. The Northampton lock is now maturing into a fine international player but back then he was a wide-eyed novice. “It was daunting coming in at that time. As a young player coming through you hear all these stories about Eddie and stuff in camp. I was apprehensive and he certainly had that aura about him.”

Among Coles’s clearest memories remains the 2022 autumn Test against New Zealand. He wasn’t selected for the game but found himself deployed as a key figure by Jones during the buildup. “The chat was that they were going to try to get into our heads and wind us up. My sole role in the team session was to just try to wind the starters up.

“I was this fresh-faced 22-year-old, scared of all the older heads like Mako Vunipola, Owen Farrell and everyone else. Eddie would run behind the defensive line and be like: ‘You’re not winding them up enough, you’re not getting in their heads.’ So, because I’d run out of ideas, I ended up coming around the side and tackling the third man in a caterpillar ruck. I then got piled on by about four or five of the starters on the floor. After that Eddie said I’d trained really well!”

This sink or swim ethos basically mirrored Jones’s entire modus operandi. Having grown up in a tough school at Randwick, where he was coached by the wily Bob Dwyer and played alongside Michael Cheika, he was constantly seeking resilient individuals rather than looking to indulge fledgling “apprentices”. What no one has ever disputed, though, is Jones’s eye for an unpolished gem; in addition to Coles, Tommy Freeman, George Furbank and Alex Mitchell were all handed their first caps by Jones and have subsequently gone on to be influential Test performers.
