Will Joseph, set to feature along with Henry Pollock and Max Ojomoh in a reshuffled England starting XV this weekend, was also given two minutes against Australia in Brisbane as a 20-year-old in 2022. Was he picked prematurely? Almost certainly. But is that proving helpful now? His teammate Coles, for his part, can now see the benefits of such experiences: “You felt a little bit on edge around Eddie but I’m so grateful to him because at that stage, in my own head, I didn’t really believe that I was ready for that level.

“He saw something in me, made me believe I could be at that international level and pushed me to work on my game. And even though I then dropped out of the team for a bit, I still think that without him it would have taken much longer to get to the point where I was ready. Mentally it was a bit of a challenge. You felt like you’d played a few games and done OK and then you’re out. But looking back now from a long-term point of view, I was a bit raw and mentally I probably wasn’t quite ready to be a consistent international player.”

In summary, Jones’s legacy remains a matter of debate. Both he and his successor, Steve Borthwick, can argue that, ultimately, the national team is only as strong as the development pipeline feeding it. And the 66-year-old Jones is also not wrong to suggest the number of absolute world-class players English rugby has produced since 2003 can be pretty much counted on the fingers of one hand. What hasn’t changed, either way, is the great survivor’s passion for rugby, nor his ability to divide a room.

What is my cat saying? I asked experts to translate

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:00:54 GMT

Slow blinking and trilling are some of the ways felines show affection – but experts say to ‘read the whole cat in context’

I talk to my cat, Blue, constantly. I say things like, “You’re my little baby,” and “Wow, good jump,” and “Can you stop being a jerk for like, two seconds?”

She also seems to say a lot, like, “Feed me,” “Feed me right now,” and “Stop working and play with me.”

Because I’m obsessed with her, I like to think we have a perfect, mind-meld level of communication. But what if I’m wrong? What is Blue really trying to tell me? And what am I really telling her?

I turned to cat experts to find out how cats communicate, and how we can better understand them.

First, it’s worth exploring how cats perceive us, as this can shape how they communicate with us. Do they see humans as big, weird, hairless cats? Food dispensers? Or something else?

“There are so many varied beliefs here,” says Jessica Mockett, a certified feline behavior, training and holistic health consultant. “In some ways, they treat us like they would another cat,” she says – they groom us, make biscuits on us, and co-sleep with us, all things they might do with other cats in their group.

“In other ways, they look to us as a caregiver or provider,” Mockett says, noting that cats miaow at humans the way kittens do with their mothers.

However they see us, cats’ relationships with humans are deeper than they tend to get credit for. There is a common stereotype of cats as aloof little dictators who see people as their personal staff and little else. But that’s far from the truth, Mockett says.

“We know from research that cats form attachments that are either secure or insecure, just as a human child forms with their parents,” she says. “Hopefully, guardians are doing what they can to create that secure and healthy attachment.”

“Cats communicate through sound, scent, touch, facial expressions and body movement,” says Mieshelle Nagelschneider, certified cat behaviorist and founder of the Cat Behavior Clinic.

Eyes, ears, tail, whiskers and posture all send signals. One can look at these individually; for example, wide eyes with dilated pupils can signal excitement or anxiety, while half-closed eyes with narrow pupils generally indicate relaxation and contentment. But Nagelschneider argues it is more important “to read the whole cat in context”.

“A comfortable cat generally has a relaxed body, softly held ears, and eyes that are not fixed in a tense stare,” she says. “They may approach with their tail upright, rub against you, settle nearby, or initiate play or contact.”

Slow blinking during an interaction can also be a good sign, as it’s a way of signaling relaxation and trust.

On the other hand, Nagelschneider says, a cat may signal discomfort with “a tense or crouched body, ears rotating sideways or flattening back, avoidance, hiding, growling or hissing”.

One of the most overlooked signs of an unhappy cat is what Nagelschneider calls the “lip lick”. This is usually the first sign that a cat is about to become aggressive. “If you see your cat’s pink tongue flick out briefly like it’s licking its lips, the stress response is rising,” she says.

These behaviors can point to different kinds of discomfort: fear, frustration, pain or a desire for distance.

If cats are talking to us with all the other parts of their bodies, what do their miaows mean, then?

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

According to experts, this seems to be a gracious adaptation they developed over time to communicate with their human companions.

“Miaowing is not something [adult cats] do to communicate with one another,” Mockett says, though they do use other sounds, like hissing, growling, spitting and yowling.

Each sound cats make has a different meaning, says Lisa Stemcosky, a certified cat behavior consultant: trilling and chirping are “social, friendly vocalizations” and chatter is “predatory excitement”.

“Miaows are just for humans; it’s usually used when requesting something,” she says.

Purring is complex. While it can happen when cats are content, Stemcosky says, it can also be a way of self-soothing when they are stressed or in pain.

Research suggests that cats understand some human language. One small study found that cats can recognize their own names, and can distinguish their owner’s voices from others. Another showed that cats may be able to form meaningful links between pictures and words.

But don’t start speaking to your cat in full paragraphs just yet. “The best place to start is by making your own behavior easier to understand,” says Nagelschneider. She suggests moving calmly, using a gentle or “baby” voice, petting lightly, and giving the cat room to approach or leave.

Allowing the cat to decide whether to initiate and continue contact is important, experts say. “If they don’t want to approach, don’t approach them,” says Stemcosky.

Nagelschneider recommends a “pause-and-observe” approach when it comes to physical contact. Offer a few gentle strokes around a cat’s preferred petting area – usually their cheeks or head – then stop. “Does the cat lean in, rub against your hand, or clearly seek more?” she asks. In that case, continue. If it turns away, remains disengaged, or leaves, give it space.

If a cat comes near you, this does not automatically mean they want to be pet. While spending time near their people is a sign of trust and affection, “a cat may sit beside you because it enjoys presence without wanting to be stroked,” Nagelschneider says. Rolling on to their back, she adds, is not an automatic invitation to a belly rub.

The key to effectively communicating with your cat, experts say, is trying to observe and understand them, and meet them halfway.

“Ultimately, understanding cats is less about teaching them to communicate, and more about becoming better observers,” says Nagelschneider. “Some of the most important things a cat tells us happen very quietly.”

Reform UK’s general secretary has left the role as Nigel Farage’s party continues to face turmoil over questions about vetting failures and professionalisation.

The departure of Tom Waterhouse comes after Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council, George Madgwick, was charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child.

Waterhouse, a public affairs executive who previously worked in the world of Westminster thinktanks and for the crown estate, was recruited in August last year. Labour described him as Reform’s “latest fall guy” for problems in the party.

A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Tom Waterhouse has left his role with Reform UK. The party leader has now appointed an interim general secretary.”

Waterhouse’s departure will be a blow to Reform’s drive towards professionalisation, a project of which he had been at the centre. He had been involved in a big recruitment push, bankrolled by wealthy donors, and in the selection of candidates for a future general election.

Waterhouse had also been involved in Reform’s internal investigation into two of its senior officials, James Orr and Dan Jukes, alongside Adam Richardson, the party’s legal secretary and a longstanding associate of Farage. Their investigation cleared Orr and Jukes of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation.

However, the recent case of Madgwick severely embarrassed the party and once again brought the question of Reform’s candidate vetting process into the spotlight. That process is now run by Paul Nuttall, the party’s deputy chair and a former Ukip leader, but Waterhouse’s departure reflects continuing organisational turmoil at Reform.

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “As the scandals pile up for Reform, everyone is being forced to take the blame except Nigel Farage. Their general secretary is the latest fall guy, but we all know nobody in Reform makes a decision without Farage’s approval.

“Farage is yet to come clean on what he knew about the arrest of his senior campaign manager and leader in Hampshire, who is now facing 35 very serious charges. And he tried to cover up a secret £5m ‘gift’ from a crypto billionaire.”

Does M John Harrison’s Booker win mean science fiction is finally accepted by a ‘snobby’ literary establishment?

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 16:44:36 GMT

Kazuo Ishiguro, Jeff VanderMeer, Olivia Laing and other writers weigh in on the publishing world’s genre wars

As M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction, with a decidedly fantastical book.

His fans, many leading authors among them, are thrilled. “For decades it was a standard – and correct – nerd whine to point out that sentence for sentence, book for book, Harrison was one of the greatest writers out there, full stop, but that ‘mainstream’ prizes never reflected that,” says China Miéville, who last week won the Goldsmiths prize with his 1,200-page speculative novel The Rouse. Back in 2002, Miéville wrote that Harrison not having won a Booker by that point proved “the bankruptcy and back-slapping generic snobbery of the literary establishment”. Now, he says: “I am so delighted, for Harrison, and for fiction.”

While some past Booker-winning authors draw heavily on SF – Margaret Atwood, Kazuo Ishiguro, Ian McEwan – Harrison is the first winner from the “bona fide SF” sphere, said Booker prize foundation chief executive Gaby Wood on Monday. The Pulitzer and the Nobel rarely take notice of SF either, though the latter has honoured Ishiguro and Doris Lessing – both of whom are considered literary writers who dabble in SF, rather than purists, and thus perhaps considered more palatable to a wider reading public.

Ishiguro says that when he emerged on to the British literary scene, he was “mystified” as to why the establishment had “fenced off SF into a ghetto”. He believes it’s done “real harm to the development of ‘literary fiction’ in the UK”, and he “personally felt liberated to go in that direction only in the early 2000s, after noticing – and envying – the brilliance of younger writers like David Mitchell and Alex Garland who were clearly inspired by SF, comics and games”. He notes, however, that his mentor and teacher Angela Carter had “no such prejudices”, often using SF elements in her work.

He points out the contrast between the patronising attitude of the mainstream literary establishment and that of cinema: “even the most highbrow of critics” venerated Fritz Lang’s Metropolis, Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey and Tarkovsky’s Solaris as “milestones of cinema history”.

Author and critic Olivia Laing agrees it’s taken the literary world “an embarrassingly long time to clock that you don’t need realism to write about how it feels to inhabit late capitalism and unravelling modernity”. Harrison has “finally got his dues” with this week’s win.

Harrison’s winning book, The End of Everything, might be called a polycrisis novel. It sees mysterious alien phenomena called iGhetti cropping up on Earth, where they increasingly warp the fabric of reality. The extraterrestrial beings may stand in for AI, climate degradation, political chaos, Brexit, runaway capitalism, or all of the above.

So while there are futuristic elements, the book very much feels like a story about now. “I gather that somebody at the award ceremony asked Harrison if he had ‘any predictions for the future’,” says the novelist Michel Faber. “That typifies the obtuseness of people who just don’t get what the best so-called ‘science fiction’ does.” The End of Everything is firmly about the present – “an elucidation of the future we’re already living in”, adds Faber.

The recognition will surely bring Harrison a host of new readers – perhaps even former SF sceptics, for whom the book will prove that the genre can be both literary and acutely politically current. NielsenIQ BookData reported that sales stood at 13,400 copies pre-win. Based on previous years, Harrison can expect to sell tens of thousands more copies in the months to come.

Harrison’s win is a “huge victory for the seriousness of genre fiction as a project”, says the novelist Julia Armfield, who cried when she heard the news. Though it is also a win for the type of fiction that “resists decoding”. Indeed, as Harrison said in an interview with the Guardian this week: “My problem has always been that I don’t believe in genre.” He described the book as “SF-adjacent”.

Certain kinds of writing “make genre concerns seem beside the point,” says the critic and novelist Chris Power. Even in Harrison’s more purely SF books, he subverts the genre, “deconstructing sci-fi tropes and questioning the militarism of sci-fi”. Since he began writing in the 60s, he’s “always been queering the pitch”.

Sign up to Bookmarks

Discover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to you

after newsletter promotion

Harrison is a “writer’s writer before he is a science fiction writer”, agrees novelist Isabel Waidner. In a commercialised publishing culture “which tends to reward conventionality, including arguably arbitrary genre conventions”, Harrison writes fiction “that pushes preconceived ideas of what a novel is”. Power suggests Harrison’s work shows that genre brackets may be more useful from a marketing perspective than an aesthetic one. “A lot of the most interesting novels have always muddled these things,” he adds.

The novelist Jeff VanderMeer says he tries to avoid the “genre v literary” debate – he believes it’s “meaningless or, quite frankly, just kind of boring or not useful”. He adds: “What I do care about is when that debate, from either ‘side’, reduces complex works of fiction to caricatures. Or when it serves a gatekeeping function that reduces access to prestige or readers that has little relationship to the quality of the work.”

Reviewing Harrison’s 2023 “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here, Power described Harrison as “the best British writer you’ve never heard of”. Three years on, the literary establishment has woken up, and Harrison is suddenly famous, his fans basking in the Booker glow. Waidner puts it like this: “His win is a win for literature, for us, and for that most endangered of things – thinking.”

Top four teams in Fifa rankings set to be kept apart until semi-finals at 2027 Women’s World Cup

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 16:03:44 GMT

Team must win World Cup group to trigger rule

Spain, US, Germany and England currently in top four

The top four ranked teams will be separated until the semi-finals at the 2027 Women’s World Cup, ­provided they each win their group, after a change to the tournament’s draw procedure was confirmed by Fifa.

Spain, USA, Germany and England are ranked one to four in the world respectively, although USA and England still need to qualify for the tournament. The seedings will be based on the 7 December updated rankings, meaning the standings could change before the draw, which will take place on 11 December in Rio de Janeiro.

The top four sides were also ­separated until the semi-finals of the 2026 men’s World Cup, which consisted of 48 teams, but it was not announced until Wednesday that the same rule would apply to the 32-team ­women’s tournament. In the men’s World Cup the top four – Spain, Argentina, France, and England – all reached the semi-finals.

The record four-time champions USA face El Salvador on 27 November as they aim to confirm their place at the tournament next summer. A victory, coupled with no changes to the world rankings, would ensure USA would be placed in the opposite half of the draw to the defending cham­pions, Spain. That would mean if they win their groups the two teams could not meet until the final, which will be played at the ­Maracanã Stadium on 25 July. Neither Spain nor USA finished top of their group at the previous World Cup.

England, the 2023 runners-up, must beat Ukraine over two legs on 1 and 5 December to ensure their qualification. The European ­champions hold a 31-point advantage over fifth-placed Japan in the world rankings before the upcoming round of internationals.

France, the hosts Brazil and ­Sweden – who finished third at three of the past four World Cups, and face Scotland in their qualifying playoff in December – would complete the set of eight Pot 1 seeds for the eight groups, if the top eight remains as it is. ­Canada, ranked ninth in the world, could pounce on a Pot 1 spot if anyone slips up.

Fifa has also confirmed that the draw will take place at 1.30pm local time (11.30am EST/4.30pm GMT) on 11 December, at Rio de Janeiro’s Museum of Modern Art. Brazil, as hosts, will be placed in Group A and will contest the opening match at the Maracanã on 24 June.

After the eight Pot 1 sides, the next eight highest-ranked teams involved will be in Pot 2, with the next eight below them in Pot 3. Pot 4 will include three places for the winners of the inter-confederation playoff ­tournament that will conclude in March, along with the lowest-ranked sides involved. No group will be permitted to include more than one team from the same continent, except for European teams, of whom there can be a maximum of two per group.

Fifa also confirmed later on Wednesday that the uncontested bids to host the 2031 and 2035 Women’s World Cups have both passed their extensive bid evaluations.

The US, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica are bidding to jointly host the 2031 event and they received an overall score of 4.4 out of 5. The UK is the sole bidder for 2035 and the bid – which includes a proposal for Wembley to host the final – received a score of 4.3 out of 5.

No venue has yet been specified to stage the 2031 final. Both bids’ infrastructure, stadiums and accommodation were praised by Fifa. Fifa’s congress is expected to formally appoint them as hosts on 23 November.

‘Young, Black and female in Brixton is hard’: ​from football to Top Boy and wordplay, the inspiring journey of UK rapper Cristale

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 16:00:52 GMT

Crystal Palace FC or Oxbridge beckoned, but the multitalented MC kept forging her way towards music. She explains how she poured every aspect of herself into her debut mixtape

Two weeks before we meet, UK rapper Cristale was scrambling down a cliff face to a secluded black pebbled beach in Dover, racing an incoming tide with fewer than 90 minutes to shoot the video for her single I’m Okay With Being Lonely. She’d never hiked before in her life. “I was wearing head-to-toe Stone Island, no hiking gear, full face of makeup, edges laid and Mum was doing my touch-ups on a rusty ladder,” she laughs.

As we sit in her publicist’s central London office, her hair half-braided and half-flowing past a black puffer coat, she says the rush of adrenaline hasn’t fully faded. In fact she seems to thrive on regular bumps of it: beyond her relentlessly articulate and energetic rap flow – put to work on tracks that span drill, introspective R&B and beyond – she has ably hopped between football, art, acting in Netflix projects and more.

Already with nearly half a million monthly listeners on Spotify alone, the 25-year-old has just released her debut mixtape, Clear Intentions. It’s her third attempt at a full-length project, but the first she has actually finished. “There’s no fillers, no bridges in between songs,” she says. “I’m very nitpicky with my art.”

Born and raised in Brixton, to a Guyanese father and half-Jamaican, half-Montserratian mother who doubles as her manager – “close is an understatement”, she says of their relationship – Cristale’s first taste of songwriting arrived in nursery when her uncle taught her how to rap.

Come year 7, her English teacher organised a school poetry slam, and sitting in a friend’s flat looking across at her own house, Cristale wrote What It’s Like to Be Young, a misunderstood kid’s response to the adults around her. She was victorious against older students, and while she cringes at the thought of anyone looking it up on YouTube, it gave her debut EP its title, and she sampled it on recent single H2O.

Her creative drive was matched by a competitive streak across her youth, including playing football for Crystal Palace’s academy, fuelled by boys at school telling her she couldn’t play because she was a girl. The plan was to go pro, but with exams looming she stepped away: “I couldn’t take the risk because you can go into women’s football and not make any money.” Teachers urged her towards Oxbridge, but she feared “maybe too linear” a path, and chose to follow what she loved at the time: drawing. Even if she hadn’t realised it at the time, music was where her imagination ran freest. “It never feels like a job. I’ve got a big blank canvas in front of me, like I’ve got 8,000 different paint brushes going in. It’s the most euphoric feeling ever.”

Alongside her art and illustration degree, with plans to become an architectural designer, she juggled university with 40-hour work weeks at a Chelsea boutique, and idly posted freestyle raps to Instagram. “It was just a hobby at first, and a reason for me to spend time with my dad.” He pushed and helped her to record them properly and, by 21, she’d signed a record deal. As she began to gain momentum, she kept up the pace, partly to honour her parents, but also to prove the doubters wrong. “Young, Black and female in Brixton is hard … you look a certain type of way, you’re categorised into a certain type of group of kids.” There have been “multiple moments”, she says; some teachers didn’t want her on their courses, assuming she’d fail. “The least I could do was block out all of the external noise, and care about myself how my mum has always cared about me,’ she says.

The payoff came quickly. Her track Bong Bing went viral, she was nominated for best newcomer at the Mobo awards, and she took acting roles in Top Boy – for which she also wrote the song Roadents – and Daniel Kaluuya’s Netflix film The Kitchen. Acting taught her more about herself – “having to put myself in someone else’s shoes made me feel even more comfortable in my own skin” – but her days ran to a strict schedule, “from like five o’clock in the morning. Routine really helps, but it also limits my creativity.” Clear Intentions, she says, speaks to finding the balance between that and a freer life.

Musically, she’s also come a long way from where she started. Her 2022 debut EP was almost exclusively drill. “I had so much more poetic music available at the time; I didn’t understand what music projects should be,” she says. “This time round, I thought I’d give them a little bit of everything.” Clear Intentions adds in grime, melodic guitars, hip-hop and subtle pockets of sound she describes as being “on the cusp of R&B”. From start to finish, it operates as a mental audit, “everything going on in my head at once,” she says. “All the different relationships with different people and things: myself, family, friends, my partner, work. It’s about what I do to maintain them, where they fail, when they succeed and what I can do to improve.”

She shrugs at genre boundaries, particularly given that they’re not always accurate for Black artists anyway – “if I was born in the grime era, they would have called me a grime artist” – and deliberately didn’t commission any featured artists for Clear Intentions: “I don’t feel like I need help telling this part of my story.”

There will be no champagne-soaked launch parties, either. Still chasing that euphoric feeling, she says she plans to spend the release day quietly alongside her mum and core team, “99.9% working”.

Cristale’s mixtape Clear Intentions is out now

Richmond upon Thames: it is Britain’s happiest place to live – but there’s a big catch

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 15:14:39 GMT

According to Rightmove, residents of the London borough are highly satisfied with their neighbourhood. But there’s one potential problem if you’re keen to move there ...

Name: London Borough of Richmond upon Thames.

Age: At the beginning of the 16th century, Henry VII – the king formerly known as Henry Tudor, 2nd Earl of Richmond (after his earldom in Richmond, North Yorkshire) – built Richmond Palace in what is now south-west London.

Is it still there? The palace? No. It remained a royal residence for England’s monarchs – including Elizabeth I, who died there – but after the execution of Charles I in 1649, it was sold (for £13,000) and largely demolished.

The town remains, though? Happily, yes. Very happily, as it happens.

I’m thinking, judging by the repetition, that “happy” is somehow significant, am I right? You are. Richmond upon Thames has just been named the happiest place to live in Britain.

By whom? By Rightmove.

The property portal? The same. They do an annual survey to update their “happy at home index”, asking respondents about issues such as local services, shops and restaurants, green spaces and so on.

Richmond Park? A good example of a green space, yes.

And why are the people of Richmond upon Thames so happy? Colleen, a property expert at Rightmove, points to the eating-out options, employment opportunities …

It’s because they’re rich, isn’t it? And the mayor, Nancy Baldwin, says: “Above all, it is our people and communities that make Richmond special.”

It’s because they’re rich, isn’t it? It’s even in the name! True – £13,000 may have bought you a palace in 1649, but it doesn’t go far in Richmond these days.

Go on. [Looking on Rightmove] So this rather lovely Georgian house is £25m. But that does include kitchen appliances. No? How about a six-bedroom Victorian house for £15m?

A bit lower, please. Ah, here’s one just over the river in Teddington, for £49,500 … oh, it’s a garage.

What’s the average asking price for a home in the borough? Over £1m.

And the whole of the UK? About £378,000.

And where else is high on the list? Happy Harrogate at No 2, then Smiling Cirencester at No 3.

How about outside England? The highest-ranked places in Wales and Scotland are Monmouth and Kirkcaldy.

What about famous happy neighbours, when I move in (to my garage)? So many in Richmond. Sir David Attenborough, Zendaya and Tom Holland, Gary Lineker, Jerry Hall, Richard E Grant …

Lucky they don’t behead traitors any more. Eh? Oh I see, you’re tidily looping back to Charles I, even if he was executed in Westminster, several miles downstream.

Do say: “Look! A deer in the park! Yay! I’m so happy!”

Don’t say: “Sorry, what? I can’t hear a word you’re saying with these planes coming in to land at Heathrow every two minutes.”

Why did it take so long to unmask Brand and Walliams? Because noughties culture told girls like me abuse was normal

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:55:39 GMT

As a survivor of the era, I welcome this reckoning – and I salute the women who were brave enough to bring it about

Mr Justice Bennathan’s sentencing remarks in the trial of Russell Brand hit me like a train, and I know I’m not the only one. This week my Instagram feed has been full of female friends, colleagues and acquaintances sharing his words: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.” Those same women are now sharing the Guardian and ITV’s investigation into David Walliams, who is accused of preying on young women for sex, with the same fury and fervour (Walliams has denied the allegations against him).

Both of these stories concerning predatory male behaviour took place in an era when I was a young woman: the “lad culture” era. It dated from about the mid-to-late 90s until the beginning of the #MeToo movement in 2016, and those of us who came of age during it sometimes joke bleakly that it’s a miracle we made it out in one piece. Some of us didn’t, and those victim-survivors live with the daily impact of male coercion, abuse and violence, still.

We were all, essentially, frogs in boiling water. Misogyny and female objectification were so common, so normalised, that all you could do was try to keep swimming before you were boiled alive. With Bennathan’s words I was catapulted back to being 17 years old and sitting in my boyfriend’s parents’ kitchen, where I read a tabloid newspaper column arguing that girls who wore short skirts essentially deserved to be raped. So many of us girls, as we were then, must have had a moment like that, where we realised, essentially, that we were prey, when we realised that we “deserved” it.

How to explain to young women today how it felt back then? Today’s girls face their own dark threats, not least from online grooming and harassment, deepfakes and being blackmailed over images, as well as the rape and sexual assault that remains prevalent. At the same time, their knowhow when it comes to consent and boundaries is far superior to what ours was then, when the word “safeguarding” was barely used. We were all learning on the job, essentially, while being surrounded by perverts.

I know girls who met rock stars more than twice their age at festivals who targeted them when they were still in their teens. Girls whose older male bosses shoved their tongues down their throats. Girls who were groomed and abused by their teachers, or preyed upon by older men with a preference for girls still doing their GCSEs. Girls whose boyfriends locked them in their flats. Girls who were assaulted, or anally raped, like Brand’s victim was.

You’d feel sick, strange, or shocked by a man’s behaviour towards you. You would know on some level that what had happened was wrong, and yet the overwhelming message from the culture around you was that this was normal because you were young and beautiful, and that was always going to be tempting to men, wasn’t it? When I was attacked by a stranger while walking home after a night out, a common rape myth at the time had it that I was a car who had left her doors unlocked. What did I, or any of us, expect?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

And so this weird sort of splitting of the self would occur: one half comprised of the pain of it all, a trauma that lives in the body, a body that knows on a cellular level that it has been violated, and the other, well, the other a shell walking around this world set with traps, surviving. Making light of it, even, or not consciously realising that what happened to you was wrong, that it mattered. Living while embodying that disconnect does odd things to you, ultimately. Especially when you’re surrounded by fully grown adults who seem to think that it’s all fine.

You forget how different the media culture was then. It wasn’t as online, as disparate and diffuse as it is now, where there are megastars on TikTok of whom whole demographics are entirely ignorant. The landscape was much more of a monoculture, its tenets, its myths and its doctrines, its language and its cadences decided by far fewer individuals, most of them older, and often, but not always, men. It was a world of lads’ mags and tabloids and telly – and if a celebrity was king of all three then their power was immense indeed. Being able to make the nation laugh was treated as a superpower. Banter and rape jokes were par for the course. That clip that is doing the rounds of Jonathan Ross, Noel Fielding and Brand joking about rape? It seems sickening now, but in the audience’s laugh you hear the truth: it was all normal then.

In 2014, I co-wrote a book with Holly Baxter about the media landscape called The Vagenda. I picked it up this morning because I wanted to remember what the world was like then. Just a sample for you: Jimmy Carr – these days rebranded as a worldly, empathic sage of social media – joking about gang-rape. The Evening Standard having a strip club correspondent. The Telegraph glowingly reporting the fact that Gymbox ran a Playboy “bunny bootcamp”. An academic study that found members of the public struggled to differentiate between statements taken from lads’ mags and those who had committed serious sexual offences. Teenage magazines having a section for readers’ photos entitled “How Sexy Am I?”.

This book, which contained a section on rape culture and rape myths and was aimed at teenage girls, was given to older men to review, as though they knew anything about what it was like to spend your adolescence in a sexist hellscape. It was trashed both by them and by the women who took money from the women’s magazines we criticised, who were complicit. There were some adults who were on our side – our mums, our editors – but by and large any woman who tried to challenge that prevailing media culture was doing so very much alone.

That is why it does not surprise me that these stories have taken so long to come to public attention, or for any justice to be delivered. That sordid, shabby era may be over, but those who endured it as the backdrop to their girlhood are still trying to reconcile those two parts of themselves: the half that knows it has been violated, and the half walking around in a world that refused to listen.

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

‘Hear the goals during the afterlife’: Barça fans get to inter ashes at club’s new memorial

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:30:15 GMT

Memorial FC Barcelona, part of upgrade to Camp Nou stadium, will consist of 26,000 niches where fans can deposit their ashes

Lifelong supporters of Barcelona football club will soon be able to cheer on the club from beyond the grave – but, like everything else at Barça, eternal devotion comes at a price.

As part of an upgrade to the Camp Nou, the club has inaugurated the Memorial FC Barcelona, consisting of 26,000 niches where fans can deposit their ashes after their own final whistle has blown.

Supporting the team from the afterlife will cost €2,490 (£2,082) for 10 years or €6,000 for 50 years, with an annual maintenance fee of €70. Guaranteeing your niche for eternity will set you back €10,000, with a further €490 for a memorial plaque.

Presenting the Memorial FC Barcelona, María Elena Fort, the club’s institutional vice-president, said: “When my grandfather died many years ago, he said the only thing he wanted was to be buried next to Barça’s pitch so that he could hear the goals go in during the afterlife. Many fans dream of the same thing.”

The memorial, designed by the architect Quique Montoya, will consist of four large illuminated squares, while the memorial plaques will be installed in a glass wall backlit with LED lights. The urns will be kept behind a mural commemorating key moments in the club’s 125-year history.

The rival Spanish clubs Atlético Madrid, Betis and Espanyol already have smaller columbariums in their stadiums.

Work on Barcelona’s will begin late next year and the club says more than 1,000 Barça fans have already booked their place. Their contributions will go towards paying the huge cost of redeveloping the stadium, which was built in 1957.

In 2023, the club embarked on a scheme to increase capacity from 99,354 to 105,000 – 15,000 more than Wembley Stadium and making it the second biggest football venue in the world, after the Rungrado 1st of May Stadium in Pyongyang in North Korea.

The cost of the changes, initially costed at €900m, is now approaching €2bn, now being borne by non-season ticket holders who have seen ticket prices double in recent years.

The work, being carried out by the Turkish firm Limak Construction, has been plagued by delays and labour disputes. In 2024, FC Barcelona recognised that, among other abuses, more than 1,000 subcontractors had not been paid for overtime.

Work is due to be completed later this year but the club will have to play part of next season at the Olympic Stadium (capacity 55,926) while a roof is installed on Camp Nou.

Jockey Tom O’Brien, Cheltenham festival winner, dies aged 39

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:20:58 GMT

O’Brien rode more than 1,000 winners over jumps

‘Tom meant so much to so many people across our sport’

Tom O’Brien, who rode more than 1,000 winners over jumps including five Grade Ones and two at the Cheltenham festival, has died at the age of 39 after being diagnosed with cancer.

O’Brien, who retired from race riding in April 2023, had a close association with Philip Hobbs’s stable near Minehead throughout his 20-year career in the saddle and enjoyed his most prestigious Grade One victories aboard Hobbs’s Thyme Hill in the Stayers’ Hurdle at Aintree in April 2021 and the Kauto Star Novice Chase at Kempton in December 2022.

O’Brien also rode two Grade One winners for Colin Tizzard, on Finian’s Oscar and Elixir De Nutz in the Tolworth Hurdle in 2017 and 2019 respectively, and two handicap winners at the Cheltenham festival: Third Wind in the Pertemps Final in 2022 and Silk Affair in the Fred Winter Handicap Hurdle in 2009.

“He came to our yard from Ireland having not ridden in a race,” Hobbs said on Wednesday, “but it soon became obvious he was pretty talented and he was with us from the start of his career until the end.

“He was in the shadow of Richard Johnson for a long time being second jockey and then became first jockey after Richard retired, which went well. His biggest win was Thyme Hill in the Grade One at Aintree and he was always very reliable and a very good bloke.

“There’s lots of good memories and there were lots of winners and I’d kept in touch with Tom since his retirement as he only lived half an hour away. He was only in our yard about three weeks ago.

“It’s very sad, particularly for his wife, Hayley, and two young children.”

Johnson also paid tribute to O’Brien on Wednesday. “Tom was an all-round great person and you won’t find anyone with a bad word to say about him,” he said. “Whether that was at the races, riding out or travelling in a car to the races, a party, he was just a great person to be around and a person we all enjoyed spending our time with.

“He left a positive mark on all of us. I spent a long time riding with him at Philip Hobbs’s and we never had a cross word, and I think that would apply to anyone you speak to as he was just an all-round good man.”

After retiring from race riding, O’Brien moved to a new role with the British Horseracing Authority’s stewarding team.

“Everyone at the BHA and across British and Irish racing is mourning the devastating loss of our friend and colleague Tom O’Brien,” Brant Dunshea, the BHA’s chief executive, said on Wednesday.

“Tom passed away surrounded by his loved ones following a long and courageous battle with cancer, which he faced with the steely determination and drive that typified the man so many of us knew.

“First and foremost, our thoughts are with those closest to Tom, especially his wife, Hayley, their two young sons and their entire family. We will do everything to support them during this unimaginably difficult period.

“Tom was held in the highest esteem and meant so much to so many people across our sport, who benefited from his kindness and loyal friendship. He touched countless lives on both sides of the Irish Sea, bringing joy to everyone who had the privilege of knowing him and watching what he did best, on and off the racecourse.

“He will be hugely missed and his loss is immensely difficult to process.”

‘Like having your brain squeezed’: Succession’s Jesse Armstrong and more on the rollercoaster of TV writers’ rooms

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:19:58 GMT

As co-writer of new thriller Hunting Alice Bell, our film critic entered the hallowed Room – and was struck by its support, buzz, abrasion and chocolate snacks. He asks legendary showrunners about their experience

‘Write, write, write until your fingers break!” That was Chekhov’s advice to writers. Until I started writing for television I thought I understood what he meant. I thought I knew what writing was: the solitude, the making yourself do it, the finger-shattering pain of doing it seriously, on your own.

As well as being chief film critic for the Guardian, I have written fiction and in some ways the basic technical challenge has not been so very different from cinema criticism; after having had the idea, or having seen the film, you have to go away on your own and turn the computer on.

But TV is different. TV is all about The Room. It’s a learning curve I have tremulously ascended having co-written and executive-produced the forthcoming Channel 4 drama-thriller Hunting Alice Bell, working with head writer and showrunner, David Baddiel. This is about a sports centre manager, living in an ordinary UK town, who gets accused online of being the onetime girlfriend of a notorious serial killer, a woman relocated after her own short jail sentence under a false name, for her own safety. It’s a story of misogyny, online paranoia and digital mob rule.

Before starting work on Hunting Alice Bell, I still had the mindset that writing, with all its mistakes and false starts, was something that happened in forgiving privacy.

The Room is not like that. The Room is about productivity and the creation of story. For Hunting Alice Bell, we convened an intimidatingly super-smart group of writers, including Kate Verghese (who has written for HBO’s Industry), Polly Buckle (who wrote the Netflix hit Love Rat), Stuart Cheetham (who writes for the cruiseship caper The Good Ship Murder) and dramatist David Persiva (who writes for The Teacher) and we gathered round a boardroom table at the production offices, crunching out narrative: plot beats and character arcs. Then the episodes get divvied up for people to go away and write.

We settle in and go episode by episode, talking about simply what happens, not the dialogue. Someone writes it up on a whiteboard in a water-based marker pen (one of the oddities of our room is that it was not typed out on a laptop and projected on the wall legibly. No, it’s the manuscript culture of the whiteboard). It is a collective experience, creativity in real time. The other writers, of whom I was in awe, zapped clever ideas and smart fixes back and forth, although David has the responsibility of final say. His is the loneliness of the long-distance showrunner.

And I learned to contribute, while feeling that creating narrative like this was like having your brain squeezed.

As David says: “The room is fantastic, in terms of creative adventure and possibility. The only thing I would say is you do, in the end, have to do the actual slog of writing the bloody thing, line by line, scene by scene, as before. The difference is that all the ideas and energy and storylining from the room remains in play as you do that work, lessening the slog. It’s like your own exhausted old writing brain is in a complex back-and-forth long-distance, hopefully still productive, non-toxic relationship with the new more youthful communal hive mind of the room.”

From the very first, I personally was obsessed with the handsome plateful of snacks that nestled in the centre of the polished table, their silvery paper glittering like jewellery. There was healthy fruit as well, such as bananas and grapes, and at first I would high-mindedly take a single grape or two while talking about the show, as if this was all the mental bandwidth I could give to eating. It wasn’t long before my blood-sugar was in freefall: I was gobbling KitKats, Penguins and Tesco treats, making a feral keening noise, my face a smudgy chocolatey mask as if it was Christmas Day and there was no work to be done.

Jesse Armstrong, showrunner and creator of HBO’s Succession, told me: “I love it. It’s the one part of working on a television show that I have uncomplicated feelings of regret not to be doing any longer. A good writers’ room can feel wonderful and light, filled with promise and a tingling sense that you’re getting close to the best version of the show. Of course, when you get stuck, on some plot thing or the shape of a whole season, that can feel terrible; you feel that you’re leading a small platoon of brave soldiers to certain death.”

He adds: “In the room, you can experiment. The second season is more relaxed because everybody knows what you’re working with. The downside of later seasons can be the queasy, uneasy feeling that you are writing fan fiction of your own work.”

However, Armstrong says a showrunner sometimes has a tricky task: “You have to make little decisions all day on what direction the room pursues. Usually, the room has its own momentum. But the showrunner has to be the ultimate decider. Someone might say: Shiv should do this. Someone else feels: no – that’s not real. If it’s important, in the end I would have to say: ‘OK, I think this is the way we have to go, for now, I have to make a call on this.’” Buckle tells me: “In the US, they can pay writers tens of thousands of dollars a week to work in rooms, enough money so you can afford to turn everything else down. There can be tension if the producer thinks that the writers should challenge the showrunner. Some people have standup rows. Not me. I’m too much of a people-pleaser. I’ve heard of rooms where people aren’t guaranteed to get an episode to write. Eight people competing for four episodes. It’s a case of ‘dance, monkey, dance!’”

For Verghese, the room is a vital US import: “In this country, I think we don’t spend enough time or money on the story part of the process, and that is what happens in the room. For me, story is like emotional maths. You work out: what the character wants, why they’re doing it, and how the pursuit of their desire ultimately changes them. I’ve been in five-month-long American rooms, some quite alpha rooms. It can be performative and competitive. When the creative alchemy is good, though, it’s such a buzz.”

And eating? “I usually get through about two packs of chewing gum a day – chewing, chewing, chewing,” says Verghese. “On one show, they gave that mannerism to one of the characters: I watched it, and thought: ‘Shit, is that based on me?!’”

So the room can be competitive, fierce, abrasive or supportive. Our room on Hunting Alice Bell was terrifically collaborative and positive, although at the end of the day I had to be stretchered out on a saline drip.

Armstrong says that we in the UK still haven’t got to the US level: “I heard about a room in America that was so big people had microphones so everyone could hear and one writer deliberately crinkled their Coke can on the punchline of every joke another writer else pitched.”

Hunting Alice Bell is on Channel 4 at 9pm on 11 and 12 November.

‘We were quite surprised’: Finland’s embassy in Australia goes viral with staff training day post on Instagram

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:00:50 GMT

After a promotion for a ‘Finnish Dinner Date’ went ‘a bit viral’, the Canberra envoy’s next post became an unlikely social media hit

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The embassy of Finland in Canberra was temporarily closed on Tuesday.

Millions of people across the world were, it turns out, quite upset by this.

A day later, with the flourish of a ribbon-cutting ceremony, the embassy reopened its doors – having garnered many millions of views on its videos, spurred memes seen by millions more and social media attention across the globe, all unexpectedly from an innocuous Instagram post about a staff training day.

“We were all having a nice planning day, then someone said: ‘Oh my goodness, it’s gone completely viral,’” Arto Haapea, Finland’s ambassador to Australia, told Guardian Australia.

The Finnish embassy, nestled in leafy Yarralumla in Canberra’s diplomatic zone just a stone’s throw from Parliament House, isn’t exactly a tourist hotspot in the nation’s capital. Flanked by the embassies of Estonia, Singapore, Mexico and Samoa, the sleek building – all grey panelling and glass – looks more like a bank or an office block than the genesis of a bizarre social media sensation stretching from Europe and the US to the centre of Australian politics.

“The embassy of Finland in Canberra will be temporarily closed on Tuesday, 10 November 2026. Regular hours will resume on Wednesday, 11 November,” @FinlandInAustralia posted on Monday, with text over video of the northern lights glowing an eerie green.

Last week, the embassy’s other Instagram videos were getting like counts in the dozens or low hundreds. The post about the building’s opening hours has, as of time of writing, been liked 622,000 times, shared 405,000 times, and been seen by up to 10 million people worldwide.

How it got picked up by Instagram’s social media algorithm, and supercharged to be seen across the world, is likely something to do with the embassy’s previous video; Haapea promoting a competition to fly single people from around the world to Helsinki for a “Finnish Dinner Date”. The dinner date video also “went a bit viral”, Haapea said, getting 8m views and 163,000 likes.

“We were quite surprised by that,” the ambassador said.

Haapea said his team hadn’t had time to do any deep analysis of why these two clips went unexpectedly viral, but he theorised that the post with the opening hours “happened to ride on the same algorithm” as the dinner date, getting even more views, and attracting influencers, companies and brands around the world to make their own videos.

“POV you’re trying to enter the Embassy of Finland in Canberra but it’s 10th of November,” posted @j. ackdale, knocking on a locked door. That has 604,000 likes on Instagram at the time of writing.

“Me, all the way from Muscat, trying to get answers about the Finnish embassy in Canberra,” posted @sand_and_heels from Oman.

“I’m flying over 300 people from Finland to Australia. Hopefully the Embassy of Finland in Canberra is open today,” posted Finnish pilot @juusojelmer, to 88,000 likes.

That included Finnish politicians and ambassadors around the world, many of whom posted their own jokes, calling their colleagues or reassuring Finns in various countries that their embassies remained open. Haapea said even Finland’s foreign minister was keen to chat.

“We were done with the planning day and did a sauna with the team, and the foreign minister wanted to call about the planning day,” he said, as they filmed a video together – Haapea fresh from the sauna – promising that normal functions of the embassy would resume the next day.

On Wednesday, Canberrans from politicians to radio hosts and journalists visited the embassy, making their own social media clips live from the scene, while ordinary people tried knocking on the door or chatting to Finnish staff. A lighthearted video with a grand reopening, complete with ribbon-cutting ceremony, had to come next, Haapea said.

“We thank the international community for your fascinating interest,” the embassy posted.

As to why the interest in the first place? The ambassador said he’s still not sure.

“I think people are just looking for good news, to take their minds off all the craziness in the world. With the algorithm, and people who are good at making memes, all it took was a few big influencers to make a meme about it,” Haapea said.

From blood group ID to cycle racks: I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:49:40 GMT

There are thousands of small tips to make our country better. People know what is wrong, and it’s clear they have solutions

Have you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your ideas for practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK – whether that’s health, schools, transport, business, housing, policing, justice, tech, shopping, money – or owt else entirely.

The spark for this happened just over a year ago, when I spoke at Politico’s fringe event at Labour’s conference. The key discussion was about Keir Starmer’s unpopularity. I was asked what I’d have advised the government when it took power, so I said: “Come up with 100 small things that piss people off and that you can fix, and they can see that you have fixed them.” Then I reeled off a list of small fixes for my subject area: the counterproductive way council tax debt is escalated; renaming “tax-free childcare”; and so on.

As I walked off stage, I emailed myself: “Set up an Institute for Small Ideas.” I started straight away, did some work, brought some people together, put it out to tender for charities to run it, and then a month ago it launched – albeit with a slight name change. Think of it as a sort of apolitical national suggestion box. And in those few weeks since launch, we’ve already had 42,000 suggestions.

At a time when public debate can feel dominated by division, outrage and disagreement, there’s something quietly encouraging about tens of thousands of people taking the time to offer constructive ideas. Clearly the timing was fortuitous, as small ideas are now all the rage. We haven’t started the filtering process yet, but here are just a few of the ideas that have been suggested:

Tell people their blood group at their first adult blood test. Knowing you’ve a common or rare type may make you more inclined to donate. It’s a brilliantly simple nudge that could widen the donor pool and save lives.

A mandatory “AI-edited” label on property photos on estate agency sites.

A “no wrong door” rule for councils and public bodies: report a problem anywhere, and they must pass it to the right place, rather than bouncing you from department to department, or from council to contractor to agency.

Cycle racks on the back of buses.

Cinema seating plans that clearly show aisles and walkways for disability access.

A voluntary wheelie-bin sharing scheme, so neighbours with spare capacity can help stop bins overflowing.

The idea is that if someone could fix enough of these frustrations and make lives easier, save time and let everyone get on with work or the things they enjoy, the combined effect – and the feelgood factor – would help shift the national mood. To make this happen, I’ve funded the Small Ideas Initiative, with two charities – Nesta and Involve – running a project in the background. (I’m telling you this because I believe funding transparency is crucial in any policy charity.) They will filter the suggestions and hopefully select and publish at least 1,000 of the best to provide a bank of ideas others may look at in future. They’ll pick 200 of these to turn into fully researched policy proposals.

Then, having got public feedback on those, we’ve brought together a cross-party panel – with representatives from Green to Reform and every party in between – who will need to unanimously agree the final 50-ish. These are meant to be useful and doable, not party political or controversial. And if that broad a church can agree on them, we’ve likely succeeded. These 50 will form the first Small Ideas manifesto we will campaign to get implemented.

Since that Labour party conference a year ago, the prime minister has changed of course, and Andy Burnham seems to have taken small ideas to heart. Which means I hope the door may be open for many of these suggestions.

Of course, I’m not suggesting that Britain needs only small ideas. These quick fixes are there to work alongside, not instead of, the longer-term big structural changes that society and the economy need. Yet if you focus only on legacy and not on legwork, it can leave the public feeling detached and with an impression that politics is futile, achieves nothing and is just talk without delivering. Small fixes are still fixes – fix a lot of them and it adds up.

‘I’d steal 10-15 times a day’: ex-offenders on the addictions driving prolific shoplifting

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:10:24 GMT

Former shoplifters say treatment and drug rehabilitation are essential to ending cycle of theft and imprisonment

Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England

When Rhys, 34, stole goods from shops across Birmingham, he would often leave notes for the staff apologising for his actions.

“I’d feel that guilty about it. I’d pass them notes, saying I’m so sorry about this,” he said. “But in the end, I was just that numb to it, and fearless as well. I’d walk in with a suitcase and ram everything into it, and not think twice about it.”

Rhys was in the grips of drug addiction and turned to shoplifting to fund his habit. He had struggled with drug use since he was a teenager and then, in 2019, he took crack cocaine for the first time. “Within a week, I was going into shops and shoplifting for it, because you just can’t get enough,” he said.

Over the next few years, he shoplifted 10-15 times a day and was sent to prison several times. However, without help to tackle his addiction, Rhys struggled to change his behaviour.

“I’d spend hours shoplifting but, at the end of the day, I still wouldn’t have anything to eat. I’d be jumping back over the fence to go through the bins to get myself a sandwich. I wouldn’t even get myself a bottle of water,” he said. “My priority was always getting the stuff to sell for drugs.”

On Wednesday, the home secretary announced plans to target 500 of the most prolific shoplifters across the country with police crackdowns in 17 areas. Measures include banning repeat offenders from high streets and town centres, closer monitoring of offenders with regular hearings before a judge and the use of electronic tagging.

But former shoplifters say many prolific thieves are in the grip of drug addiction or experiencing mental health crises, and without more funding for support services, the problem will not go away.

Keeley, 44, was once labelled Birmingham’s most prolific shoplifter, stealing between £5,000 and £9,000 worth of goods a day. She was sent to prison 28 times. Keeley had been addicted to drugs since the age of 13, after being groomed by an older man, and stole items such as designer handbags, which she could sell quickly to fund her habit. Her biggest fear was withdrawal, which had previously left her in hospital for 10 days.

She said shoplifting was an exhausting necessity – one that often led to her walking 30,000 steps a day. “Shoplifting, to a lot of us, is the closest to a victimless crime as you can get. You’re not violating anyone’s house or privacy, or robbing food out of their mouth.

“I know it’s not right, but it’s what we tell ourselves to justify it at the time – that you’re not hurting anyone – because none of us want to be doing what we’re doing.”

Keeley said she “didn’t get caught much for the amount of stuff that I stole”. Yet she spent three decades in and out of prison, never receiving the help she needed.

She eventually turned her life around when an off-duty security guard referred her to a drug support service, which led to her receiving buprenorphine injections to treat her opioid dependence.

“We’re crying that we’ve got a shoplifting crisis, and we’re crying that we’ve got a drug crisis, but no one’s doing anything about the two together,” Keeley said. “If you treat the root cause and take the addiction away, we’ve got no reason to go out and commit crime.”

For Rhys, help came in the form of an outreach navigator – a professional who connects vulnerable people to social services, housing and healthcare. He has been in recovery for 18 months, spends his time volunteering and has left shoplifting behind.

“I went into Aldi the other day, and I asked for a carrier bag and scanned it straight away. It’s such a weird comparison – now I’m scanning these 30p bags. But before, I was going in there and filling a suitcase to steal,” he said.

The social justice charity Revolving Doors said addiction, poor mental health and homelessness – often all three at once – were substantial drivers of Britain’s shoplifting epidemic.

Pavan Dhaliwal, the charity’s chief executive, said: “The anger of retailers and shop workers is justified. Theft is not victimless, and abuse of staff is intolerable.

“But if we want fewer thefts, rather than just more arrests, we have to ask a harder question: why does the same small group of people keep cycling through crisis and custody repeatedly?”

She said services that can direct people away from addiction and into stable housing were essential. “The people we work with show that recovery and rebuilding lives are possible with the right support.”

Sean, 44, has been to prison 42 times since 2000. For decades, he had not spent more than six months out of custody and felt “powerless to addiction” that drove him to crime after a traumatic childhood.

He stole food and clothes because all his money was spent on drugs, and prison brought no long-term solutions.

“The last five times I was in prison, I was a recovery mentor, taking people on circuits every day in the yard, feeling on top of my game,” Sean said. “But back in Wigan, usually within a couple of days or even a couple of hours, I’d be back doing what I’ve always done. I was completely let down by services.”

It was only when he was picked up at the prison gates by an addiction recovery service and started therapy that his life turned around. Sean now runs Rehab Fitness, which helps people recovering from addiction through group exercise and wellness activities.

He said many of his friends had turned to shop crime because there were “no consequences”, adding that the intervention should be help and support, not prison.

Prison also failed to rehabilitate Roy, 36. He was jailed several times – on one occasion after stealing wine from a shop while under the influence of drugs and alcohol.

“I had money in my pocket. I don’t know why I did it – I couldn’t even remember it afterwards. I was a different person; dead behind the eyes,” he said. “Prison would be a reset but I’d be straight in with the old crowd when I came out.”

Roy managed to get clean, and now runs Iron Minds Academy, which offers physical fitness and mentoring to young men in Wigan. “I just want to stop other young people getting to that point, for them to see there’s another path,” he said.

“When you’re leaving school, no one says I want to be on the streets addicted to heroin. We need to stop it before it gets that far, it can save someone’s life.”

David Walliams: Power and Silence review – some of this footage will make your head spin

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:02:20 GMT

From the visceral accounts of those the comedian allegedly groomed to archive footage of Jonathan Ross joking about him taking 15-year-olds home, this is dizzying TV

David Walliams and his lawyers fought to the last to keep secret the results of a three-year investigation by ITV and the Guardian into claims by multiple women of the comedian and author’s predatory behaviour dating back decades, but those attempts failed and now they have been laid bare before the public.

Accompanying the Guardian’s reports, an hour-long documentary has been released – first on YouTube and now on ITVX. It largely follows what is rapidly and increasingly enragingly becoming a traditional format. Women with claims of historic abuse, perpetrated against them by a famous man apparently enabled by his fame and the people intent on maintaining the freedom of a lucrative asset, sit before a camera and give their testimony. Contemporary footage attesting to the jokes and insinuations in the public domain at the time are shown and mental vertigo sets in. Jonathan Ross introduces the 15th year of the British Comedy awards in 2004 with: “Like all 15-year-olds, it’s drunk, it’s unpredictable and it’s probably going home with David Walliams,” and Alan Carr a few years later likens his approach to women to that of “an illegal taxi driver – you lure them in to a false sense of security and then you pounce”. You wonder at how shocking this now seems, given how little has – in meaningful, practical terms – changed since.

Some of the women have asked for their identities to be disguised, some have not. Some were 15 when they met Walliams, one was 17, some were 18, one was 19. Walliams would generally clock in at around twice whatever age they were. Some were vulnerable because of their youth, some for other reasons – an upbringing in care, perhaps, or previous experience of sexual abuse.

But they all tell similar stories, of being approached and charmed by Walliams, of having attention, invitations to parties, show tickets and gifts lavished upon them, and then of being manoeuvred into sexual scenarios they were not expecting, didn’t want or didn’t feel able to say no to – by virtue of their isolation, his celebrity status, or the psychological debt we now call “grooming” that they were in; usually all of the above. Most of them mention his physical size too: “He’s a big guy”; “His huge head in my lap”; “Quite a looming figure … coming at me.” Rare will be the woman watching who does not respond viscerally to such phrases due to her own experiences of men approaching her.

They also talk of the familiarity that fame breeds, encouraging a degree of trust – especially if you are young enough to have no real idea of how the world works or that you should perhaps not believe in an avuncular facade presented, say, by an endlessly encouraging judge of acts on a popular show such as Britain’s Got Talent.

Occasional phrases strike through the thickening miasma of horrors, often because they suddenly bring the innocence of youth into such painfully stark view. “Alex” was 15 when she and her mum met a 32-year-old Walliams at a Little Britain show signing and she gave him some sketches she had written and a covering letter containing her phone number. He rang her and they talked for an hour. “I was just, like, full of hope and excitement.” “Jade”, also 15 when she met the then 36-year-old Walliams, agreed to go back to his house because “I didn’t think he would want sex. Especially that quickly.” He said they would wait until she was 16 and to stay in touch. She did not.

Beyond the spotlight on Walliams, of course – who denies all the allegations and is variously “mortified” and “devastated” to hear the now-women’s accounts of their experiences – is the vast penumbra in which all those who enable alleged predators reside. A former friend of Walliams, “Ben”, who says he witnessed the pattern of behaviour the women describe, says, “Money, fame, success – everyone wants to be around it, everyone wants to protect it.” “Katie” reported her concerns about Walliams to HR at HarperCollins, the publishing company for whom he was a longstanding bestselling author (they have recently cut all ties with him). She describes unofficial arrangements evolving (not, apparently, in response to her complaints) so that young women were not left alone with Walliams, and adds succinctly that if he had not been such a cash cow, “he would just have been some random creep called Dave.” It is a meticulous hour detailing a meticulous investigation. It is only left to hope that it brings about equally meticulous change.

David Walliams: Power and Silence is on ITVX and YouTube

AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:00:48 GMT

181GW of gas-fired capacity proposed for sites in US and Europe because of delays in connecting to national grids, says report

Developers of AI datacentres plan to build on-site climate-destroying gas power stations on a huge scale to meet their energy demands, research reveals.

Datacentres planned across the US, the UK and mainland Europe have proposals to build fossil fuel plants on-site to create 181GW of gas-fired capacity because of delays to connect to national grids, according to the findings. This is almost four times the total peak electricity demand of Great Britain.

The research by BloombergNEF says this “speed to power” will – if the planned rollout happens – emit about 345m metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year in the US, where 90% of on-site gas-fired power stations are planned. This is equivalent to annual greenhouse gas emissions from about 72.8m fossil fuel cars.

The report was published on Wednesday as global leaders gathered in Turkey for the 31st UN climate summit, where increasing electrification – ideally from clean sources – is a central part of discussions. However, a number of key European leaders, including from France and Germany, will not be at Cop31, instead heading to Dublin where EU leaders will hold their first dedicated AI summit on Friday.

Mark Daly, the head of datacentres and emerging tech at BloombergNEF, said: “The extraordinary economics around AI are making speed to power one of the most important priorities for defining constraints on datacentre developers.

“The climate outcome will depend not only on how much electricity these facilities use, but on how quickly grids can connect them and whether power systems add cleaner generation alongside that demand.”

By 2035, the electricity demand of AI datacentres was predicted to almost quadruple to 2,354 terawatt-hours – equivalent to 7% of global electricity demand – the report said.

AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cool equipment, and to run facility systems.

Daly said while the developers of the future datacentres claimed their gas-fired power supplies would be temporary while they waited for grid connections, once they were online, the economics could encourage them to continue generating energy, creating a longer-term fossil-fuel lock-in risk.

The report said ensuring new datacentres were connected to the grid was the more sustainable option. Faster grid connections were crucial to limiting emissions impacts and locking in fossil fuel risk, it said.

UK planned datacentres made more than 100 inquiries in 2024-5 to connect to gas as a result of delays in securing access to the electricity grid, according to Future Energy Networks, the representative body for the UK gas networks.

For example, Wapseys Wood, Buckinghamshire and Quest Park, Bedfordshire are seeking to build their own on-site gas-fired power stations because of the long wait to connect to the grid. The datacentres are among the first to be fast-tracked through the government’s nationally significant infrastructure project regime, which allows developers to rapidly deliver major infrastructure, bypassing locally elected planning authorities.

But the use of fossil fuel power generation on site is likely to be repeated by many more UK sites after the chancellor, John Healey, gave the green light for datacentres to build and run temporary on-site fossil fuel power stations while they wait for connections to the grid, as part of a so-called datacentre covenant.

Oliver Hayes, the head of policy and campaigns at Global Action Plan , said: “Private gas power stations for datacentres should be a red line for any government serious about climate action, so it’s shocking to see the chancellor give them his explicit backing.

“No one seriously believes these gas power stations will be temporary – once they’re built, they’ll lock in high emissions for years.”

Danny Kelly, football broadcaster and renowned editor, dies aged 69

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 11:56:39 GMT

Danny Baker pays tribute to the ‘funniest man I knew’

Kelly was former editor of the NME and Q magazines

The journalist and broadcaster Danny Kelly, who helped define coverage of music and football in the UK for a generation, has died at the age of 69.

Kelly edited the NME and Q magazine, and launched the Football 365 website before going on to be a presenter and pundit on the BBC and TalkSport. He had been receiving treatment for oesophageal cancer.

Tributes were led by Kelly’s longstanding broadcast partner Danny Baker. “My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon,” Baker wrote on social media, the pair having worked together on any number of radio, TV shows and podcasts. “I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.”

Tottenham Hotspur paid emotional tribute to Kelly, a lifelong Spurs fan. A statement said: “The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly. Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time.”

TalkSport, for which Kelly worked as a presenter for nearly two decades, said it was “heartbroken” by the news. “A cherished part of TalkSport for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves,” the station said. “His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.”

Another broadcaster, the former Sky Sports host Richard Keys, said Kelly “was all of the things – and more – being said about him – ‘warm, witty and knowledgable’”.

Kelly was born in north London in 1956 and first made his name writing about music. He began contributing to the NME in his 20s and went on to edit the agenda-setting weekly newspaper at the end of the 1980s. From there he took charge of the top-selling music monthly Q magazine, where he was named British magazine editor of the year.

Manic Street Preachers paid tribute to “a brilliant broadcaster-writer-ideas factory. Danny was editor of the NME when we first started getting press, a wonderful man, his musical knowledge was vast and deep, his radio voice has been part of our lives for so long … We will all miss him.”

In the second half of the 1990s, Kelly threw himself into the nascent world of digital media and launched Football365, which became one of the leading online voices on the sport. In the noughties, he spotted another development – podcasts – and launched the Game, a weekly football podcast, for the Times.

Over the past 15 years Kelly became best known as a radio presenter and podcast host, including presenting the Tottenham-focused show View from The Lane. Paying tribute to “our host, our leader” on its X account, the View from the Lane said: “We all loved him as much as he loved Spurs.”
