Why are Britain’s streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 06:00:31 GMT

The transition to electric vehicles should be moving apace, but it is not. And why? Incompetence, expedience and cowardice

This is how it works. An industry puts tremendous effort into resisting change: lobbying governments, mobilising the media, pouring money into junktanks. It argues that a transition would threaten jobs, or damage the national interest, or harm poor people, while what it really fears is the cost of retooling its plants or developing new protocols. Then, when the inevitable cliff edge approaches, it whines that change is coming too soon. For reasons beyond its control, it isn’t ready, so the government must delay its plans.

This is what triggered the Dutch nitrate crisis, and the UK’s repeated “emergency” exemptions from the ban on a devastating class of pesticides. Now the same dynamic is driving the UK’s crisis over the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). The result is that, as the global climate summit, Cop31, begins, it looks as if our gift to the world will be a major, predictable and entirely avoidable increase in the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions.

Car manufacturers could have seen this coming more than 130 years ago, when the first electric automobiles were sold. For at least the past 30 years, as new electromotive technologies have progressed at speed, they plainly represented the future, and internal combustion engines, with their hard efficiency limits and vast impacts on human and planetary life, the past. Since 2010, it’s been obvious that China, which has not only seen the future but seeks to own it, would flatten our manufacturers like hedgehogs if they didn’t speed up. In 2023, the Conservative government gave automakers seven years to get their act together. And now they wring their hands and claim to be unprepared. To which the only reasonable answer is: tough.

But, unfortunately, this doesn’t seem to be the answer the government is giving. Instead, on Wednesday it’s expected to cut the target for zero-emission cars from 80% of new car sales by 2030 to approximately 60%. If so, this will be the latest in a series of concessions that governments have agreed since the Conservatives announced the deadline.

Both Conservative and Labour governments have permitted a series of “flexibilities” (otherwise known as loopholes). These allow companies to sell hybrid petrol-electric cars instead of purely EVs. They can also sell a lower proportion of EVs by 2030 on the promise that they’ll accelerate sales after that date. Now the government is also expected to extend the “flexibilities” to 2034, making a mockery of the promise to accelerate after 2030. One retreat after another.

Every one of these slippages has major consequences, for climate breakdown, air pollution, energy security and the cost of living (electric cars, if you can charge at home, are much cheaper to run). The transition to EVs was supposed to be the biggest of all the government’s decarbonisation measures. Now it’s in pieces.

Once again, the problem is the domination of our nominally democratic systems by money. Commercial lobbyists reach ministers long before environmentalists can. As soon as the Conservative government proposed its transition plan, manufacturers pressed to weaken it. This year, they hinted that they wouldn’t invest in future manufacturing here unless the government made further concessions. It looks to me like a legal form of blackmail.

Perfecting the art of unreadiness, the car companies help to ensure that society is also unready for the great crises – from oil supply shocks to climate breakdown – we face. The people they hire deploy an armoury of clever arguments. But while these might sway British politicians, they do nothing to persuade reality, whether that reality consists of the atmosphere or Chinese competitors.

Last month, the Chinese company BYD launched a new Seagull electric hatchback for the home market at just $10,000 (£7,500). It can be flash-charged in five minutes. And where are western manufacturers? Well, Jaguar recently unveiled its reply to Elon Musk’s ill-fated Cybertruck, an unaffordable monster that can scarcely be driven – let alone parked – on our streets. Perhaps the nearest European equivalent to the Seagull, the Volkswagon ID Polo, is much more expensive and you might not get it for months. As the website Autonext comments, “Europe’s carmakers spent 2024 and 2025 telling Brussels that the CO2 targets were unrealistic because buyers would not take small electric cars in the volumes the rules assumed. Volkswagen has now put three of them on sale and cannot build them quickly enough.” Why? Because it didn’t invest in sufficient plants.

The government is now considering imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs, as part of an EU scheme. If you can’t beat them and you can’t join them, block them. So much for addressing the cost-of-living crisis.

As for allowing companies to keep building hybrids rather than EVs, this solves nothing. Hybrids are almost as polluting as 100%-petrol or diesel vehicles; more expensive to run than EVs; incompatible, in most cases, with rapid chargers and destined, very soon, for the scrapheap of history. But, thanks to government policy, last year they accounted for 14% of new car sales, which means 14% of buyers were suckered. The hybrid is the perfect motif for government dithering: given a choice between two technologies, two worlds, two futures, it says yes to both.

after newsletter promotion

The public information campaigns and public honesty required from the government in explaining why a rapid all-electric transition is necessary and what its implications are, as usual, are entirely missing. Public communications remain in private hands. The marketing budgets of the car companies are still used to sell ever bigger child-killing, planet-killing trucks.

An EV transition doesn’t solve all of our transport issues. We should be reducing transport demand, through a shift towards the 15-minute city model of which Paris is an exemplar. We need better and safer provision for cyclists and pedestrians. We need more investment in public transport. But if we can’t even get the end-of-pipe – or end-of-the-tailpipe – issue right, what hope is there for the rest of the system?

This is, or should be, easy politics. Tell the foot-dragging, planet-trashing car companies, the authors of their own failure, where to get off. They face a stark choice: move or get squashed.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

UN chief urges Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia to turn fossil fuel promises into action

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 18:49:36 GMT

António Guterres calls for ‘clear next steps’ as countries face pressure to agree concrete measures

Turkey and Australia, the co-hosts of crucial climate talks, must urgently move from discussing the end of fossil fuels to delivering it, the UN chief has said.

“It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable,” António Guterres said, in a dramatic intervention on the second day of the conference on Tuesday.

“Now, here at Cop31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it.”

The two countries hosting Cop31 are significant exporters of fossil fuels. Early on Tuesday, the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, was extolling his country’s oilfields even as he prepared for his appearance at the summit on Wednesday.

Guterres said the talks should end with “clear next steps” to advance a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels presented to delegates on Tuesday by Brazil, which presided over last year’s talks.

During a presentation with the Brazilians, Guterres – who will step down as UN secretary general at the end of this year and has made the climate crisis a central part of his agenda, often intervening on issues with dramatic language – was energetically backed by the former US secretary of state and climate envoy John Kerry, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, and his predecessor, the Mexican diplomat Patricia Espinosa. He was met by rapturous applause as he left the stage.

Brazil announced at the close of last year’s Cop30 climate summit that it would produce the roadmap. Previewing it last week, the country said an exit from fossil fuels would boost economies and help pull people out of poverty.

Kerry said the roadmap had come “at a critical moment” but “words in conversation don’t cut a single ton of emissions – action does”.

There is growing pressure on this Cop to deliver after several years in which the summits have been criticised for a lack of progress. It took 28 years of annual UN Cop negotiations for the first mention of a transition away from fossil fuels to be included in a final decision, at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023.

Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who inspired global climate protests several years ago, attended this year’s Cop for the first time since 2021,. “Cops have become greenwashed circuses. That is the reality,” she told reporters.

The drama came on the eve of a two-day leaders’ summit at which more than 90 world leaders, including the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, his Australian counterpart, Anthony Albanese, and the newly elected Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, were expected to speak and join negotiations.

Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate thinktank E3G and a Cop veteran, described the presentation of the roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels as “an incredible display of collective firepower”.

“There’s clearly now an expectation that the presidencies [of Australia and Turkey] will pick up the baton from Brazil in some way,” he said. “But it won’t be agreed by consensus here. It took us 28 Cop meetings to get the need to transition away from fossil fuels into a Cop decision.

“This is what we are getting down to and it will be interesting to see how this hybrid presidency responds to this. This is the challenge to this presidency and how they pick up this baton and keep this discussion going.”

A spokesperson for Australia’s climate minister, Chris Bowen, said: “Our message had been clear: countries working together is not only the best way, it is the only way of dealing with climate change and the other crises that countries are facing.

“Before us is the opportunity to make our nations more prosperous, our energy system more secure and the climate more safe.”

The Turkish hosts were approached for comment.

The second day of the conference also saw more than 700 groups, ranging from trade unions to disability advocates, urging diplomats to prioritise a “just transition” for the people who will be hit hardest by a shift to a clean economy.

Organisations from 88 countries demanded a mechanism at Cop31 to turn promises of a just transition into action. Known as the Belém-Antalya Mechanism (BAM), it would seek to support issues including human rights, gender equality and good jobs, while respecting Indigenous rights.

Lidy Nacpil, the coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, said: “Workers and communities, especially in the global south, welcomed and celebrated the Cop30 decision to develop a just transition mechanism – or BAM – which has the promise of delivering real support and action for just transition on the ground.

“However, in pre-Cop, governments of the global north have once again exposed their determination to pour cold water over this promise, by limiting what a mechanism can do and delaying the process of its operationalisation.”

On Tuesday, with 100,000 people attending the talks, many delegates were stuck in traffic for hours. Tram services were crammed with attenders, while some bus journeys took more than three hours.

‘I looked at the sky, something didn’t feel right. Then my buddy messaged: “I see open flame”’

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 12:00:50 GMT

Location: Jasper, Canada

Disaster: Wildfire, 2024

This is Darcy Ruddy’s story

Darcy Ruddy is the owner-operator of an excavation company in western Canada. Just before a wildfire swept through parts of his home town, Jasper, he was finishing work at a nearby luxury heliskiing lodge. Climate change made the higher temperatures the week before the fire and the day it ignited more likely.

I’d landed this big job at a heliskiing lodge in Valemount. I finished 95% and was excited because I was going on this mountain biking trip in the Chilcotins [mountain range]. I was like: “I’m just going to leave the machines here. I’ll go home tonight, grab my camper van, and I’ll move them when I get back.” Had I not done that, I would have lost everything.

As I was driving back into town, there was this intense warm air. It was nice out, but it was stormy. I made a joke that morning: “Big lightning come to town tonight? About time Jasper burns.” Didn’t expect it to happen but, as I drove into town, I looked at my gas gauge and I was like: “I better go fill this thing up.”

At home, I pulled my van into the back. I was looking at the sky and enjoying a leftover gin and tonic. I was like: “Something doesn’t feel right.” My buddy Alex messaged me: “There was a lightning strike out here. I see open flame.” I turned on my radio and my buddy, who works for parks, was evacuating a campground. I could hear the intensity in his voice. Holy fuck, this is it.

I called my dad. He was out for dinner with a friend. I was like: “Dad, pay for dinner, get the hell out of there. We got to start packing.” I ran back into my house and started grabbing things. I got lucky because I had packed all my stuff for that mountain biking trip and it was sitting by the door.

We started getting the alerts. I jumped in my work truck, burning around helping my family. Then I went to my dad’s house. I’m helping him strap his trailer on a truck someone loaned us. I was telling my dad: “Get in the gridlock. I’m going to get in it too.” It was bumper to bumper all the way to Valemount. It was really dark at that point. There was ash starting to sprinkle down. A storm rolled in and there was lightning at Mount Robson. Jesus, it was intense.

The heliskiing lodge manager called me: “You bring all your family.” It’s got 20 rooms. Not many people knew how to get to the lodge. I was up all night finding my aunts and cousins on the highway. Landing my grandmother at 3am in a CMH bed and telling her that there’s a chef for her to cook in the morning was pretty special. I slept in my van out near the road waiting for my dad. I could see how tired he was when I was helping him put the trailer on. He got 30 minutes out of town and, being an old railroader, pulled over to sleep it off.

The next day my family was like: “You could sit here and hold our hand and cry with us, or you could go enjoy the trip you paid for with your friends.” I left early the next day to the Chilcotins. On the way, I had gotten a picture of the Wicked Cup on fire. Fuck, it’s actually happening. I pulled over at the end of Carpenter Lake. It was sunny and beautiful. I sat on the beach, grabbed a beer out of the cooler, and started crying.

That night, Jasper burnt down. But there was no confirmation. Eight of us were sitting on the dock on this little lake, going over photos that leaked online. There was one of the church on fire. My dad’s house is 200 metres away, burning. His house was 200 metres away from mine. So my house is gone.

The next day we tried to enjoy our day and go mountain biking. All of us weren’t thinking correctly, for good reason, and brought only summer clothes. We hit some weather on the top of one of the passes. My house burnt to the ground, but I’m freezing my ass off. At the end of the ride, all our phones lit up because of the news and photos. It was like bang, bang, bang. I remember we were going to do a bunch of biking after that. I felt like I was going to faint if I got my heart rate up. I was like: “Hey guys, I can’t focus on the mountain bike. I’m going to go over the handlebars.”

After the bike trip, I got a call from the municipality. I made a joke: “I bet you don’t need me to do that retaining wall now, eh?” He’s like: “We have to get the pharmacy open, a gas station open, the hospital open, the grocery store open, and fences all around the danger sites in town.” I had a job to do. I’m going back to fix Jasper.

Pulling into town with my excavator, they had police blockades. I thought I was going to have to show them a card, but the guy was like: “Open the gate. Let him in.” Driving through, the town was smouldering. The airfield had just lit on fire. It was all charred black grass that was smoking. The fire was still happening up in the distance. All the municipal guys were standing there with vac trucks, waiting for me to start digging.

When the fire came through, I was like: “OK there’s going to be some damage.” I didn’t think rows upon rows upon rows was completely gone. The log home my dad built with my mom, also burnt. The fire took out my cousin Adrian’s garage and my brother’s shop. My grandpa’s house, now my aunt’s house, burnt to the ground. That was my cousin’s inheritance.

Standing in the ashes, the smell was way different than burnt forest. You’re around burnt chemicals, burnt house, or burnt car. You’d go down alleyways and there would be little streams of aluminum coming from cars because the radiator melted and turned into liquid. I remember this house had one of those aluminum roofs. It had gotten so hot that it turned into rain, dripping all over the back yard. I asked: “Where do you want me to go?” The lowbed driver was like: “Go to Grandma and Grandpa Don’s old house, the back alleyway.” I was like: “You jerk. That’s my next-door neighbour. You’re sending me to my house first?” I go to my house. It was weird seeing things of mine melted and laying on the ground. My great-grandfather had this beautiful old rifle that had been all over the park. You can’t even make bullets for it any more. When I was young, I asked my grandfather: “Can I take that rifle? Maybe we’ll shoot it one day.” I had it up on the shelf locked up in a case. It was laying there, right on the surface, all distorted.

I started demoing and cleaning up Jasper as best I could: driving excavators all over the place, loading up ashes, and pushing them around. I had a lot of pride in fixing town and making sure things were done right because I could sense the vultures trying to swoop in. I think there’s people that made a lot of money on this fire that have never even stepped foot in Jasper. There was even tour buses. People were going to be coming to Jasper to look at bears, now they’re just coming to look at the disaster. Some 60-year-old couple’s in tears as people pick through their ashes looking for the wedding ring. Then a tourist walks up and says: “Hey, what’s going on here? How do you feel right now about this?” Some people were really rude about it. Like: “Go home, dude.” Others were kind.

There was a lot of up in the air. Every day I got up, it was: “What’s the next step?” My friend Pete came to me and was like: “I want you to clear my lot.” He lost his kids in their 20s. Jason was in a driving accident. He was like a brother to me. Calla was two years younger than us. She was at that country show in Vegas and got shot by that dude. Pete’s like: “I want you to go slow and search for Calla’s urn.”

My buddy Greg, who’s working for me, grew up with Calla as well. I was like: “We’re looking for a box this big. Calla had a deer on her urn.” I could see her face when I was searching for her. I remember a photo album popped out of the ground, open to a picture of me and Jason at a toga party. I don’t do much spiritual stuff, but Jason was with me.

Then, Greg was like: “What’s that?” I walked over and there was a little porcelain black box covered in dirt. I picked it up and swiped it off, and there was the deer. Holy shit. She was under a metre and a half of broken concrete and rubble. We found her with an excavator bucket, 100% intact. I called Pete and he came down. I gave Calla to Pete, and he was like: “Intact?” I was like: “Fucking intact.”

On top of learning how to help homeowners, how to do the demos, and how to please Parks Canada, I was also trying to get temporary housing. When I first got to town I was living in my van on the street. A guy that I work with felt bad for me. They shut down their bed and breakfast for the rest of the year, and I moved in for the winter. But, at the end of spring they needed to open up their bed and breakfast.

I moved into my brother’s basement for another month and a half. Then I bought RVs and took my excavator to a friend’s property. I call it my compound. I hold this septic installation ticket [licence] – probably the only one in 200km – and they’re calling me: “Hey can you sign off on above ground tanks at these staff accommodation camps.” I was like: “I’m working so fricking hard cleaning up I think I deserve one of these 25 temporary housings.” They offered me a dorm room, a 38-year-old. I said: “No”. It was almost a year and a half that I didn’t have a full kitchen. I hate eating out now because I did so much of it.

A month and a half or two after people were back, I was invited to a back yard barbecue. It was a friend’s birthday. I walked past my dad’s house and I broke down. I’ve seen my dad’s house 100 times, but I exploded. I stood in the back alleyway for an hour trying to stop crying and I just couldn’t. I had to go home, go to bed. I’m not afraid to cry or anything but I felt like, being a construction guy, I’m a little tougher. I cried after the fire many, many times, but never where I stopped operating. Never that hard.

It feels like the fire might change Jasper’s unique mom-and-pop feel. Growing up here, all the businesses, restaurants, the movie theatre, the hotels, were owned and operated by local families. There’s still a bit of it, but there’s all these big corporations swooping in and buying things up. You had grown up here in character homes. Now, all the houses are going to be from this one era. They’re all going to be green and grey.

It’s changed the community, not only by its appearance. One day, it got really hot out and windy – the fire activity picked up again. One friend just bolted. I’d never seen him so rattled before. That valley didn’t burn and still sits out there with all the dead trees. That’s a lot of anxiety for people. We’re rebuilding this place to potentially burn again.

If I could say anything to you: have an evening with your partner one night and talk about what you would do, which direction you would go, the things you would take, the things you would leave. Get good insurance, and read your insurance, and understand it. Have a few different gameplans. Because I’ll tell you what, I would way rather return to a new house and be able to put your painting back up on the wall than just be like: “No, it’s not actually going to happen.” I joked for 15 years of my life about my home town burning down and then it actually did.

Republicans Begin Aggressive Lame-Duck Push to Install Trump Judges

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The G. O. P. intends to win confirmation of about two dozen federal judges before the party loses power. But Democrats promise to do what they can to stop them.

By Carl Hulse

Reporting from Capitol Hill

Senate Republicans, recognizing that President Trump’s chances for filling federal court vacancies will be slim under a new Democratic majority, intend to muscle through about two dozen federal judges before losing control of the Senate in early January.

Democrats promise to do whatever they can to slow the lame-duck judicial juggernaut that began Tuesday as the Senate Judiciary Committee approved four nominees and sent them to the floor for consideration. But their ability to block it is limited, since Republicans can win Senate confirmations as long as they are willing to devote the necessary time to doing so and can deliver a majority vote.

Top Senate Republicans say that confirming judges is a top priority for them and the president, and that they will keep the Senate in session as long as needed to seat as many on the federal bench as possible. Aides say up to 25 nominees are in the pipeline, including four appeals court candidates and 21 for district courts. They estimate that doing so would consume considerable floor time and keep the Senate in session well into December.

The group includes two nominees to fill vacancies in Texas, whose names were hastily added to the list last week — one without going through the typical review process by senators — after Democrat James Talarico won a Senate seat there last week. Democrats suggested the White House was rushing their nominations in a bid to install them before Mr. Talarico arrived in the Senate and gained the power to derail home-state judicial nominees.

Senator John Thune, the South Dakota Republican serving as the majority leader until January, said members of his party were committed to staying in Washington to seat as many judges and push through as much Republican-backed legislation as they could before being relegated to the minority.

“We’re going to make the most of the time that we’ve got,” Mr. Thune said. “Our conference is committed to being here to do whatever it takes to get as much done as we can.”

The nominees, all conservatives, would fill court vacancies in states represented by Republicans, since Democrats have the power under longstanding Senate tradition to block court picks for their states whom they find objectionable. They have largely resisted those proposed by the White House.

The Texas nominees, in particular, have drawn attention because of the timing of their nominations and the political shift that took place in the state last week.

“We are going to do our best to make sure that Talarico is not denied the basic right of a senator to decide whether a federal district court judge goes forward,” said Senator Richard J. Durbin of Illinois, the senior Democrat on the Judiciary Committee.

The new Texas district court nominees are James Sullivan, a member of the Texas Supreme Court who lost his bid for re-election to that court last week, and Elliott Gaiser, a top Justice Department official who just resigned his job in the agency’s Office of Legal Counsel.

Mr. Durbin called Mr. Gaiser’s connections to the state of Texas tangential, and said that he had issued “unhinged” opinions while serving in the Justice Department.

Senator John Cornyn, a Texas Republican, noted that Mr. Gaiser’s nomination did not go through the usual Texas review process established by him and Senator Ted Cruz, his fellow Texas Republican. He said that he and Mr. Cruz had offered the White House the names of other qualified candidates for the opening in the state’s Northern District.

“I will look at his record and make a decision,” said Mr. Cornyn, noting that it was unusual to “airdrop” in a nominee at the last minute.

Mr. Durbin also accused Senator Charles E. Grassley, the Iowa Republican who chairs the Judiciary Committee, of violating some customary practices of the panel by hurriedly scheduling hearings and not allowing enough time to review paperwork about the nominees. Mr. Grassley dismissed those complaints, saying that Democrats took similar steps in the past and that he broke no committee rules.

“The chairman has always had discretion to set hearings,” Mr. Grassley said. “This committee has always shortened timelines when circumstances warrant it.”

Because of Senate rules changes, judicial nominations are no longer subject to a 60-vote threshold. With Republicans still holding a 53-47 majority, they have the power to overcome any Democratic procedural objections. Federal district court nominees can move through the Senate on an expedited basis in one day once they reach the floor. But those up for an appeals court position can take multiple days to confirm. Democrats can also force other procedural votes to slow the process, and say they will do so.

“We should spare no effort to stop judges who will be on the bench long after we are gone,” said Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut and a member of the Judiciary Committee, about the nominees for lifetime appointments. “I’m going to do everything I can to fight them.”

Democrats were being encouraged to do so by progressive groups who say they should try to hold off Senate Republicans and the president after they were repudiated at the polls.

“The outgoing Republican majority has no mandate to use its final weeks in power to ram through even more extremist judicial nominees who will put loyalty to the thoroughly rejected MAGA agenda above all else,” Svante Myrick, the president of People for the American Way, said in a statement. “Democrats must do all they can to stop this power grab.”

Even if Republicans confirm all 25, it would still put the number slightly short of the 84 judges both Mr. Trump and President Joseph R. Biden Jr. each installed on the courts in the first two years of their terms, according to Mr. Durbin’s office.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

Massie Vows More Tough Votes for G. O. P. in His Final Days

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Representative Thomas Massie, the Kentucky Republican, said he would use his waning time in office to prod his party to vote for “sanity” and break with President Trump.

By Catie Edmondson

Reporting from the Capitol

Before lawmakers even began voting on his effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday, Representative Thomas Massie, Republican of Kentucky, was teeing up another uncomfortable vote for his party, this time a resolution directing President Trump to end the Iran war.

All year long, Mr. Massie, a libertarian who was ousted after feuding with Mr. Trump, has used arcane procedural maneuvers to exert extraordinary control over the House floor, clogging up the schedule with politically tricky votes for the G. O. P. against the wishes of its leaders.

Speaker Mike Johnson has sent the House home early twice this year to shield Republicans from voting on measures that Mr. Massie has raised, first on releasing files related to the accused sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein, and again on the impeachment resolution.

With just a few weeks left on the legislative calendar before the G. O. P. loses control of Congress and Mr. Massie surrenders his seat, he shows no signs of stopping, promising more forced votes and inconvenient moments on the floor even after his impeachment drive failed to pick up a single Republican vote.

On Wednesday, Mr. Massie secured enough bipartisan support for his bid to force the House to vote on another law tied to the Epstein files, this one to compel the release of more files and allow for lawsuits to obtain withheld material.

“I’ll give them every chance I can for them to vote for sanity before I leave,” Mr. Massie, 55, said in an interview after the vote to block the Hegseth impeachment charges. “And if they pass on the sanity vote, then — I mean, they’re all going to be up for election in 2028.”

It is a fitting coda to Mr. Massie’s 14-year career in Congress. Known as “Mr. No” for much of his time on Capitol Hill, the Kentucky Republican has exulted in weaponizing the minutiae of congressional procedure to suit his libertarian agenda of shrinking government, slashing spending and disentangling the United States from foreign conflicts.

In 2015, he helped write the motion to oust Speaker John Boehner that ultimately sent the Ohio Republican into an early retirement, a screed framed on his office wall. In 2020, he single-handedly called the House back to cast an in-person vote on the $2 trillion coronavirus pandemic stimulus bill, a one-man revolt that sent lawmakers across the country scrambling back to the Capitol, earning him heaps of bipartisan scorn.

More recently, he has gleefully played the role of his party’s foil as Mr. Trump has commanded near-total loyalty from other Republicans. In addition to the Epstein files and the Hegseth impeachment, he forced a vote on whether to oust Mr. Johnson for allowing a Ukraine aid package to come to a vote.

He also refused to back Mr. Trump’s marquee tax and spending cuts legislation because he argued it added too much to the debt, and has repeatedly voted against the war in Iran. He backed Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida in the 2024 G. O. P. presidential primary, even joining him on the campaign trail.

All of it has earned Mr. Massie invectives from the top of his party all the way down. Mr. Trump called him “a total loser.” Mr. Hegseth at a news conference on Tuesday dismissed the impeachment resolution as “a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” led by “one disgruntled guy.”

By the end of the day, Mr. Massie’s G. O. P. colleagues were piling on.

“Massie losing his primary doesn’t make policy disagreements impeachable offenses,” Representative William Timmons of South Carolina wrote on social media.

Mr. Massie met his defeat with equanimity.

“The Republican conference hit an iceberg on Nov. 3, and I felt like I was bringing them a life raft,” he said in the interview after the vote. “I felt like the most likely people to vote for this wouldn’t be the ones who lost their elections, but the ones who are looking toward 2028 and are trying to put some daylight between themselves and the president. And none of them decided to get on my life raft.”

Mr. Massie, almost shrugging, continued: “The whole town has lost it over Trump. It’s a form of Trump derangement syndrome, where they can’t break away from Trump. They can’t even cut a path that’s a little bit away from Trump.”

There is, famously, little love lost between the two men. Mr. Trump marshaled his power as the most influential force in Republican primaries to find and back a G. O. P. challenger to Mr. Massie, Ed Gallrein, who prevailed earlier this year in a race that became the most expensive primary in the country.

“I think because I’m the only one who has broken from this administration, it was easy to make an example of me,” he said.

But Mr. Massie’s electoral loss only appears to have emboldened the puckish congressman, an M. I. T.-trained engineer and self-styled homesteader who champions raw milk and has invented dozens of gadgets, including the tiny electronic badge he wears on his lapel that displays the national debt.

Having extensively studied the precedents that govern the House, he recently took advantage of a little-used rule that allows any member of Congress an hour of time on the floor to rebut a colleague’s denigrating remarks.

He invoked that rule in September, after a visibly annoyed Mr. Johnson dismissed his prediction that G. O. P. leaders would send the House home early to stymie progress on the second bill related to the Epstein files. Mr. Johnson called Mr. Massie’s comment “nonsensical” and made by someone “who is not participating as a full member of the Congress.”

The result was a broadside by Mr. Massie that spanned his legislative career, from his work to release the Epstein files to the national debt. He also lamented what he suggested was the dumbing-down of Congress, at one point stiffening his arms and making mechanical-sounding noises to mimic what he called “robot” congressmen reciting speeches written by aides or generated by artificial intelligence.

In the interview on Tuesday, he said he worried that once he was gone, no Republican would have the nerve or ability to employ the kinds of guerrilla tactics with House procedures that he had made his calling card. Mr. Massie has only been able to circumvent House leaders with the support of a handful of other Republicans who will also be leaving Congress next year.

“I would like to transfer this knowledge to somebody,” Mr. Massie said, “but I don’t know that people would do anything with it. They’re terrified.”

Instead, he predicted that Republicans would “stay in this suicide pact with Trump, and the Democrats, recognizing that, are going to force some crazy votes” on the president’s statements and actions.

Not long after the failed impeachment vote, it was Democrats who signaled they would follow Mr. Massie’s lead once he was gone. Representative-elect Richard Ojeda, Democrat of North Carolina, who flipped a Republican-held seat in one of the early upsets of last week’s midterm elections, approached Mr. Massie in a hallway in the Capitol to thank him.

Mr. Ojeda, using an expletive, told Mr. Massie: “We’ll finish this next session.”

Michael Gold contributed reporting.

Catie Edmondson covers Congress for The Times.

If America Isn’t a Center-Right Country, What Is It?

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

By David Wallace-Wells

Opinion Writer

Come January, three-quarters of Americans will be living in states with Democratic governors, including nine of the 10 biggest states and nine of the 10 richest ones.

This isn’t just a blue wave, or a repudiation of the president, or a cost-of-living revolt. It tells us something profound about the nature of the country and the spiritual life of our politics, where not just policy and ideology are hashed out but also the deeper meaning of everything from music and movies to fashion and food culture, educational attainment, economic opportunity, income inequality and much more besides.

For a long time, Americans thought of their country as decidedly right of center and irreconcilably polarized, divided by partisanship so intense that the conflict was sometimes compared to a civil war. But in the aftermath of an electoral rout, the map looks quite different. To put it bluntly, it all looks pretty deeply blue.

The reconfiguration of the political map by this blue tsunami probably isn’t permanent. I would guess Democrats will notch another victory in 2028, much as they did in 2008 after a huge midterm victory in 2006. But those races are obviously still up in the air, and these days it often seems that politics is balanced on a knife’s edge, with neither party capable of securing a significant advantage.

This is precisely what makes the scale of the romp so remarkable. By popular vote, Democrats seem to have notched the biggest victory any party has achieved in congressional elections in 50 years. In the new Congress, Democrats will have more House seats than Republicans have at any point since the Depression. If Scott Colom’s lead in Mississippi and Mary Peltola’s lead in Alaska both hold up, Democrats will have more Senate seats than Republicans have had at any point since the early 1920s.

The state-level triumph is so broad — Democrats will now control a majority of legislative chambers, and have more trifectas than Republicans for the first time since 2009 — that Democrats could pass the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact to bypass the Electoral College. And yet as a purely partisan matter that particular project seems much less pressing, suddenly, because there isn’t such an obvious Democratic disadvantage left to erase. Those swathes of the electoral map that used to look like Republican fortresses — the Old South, the Sun Belt and the Great Plains — are no longer red but purple. In some cases, just blue.

There could very well be a Democrat representing Mississippi in the Senate come January, and there will be another representing South Carolina. Blue Texas isn’t a progressive dream anymore. It has happened, and pretty emphatically: Democrats won not just the open Senate seat and the governorship but also control of the State House. The Texas land commissioner is now a Democrat, as are the agriculture commissioner and the railroad commissioner. Ted Cruz is the only Republican who will still be holding statewide office.

The biggest shock is how consistent it all seems: Nationwide, Democrats won the House popular vote by more than 13 points.

Above all, the midterms were a devastating verdict on Donald Trump and a rebuke to MAGA — which is now, according to exit polls, a phenomenon not much bigger than Democratic Socialism. A liberal coalition this big contains multitudes, which is one reason the election has given way to some intense factional infighting about what the victory tells us about the future of the Democratic Party.

In truth, it told us a lot of different and contradictory things. Candidates mixed remarkably strident class-warfare messages with a variety of gestures toward big-tent social moderation. But there was little in the way of an actual policy agenda visible to a national audience. Instead, candidates seemed to want to coast in on anti-Trump vibes: anti-inflation and anti-corruption, anti-plutocracy and antiwar.

One cautious way of interpreting the results is to say they don’t tell us all that much. You could see them as only the latest backlash election in what I’ve been calling our age of whiplash politics, in which even large majorities are fleeting almost everywhere in the world and meaningful political change has become incredibly difficult as a result.

That context still holds. But you simply can’t get liberal majorities like these in what has so often been described, across that long history, as a libertarian nation, or a conservative one, a center-right country or, more recently, a MAGA majority. The math gets even harder given gerrymandering, the imbalance of campaign financing and the structural bias of Senate power, which hugely advantages rural and sparsely populated states over denser and more urban ones.

A tremendously unpopular president helps, of course, and the results should humiliate anyone who ever argued Trump possessed some supernatural hold on the country. But under conditions like these, you can only win big liberal majorities if the country itself, as a whole, is left of center.

How far left remains up for debate — or, rather, determination. Yet even in this whiplash period, the Democratic backlashes are proving much bigger than the Republican ones, because the country’s actual center of gravity remains much more Barack Obama than Donald Trump.

Nationwide, the Democratic victory in the House is, by popular vote, twice as large as Republicans have managed in any race since 1984. Republican presidential candidates have reached 50 percent of the vote just once since 1988, when George W. Bush beat John Kerry by 2.4 percentage points in 2004.

The structural bias in the Senate isn’t about to change anytime soon, but whatever you might’ve heard a few years ago about what it would take to flip that chamber — about the need for more anti-abortion Democrats, or liberal independents who might avoid the toxic Democratic brand — if Scott Colom prevails in Mississippi, the party will have won Senate seats in 43 different states since 2008, as Nate Silver pointed out. With all their structural advantages, Republicans have won them in just 35.

This is a chaotic and disorderly nation politically, full of plenty of conservatives and even more citizens full of nonpartisan frustration and rage. The Democrats do not now have the mandate of heaven thanks to just one electoral blowout, and even this huge majority doesn’t quite vindicate the long-derided “emerging Democratic majority” thesis of the early Obama years — let alone secure that majority for a generation. No political majority looks all that long-lasting anywhere in the world these days, though the success of Mark Carney in Canada and Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico suggests that we may be turning a corner globally, as well.

But perhaps conservatives were onto something when they insisted on describing themselves, across both Trump presidencies, as embattled insurgents fighting an entrenched liberal elite. For all their norm-breaking swaggering and imperious brutality, theirs was always a fleeting, minoritarian claim on power. It’s a shame and an embarrassment, looking back, that so many universities and law firms and media organizations failed to see things as clearly — capitulating, just in time for the vibes to shift again.

Remember hearing that MAGA had laid claim to the future of pop culture? The biggest act the Trump White House managed to book for the country’s 250th birthday party was Flo Rida. Hollywood never went centrist, let alone MAGA, and Tesla just announced the Cybertruck was being discontinued. “The Daily” from The New York Times has been at or near the top of the podcast app list for years.

On the campaign trail in 2019, Joe Biden described MAGA as a kind of national fever that would break once Trump was defeated, with Republicans who’d enabled the president so slavishly shame-facedly coming to their senses. Biden was mocked when, after his victory, that fever didn’t break but intensified. It does feel like it’s broken now. But what has been revealed?

In certain ways, the political landscape looks like it did 12 years ago — Obamaism with a new Zohran twist. The 44th president is the most popular political figure in the country, and many of the Democratic leaders given new prominence by this wave election came of age in the Obama years, as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez pointed out after election night, which she described as a hopeful redux of 2008.

The rhetoric of Democrats, too, fused quite explicit and moralistic populism with old-fashioned appeals to homespun common sense and community tradition — with some of the party’s leading lights literally sounding like Obama every time they took the stage. “The Resistance” was really rump Obamaism by another name, and it emerged from this election much mocked, looking nevertheless like a resurgent force in Democratic politics — now given new energy by anti-establishment populism as much as it was genuinely displaced by it.

The map, too, looks like a delayed prophecy from the Obama years. The Washington suburbs, the research triangle, the Atlanta sprawl and the big blue cities of Texas — these knowledge-economy cities and suburbs of the broad Sun Belt are the country’s growth spots of the last 15 years, and they are all drifting left.

And yet what has given Democrats the biggest wave election in living memory is not exactly liberal triumphalism. It’s more like the opposite, with national confidence in the Democratic Party far from some all-time high. The country has been battered by a decade-long assault on its institutions and its ideals, which has left some liberals skittish, nervous to dare anything, and others angry and unwilling to compromise.

The policy landscape looks different, too, with many of those longstanding crusades we once used to orient ourselves, has dropped away in salience. Perhaps the country has grown somewhat less anxious about climate chaos; abortion and crime have almost fallen off the radar entirely. Immigration has become less charged as the number of migrants apprehended at the southern border has fallen dramatically, though the fight may well reignite again, and it’s not exactly clear what new bargain Democrats are aiming for.

More broadly, the party doesn’t seem inclined to raise taxes on anyone except perhaps the very, very rich, and though Democrats are coming into power on the basis of cost-of-living complaints, they don’t seem prepared to propose any large new social programs to alleviate them. It’s not hard to imagine an out-of-power Republican Party getting religion again on the deficit and size-of-government issues, but one notable feature of the Trump years has been how much less focused on cutting entitlements the G. O. P. became. And it’s not at all clear what a post-Trump conservative coalition would really be for.

The result is a kind of political agoraphobia, in which both the political landscape and the policy agenda look dizzyingly indeterminate. Presumably, in the next few months, we’ll begin to hear from congressional Democrats about A. I. policy proposals, good-governance legislation, anti-corruption investigations and perhaps some more of health care expansion, likely short of Medicare for all. On the very first day of business for the new Texas state legislature, Democrats filed bills to expand Medicaid, repeal the state abortion ban, raise the minimum wage, end tax incentives for data centers, limit the use of Flock cameras and stop the construction of border walls in state parks.

But where will national Democrats go on immigration or Gaza? Will there be permitting reform? Will there be an actually effective affordability agenda? Will any of these policy proposals actually matter to voters? The horizon looks pretty wide open to me. But that sky looks pretty blue, too.

Trump Hints at Immigration Deal, Then Reverses. He’s Done That Before.

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Democrats and some Republicans say President Trump is missing an opportunity to find consensus on an issue that has bedeviled past administrations.

By Zolan Kanno-Youngs

Zolan Kanno-Youngs, who covers the White House, reported from Washington.

When President Trump suggested he was open to finding a compromise on immigration after last week’s midterms, Democratic lawmakers and conservative allies rushed to assess whether the president was truly pulling a U-turn on a policy central to his political identity.

Senator Richard J. Durbin, Democrat of Illinois, called for Mr. Trump to “keep your word” and work with lawmakers to pass legislation that would provide legal status to certain undocumented immigrants brought into the country as children. Mr. Trump’s homeland security secretary acknowledged he was fielding calls from Democratic lawmakers interested in a deal on immigration policy. Mr. Trump’s conservative allies accused him of pursuing “amnesty” for immigrants.

Then, just as quickly, the president flipped again, shutting down the idea that he was softening his position.

“We have a very strong deportation policy; there’s no amnesty, no, no anything. We keep that,” Mr. Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday, adding that he had not told Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration agenda and his new chief of staff, to make any changes to the administration’s efforts to deport millions. “My policy hasn’t changed.”

The president’s conflicting signals were the latest case in which he has indicated he is open to scaling back his hard-line policy when faced with pressure from voters or business leaders, only to revert to aggressive deportation and border policies.

Newly empowered Democratic lawmakers and even some members of Mr. Trump’s own party say the president is now botching an opportunity to do what many of his predecessors failed to achieve: forge consensus on changes to an immigration system long seen as broken.

Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, released a television ad during the midterm campaign criticizing Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown for going too far. She noted it was a Republican president, Ronald Reagan, who signed a landmark immigration bill in 1986.

“You can surpass Reagan’s legacy,” she wrote on social media, “by delivering a historic immigration reform.”

Mr. Trump’s rapid zigzagging in the last week shows how much he recognizes the political cost of what has been one of the defining policies of his presidency.

During a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday, the president suggested that immigrant workers who have lived in the United States for years — many of whom have been targeted by his own administration — should be granted some kind of protection from deportation.

“When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that’s worked there as — you know, as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden, they’re being taken out of the country, it’s tough,” Mr. Trump said. “But there’s a group of people that, I would say, on the sort of pretty far right that would like everybody taken out.”

Mr. Trump said he still wanted to deport “killers” and “drug dealers” but also “let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them.”

The president’s remarks, which aired on Sunday, jolted both the left and the right.

“The takeaway from the midterms should NOT be to moderate our views on immigration,” Representative Keith Self, a Republican of Texas, wrote on social media. “Amnesty of any form would be a massive betrayal of this trust.”

Representative Delia Ramirez, a Democrat from Chicago, whose mother crossed the border while pregnant with her, challenged Mr. Trump to emulate Mr. Reagan on immigration.

“If Donald Trump decides it’s been 40 years, it was a Republican who did it in 1986 and I’m going to be the Republican that does it again, then prove it, show it,” she said.

Indeed, on the very same afternoon that Mr. Trump taped his “60 Minutes” interview, he named as his chief of staff Mr. Miller, who has helped set in motion a mass deportation policy that has widely targeted immigrants without legal status in the nation.

Mr. Miller held a call with homeland security officials the morning after the election encouraging them to carry out the deportation agenda as usual, even as the president was suggesting in public he was open to making a deal with Democrats.

Mr. Trump’s aides have dismissed the idea that many voters rejected the administration’s immigration agenda, citing polling showing that immigration enforcement remains deeply important among Republicans. Public polling, however, also showed that voters trusted Democrats more on the issue, on which Mr. Trump had an advantage in 2024.

“The reality is that the Democrats’ immigration policies are massively unpopular,” Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement, calling that “a key reason President Trump won in a landslide in 2024.”

She noted Mr. Trump’s success in reducing border crossings and ramping up deportations. “If the Democrats want to advocate for another mass invasion of illegal immigrants into our communities, it’s political suicide for 2028,” she added.

Ms. Rogers did not respond to questions about whether Mr. Trump supports any of the various immigration proposals currently stuck in congressional gridlock, including one that would provide protection to so-called Dreamers, immigrants who came into the country illegally as children.

During an interview with Fox News on Tuesday, Mr. Trump’s homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, expressed some sympathy for such individuals, saying that “they were brought here at no fault of their own.” But he added that the administration would consider a deal providing protection to those immigrants only if “our base is with us on it.”

“They’re not with you,” responded Laura Ingraham, a Fox News anchor.

Mr. Mullin noted that Mr. Trump would not back anything that “isn’t in the right movement for this country and the Republican Party.”

Andrea Flores, an immigration analyst who worked as an adviser for the Biden and Obama administrations, said Mr. Trump had an opportunity to become ”the president who finally legalized millions of undocumented immigrants while keeping the border secure.”

She and other experts note that Mr. Trump had already successfully changed the politics of immigration. For decades, Democrats pushed Republicans to agree to provide immigration relief in exchange for investments in border security or enforcement. But after Mr. Trump attacked the Biden administration over a ballooning border crisis, many Democrats came to gradually emphasize the need for strong border security.

“Trump has fundamentally changed the politics of immigration in the United States, and Democrats have been on their back foot on this issue ever since he came to power,” Ms. Flores said. She added, “His miscalculation in pursuing a mass deportation campaign on a scale no other president has attempted has created an opening for a new immigration debate that is about more than just the border.”

It is not the first time Mr. Trump has teased his openness to an immigration deal, only to move ahead with his restrictionist agenda.

David Lapan, a former spokesman for the Homeland Security Department in Mr. Trump’s first term, recalled how the president initially pledged to help protect people brought illegally to the United States as children only to abandon a bipartisan compromise to shield them.

“He’s given us no reason to believe things that he says like that,” Mr. Lapan said. “He switches positions frequently.”

When the Dreamers bill fell apart in 2018, Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican, blamed the man who is now Mr. Trump’s chief of staff. “As long as Stephen Miller is in charge of negotiating immigration, we are going nowhere,” Mr. Graham told reporters on Capitol Hill.

Mr. Trump also helped sink a bipartisan border security bill in 2024, at the end of President Joseph R. Biden’s term, that would have also provided money for Ukraine. Mr. Trump and House Republicans were pushing for severe immigration measures that would have not have passed the Democratic-controlled Senate at the time.

In his second term, Mr. Trump has at times shown his willingness to carve out exceptions to his hard-line policy, albeit temporarily.

When farmers and agriculture groups voiced alarm over the immigration crackdown last year, Mr. Trump posted on social media that immigrants in those industries were “very good, long time workers” and that he would be making changes to protect them.

The administration then issued guidance to largely pause raids at agriculture sites, meatpacking plants, restaurants and hotels — absent other criminality like human trafficking or drug smuggling. That caught some in the White House by surprise.

While agents were directed to ease enforcement at those sites, some advocates say immigration enforcement has continued on farms throughout the United States. And immigrant workers are still at risk once they leave their work sites. Just before the midterms, an uptick in ICE activity rattled agriculture communities in California, discouraging many workers from showing up at their jobs.

In January, after immigration officials fatally shot two American citizens in Minnesota, Mr. Trump said the administration could use a “softer touch.” The administration briefly scaled back its deportation strategy amid national outrage over the shootings.

Immigration arrests surged again this summer as the administration targeted people through operations at hospitals and at airports, traffic stops, courthouses and along rural construction sites and truck stops.

Mr. Miller, who convenes regular calls with homeland security officials to monitor progress on deportation goals, has in the past year encouraged them to find new ways to target and arrest people without legal status. He has also championed the removal of immigrants to third-party countries where they have no ties, a program that has resulted in many migrants being sent to countries with poor human rights conditions.

Mr. Trump has acknowledged Mr. Miller’s influence in shaping immigration policy.

“Stephen’s a very strong voice,” Mr. Trump said during an Oval Office interview with The New York Times in January. “I don’t think I disagree with him, no.”

Madeleine Ngo contributed reporting.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

How Democrats Invested Online to Overcome Their Cash Disadvantage

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Strategists for Senate Democrats say they spent record sums reaching voters, particularly younger ones, on nontraditional platforms such as YouTube and various streaming sites.

By Emily Davies

From the start of the year, Senate Democrats knew they were unlikely to catch up to the Republican Party’s significant cash advantage.

So they devised a way to make their money go further, by investing heavily in a digital advertising program that strategists now say became one of the building blocks of their sweeping success in last week’s elections.

The Senate Majority PAC, the political arm of Senate Democrats, spent $215 million on its digital program this cycle, a 60 percent increase from such spending in 2024, Lauren French, the group’s communications director, said in an interview.

Buying ad time on streaming services and smart TVs is not only cheaper than doing so on broadcast or cable, but it also allows advertisers to more precisely target the voters they are trying to influence, whose fractured viewing habits limit the reach of traditional ads.

One of the key groups they reached this way, Ms. French said, was younger voters. Indeed, voters between the ages of 18 and 29 shifted toward the Democrats by 34 points, a New York Times analysis found, the most dramatic swing of any demographic.

The emphasis on digital spending marks a full circle moment for the party, which had been playing catch up to the Republicans’ online presence for nearly a decade, but now has a moment to show off its progress. In 2024, when Democrats had the financial upper hand, President Trump’s super PAC invested significantly in ads on streaming services and smart TVs.

While the Democrats’ new majorities in the House and Senate were driven by a number of causes — including widespread dissatisfaction over President Trump’s war in Iran and persistently high prices — Ms. French attributed some of the victory to the digital program. In general elections this cycle, Republicans spent about $250 million more on ads than Democrats in Senate races. Of 14 battleground contests, they lost all but two.

“They are going to beat us on money,” she said of the Republican Party apparatus this year. “But we are going to beat them on strategy, efficiency, creativity and effort.”

Republicans invested online, too. The Senate Republicans’ top super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, spent more than $200 million on streaming and social media this cycle, Axios reported last week. Mr. Trump’s political operation also flooded Facebook and Instagram with ads in the final days of the election as part of its digital push.

One of the front lines of the battle for voters’ attention this cycle was YouTube, where the Senate Majority PAC spent more than $75 million, the most of any Democratic spender this cycle, Ms. French said. The super PAC also continued to invest in the network of online influencers it began building through its nonprofit in 2020.

The Democratic National Committee, too, saw an opportunity not only to focus on turning out its loyal base, but also to persuade fence-sitters to break its way. The organization said it worked with more than 500 influencers and set up unbranded accounts to focus specifically on such persuasion tactics.

The Democratic Governors Association spent seven figures on its influencer program, said Olivia Davis, the group’s spokeswoman. That spending involved hiring and setting up infrastructure to work with influencers across the country.

“It paid off, with Democrats now holding the majority of the nation’s governorships for the first time since 2010,” she said.

To work with influencers, the Senate Majority PAC created “clip libraries” of opposition research and other information on marquee races, then distributed them to hundreds of progressive content creators, said Amanda Ach, the super PAC’s digital director.

Some of those creators were paid to work with the party. The super PAC treated others more like mainstream reporters, leaking them information to aid the party’s candidates and hurt its opposition.

The super PAC also worked with what it deemed “lifestyle creators,” or online influencers who post less than a quarter of the time about politics.

Early in Alaska’s Senate race, the super PAC conducted a study that showed exposure to just one of its creators increased negative feelings about Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, by 11 percent, Ms. Ach said.

Ms. French and Ms. Ach both declined to identify the influencers they paid to amplify the Democratic Party’s message. Such paid advocacy is difficult to track. The Federal Election Commission’s rules governing disclosure of traditional political advertising do not apply to social media, and the Federal Trade Commission’s rules requiring disclosure of paid commercial posts on social media do not apply to political content.

By the end of the cycle, the super PAC had worked with more than 800 influencers to generate 750 million views, Ms. French said. In the final week of the cycle alone, the program was generating more than 10 million views a day.

“You want people to see great exchanges from Democratic politicians and not so great comments by Republican politicians in the format that they’re consuming all other media,” Ms. Ach said. “Because then it doesn’t feel like an ad and it doesn’t feel like spin.”

Emily Davies is a political correspondent for The New York Times.

An 8-Year-Old Was Separated From Family and Taken by ICE at a Check-In

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The third grader from Haiti had been living with his uncle’s family since his father was deported last year. From a shelter where ICE sent him, “he cried and just begged to come home.”

By Miriam Jordan

Miriam Jordan is a national immigration correspondent chronicling the effects of the Trump administration’s policies.

The boy walked silently, flanked in front and back by immigration officers. He had reported for an appointment with U. S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in San Diego with his uncle and his uncle’s family. He was taken away alone.

A 36-second video of agents escorting the child from an interview room to an elevator ricocheted across social media this week — in part because the footage shows the boy holding his arms in front of his body, prompting speculation of restraints.

Immigration agents determined that the boy, an 8-year-old from Haiti, was an unaccompanied minor, despite documentation from his uncle that his family had been tapped as the boy’s caregivers. Members of Congress wrote to Trump administration officials on Tuesday, demanding information about the boy’s case, his whereabouts and the possible use of restraints.

In his first interview since the boy was detained, his uncle Edmard Volmy said he had cared for the boy since his father, who worked as an Uber driver, was deported in 2025 after mistakenly crossing into Mexico and trying to re-enter the United States.

“He’s part of our family,” said Mr. Volmy. The boy and his father had lived with Mr. Volmy’s family since their arrival in the United States in 2019. They later gained Temporary Protected Status, a legal safeguard that allowed them to live, work and go to school without risk of deportation. The Trump administration revoked T. P. S. for Haitians in July, leaving hundreds of thousands vulnerable to detention and deportation.

The boy called his aunt “mama” and was treated as a beloved little brother by his two teenage cousins, Mr. Volmy said. The boy was thriving in the third grade, said Johana Bielma, the principal of Fay Elementary School, which he had attended since preschool.

“This has devastated us,” Mr. Volmy said. His lawyer, Robert Ferretti, who was not officially representing the child, said in an interview that Mr. Volmy had provided a notarized letter in which he was appointed by the boy’s father as the child’s caregiver.

Mr. Ferretti said an officer told him that the letter was not acceptable and that a court guardianship order was required.

The boy was separated from his family and escorted to a room where four officers stood watch, as an ICE agent delivered the news that the boy was being detained and would be sent to a migrant center, Mr. Ferretti said.

He also recalled that an ICE officer had told the boy, “It’s going to be fine. They have ice cream and video games.”

In response to questions, the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “a man claiming to be the child’s uncle” had brought the boy to the immigration check-in, his first since his father was deported.

“Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement,” the statement read. The agency said the boy was taken into custody as an “unaccompanied alien child.”

D. H. S. did not confirm or deny that the boy had been restrained.

As the Trump administration has intensified its immigration crackdown, lawyers and advocates have encouraged parents at risk of deportation to prepare legal documents, such as powers of attorney, authorizing relatives or friends to care for their children if they are detained. However, many do not have this safeguard.

“Unfortunately, when parents gets detained or deported, they aren’t allowed to go back and put a legal guardianship in place,” said Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, a national advocacy group.

Immigration authorities could have allowed the boy to stay with his family, said Mishan Wroe, directing attorney at the National Center for Youth Law, a legal advocacy organization.

“D. H. S. could have exercised discretion,” she said. “Instead, they chose to send him to a shelter where he will be alone rather than in school and with people who love him.”

On Tuesday, Democratic members of the House and Senate from California sent a letter to Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security secretary, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health secretary, demanding answers about the case and what steps were being taken to reunify the boy with the family.

“Video footage appears to show the use of restraints on a child who seemed to pose no threat to those around him, raising serious questions about the handling of this incident,” the lawmakers wrote.

The office of Representative Juan Vargas, among the signatories, said it had not yet received any information on the case or the child’s whereabouts.

Mr. Volmy, the uncle, said that he and his family reported to ICE with the child after receiving letters instructing them all to appear for a check-in on Nov. 4.

The woman who recorded the video, Karen Pohl, a 70-year-old retired Master Chief and civil servant in the Navy, said she spends three days a week at the federal building as an observer of ICE check-ins.

“This is the youngest person I have ever seen detained alone,” Ms. Pohl said.

Because she filmed from behind, Ms. Pohl said that it was impossible to see whether the child was restrained.

After the boy entered the elevator with the men, Ms. Pohl said that she rushed to a railing that overlooks the lobby, hoping she would spot him. When he failed to appear, she feared he had been detained.

Near the waiting area, she encountered Mr. Volmy and his family as they were leaving. The children were sobbing, Ms. Pohl said.

Late on Monday, Mr. Volmy said that he had spoken with the boy on a video call earlier.

“He just cried and begged to come home,” he said. “He was distraught. He didn’t know where he was.”

Back at home, “everyone is heartbroken,” he said. “We just want the boy back with us, his family.”

Miriam Jordan reports from a grass roots perspective on immigrants and their impact on the demographics, society and economy of the United States.
