The S. S. United States, a Historic Supership, Heads to the Ocean Floor

The New York Times November 11, 2026

The 20th-century ocean liner will become an artificial reef, ending efforts to save a ship that was fast, luxurious and (almost) indestructible. Watch the livestream.

The 20th-century ocean liner will become an artificial reef, ending efforts to save a ship that was fast, luxurious and (almost) indestructible. Watch the livestream.

Credit...

Supported by

By Jesse Pesta

Photographs and Video by Micah Green

Jesse Pesta and Micah Green are with the S. S. United States, off the coast of Destin, Fla. This article was reported over several years from Destin, Philadelphia and Mobile, Ala.

​In its glory days, the S. S. United States was fast, luxurious and all but indestructible. As the ocean liner’s designer, William Francis Gibbs, liked to ​say, “You can’t set her on fire, you can’t sink her, and you can’t catch her.”

​And he was right, up to a point.

On Wednesday one of the greatest ships to sail the seas​ was set to make its final journey, 180 feet down to the bottom of the ocean.​ Starting around 1 p. m. Central time, the ​S​. S. United States ​— a midcentury monument to postwar American technology and ambition — was scheduled to start its journey below the waves, opening its next chapter as an artificial reef and diving destination.

​But it turned out to be tough to sink the S. S. United States. In fact, it took years of planning and preparation to reach this point. ​And some fighting. A preservationist group filed a last-minute lawsuit to try to block the effort, though a judge dismissed the suit.

​So on Wednesday, hundreds gathered ​about 22 nautical miles off the coast of Destin, Fla., ​aboard sailboats, speedboats and yachts to watch one of the most unusual intentional sinkings to ever take place. Rarely is a vessel so big sunk in this way.

Stripped of its signature red-white-and-blue smokestacks — they were removed for a planned museum nearby — the S. S. United States cut a somewhat more low and lean profile than it once did. You could say it looked more like a cigarette boat than an ocean liner, if cigarette boats were as long as three football fields.

Still it was a fitting look, because the ship was the fastest ever to cross the Atlantic Ocean.

The ship’s designer, Mr. Gibbs, was a giant of ​20th-century naval architecture, and the S. S. United States was his magnum opus. Built in the boom years after World War II, ​it was an ocean liner so fast, its top speed was a Cold War state secret. On its first trans-Atlantic round trip, in July 1952, it set a speed record that still stands today.

The S. S. United States spent most of the 1950s and ’60s ferrying people between New York and Europe, its shipboard orchestras and cocktail lounges entertaining countless travelers — presidents, royalty, immigrants and vacationers. Marilyn Monroe sailed on the ship. Walt Disney. Duke Ellington. Princess Grace. But its most famous passenger was probably the Mona Lisa, in 1963, when the painting visited America.

But as jet travel turned ocean liners into relics, passengers dropped away. In 1969, the ship was mothballed.​ Until relatively recently, it hadn’t budged from its Philadelphia pier for decades.

For the ship to become a​ reef, its dark, labyrinthine interiors needed to be made safe for divers. Its huge fuel tanks had to be drained of decades-old goop. And for that to happen, the ship had to be towed halfway around the country, to a shipyard in Mobile, Ala., by a special oceangoing tugboat.

But first, the Coast Guard needed to be persuaded that the ship​, which is as long as the Chrysler Building is tall, was safe to move.

The effort to turn the S. S. United States into an artificial reef was led by Alex Fogg, the natural resources chief of Okaloosa County, Fla., which bought the ship in 2024 for $1 million. The county is assembling a menagerie of sunken ships for divers to explore off the coast of Destin on Florida’s panhandle.

On Tuesday, Mr. Fogg was on hand to help make final preparations for a sinking he’s been working toward for years. Once it’s done, he said, “I really don’t know how I’m going to feel.” He ran through a few possibilities. Relief. Joy. Sadness. Excitement.

“Right now it’s kind of surreal,” he said.

The waters around Destin are the final resting place for World War II Liberty ships, tugboats with names like Miss Louise and Mohawk Chief, and something that’s described on dive maps as a “steel vessel with chicken transport devices.” There’s a casino ship down there, a paddle wheel boat and Big Dawg, a military water-survival training ship. The list goes on.

The S. S. United States will be the crown jewel in the collection.

Okaloosa County bought the ship from a nonprofit group, the SS United States Conservancy, which for years had been trying to give it a new life as a hotel, entertainment complex or other development. But the ship’s fate was sealed in 2024 when it was evicted from a dock in Philadelphia by its landlord, the pier’s owner.

The eviction turned nasty. The group even accused the landlord of trying to negotiate a sale of the ship, an asset it didn’t own.

When an urgent search for a new pier failed, the conservancy decided that an artificial reef would be a more dignified end than selling its beloved ship for scrap.

Okaloosa bought it. Then Okaloosa needed to move it. After months of false starts, it finally happened on a freezing February day in 2025.

That morning, Mr. Fogg and his team gathered beside the ship in Philadelphia. A half-dozen uniformed Coast Guard officials strode up the dock, led by Capt. Kate Higgins-Bloom. She held a piece of paper, and the fate of the ship, in her hands.

Someone whispered: Here comes one of the most powerful officials on the East Coast.

Captain Higgins-Bloom handed Mr. Fogg the thing he’d been pursuing for months, a permission slip to pull the ship out into the Delaware River and tow it to Alabama. The Coast Guard was finally satisfied that this could be done safely — basically that the ship wouldn’t sink or cause a disaster somewhere.

Holding the document, Mr. Fogg said, “I’m literally going to frame this.”

Around midday, a radio crackled with the words, “A horn for the crowd!” and the tugboats obliged, sounding a long blast. And for the first time in nearly 30 years, the S. S. United States moved away from the riverbank.

As the tugs pulled the ship along the pier and past the team from Okaloosa, a ghostly warning, “Danger Keep Clear of Propellers,” floated by in faded paint on the hull, just above the waterline.

Mr. Fogg and a colleague jumped in a car and began weaving and racing through traffic, trying to keep up with the ship as it headed downriver toward the sea.

Along the Delaware, people had gathered to witness the spectacle. As the huge ship slid beneath the Walt Whitman Bridge with almost no room to spare, Terrie Williams hopped out of her car to get a snapshot. Her grandfather, she said, had worked aboard the ship as a chef.

A few miles down, along a weedy riverside, mother and daughter Anastasia and Harper Goldman stood arm in arm to say farewell to a neighbor. “The S. S. United States was part of our lives for so long,” Anastasia Goldman said.

They waved little American flags that they had grabbed from their Fourth of July decorations in the basement. After all, she said, “it’s the S. S. United States!”

A few steps from the Goldmans, Mr. Fogg took it all in. The ship was on its way. Down the East Coast, then past Cuba, destined for Alabama. But there was still more than a year of work ahead.

Sinking ships is a business, one that Coleen O’Malley knows well. She and her husband, Tim Mullane, run Coleen Marine, which they estimate has intentionally sunk, or “reefed”, about 140 ships. And the S. S. United States was one of their best-known customers.

Six months after the ship made it to Alabama, Ms. O’Malley was at work, deep inside the vessel. In a tiny room behind a door marked “Relief to Atmosphere,” she explained what was being done.

It was her job to safely send the S. S. United States to the bottom.

Old deck plans papered the walls. The room vibrated from the thumping of a thick hose in the hallway outside, pumping out oil.

“Every ship is different, but every ship is the same,” Ms. O’Malley said. The wiring had to come out, along with ductwork, glass and things that might entangle or injure divers. “Snag hazards,” Mr. Mullane said.

There was a need to cut passages strategically throughout the ship, so that divers could easily see pathways to open water and don’t get trapped. It helps sea life, too, by reducing stagnant waters.

And an important one: Making sure the ship, when sunk, sits upright on the bottom. If it lands on its side or flips, it could wobble and be unstable for divers. The secret is to make sure no big air pockets remain inside.

“Do you know what the ‘free surface effect’ is?” Mr. Mullane asked. Thus began a lesson in properly sinking a ship.

Imagine a baking pan floating in a bathtub, he said. Start filling it with water and what happens? The water shifts and the pan rolls to one side. “Now do a muffin pan and tell me what happens,” Mr. Mullane said.

The S. S. United States is a muffin pan, he said, as Ms. O’Malley laughed.

As they worked to prepare the ship last August, the decks were heaped with crumpled ductwork, piles of wires and stacks of mad-scientist control panels with labels like “Shaft Revolution Indicators.” A tanker truck parked out front was slurping out the oil.

It was an especially big week in the ship’s transformation. Its two iconic, teardrop-shaped smokestacks, or funnels, each the height of a six-story building, were ready to be lifted off.

Along the Mobile waterfront, at the end of a dead-end street and just past a bail bond shop, well-wishers had stuck several flags in a mound of dirt.

Mr. Mullane stood at the top of the ship, conducting an orchestra of cranes, barges and people with cutting-torches, and dropping F-bombs.

At 1:06 p. m., “Clear the stack” came across the radio, warning everyone to move away.

At 1:10 Mr. Mullane emphasized the point with a touch of profane urgency. “Clear!” he shouted.

“It’s only under 16 tons of tension,” he said to no one in particular.

A series of gut-vibrating booms rumbled through the ship. A man stepped out of a small hatch near the bottom of the forward funnel and made a cutting motion across his neck.

“I’ve got goosebumps,” Mr. Fogg said.

More pounding and groaning of metal, and at 1:50 p. m. the funnel swung free in a puff of rust. Ms. O’Malley ran up the starboard side toward the bow, where she and her husband shared a kiss.

Which brings us to Wednesday, when years of uncertainty about the ship’s future and then all that preparation — months of cleaning, decontaminating, hoisting and cutting — came down to one big moment off the Florida coast.

Starting around 1 p. m., holes would be opened in the hull just above the waterline. Then water would be pumped into the ship, causing it to settle lower and lower, until seawater started to rush into the holes that were cut in the hull. Mr. Mullane would be the last person to stand on the ship before transferring to a waiting boat.

And the S. S. United States would make its final journey.

Mr. Fogg called the sinking “the most honorable next chapter.” He planned to be the first person to dive to the S. S. United States, once it came to rest on the bottom.

Jesse Pesta is the deputy editor of the Climate team, helping to lead The Times’s coverage of climate change and the environment.

I Visited Big Bear Lake’s Famous Bald Eagles and Found Very Human Shenanigans

The New York Times November 11, 2026

My I. R. L. adventures in the strange human world behind the enormously popular livestreaming eagle cam.

Trisha Dale Green and Owen Phairis at Dana Point Park on Big Bear Lake. Credit... Sinna Nasseri for The New York Times

Supported by

By Sam Anderson

The eagle cam entered my life like most things: through my phone.

It was the middle of winter, the sad dark stretch when the sun seems to set before it rises, when the snow outside is dishwater gray, and I was handling it the way I always do: vegetating under a mound of pillows, poking at my glowing screen, praying that the internet would serve me something good — not the usual toxic fire hose of spam, slop, bots, gambling ads and phishing links.

Finally, my phone buzzed.

You have to check this out, my friend texted. It’s the only thing bringing me joy right now.

And he sent a link to the eagle cam.

It looked promising. Apparently, somewhere out in the wilderness of California, at the top of a very tall tree, two bald eagles were living in a nest, doing their best to survive and thrive and produce the next generation of eagles. The whole adventure was being livestreamed, 24/7, via a camera clamped to the tree. My friend said he couldn’t stop watching.

I clicked.

Instantly, a new world filled my screen. At the bottom, dominating the foreground, was the nest: a big messy tangle of sticks and branches. Behind that, stretching off to infinity, was a panoramic view that looked too good to be true: green forest, blue water, purple mountains. It looked like a Renaissance painting of the Garden of Eden — the sort of sun-splashed paradise the word “sublime” was invented to describe.

The feed seemed to have a good microphone, because as soon as I clicked, all the noises of the forest came pouring into my house: songbirds chirping, ravens croaking, woodpeckers hammering out their overlapping drum rolls — and, over it all, the constant roar of an oceanic wind, a big crashing whoosh that thrashed the treetops, so loud and harsh it sounded like fire.

Just a glance at the eagle cam made me feel lifted, extracted, as if I’d been plucked out of my sad little ground-bound life and set back down somewhere primal and real. (To be clear, I was still under my pillows.) I wanted to live there, in this fresh, wild world.

The biggest surprise was the eagles themselves. It turns out that actual eagles are not like the eagles we see on coins and flags and football helmets. They are fully embodied beings: loud, fierce, clumsy, majestic, grouchy, funny and (I say this affectionately) weird. Real bald eagles have big, round, yellow eyes that make them look as if they’re in a constant state of shock and rage, as if someone has just leaned down and whispered the most scandalous possible secret and they are trying to find someone to murder. They have no sweat glands, so on hot days they open their beaks and pant like dogs. Real bald eagles don’t make epic shrieking noises the way they do in movies — they grunt, honk, purr, squeak and chirp. Above all, bald eagles seem to be obsessed with collecting sticks. They pick them up in their deadly beaks and then clack them around, semirandomly, until they fit into the ever-growing puzzle of the nest.

Animal cams! The world is full of nests and dens and warrens and holes — private spaces full of creatures doing secret things. For nearly all of history, what happened in those places stayed hidden. But modern humans, stuck in our offices and studio apartments, armed with tiny cameras and pocket computers, have breached the boundary. We spy. These days, the animal-cam options are endless: flamingos in Houston, red pandas in San Diego, naked mole-rats in Washington. (The National Zoo even designed bingo cards: Fill in squares for “a mole-rat eats corn” or “a mole-rat kicks bedding around” or “a mole-rat runs uphill in tunnel.”)

Amid this cornucopia of cams, the eagle cam has built up an unusually passionate following. It was installed, back in 2015, by an environmental group called Friends of Big Bear Valley, an area that contains Big Bear Lake. The group hired a wildlife biologist to scale the 150-foot tree using ropes, no spikes, and stand in the nest to attach the cam. During the first few years, its popularity grew modestly. Then the pandemic hit, and — as with many other forms of virtual escape — the livestream took off. A whole global community, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, sprouted up online.

All over the world, the eagle cam functions as a sort of existential screen saver — a positive alternative to the doom and gloom of the 24-hour news cycle. Elementary school teachers often play it in their classrooms. Doctors play it in waiting rooms. Eagle-cam fans flock to message boards to discuss the birds’ lives. They post supercuts on YouTube and buy official merch and study charts cataloging all the activity around the nest: intrusions from pesky ravens, night visits from flying squirrels.

By the time I started watching the eagle cam, its two stars — Jackie (female) and Shadow (male) — had already worked their way through the fragile early stages of eagle procreation. In late February, cam fans celebrated as Jackie squeezed out two eggs: off-white globes roughly the size of human fists. Then people crossed their fingers as the parents took turns incubating the eggs, hunkering down day after day to protect them through rain and snow and hurricane-force winds.

This is what separates the eagle cam from most other animal cams: stakes and intimacy. We are not watching a carefully managed zoo enclosure — we are watching a life-or-death struggle at the top of a tree. Also, the eagle cam makes us feel as if we are inside that nest — almost part of that family. Every year, with each new mating season, the stakes refresh. Will the eggs hatch? Will the babies grow up and successfully fly? Because of the intimacy, those questions don’t feel abstract. They feel personal.

In early April, there was an eruption of online celebration when the first tiny cracks, known as pips, ruptured the surface of the shells — and then more celebration, in the following days, as the eggs cracked open to spill out two gray-white puffballs. Viewership spiked as the babies squeaked and chirped and whistled at their harsh new world, as the parents fed them chunks of fish from the lake, as the puffballs’ bodies began to grow and stretch to gangly proportions, as their feathers turned from gray-white to dark gray to brown. On the livestream, viewers sent constant streams of little hearts floating up the screen.

By late spring, the baby eagles had reached adult size. They looked streamlined and predatory. The nest was getting crowded. Jackie and Shadow spent most of their time perching on nearby branches.

But the babies couldn’t fly. Not yet. This was the next step in the drama, the moment we were all waiting for: fledging.

I found myself opening the eagle cam constantly, especially when I was stressed.

At the moment, the babies were spending a lot of time “wingersizing,” flapping and flapping, building up strength, feeling the wind. But soon they would leap. I became invested in their success. I started to fantasize about going to Big Bear Lake to try to see it happen. I wanted to cross the bridge between the digital and the real, to replace that onscreen paradise with something solid. What if I could be there when the babies finally took off? And then I could crawl into the nest in their place? Maybe all my problems would be magically solved.

The closest you can get to the nest is out on the water. So one morning in mid-June, after flying to Los Angeles and driving 90 miles east up twisty mountain roads to Big Bear Lake, I found myself boarding a pontoon boat for an eagle tour. My guide was Jenny Voisard, the media liaison for Friends of Big Bear Valley, the nonprofit organization that runs the eagle cam. Voisard was basically Jackie and Shadow’s official P. R. rep. Whenever something major happens on the livestream — egg-laying, hatching, fledging — she works round the clock to answer emails, field interview requests and appear on radio and TV.

I asked if she ever got sick of talking about eagles.

“Never,” she said. “It’s my favorite topic.”

I 100 percent believed this. Voisard, it quickly became clear, revered these birds. She started watching the eagle cam in 2022, obsessively, after a series of personal heartbreaks: the death of her first husband, the discovery that she couldn’t have children. The eagles swooped in to help fill that huge space of loss. Watching the eagle cam brought her peace. She loved, in particular, a charismatic baby eagle born that year named Spirit. In 2023, some months after Spirit fledged, Voisard started working for Friends of Big Bear Valley.

Sadly, Voisard said, bald eagle life is not always peaceful and relaxing. It can be ugly and harsh — as tragic as the tragedies we are trying to escape. As it turned out, 2023 was a hard year. Jackie and Shadow’s eggs didn’t hatch. Ravens invaded the nest. Shadow, in particular, seemed to struggle with the loss. He would just stand there, Voisard said, not knowing what to do.

“Jackie helped him,” she told me. “It took a couple days. And then he kind of got back to normal. He started bringing sticks back. And then they started mating again.”

Voisard said that the eagles’ resilience inspired her. If they could get through this stuff, she thought, the rest of us could too. She said she frequently finds herself thinking, in her daily life, What would the eagles do?

On her first in-person trip to Big Bear Lake, Voisard had what she describes as a “religious experience”: Shadow came diving out of the sky, right next to her boat, and snared a fish out of the water.

This is exactly the kind of magic I was hoping to see out on the lake.

The boat motored on until we reached a little cove — and then Capt. Mike Marzell, the Big Bear Valley resident at the wheel, cut the motor.

We sat there, bobbing, several hundred feet from shore. I stared but couldn’t find the nest anywhere. I saw distant gray boulders. A chunk of deep green forest.

Finally, Voisard pointed my attention to a thin trunk poking up, all alone, with a dark smudge at the top. That was the nest.

And at this decisive moment I thought, Hmm. Based on my research, I knew that eagle nests are huge. The word “nest” hardly does them justice. Jackie and Shadow’s nest is roughly the size of a small car — six feet across and nearly that deep, weighing hundreds of pounds. It sits wedged, solid as a bunker, near the top of this tall, skinny tree.

From the water, to my weak human eyes, the nest was just a blob. Above the blob I saw a tiny space — a pinhole of blue sky — which occasionally seemed to flicker in a way that reminded me of a blinking eye.

That, apparently, was the eaglets, Sandy and Luna. (Friends of Big Bear Valley received nearly 64,000 submissions for this year’s naming contest; the winning names were chosen by local third graders.) They were flapping their wings, practicing, building up the strength to fly.

We sat in that cove for a long time. As we talked, fish kept popping out of the water to snag bugs, splashing back down at odd rhythms around us.

Up to this point, my visit to Big Bear Lake was going just as I expected. Big nature, big nest, big feelings. Then things got slightly weird. It started with Captain Mike.

He struck me as a perfect embodiment of Southern California. He was 60ish, with a grizzled white beard that contrasted starkly with his tan skin. He wore a backward baseball cap, plus a Los Angeles Dodgers tank top, plus a pair of those reflective blade sunglasses that appeared suddenly on many Californians’ faces in the 1990s in the same way that hoofs once appeared on certain mammals during the Eocene Epoch. His voice was low and gravelly, but he had one of the purest California accents I’ve ever heard, almost like a Valley Girl in a movie: His vowels were squashed, and his speech rhythms went pogo-sticking up and down in ways I can’t possibly convey without sprinkling in a bunch of diacritical marks like a linguist or a 1980s heavy metal band.

Captain Mike’s tour of the lake was jaunty and loosey-goosey and fun. Early on, when I asked him how fast his boat could go, he answered, cheerfully, “The mile-per-hour thing is broken.”

He steered us past the highlights: the dam, Boulder Bay, multimillion-dollar mansions on the shoreline. He pointed out a spot where the eagles used to perch — until the owners cut the tree down because they got tired of all the eagle poop. We stopped for a while to watch teenagers do cannonballs off a giant boulder. The whole time, we scanned the sky for eagles. But they were nowhere to be seen. We would get excited — but it would turn out to be just a hawk or raven or vulture. (Cam fans have a word for these kinds of false sightings: eagle-lusions.)

As Captain Mike steered, I kept admiring his tattoos: two big portraits of Jackie and Shadow, one on each shoulder. When I asked when he got them, he chuckled.

“Five years ago,” he said. “I was married for 30 years. I got a divorce. And I got these tattoos right after my divorce.”

Over the course of our tour, Captain Mike told us a number of things about his divorce. It seemed to be woven into every other subject, including the eagles. At one point, he said he would like to wear a shirt that says: “I IDENTIFY WITH MR. B.” Mr. B was an eagle that used to live at Big Bear Lake — Jackie’s mate before Shadow came along. Captain Mike spoke about the bird wistfully, like an old drinking buddy.

“He’s the original,” Captain Mike said. “Shadow chased off Mr. B.”

At this point, Voisard jumped in. Technically, she said, Shadow just hung around near the nest, and Mr. B left of his own accord. There was no fight or confrontation.

“As far as I’m concerned, he chased him off, darn it!” Captain Mike said, laughing.

Partway through the tour, we made a brief stop. Voisard wanted to show me Dana Point Park — a local birding hot spot, just off the water, where eagle lovers come from all over the country to congregate and admire the nest. We docked the boat and made our way to an open area, where a smattering of people sat hunkered down with telescopes and binoculars and telephoto lenses the size of Civil War cannons. We were just getting our bearings when, out of nowhere, pandemonium broke out.

The first thing I heard was Captain Mike’s shouting.

“Guys, that’s her!” he boomed. “She’s here! That’s my ex-wife! I can’t be here!”

He started moving back toward the boat.

It turned out we had, unwittingly, stepped right into the teeth of a serious local drama, and the drama seemed to have multiple rows of teeth — because, as I did my best to listen to Captain Mike’s explanation of the complicated and agonizing aftermath of his divorce, an argument was breaking out somewhere off to my right. Mike’s ex-wife was also apparently an eagle enthusiast, and she had some longstanding criticisms of Friends of Big Bear Valley, which she was making known. “We can’t be here!” Mike shouted.

I was stunned. I felt as if I had walked into a meditation class and ended up in the middle of a brawl.

Somehow, a little shellshocked, we all ended up back on the boat. We rode for a while in silence. The eagles did not appear.

Friends of Big Bear Valley was led, for more than 20 years, by Sandy Steers, a fierce environmentalist whose life mission was to stop developers from swallowing Big Bear Lake. Steers was a mystic and a nature-lover — but also a fighter. Everyone I talked to had stories about her. She drove like a maniac. She let wild animals — chipmunks, birds — have free access to her house. She was a shaman and an energy healer. Once, when officials thinned out the forest in the name of fire prevention, Steers walked through the area and said she could feel nature suffering.

She was determined to stop that suffering using every possible tool. And her most powerful tool, arguably, was the eagle cam.

In Southern California, fighting development is like trying to fight gravity. One of the greatest impediments to conservation is that, most of the time, it is hellaciously boring: slow, grinding, legalistic. The eagle cam gave that fight a face — two faces, actually, with sharp, bright yellow beaks. Friends of Big Bear Valley no longer had to ask for help with abstract things, such as donations to defray legal fees that might delay developers from getting permits. They could just say, “Help us save the eagles.” It was a fund-raising bonanza.

But with global attention comes local resentments. In a small territory like this, it’s no surprise that people get territorial. And sometimes the fighting turns nasty.

Late one afternoon, as the sunbeams slanted low over the lake and the eaglets flapped in their nest, I took a break from watching the eagle cam to go interview Mayor Randall Putz, of the city of Big Bear Lake. Although it turns out I didn’t actually have to take a break from the eagle cam, because there are screens everywhere in Big Bear Lake — it feels as if the town is throwing a citywide Super Bowl party, except the football was birds and the game never stopped. Right behind Mayor Putz’s head, on a big flat-screen, was the eagle cam. I kept glancing at it as we talked. One of the eaglets seemed to be watching us, listening in, turning its beak in a way that made its head line up with the mayor’s.

We were talking in the mayor’s shop. You are going to think I am making this up, but I swear: The mayor of Big Bear Lake owns a bird supply store. It’s called Chirp Nature Center, and it offers not only sommelier-level blends of seeds (“tested and approved by Big Bear Lake’s pickiest backyard birds”) but also everything else a birder could ever want: binoculars, field guides, birdhouses, birdbaths, birdbath accessories that make the water warm and bubbly so the birds can enjoy some hot tub action, etc.

Mayor Putz confirmed my impressions of Big Bear Lake. It is, he said, a complicated place, for multiple reasons. One is geography. The place sits up in the mountains, and they are not normal mountains but what geologists call a “transverse” range, which means they run sideways across the map, east-west, on a continent where most ranges run up and down. This produces, among other things, extreme weather. Big Bear Lake is prone to monsoon rainstorms, hurricane-force winds, sudden wildfires, punishing blizzards. Several winters ago, it suffered an event locals remember as “snowmaggedon” — a storm so heavy and sudden and cold that people in the valley actually died.

Big Bear Lake, then, is not exactly the natural paradise we imagine from the eagle cam. Even the lake itself, I learned, isn’t natural: It was first created, 150 years ago, by a San Bernardino Valley citrus farmer who dammed the marshy valley to make himself a reservoir, drowning 9,000 trees in the process. Like much of the rest of Southern California, it is human-made — as artificial, in its way, as Disneyland.

I shouldn’t have been surprised. I mean, this is the lesson of many of the oldest stories in the world: Paradise, the thing we want so desperately, not only does not but cannot exist — not for us, not in this world. And yet we won’t stop running toward it. It is the banana peel we will never stop slipping on.

Complicated places spawn complicated politics. Over the decades, many different cultures have collided in the tiny space of Big Bear — hippies and libertarians and Hollywood moguls — and they all tend to have different agendas. One long-running battle is over the development of a place called Moon Camp, the last undeveloped piece of shoreline on the lake. Steers worked, for many years, to hold off developers.

The fight over Moon Camp was coming to a head that summer. Friends of Big Bear Valley was desperately trying to raise $10 million to help a conservation trust buy the property before a July 31 deadline. Despite their best efforts, they were more than $5 million short.

Sadly, Steers died of cancer in February, just a couple of weeks before Jackie laid her eggs. The eaglet Sandy was named in her honor.

Most Big Bear residents I spoke with love the eagle cam but also complain, good-naturedly, about the side effects of its popularity: traffic from tourists, screens all over town. One afternoon, in the lobby of my hotel, a desk clerk named Bethany was making me laugh. There was a big flat-screen mounted behind the desk, and on the screen the babies were really going for it: sticking their huge wings up into steep V’s, flapping down hard and also jumping up and down as if the nest were a trampoline. It looked to me as if this might be our moment: I might get to see the eaglets fledge right here in the hotel lobby.

Every time the eagles jumped, Bethany yelled at the screen: “GO! FLY! YOU’RE SO CLOSE!”

She was not yelling in the spirit of gentle encouragement you would have heard from most tourists. She was yelling like a parent whose children were irritating the hell out of her in the kitchen an hour before a dinner party.

Bethany told me she grew up in Big Bear Lake and could remember the place before the eagle cam took over. Although she wished the babies well, she was also tired of looking at them. She wanted them out of her life. She said she had an irrational fear of birds, including the eagles: Whenever she drove around the lake with her windows down, she imagined Jackie or Shadow flying into her car, crashing around. As soon as these eaglets fledged, she told me, she would be allowed to switch the hotel TV to something she found more interesting: a live feed of bears in Alaska.

“GO!” she yelled at the screen. “GET OUT OF HERE!”

During my time in Big Bear Lake, I went as often as I could to Dana Point Park. I went partly to see the eagles, but mostly to see the people who were seeing the eagles.

The name Dana Point Park makes the place sound fancy. It’s not. The first time I went on my own, I almost drove right past it. It’s on the wild north side of the lake, near Moon Camp, on a road so narrow and windy I was always imagining 50-car pileups. There’s not much there: a little parking lot, some docks. Right on the dirt, in clearings among the trees, people set up camping chairs. They pull out binoculars and telescopes, aim them at the eagles’ tree and then just hang out for hours. It’s like a family reunion.

I talked to Scott Hicks and Dawn Dimanno, a couple who had driven several hours to set up their big orange telescope, which was now trained on the nest, and were sharing it freely with other eagle watchers. They told me they’ve been watching the cam since 2019, back when there was a baby in the nest named Simba. Remembering him still made them grin. “He was just loud and obnoxious and funnier than anything,” Dimanno said.

Dimanno told me that, during Covid, she watched multiple animal cams at once — but she racked up a such a big cellular data bill that Hicks told her she had to choose just one. It wasn’t a close call. She chose the eagle cam.

Up in the parking lot, I met Alicia Ferraro, an eagle-cam superfan who had driven eight hours from Carson City, Nev. On her dashboard was a yellow rubber duck with its head painted like a bald eagle’s. She said the long drive was absolutely worth it. She got to go to Sandy Steers’s memorial service, where people sang and shared stories. And a couple of days before, for the first time ever, she saw Jackie flying across the lake, chasing a raven. Ferraro said her heart was pounding the whole time.

At Dana Point, I kept asking the eagle watchers a question that wouldn’t stop needling me. Why were we here? Why had we come all this way to visit the eagles in person — to get a worse view of something we could have stayed home and watched up close, in high resolution, on our screens?

“When you’re looking at it from the camera, you only see the nest,” Dimanno said. “And there’s so much more that goes on around it.”

Just before we talked, Hicks and Dimanno had spotted Shadow bringing a fish into the nest. And as they looked at the eagles through their telescope, the eagles kept staring directly back at them. Dimanno said the birds must have noticed the sun reflecting off the mirror.

“It’s a shared experience,” said Andrea Prince, who was watching the nest through a pair of binoculars she kept on a gold chain. “I feel like I’m here with them. I’m part of that moment.”

Prince lives in Los Angeles but drives to Big Bear Lake as often as she can. She told me that watching the eagle cam helped get her through chemotherapy, when her mind was so foggy she couldn’t concentrate on anything else, even short TV shows. Her kids tease her for coming here so often, but she said the cam is no substitute for the reality of this place. She said it’s like going to a concert instead of just watching a recording.

This was true. The view on the eagle cam is beautiful and close and special and precious. But it’s also flat and disconnected. It lacks context. The view in the background is a just that: a view. It’s not a three-dimensional space. But here in Big Bear Lake, everything was real and interwoven. The fish that jumped offshore, at Dana Point, were the same fish the eagles ate. The wind that ruffled my hair was the same wind that ruffled the eagles’ feathers. You understood, viscerally, where these eagles fit into the world, and where the world fit into the eagles.

In the end, despite staring at the sky until my eyes hurt, I never saw Jackie in person. I saw Shadow, in the distance, perching. But the great mother stayed hidden. On my last evening at Dana Point, I sat alone on a dock, facing the nest, for a long time, hoping to see Jackie flying. Fish kept jumping all around me, and I kept picturing her swooping down, through the dusky light, to snag one before bedtime. But she didn’t. The light was nearly gone; the mosquitoes were eating me. I gave up.

Driving away, back down that twisty mountain, I remember feeling sort of proud of her. Jackie was a wild creature — a real bald eagle. We can surround her and set up cameras and lie in wait all we want. But no human can force her to perform. And that was the way it should be.

When I left Big Bear Lake in late June, the fund-raising for Moon Camp — despite more than 25,000 donations — was still well short of the $10 million purchase price. On July 24, a week before the deadline, Friends of Big Bear Valley announced miraculous news: A $5.5 million donation had arrived to fill the gap. It came from the OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna. Anna, it turned out, was a huge fan of the eagle cam.

Sandy and Luna continued jumping and flapping, preparing for their big moment of flight, until nearly the end of June. People fantasized that they might actually fledge on July 4, America’s 250th anniversary — an irresistible confluence of patriotic symbolism. But they didn’t wait that long. On June 28, the eaglets were exploring the branches just outside the nest — an area cam fans call “the front porch” — when Luna made a misstep and accidentally knocked his sister off the branch.

This happens sometimes — cam fans call it “fludging” (a fudged fledge). Still, it was terrifying. People didn’t know, for a while, if Sandy was OK. They could hear Luna, in the nest, making desperate “squee” noises.

Turns out, Sandy was fine. And, stuck outside of the nest, at this strange lower elevation, distressed and confused, Sandy took the only way out: She flew.

Luna, suddenly alone in the nest for the first time in his life, stared out on that landscape with new eyes. The next day, after testing his wings some more, he leaped and soared.

It was June 29. After all that drama, the nest was empty.

For a few weeks after they fledged, the baby eagles came back to the nest, occasionally, until they got the hang of things. Then they left to explore new territories, to meet new eagles, to build their own nests and start their own families in some other paradise — almost certainly one that would not be on camera.

At Big Bear Lake, meanwhile, the parents’ lives went back to normal. They gathered their strength to prepare for the cold weather. Soon, together, they would start to fix up the nest for the following season.

Except not this time.

In early July, after the big fireworks shows, Jackie fell into a rapid decline. The biggest, strongest eagle on the Big Bear Lake suddenly appeared to be weak and lethargic. On July 12, she flew out of the nest for the final time. Later that week, she was spotted standing on the ground near the water. She had collected some fish, and two younger bald eagles, apparently visiting from another territory, swooped down and tried to take them. Jackie rolled over, fending off the invaders with her talons. Finally, they left. Jackie just stood there, exhausted, unable to fly.

In the aftermath of that fight, Jackie was captured and taken to a bird hospital in Ojai. As the news got out, eagle lovers sent tributes and supplies: letters, water, salmon from Alaska. The doctors did the best they could, but Jackie kept declining. She got weaker and weaker. Then, shockingly, she died. (An autopsy later revealed that she had been suffering from avian flu.)

Expressions of grief poured in from around the world. Jenny Voisard did 22 interviews in two days. The Friends of Big Bear Valley shop sold out of everything. Memorial posts flooded all the eagle-related corners of the internet. Someone posted an elaborate memorial to Jackie in the temple at Burning Man.

Now it was only Shadow.

Soon, however, a new bald eagle was hanging around the area. It perched nearby, not getting too close but also not going away — just as Shadow once had, back in the era of Mr. B. Shadow seemed to tolerate this new bird. Biologists identified it as KD1, a female from the Prado Basin area, roughly 70 miles to the southwest. Soon, eagle cam fans seemed to accept her. They started calling her Kaydee. She got closer and closer to Shadow. On Sept. 12, exactly two months after Jackie left the nest for the final time, Kaydee flew off — and then returned, with a stick in her beak: the first move in the yearly ritual to prepare the nest for next season.

Sam Anderson is a staff writer for The New York Times Magazine.

He Voyaged on the Ship as a Boy. Now He’s Recording Its Final Journey.

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Times Insider

A New York Times editor has had a lifelong connection to the S. S. United States, which is becoming an artificial reef off the Florida coast.

By Jesse Pesta

Jesse Pesta edits investigative and narrative articles about climate change, and has a side hustle writing about the S. S. United States.

Isn’t that a cute kid? I’m inclined to think so, because the kid is me. I’m 2 years old in the photo, sailing the high seas aboard the fastest ocean liner ever built.

That family trip, nearly 60 years ago, helps explain why I find myself writing about the very last journey of that ship, the S. S. United States. On Wednesday, it was intentionally sent to the bottom of the ocean near Destin, Fla., to become an artificial reef and diving destination.

I’m in Destin and watched the ship’s final moments.

For the past two decades or so, I’ve written off and on about the ship and the efforts to save it. I got interested for a simple reason: that family trip.

I don’t remember a thing about it, of course. I was 2.

But through my childhood, it made for great family lore. Mom and Dad would reminisce about the time we moved across the Atlantic with our entire lives stuffed into a single steamer trunk.

My dad had gotten a scholarship in London and the price of tickets was covered, either by air or by sea. The choice was easy, my mom, Maureen O’Hara Pesta, told me this week. “We wanted to ride the big ship,” she said. It sounded like an adventure.

The S. S. United States, fast and luxurious, carried passengers back and forth between New York and Europe for most of the 1950s and ’60s. My parents made the right decision in 1968 to go by sea — barely a year later, the liner went out of service, never to sail again.

Fast forward to about 20 years ago. My parents mentioned they’d seen a documentary about the ship.

I knew the family story about the trip, but until then I hadn’t given it too much thought. It was one of those yarns told from time to time around the dinner table, and forgotten until the next time.

But now I learned that the S. S. United States was docked in Philadelphia. It looked like a ghost ship. And a group of people who loved the ship were trying to to save it.

A few of them were so dedicated that they’d occasionally hire small boats and sail into the Delaware River, where the ship was docked, just to touch its rusty hull. I wrote about their exploits, and I’m still in touch with some of them today. That was the start for me.

This week I asked my mom for her memories of the 1968 trip. What was in that single steamer trunk, the thing that contained everything we owned?

She thought about it and decided she wasn’t quite sure, but it must have been clothing and little else. “In my mind’s eye, walking through those rooms in London, I can’t see one thing — not even framed photographs — that we’d have brought with us,” she said.

But she did vividly remember something about the ship sailing out of New York Harbor. “The receding of the Statue of Liberty,” she said, “and thinking how momentous that was.”

And then, laughing, she recalled hearing the little three-note chimes that the crew would ring to announce dinnertime.

She couldn’t remember the circumstances around the porthole photo of the two of us. But here’s a twist. A year or so ago, I showed the snapshot to someone who knows the layout of the S. S. United States particularly well.

Of all the hundreds of portholes on the huge ship, she said, she knew this specific one. Amazing.

So about a year ago, when another reporting trip put me back aboard the ship, I located that porthole and asked the photographer on the story, Micah Green, if he’d snap a photo of me looking through it again.

Memory is a funny thing. We don’t remember what’s in our box of worldly possessions, but we do remember the dinner chimes. We can identify one porthole among many.

I like the two porthole photos. They’re like accidental bookends: little me being taken on an adventure, and big me marveling at the journey.

My parents made an interesting choice, sailing off to London with a steamer trunk and the kid. I suppose that became part of who I am, even if 2-year-old me looked a little nervous about it.

Jesse Pesta is the deputy editor of the Climate team, helping to lead The Times’s coverage of climate change and the environment.

White House Threatens Congress, Saying Aggressive Investigations Could Be Crime

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

As Democrats prepared to begin oversight inquiries, it was not clear what legal basis could support the threat. The Constitution grants lawmakers immunity for legislative acts.

By Charlie SavageJonathan Swan and Michael Gold

Reporting from Washington

The White House’s top lawyer has warned the Democrat in line to lead the House’s chief investigative committee that aggressive oversight of the Trump administration “may cross the line into blatant criminality,” a threat that experts called legally dubious.

In a three-page letter to Representative Robert Garcia of California, the incoming chairman of the Oversight Committee, the White House counsel, Will Scharf, said Democrats had “evinced a clear intent to transgress” constitutional limits on congressional investigations. He predicted that their inquiries would be used “to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end.”

The warning from the White House was dated Monday, a day after Attorney General Todd Blanche said on CNN that members of Congress had “done nothing but threaten everything that’s happening in this administration.”

“That is not governing, that is not leading, that is not oversight,” Mr. Blanche said. He, like Mr. Scharf, once represented Mr. Trump as a defense lawyer.

Taken together, their statements signal that Mr. Trump’s administration is likely to follow the playbook his first administration used after Democrats took the House in 2019. Then, Mr. Trump vowed to fight “all” subpoenas, his administration routinely refused to comply and the disputes ended up in court.

But the threat of launching criminal investigations goes even further than the stance he took in his first term. It indicates how far Mr. Trump is willing to push the Justice Department to try to protect the White House from legislative investigations.

In a statement, Mr. Garcia dismissed the letter, which his office said it had not received as of Wednesday morning. Arguing that Congress has broad authority to conduct investigations, Mr. Garcia suggested Mr. Trump had “something to hide” and accused the White House of threatening legislators.

“The Trump administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress,” he said. “We are a coequal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized D. O. J. or from the president’s lawyers.”

Punchbowl News first reported the letter, which was later shared by the White House.

Peter M. Shane, who teaches public law at the New York University School of Law and is an author of a separation-of-powers casebook, criticized Mr. Scharf’s threat as legally baseless. “Our Constitution protects legislators from the threat of criminal prosecution while performing official duties as an essential bulwark to repel executive overreach and defend checks and balances,” he said.

He continued: “Congressional oversight and the issuance of subpoenas by definition cannot be the focus of legitimate criminal prosecution. It may be that an occasional subpoena may be quashed as outside the committee’s jurisdiction or for some other reason, but that is not a criminal offense.”

The portion of Mr. Scharf’s letter raising the prospect of criminality cited no precedent.

“Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality,” the White House counsel wrote. “And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation.”

Mr. Scharf’s reference to depriving people of constitutional rights and privileges appeared to be a reference to a statute that makes that a crime. It is generally invoked in the context of people who abuse coercive law enforcement power, like police officers and prison guards.

Mr. Scharf, a 2011 graduate of Harvard Law School, did not address how any attempt to investigate aggressive congressional oversight as a crime could square with the “speech or debate” clause of the Constitution, which shields lawmakers from being subpoenaed or prosecuted by the executive branch over their legislative acts.

On Wednesday, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic minority leader who is in line to be the next House speaker, dismissed the White House threat.

“A Democratic Congress is going to be a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch in the face of unprecedented corruption that they’ve unleashed on the American people,” he told reporters. “And if they don’t like it, consult the Constitution.”

Much of his letter rests on legal principles courts have used to separate legitimate congressional subpoenas from ones that can be quashed: Congress may compel testimony and documents tied to a valid legislative purpose, like weighing whether new laws are needed or whether there is a basis on which to impeach an official, but not merely to harass people or invade privacy for the sake of exposure.

The first Trump administration made the same argument against congressional subpoenas, including one seeking Mr. Trump’s financial records after he had violated the norm that candidates for president release their tax returns. He said Democrats were just trying to harass him and score political points, while lawmakers maintained they had a valid legislative purpose because they were weighing whether to enact a law requiring such disclosures.

The Supreme Court set clearer limits on subpoenas for a president’s personal records, sending the case back down for further consideration and narrowing the files Congress ultimately received in a 2022 settlement. In the meantime, the litigation also helped Mr. Trump run out the clock on disclosures before the 2020 election.

Mr. Scharf’s letter follows more than a year of efforts by the Trump administration to prosecute officials who have investigated the president. For much of his second term, prosecutors in South Florida have pursued a sprawling inquiry, called the “grand conspiracy” investigation by Mr. Trump’s allies. It is examining whether former F. B. I. and intelligence officials who investigated Mr. Trump over the past decade conspired to violate his constitutional rights. But, so far, that effort has not succeeded in establishing a basis for an indictment against former officials, and several Trump loyalists who worked on the inquiry recently resigned.

Much of Mr. Scharf’s letter is a catalog of Democrats’ post-election social media posts and commentary. As election results came in last week, Mr. Garcia issued a terse statement warning Trump administration officials and others to “lawyer up.” Since the election, Democrats have promised to pass out subpoenas “like candy” or “Mardi Gras beads,” and one representative-elect said he wanted to watch Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “squirm.”

Mr. Trump has made threatening to prosecute his personal and political adversaries a hallmark of his rhetoric since his 2016 campaign, when his rallies featured “Lock her up!” chants about Hillary Clinton. In his second presidency, he has openly challenged the principle that the Justice Department and F. B. I. should make criminal investigation and charging decisions independent of White House political direction, and courts have repeatedly suppressed subpoenas and thrown out charges based on findings that they lacked a legitimate basis.

Congress has long taken an expansive view of its own investigatory authority, with lawmakers arguing that they cannot legislate properly without being able to seek information. Historically, members have asserted their right to investigate nearly any area where Congress has the power to pass legislation or appropriate funds.

The party out of power often campaigns for the midterm elections on a promise to investigate the president and his allies. When Republicans narrowly won control of the House in 2022, scores of lawmakers vowed to investigate President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s family members and their businesses, particularly his son Hunter. That year, Republican candidates across the country also campaigned on a promise to investigate Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, then the country’s top medical adviser on the coronavirus, including at least one who vowed to prosecute him. Once in office, they followed through on many of those threats.

Charlie Savage writes about national security and legal policy for The Times.

Jonathan Swan is a White House reporter for The Times, covering the administration of Donald J. Trump. Contact him securely on Signal: @jonathan.941

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Raman and the D. S. A.: Wariness, Skepticism and Hope

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Democratic socialists had another success with Ms. Raman’s ascent to the Los Angeles mayoralty. But she is no sure bet to align with all of the group’s priorities.

By Jill Cowan

Reporting from Los Angeles

Election Day produced what seemed like dream results for the democratic socialists of Los Angeles.

Nithya Raman, a member of the progressive movement, was elected to lead the city, following a hard-fought battle against Mayor Karen Bass. Marissa Roy, also a democratic socialist, easily won her race for city attorney — a role that, while lesser known, wields significant power.

The two will join a city controller aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America and three democratic socialist City Council members, making the small but ascendant D. S. A. as powerful as it is in any major American metropolis, joining New York, where Mayor Zohran Mamdani has pledged to remake urban government.

“It’s hugely exciting,” said Frances Gill, a member of the D. S. A.’s national political committee who lives in Los Angeles. “It marks strong potential and possibility for how we build the socialist movement in L. A.”

But Ms. Raman is no sure bet to advance a strictly democratic socialist agenda as mayor. Throughout her campaign, she maintained an arm’s-length relationship with both the national organization and the Los Angeles chapter, and D. S. A. members in turn expressed skepticism about whether she was ideologically aligned enough with the group’s priorities.

Her relationship with other left-leaning leaders in the city could also present challenges. All three of the other members of the D. S. A. on the City Council backed Ms. Bass for mayor, for instance.

Ms. Gill acknowledged that the decision to back Ms. Raman had been “contentious within the organization — that’s no secret.” But she pointed out that the D. S. A. itself is far from monolithic, and ultimately, she said, the group claims the mayor-elect as one of its own.

Political analysts say that, especially in Los Angeles, where virtually everyone is a Democrat, conflicts between leaders and the groups that have helped get them elected are unavoidable.

“When a movement is this successful so quickly and has so many of its allied candidates winning, there’s inevitably kind of a creative tension between the policy positions that the organization has and the governing actions of those who win,” said Raphael Sonenshein, an expert on Los Angeles government and an architect of the 1999 city charter overhaul. “That’s the stage that’s probably coming.”

Ms. Raman’s campaign downplayed her connection to the D. S. A., saying it was just one of many groups that had helped propel her to victory. It cited several major labor unions whose members knocked on thousands of doors trying to persuade Angelenos to vote for Ms. Raman.

“I just don’t want the interest in D. S. A. to overshadow the real work that those partners did,” said Ian Manheimer, Ms. Raman’s campaign manager.

Ms. Raman announced on the last day possible that she would challenge Ms. Bass, a longtime Democratic politician whose popularity plummeted in the wake of last year’s devastating Palisades fire and never recovered.

In the midst of a tight primary campaign, the D. S. A. declined to formally endorse Ms. Raman, instead opting to merely “recommend” that voters choose her in the absence of better options. Ms. Raman was an imperfect candidate from an ideological perspective — she hadn’t been sufficiently vocal about opposing Israel’s actions in Gaza, some argued, or about targeting Israel with boycotts, divestment and sanctions. But the group said in its voter guide that she was most closely aligned with its practical goals in the city.

In particular, they agreed with her pitch to reduce spending on the Police Department and increase funds on basic services, like paving streets, planting trees and investing in public transit.

But members of the group were frustrated when she sought changes to Los Angeles’s mansion tax, which she had originally championed, because it had the unintended consequence of squashing apartment construction. Some in the organization thought she was caving to developers, exposing perhaps the biggest policy rift between Ms. Raman and the D. S. A.

While democratic socialists believe that housing should be “decommodified,” or taken out of the private sector’s hands, Ms. Raman has frequently talked about how important it is to make it easier to build — and make money from — multifamily housing. The city needs more housing, and she has said that requires buy-in from for-profit developers.

Ms. Raman was also criticized by some on the left for staying mostly silent on Proposition 40, which would have taxed billionaires’ wealth, a measure that was backed by the D. S. A. It was defeated this week. Liz Garcia, a campaign spokeswoman, said that Ms. Raman supported the measure but was not vocal about it because she was focused on her own race.

It took the local chapter of the D. S. A. months before it finally endorsed her in the general election.

Ms. Raman, for her part, has toed a line between courting the group’s base of highly educated millennials and distancing herself from the more extreme associations that come with the label of democratic socialist.

She has appeared in videos with D. S. A.-aligned influencers, comedians and podcasters. And progressive organizations, including what was then a much smaller D. S. A., were instrumental to her grass-roots campaign for the Los Angeles City Council in 2020, when she ousted an entrenched incumbent.

But she has also carefully framed her own rise as a natural trajectory from a Harvard graduate with an urban planning degree from M. I. T. to mayor of the nation’s second most populous city. Her decision to join the D. S. A., she has said, came after she found that the organization was one of the few that prioritized addressing the city’s catastrophic housing crisis.

California voters were more inclined to support candidates described as progressive than as mainstream Democrat and were evenly divided on whether they were more inclined to support candidates described as democratic socialist, according to a poll released in August by the Institute of Governmental Studies at the University of California, Berkeley.

As she celebrated her victory with her team on Thursday, Ms. Raman told reporters that she was already hard at work mending fences with people including the chief of the Los Angeles Police Department, Jim McDonnell. At various points this year, she said she would replace him because of the department’s handling of protests against federal immigration enforcement in the city.

Her opponents said that plan was naïve, arguing that it would leave the department, one of the nation’s biggest law enforcement agencies, rudderless ahead of the 2028 Olympics.

She has since tempered her determination to oust him. She said she wanted to ensure “that we are prepared to deliver that service at the level that Angelenos expect when I take office,” adding that “I know Chief McDonnell is committed to that.”

(The Los Angeles Police Department’s union spent big sums to oppose Ms. Raman.)

While Ms. Raman has been hesitant to commit to governing as a democratic socialist, Ms. Roy, the city attorney-elect, more explicitly campaigned with the D. S. A., and her agenda closely aligns with the group’s priorities. She also has unusual autonomy to enact it.

The office, which has roughly 1,000 employees, has two main functions: It acts as legal representation for the mayor, the City Council and other city departments, and it can sue people and businesses on behalf of residents.

Ms. Roy said that she plans to sue more bad landlords and employers that take advantage of their employees, and to hold police officers accountable when they violate department policies.

She didn’t explicitly campaign alongside Ms. Raman, Ms. Roy said, but she is open to collaborating when she feels the mayor’s interests are aligned with those of her constituents.

On Tuesday, under the soaring arches of Los Angeles City Hall’s Council chambers, Ms. Raman’s City Council colleagues, none of whom backed her in the race against Ms. Bass, congratulated her one by one. A few acknowledged that they had opposed her campaign but said they were ready to move on.

“Our city will thrive if we can have a relationship where we can work together, we can build together, we can disagree with each other and come back to the table to move our city forward,” said Eunisses Hernandez, a D. S. A.-backed Council member.

“The trees, the streets, the lights, the sidewalks — you know I never shut up about that,” Ms. Hernandez added, smiling at Ms. Raman from across the horseshoe-shaped dais. “I have been following what you’re saying, and I’m excited to advance those things, too.”

Orlando Mayorquín contributed reporting.

Jill Cowan is a Times reporter based in Los Angeles, covering the forces shaping life in Southern California and throughout the state.

U. S. Efforts to Tighten Blockade of Iran Rely on Reluctant Neighbors

The New York Times November 11, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Washington wants to intensify its economic pressure campaign on Iran by closing its land borders. Neighboring states, fearing economic fallout, are pushing back.

By Erika SolomonEric Schmitt and Tyler Pager

The first step in the United States’ campaign to economically strangle Iran was a naval blockade of its ports, cutting off Iranian trade by sea. Next came a raft of new sanctions, grounding much of the country’s air transport network.

Now, the United States is going after Iran’s last economic artery: its land routes. Only there, Washington has hit upon a problem.

For weeks, U. S. officials have tried — and failed — to diplomatically pressure Iran’s neighbors into shuttering their border crossings, according to three Iraqi officials and one U. S. official with knowledge of the talks, who requested anonymity to speak candidly.

Those neighboring states, primarily Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan, are increasingly wary and disgruntled by U. S. policies they say could hurt them as much as Tehran.

So, on Saturday, the U. S. military joined the effort, announcing Task Force Iron Gate, which it says will work on “preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.”

It is unclear how the task force will operate in practice, and it is unusual for such an economic and security campaign to be run by U. S. Central Command, known as Centcom, which oversees military operations in the Middle East.

Former U. S. military officials and analysts say the move was likely aimed at taking advantage of Centcom’s intelligence capabilities and resources, which were already focused on Iran amid the war. Centcom, they said, could sharpen the focus and organization of previously uncoordinated efforts among diplomats, anti-money laundering units and intelligence agencies to clamp down on land routes.

For Iraq — one of Iran’s largest cross-border trading partners — the latest U. S. effort could be particularly dangerous. The Iraqis fear unrest among smuggling networks and militants along a rugged, 994-mile border they cannot fully control. Washington has long been aware of Iran’s use of the porous frontier with Iraq to smuggle weapons and money to its militia allies there.

The task force will consist of 20 civilian and military personnel based in Florida, Centcom said in its statement. An American military official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, said they would not conduct military operations, but may instead push neighboring states to use their own militaries to crack down on illicit or sanctioned trade.

The effectiveness of Task Force Iron Gate remains to be seen, but Dana Stroul, the Pentagon’s former top Middle East official in the Biden administration, said it was a “‘Kitchen sink’ strategy.” It will aim, she said, to “squeeze any pressure relief valves the Iranian regime is using to circumvent the sanctions and naval blockade.”

The U. S. official familiar with the talks with neighboring states said that many had voiced fears of “civil insurrection” if they were to cut off smuggling and trade routes vital to businesses and populations on both sides of the border. The official said that the latest U. S. efforts were stoking resentment among its regional allies.

Many of those countries were already frustrated with Washington for ignoring their pleas not to start a war with Israel against Iran in February, a conflict in which they have suffered economic costs and physical destruction.

Yet, for President Trump, tightening the blockade may be the best among bad options to try to end the war.

There is still no nuclear deal in place with Iran. And the once freely navigable Strait of Hormuz, vital for oil and gas shipments in the Persian Gulf, is now a dangerous route contested between Iranian and U. S. naval forces.

After months of stalemate, the Trump administration was widely expected to launch renewed strikes on Iran after the midterm elections. But momentum for that has fizzled as officials took stock of a sweeping Democratic victory that many of them, including Vice President JD Vance, linked to the war’s unpopularity with American voters.

The Trump administration is now casting about for other options to pressure Iran to accept a deal more favorable to the United States.

By deepening the blockade, the hope is “it just weakens the system so much from within that there will be implosion,” said Alex Vatanka, a Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute in Washington. Analysts say U. S. officials are hoping to turn the economic screws until domestic turmoil forces Iran’s clerical rulers to capitulate to U. S. demands, or the government simply collapses.

Since announcing Task Force Iron Gate, administration officials have argued the economic campaign made renewed strikes unnecessary.

“The economic pain that is being inflicted on Iran ​right now is extraordinary,” Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, told reporters after a G7 meeting in Paris on Tuesday. “We don’t need to conduct military strikes if we’re achieving the same objective through economic means.”

The U. S. naval blockade, analysts say, has effectively cut off Iranian oil exports, the backbone of its economy. Some Iranian officials this summer publicly stated that exports were near zero.

With some 90 percent of Iran’s trade dependent on maritime routes, the blockade was also devastating for Iranians trapped in a spiraling economic crisis.

Iran’s leadership, however, has had decades of learning how to develop secret business and smuggling networks to circumvent U. S. economic sanctions and withstand sustained economic pressure.

The new task force, Mr. Vatanka said, was effectively “a recognition that the Iranians were moving fast to compensate” for their maritime losses through reliance on land routes.

Analysts and diplomats say Iraq, Turkey and Pakistan have been the focus of U. S. efforts so far. Turkey has largely refused to change its border policies, they said, while Iraq has struggled to placate both sides.

The Iraqi leadership has held weekly talks with U. S. diplomats, including the regional envoy, Thomas Barrack, according to two of the three Iraqi officials, who said Iraq was asked to close all but two of the country’s border crossings with Iran.

The officials said Iraq had so far refused but, in a gesture to U. S. demands, had temporarily closed one or two crossings — often to huge uproar among its own population.

Publicly, Iraqi officials have said the closures were made to upgrade monitoring and security measures that would help curb money laundering and weapons smuggling at the border.

Pakistan, whose official yearly trade with Iran amounts to $3 billion, may have taken an approach similar to Iraq’s, analysts said, as it has opened and closed some of its border crossings with Iran in recent weeks.

Pakistani officials have said those recent border shutdowns were based on security issues, or the implementation of new electronic import processes — a move Iranian officials said was linked to U. S. sanctions on their country.

Peyman Sanandaji, head of the Transportation Commission at the Tehran Chamber of Commerce, told Iran’s Mehr News Agency that “banking restrictions related to Iran” risked “effectively bringing Iranian exports to Pakistan to a halt.”

Iran is now moving quickly to exert its own pressure on these countries, telling them not to acquiesce to U. S. demands.

“We, too, are continuing to pursue our efforts with neighboring countries and maintain our discussions with them,” said Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in a speech last month, in which he criticized U. S. efforts to pressure countries to stop trade. “We hope we will succeed.”

Working in the Iranian government’s favor is the presence of powerful regional actors, like China and Russia, that are also still willing to work with it.

On Tuesday, Iran’s deputy foreign minister announced he had held a meeting with the Russian ambassador to Iran to discuss “how to counter unilateral U. S. actions, and the so-called Iron Gate plan.”

Iran can exert economic leverage over its neighbors, said Ellie Geranmayeh, an Iran expert at the European Council on Foreign Relations. Pakistan, for example, is heavily dependent on Iranian fuel imports, particularly liquid petroleum gas.

Iraq, meanwhile, relies on Iran for more than a third of its gas, which is used to power its electrical grid. When Tehran has cut off those supplies in recent years — often because of U. S. sanctions that hindered Baghdad’s ability to pay — that has triggered huge power cuts and street protests.

The U. S. midterm election results were seen as such a resounding rebuke to the Iran war that countries in the region may simply choose to ignore U. S. demands, Ms. Geranmayeh said.

“The U. S. is currently an unpredictable and, in some cases, unreliable ally,” she said. “Iran is going to be their neighbor, they know they’re stuck with Iran for life.”

Falih Hassan, Sanam Mahoozi and Shirin Hakim contributed reporting

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley figures cast the Nvidia chief’s relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy as a personal lapse, not a security failure.

By Emmy Martin

Reporting from San Francisco

Within hours of Jensen Huang’s admission on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife, some of Silicon Valley’s most influential investors closed ranks around him.

Their messages, delivered mostly on social media, were consistent. Mr. Huang’s relationship with a woman identified by U. S. officials as a Chinese spy was a personal failing. Losing the Nvidia chief executive, they argued, would be a far bigger blow to the country, and America couldn’t win the artificial intelligence race without him.

“Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote in a post on Sunday afternoon. He said that Mr. Huang “did something incredibly dumb,” and that it was bad for America, “but my guess is there was no bad intention.” He concluded that Mr. Huang is “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”

About an hour later, Elon Musk quoted the post and added: “I agree.”

The show of loyalty reflects Mr. Huang’s rarefied standing in Silicon Valley. In the three decades since he co-founded Nvidia, he has gone from running a maker of video game graphics cards to presiding over the company at the center of the A. I. boom, now one of the world’s most valuable companies.

Nvidia’s chips are the scarce resource every A. I. company needs, a position that makes Mr. Huang something of a kingmaker. Decisions about who gets his products, and how many, can shape which start-ups and tech giants pull ahead. Nvidia’s finances are also deeply intertwined with other leading A. I. companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.

(China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)

Bill Ackman, the billionaire hedge fund manager, called Mr. Huang “an incredible human” who took “full responsibility as he should,” and urged people to “support him and his family.” Later on Sunday, Mr. Ackman added that he was “not suggesting he gets a free pass.”

On Monday, the investor Gavin Baker argued that many venture capitalists were “patriotic Americans” who believed Mr. Huang’s policy views served the country against China. He wrote that it would be “a disaster for America — and a gift to China — if Jensen goes down.”

“100% in agreement,” replied Jason Calacanis, a host of the All-In podcast, which is a popular podcast hosted by a group of venture capitalists including David Sacks, President Trump’s former A. I. and crypto czar.

Antonio Gracias, the founder of Valor Equity Partners and a longtime associate of Mr. Musk, agreed on Tuesday: “America would not be ahead in the AI race without Jensen,” he wrote. “He clearly made a mistake. One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership.”

The All-In hosts have been close to Mr. Huang. During an appearance onstage with the podcast’s hosts in September, Mr. Huang took a phone call from Mr. Trump.

Mr. Trump, too, has stood by Mr. Huang. “I really believe him,” he said on Monday, recalling a conversation when Mr. Huang told him he did not know that Ms. Huang was a spy. The Times has reported that Mr. Trump was briefed a year ago about intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was an operative for the Chinese government. Mr. Trump on Tuesday demurred when asked whether he received the briefing last year.

Mr. Huang has been among Washington’s most forceful voices against cutting China off from American chips, and has been an ally of Mr. Trump since his return to office. That, Mr. Calacanis acknowledged, makes him and his company “a critical target, and we need to protect them both.”

In Congress, the Republican leaders of three influential House committees have asked Mr. Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Ms. Huang.

The Times reported last month that U. S. officials had concluded Ms. Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore company that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips, had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.

Nvidia’s board has opened an investigation, and says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Beijing dismissed the allegations as smears.

Emmy Martin is a reporter covering the technology industry from San Francisco and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship class.
