Trump Visits Arlington Cemetery as His Proposed Arch Faces Growing Opposition

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Trump Remakes Washington

Advertisement

Supported by

An expanding legal fight over the proposed site of President Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch looms over his visit to Arlington National Cemetery on Veterans Day.

By Zach Montague

Reporting from Washington

President Trump traveled to Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday to lay a wreath in honor of fallen service members, a time-honored presidential tradition on Veterans Day at a site that could be dramatically reshaped by his proposal to build a 250-foot triumphal arch in a traffic circle just outside the cemetery’s main entrance.

Mr. Trump’s arch project is being challenged in court by a trio of Vietnam War veterans; Arlington County, Va.; the state of Virginia; the District of Columbia; and as of Tuesday, members of the Kennedy family, whose relatives’ graves sit at the emotional heart of the cemetery.

A common thread throughout the suits is the contention that the giant arch, which would loom over the nearly 640-acre military cemetery in Virginia, would have a negative effect on it.

The Times created a 3-D model of the 250-foot monument to show how it would affect a symbolic sightline.

The planned site of the arch holds “symbolic significance as the physical and ceremonial connection between Washington, D. C. and Arlington National Cemetery — the final resting place of more than 400,000 active-duty service members, veterans, and their family members,” Virginia and the District of Columbia contended in their joint lawsuit.

“For more than a century, that direct sight line has stood as a testament to the reunification of the nation after the Civil War and a point of reflection for visitors,” Arlington County said in a legal filing.

For months, Mr. Trump has vowed to push forward and celebrated the proposed arch as one of his grandest contributions to the city, dwarfing similar triumphal arches around the world. The administration has argued that aesthetic concerns about the area are not enough to win a federal lawsuit, and that various historical proposals for the bridge linking Virginia to Washington at the entrance to the cemetery included proposals for an arch built in the same corridor.

But as plans to break ground have accelerated, government bodies on both sides of the Potomac River have said the idea would bring unwelcome service interruptions to the region — and overshadow the solemn site.

Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, said the arch “will serve as a gateway to Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen and all Americans alike, serving as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes throughout our 250-year history so we can enjoy our freedoms today.”

The White House also shared a statement from the Interior Department, which said the circle itself would be improved by the project, benefiting traffic flow and pedestrian safety in the long run.

The cemetery hosts around 150 funerals in a typical week, with processions of cars traditionally entering through the main gate.

The arch would sit on an island in the Potomac River at the southwestern boundary of the District of Columbia, just across a 2,100-foot bridge. The bridge was designed to trace a vista to the Lincoln Memorial from the Robert E. Lee Memorial, also known as Arlington House, which sits atop a hill in the cemetery.

The New York Times

All sides agree the arch could be built without closing the cemetery. But the suits argue the national site could be affected in other ways.

Several of the lawsuits anticipate that preliminary excavations for the construction, which could ultimately include paving more than 62,000 square feet, would badly disrupt traffic heading into the cemetery’s main grounds.

In their new filing, nine members of the Kennedy family contend that the arch would also interfere with the intended sightline from the eternal flame at President John F. Kennedy’s gravesite, and “permanently cast shadows” over memorials throughout the area.

The board of Arlington County, a five-member legislative body, has said the arch would snarl traffic for tourists and family members visiting the cemetery, not to mention local residents commuting in the area. They have also noted that the county provides emergency services for incidents at Arlington National Cemetery, and the extended construction could impede responders.

“Memorial Circle sits on federal land, but is right next to Arlington, and connects directly to roads the county maintains and that our residents use every day,” a spokesman for the county said in an email statement.

Citing projections by the National Park Service, Arlington County has said that if Mr. Trump’s vision for his arch is successful, visitors to the area could swell by as much as 1,500 percent. The Park Service’s assessment found that when the arch is finished, traffic could “approach the upper limit of roadway capacity” in the circle.

The New York Times

The veterans, who include a former Army soldier who later served as the U. S. ambassador to Armenia and a former sailor who went on to serve in Kosovo with the Senior Foreign Service, have noted in court filings that the unobstructed view between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House across the river was intended to be “reciprocal.” It echoes the corridor between the Capitol and the White House, as planned by Pierre Charles L’Enfant, the French-born military engineer who designed much of the city.

Several of the men say in their lawsuit they hope to be buried at Arlington, and that they regularly drive across the bridge to reflect on the sight en route to honoring comrades laid to rest in the cemetery.

Mr. Trump first proposed his arch last year. He has said the project was conceived to mark the nation’s 250th anniversary, but told reporters it would also be built in his own honor. With plans to rise nearly 100 feet higher than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and to be topped by golden angels and flames, the arch could take two to three years to build, according to court filings by the government.

The veterans sued in February. They were joined in October by Washington and Virginia, which argued that the arch had been fast-tracked without proper environmental reviews or the approval from Congress necessary to add a soaring monument to the city skyline.

The president’s allies on a federal planning board formally approved construction of the project on Thursday. But minutes later, a federal judge in Washington temporarily blocked work from starting.

Judge Tanya S. Chutkan, an Obama appointee, has been skeptical that the veterans had legal standing to challenge the project. But she wrote that the District of Columbia and Virginia “face tangible economic harms from the construction of the arch.” She will next consider whether to impose a more lasting block on the project while she weighs the legal challenges.

A federal judge in Virginia will review the concerns raised by Arlington County during a hearing next week.

In recent weeks, the Trump administration has begun to argue that the arch will double as a military installation, echoing claims the president made when judges questioned his authority to replace the East Wing of the White House with a massive ballroom. Mr. Trump described the ballroom as merely the aboveground portion of a new military command center being built below. The claims gave judges pause and allowed construction to continue unimpeded for months.

As for the arch, the president has described the structure, which outwardly resembles other triumphal arches, as a “military complex” that would house fleets of drones and sniper’s nests.

But the lawsuits challenging the arch have argued that such features would make it even less appropriate to anchor a busy public intersection outside the most prominent military cemetery in the country.

“Using the arch to store large stockpiles of ammunition and as a staging point for drones and snipers, so close to commuters and tourists, will dramatically worsen these public-safety harms and the risk of accidents,” the Arlington County lawsuit said.

Marco Hernandez, Junho Lee and Doug Mills contributed graphics.

Zach Montague is a Times reporter covering the federal courts, including the legal disputes over the Trump administration’s agenda.

Trump Officials Clashed Over Firm at Heart of Nvidia Affair

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Investigation

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week about why the administration had not put restrictions on advanced chip sales to Megaspeed.

By Ana Swanson and Tripp Mickle

Ana Swanson reported from Washington and Tripp Mickle from San Francisco

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week over his handling of a Singaporean company at the heart of revelations about Chinese spying on Nvidia, demanding to know why the United States had not already banned sales of advanced A. I. chips to the firm.

The exchange, which took place at the White House on Thursday and was described by people briefed on it, highlighted growing tensions inside the Trump administration over A. I. policy in general and the Commerce Department’s posture toward Nvidia in particular.

The internal debate has only intensified after Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, acknowledged he had an affair with a woman who had helped lead the Singaporean data center company, Megaspeed. The woman, Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, has been identified by U. S. intelligence as a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported.

Mr. Lutnick responded to Mr. Bessent that the Commerce Department could now move quickly to put restrictions on Megaspeed in place, said the people briefed on the exchange, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the discussions were private.

A spokeswoman for the Commerce Department denied that the conversation between Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick had taken place. She said that the decision about whether to add companies to the entity list was an administration-wide one.

The Treasury Department did not provide a comment.

The United States has imposed restrictions since late 2022 on selling advanced chips directly to China. But Megaspeed and other companies have sidestepped those rules by setting up data centers in Southeast Asia to cater to Chinese clients. U. S. officials have also been investigating Megaspeed for potentially diverting those chips illegally into China, a charge that Megaspeed has denied.

The move to blacklist Megaspeed had earlier been discussed at a meeting of the deputies of cabinet officials, where Jeffrey Kessler, an under secretary in the Commerce Department, deferred on taking action, saying that the decision was up to Mr. Lutnick.

The confrontation between Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick was reported earlier by Axios.

In recent months, the fight over how to regulate U. S. technology has increasingly left other departments at odds with officials from the Commerce Department, which oversees technology export rules. Megaspeed’s purchases of more than $4 billion of advanced Nvidia technology have helped to reignite a debate in the administration and Washington more broadly about how rigorous U. S. controls over technology exports should be.

One of the Commerce Department’s most powerful rules is the entity list, a trade blacklist. U. S. companies are prohibited from shipping products to any firm on the entity list without first obtaining a license from the U. S. government.

During the first Trump administration and throughout the Biden administration, the government started to use the entity list more aggressively toward China’s technology sector. In March of last year, the Trump administration also issued a large update to the list, adding more than 80 companies and organizations.

But the administration has backed off use of the list more recently, as it tries to maintain a trade truce with China. More than a year has passed without any firm being added to the entity list, the longest stretch in 18 years. The Trump administration has considered entity listings of Chinese A. I. firms like Deepseek and Alibaba, but has not yet decided to move forward with them.

Still, many Trump officials have argued that Megaspeed should be added. A few months ago, officials at several agencies who oversee technology licensing agreed that Megaspeed should be put on the list, including the State Department. But the Commerce Department, which has final responsibility for issuing rules, did not take action.

The Commerce Department’s inaction led to frustrations across the administration and to Mr. Bessent’s confrontation with Mr. Lutnick.

U. S. officials in the Commerce Department began looking into Megaspeed in 2024, after the company started importing billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Nvidia A. I. equipment into Malaysia. Megaspeed had been planning and constructing data centers in Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba. That behavior is legal, but U. S. officials were concerned that some of the Nvidia chips the company had bought were illegally routed to China.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Tripp Mickle reports for The Times on some of the world’s biggest tech companies, including Nvidia, Google and Apple. He also writes about tech industry trends like layoffs and artificial intelligence.

ICE Officer Involved in Maine Shooting Expressed Hatred of Immigrants

The New York Times November 11, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The agent talked of foreign bloodlines, denounced noncitizens and more, according to emails obtained by The Times. His fatal shooting of a Colombian-born motorist in July remains under investigation.

By Katie Benner and Alexandra Berzon

Benner reported from Augusta, Maine.

David Brouillette, the rookie Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who fatally shot a Colombian migrant in Maine this summer, has a troubling work history, past complaints of domestic violence and abuse, as well as mental health issues.

He also has a record of deep-seated anti-immigrant hostility, especially against Colombians.

In 2021, four years before he joined ICE, Mr. Brouillette, a former U. S. Army sergeant, raged against his sister and their relatives in a series of emails, castigating her for her longtime relationship with a Colombian man, with whom she had two children.

“He can takes his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries,” Mr. Brouillette wrote in an email thread riddled with typos, a copy of which was shared with The New York Times.

“He does not emulate what it means to be an American” but “rather he emulates what it’s like to be entitled and think he has a seat” at a table “that has no room for his (or your ignorance),” he wrote. Mr. Brouillette continued that the man’s “bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers.”

The man who sparked Mr. Brouillette’s anger was at the time a 37-year-old graduate student studying for a Ph. D. ​in education. Born in Colombia, the man was living in the United States legally and had dated Mr. Brouillette’s sister for five years.

The email exchange was shared by Elizabeth Emen, Mr. Brouillette’s sister, and confirmed by a friend who discussed the email with her at the time, as well as a family representative. Mr. Brouillette’s comments were a snapshot, they said, of his views and anger toward people born outside the United States.

“David had no basis for saying that my partner was undocumented,” Ms. Emen, a licensed therapist in Maryland, said in an interview. “It was about how he saw him based on his race.”

Mr. Brouillette, 38, fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 during an attempted traffic stop in Biddeford, Maine.

The emails, which have never been made public, add another layer to Mr. Brouillette’s high-profile shooting and could factor into the pending state and federal investigations.

It is illegal in Maine to infringe on a person’s rights because of their actual or perceived race, color, ancestry or national origin, among other identifiers. Federal law prohibits an officer from depriving a person of their constitutional rights “on account of such person being an alien or by reason of his/her color or race.”

Mr. Brouillette’s family said he didn’t hide his sentiments about immigrants. Those views, along with publicly accessible court records documenting claims of abuse, mental health challenges and workplace struggles underscore concerns about the federal government’s hiring of Mr. Brouillette, who applied for a job with ICE as the agency relaxed its vetting process and added thousands of new officers.

“He is dangerous and should not have weapons,” Mr. Brouillette’s mother, Susan Bedard, said of her son in a text message to The Times. “Believe his victims, not him.”

Mr. Durán Guerrero, 25, was shot four times in the face and neck, said Sean P. Murphy, a lawyer for Mr. Durán Guerrero’s family.

The Department of Homeland Security said “the vehicle attempted to flee” and the officer, “fearing for public safety,” fired his weapon. Evidence confirming this account has yet to emerge.

The agency declined to confirm that Mr. Brouillette had fatally shot Mr. Durán Guerrero or describe his employment status. Mr. Brouillette’s family, however, identified him as the man pictured at the scene of the shooting being consoled by other officers.

His ex-wife and daughter told The Times that Mr. Brouillette said he fired the fatal bullets. Also, federal and state investigators examining the shooting have asked people who knew Mr. Brouillette about his background and whether they thought he should be fired over the killing of Mr. Durán Guerrero.

D. H. S. initially said that Mr. Durán Guerrero had illegally entered the country but later recanted that statement to Senator Angus King of Maine, the senator’s office said. The lawyer for the Durán Guerrero family said he was authorized to work in the United States and was not the target of ICE’s investigative efforts.

The shooting sparked a sharp outcry in Biddeford, and state officials from both parties condemned ICE’s actions. Susan Collins, Maine’s Republican senator, asked that ICE “cease all non-urgent vehicle stops.”

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “any claims of substandard training or vetting are FALSE” and that ICE officers were “trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations.”

Mr. Brouillette declined to speak with a Times reporter who knocked on the door of his home in Maine and left a letter for him. In response, he called the local sheriff to warn the reporter not to return.

According to an incident report, Mr. Brouillette told the sheriff’s deputy he was under “‘executive protection’ through the U. S. Department of Homeland Security.”

This article is based on court records, emails and interviews with Mr. Brouillette’s relatives, including Ms. Emen; his mother; his first ex-wife and daughter; as well as a former classmate, neighbors, former colleagues and people with knowledge of his hiring at ICE. His two ex-wives and some former co-workers had previously spoken to the media about their concerns.

The accounts portray Mr. Brouillette as a man who longed to wield authority as a soldier and an officer of the law. (His teenage online message handle was citizensoldier22.) Yet he worked for only short stints as a corrections officer, a security guard at a V. A. medical center and an enforcement officer for Maine’s Health and Human Services department.

He struggled with mental health challenges, having been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and hospitalized “multiple times,” his mother, Ms. Bedard, told The Times. This type of health history is typically disqualifying for federal agents, according to federal hiring guidelines.

His two former wives said in court filings that he had physically abused them — claims that he disputed. In addition, Mr. Brouillette gave false statements at least twice in court filings. For example, he told a family court judge in 2019 that he had worked as a police officer in Hallowell, Maine, according to court records. The Hallowell police chief told The Times Mr. Brouillette had applied for a job with the department but was not hired.

Several former federal prosecutors said that this kind of false statement would make it hard for Mr. Brouillette to testify in court cases, impairing his ability to do his job.

Mr. Brouillette was cleared to start at ICE on Dec. 1 after being fast-tracked through a preliminary vetting process that had become much more lenient during that period, according to a person with knowledge of his hiring, who was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. He joined the ranks amid a hiring surge that was prompted by Trump administration demands to more than double the number of deportation officers.

Hiring guidelines were changed, lowered or ignored to meet that demand, according to current and former officials involved in the agency hiring process. One agency whistle-blower told the Office of Inspector General that an “unprecedented lowering of standards” allowed improperly vetted, unqualified candidates to get job offers before they had passed basic fingerprint, identity or credit checks.

Mr. Brouillette was allowed to skip ICE’s full training course in Georgia, according to two people who were briefed on Mr. Brouillette’s work history at ICE and spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter. The decision was in keeping with ICE’s practice to have recruits with some law enforcement experience complete a shorter online training program.

After he was hired, his full background check was completed by an outside contractor, as is a standard part of the security clearance process for new officer hires, according to one of the people with knowledge of his hiring. But the agency had started to build a gigantic backlog of background reports. At the time of the shooting in Maine, officials still hadn’t gotten to look into Mr. Brouillette’s background report for red flags that could result in his termination, the person said.

Without his full clearance, Mr. Brouillette was limited in his access to some secure computer systems. But he was still deployed on the streets of Maine, armed and empowered to carry out President Trump’s immigration enforcement mandate.

In April he arrested a man born in Angola; in June, a man born in the Democratic Republic of Congo; on June 30, a man born in the Ivory Coast, federal arrest reports show. None of the men had criminal histories, the records show, and all three were detained for overstaying their visas.

On July 13, Mr. Brouillette shot Mr. Durán Guerrero.

Mr. Brouillette’s work history contained several red flags.

He held at least seven full- and part-time jobs from 2015 to 2025, including as a state corrections officer, a policeman at a V. A. hospital and an agent at Maine’s Health and Human Services Department, where he tracked down family court scofflaws.

His workplace struggles burst into view in late 2021, when he became a volunteer firefighter in Manchester, a small town near Augusta.

“It didn’t take me long to recognize that I’d made a mistake,” said Frank Wozniak, who was the fire chief at the time. “He was a loose cannon.”

While in a firefighter training program at Southern Maine Community College, a steel beam struck Mr. Brouillette in the head, causing a severe injury, according to a lawsuit that he filed against the college. Shortly after, Mr. Brouillette drove to the fire station to find Mr. Wozniak.

“He’s bandaged up and screaming at one of the guys, upset that I wouldn’t let him train or go on calls,” Mr. Wozniak said. “He was screaming, ‘I’ll punch you in the face and take your job!’” Mr. Brouillette then left the department.

Two years later he sued the college, claiming that his cognitive functioning and memory were still impaired. The lawsuit was settled.

In 2025, he ran through three jobs: He was let go from a pest control company over behavioral issues, according to two people briefed on his departure. He quit his job as a truck driver, citing health issues, and he joined a real estate agency, where he received a few thousand dollars in commissions, according to filings in a child support case.

In the fall of 2025, he applied at ICE.

The Times could not find any employer or family member who was contacted by the federal government about Mr. Brouillette until July 2026, after the fatal shooting.

When his first wife, Ashley Brouillette, found out in November that he was joining ICE, she recalled asking him how he continued to get jobs with guns. “He laughed,” she said.

She, like his sister, Ms. Emen, was surprised to learn of his new job. Ms. Emen said Mr. Brouillette’s mental health seemed to have declined after he returned from his service in Afghanistan in 2013.

“We talked about his behavior before, during and after he was in Afghanistan, and about his ongoing PTSD and mental health challenges,” said Ms. Emen, who never treated her brother or spoke with him in a professional capacity. “He conveyed to me that he protected himself in Afghanistan by racially profiling the people there. If he could dehumanize the people, he could be more self-protective and less empathetic.”

Ms. Emen said that Mr. Brouillette had made statements that certain races of people should not live in the United States. Their relationship ended in 2021.

When Ms. Emen invited her relatives to celebrate her son’s birthday, Mr. Brouillette responded with the email tirade, expressing his disapproval of her partner’s “bloodline” and his supposed “anti-American ideologies.”

“Your choices have cost you a brother. I am so so so ashamed of you,” he wrote. “You’re dead to me Liz. Enjoy it. Dead to me. DEAD.”

The email exchange could come into play as investigators examine the shooting in Maine.

“Federal statute doesn’t require a prosecutor to prove racial animus, but such bias could support the idea that the officer used excessive force,” said Michael Gennaco, a former federal prosecutor in California who oversaw civil rights prosecutions against officers accused of excessive force.

Attorney General Aaron M. Frey of Maine launched the probe immediately after the shooting, saying his office “has exclusive responsibility both for any criminal investigation of a homicide and for the use of deadly force by law enforcement.”

Mr. Frey, through a spokesperson, declined further comment, citing the pending investigation.

Biddeford police captured footage from the aftermath of the shooting on their body worn cameras, including statements made by Mr. Brouillette, according to two people briefed on the inquiry.

Separately, the Department of Homeland Security’s Inspector General, the agency watchdog, said that it was also investigating the use of deadly force in Maine.

Toby Dilworth, a former federal prosecutor in Maine, said that before the Trump administration, federal and state investigators worked in lock step on these inquiries.

In the Brouillette case, a detective from the state attorney general’s office and a special agent with the D. H. S. Inspector General’s office interviewed Mr. Brouillette’s first wife, Ashley.

But three people briefed on this investigation, none of whom were authorized to discuss the case, said that the federal government’s cooperation with Mr. Frey’s office has been more limited.

This is in keeping with friction that has arisen between federal and state investigators in multiple cases, including the shooting of Alex Pretti, a nurse who was killed by a Customs and Border Protection agent in Minneapolis. Mr. Pretti’s parents said that the Justice Department refuses to confirm the identity of the man who shot their son and has stopped sharing evidence related to the shooting with local investigators.

Local authorities are investigating several high-profile incidents involving federal immigration agents, including deadly shootings, and have indicted four officers in Colorado, Minnesota and Texas.

In Maine, some resolution could come soon. Mr. Frey’s term in office ends this December, when the State Legislature seats the next attorney general. Mr. Murphy, the lawyer for the Durán Guerrero family, said investigators recently told him that Mr. Frey plans to announce any decisions in the case before he leaves office.

Susan C. Beachy and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

Katie Benner is a correspondent writing primarily about large institutions that shape American life.

Alexandra Berzon is an investigative reporter covering American politics and elections for The Times.

Behind the Trump-Xi Bonhomie, a Fierce Spy War Rages

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

That the United States suspected Nvidia’s leader was a Chinese spy target underscores the deep distrust between the two powers, even as their leaders try to stabilize ties.

By David Pierson

Reporting from Hong Kong

As President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, prepare to meet next week to extend a fragile trade truce, a fresh espionage scandal has shown that behind their diplomacy is a fierce intelligence rivalry.

At its center is Jensen Huang, the Nvidia leader and an influential ally of Mr. Trump’s, who has acknowledged having an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom U. S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for Beijing. China has denied the espionage allegation.

Under Mr. Xi, the Chinese Communist Party has built a more sophisticated and assertive spy service that regularly highlights the importance of technological security and of threats posed by the United States. At the same time, the Central Intelligence Agency has said that Chinese companies are a legitimate target for espionage in areas like artificial intelligence, semiconductors and biotechnology.

Nvidia’s computer chips power the global A. I. boom and sit at the center of Washington’s efforts to keep that technology out of China’s hands. That makes Mr. Huang, who has lobbied Mr. Trump to ease restrictions on the export of advanced chips to China, a prime target, analysts say.

“It is not at all surprising, given the centrality of Nvidia to U. S.-China tech competition, and the importance of tech competition in the overall U. S.-China rivalry, that someone like him would be a top target for Chinese intelligence collection,” said Sheena Chestnut Greitens, an expert on Chinese security at the University of Texas at Austin.

U. S. agencies concluded that the Chinese businesswoman, who goes by Alice Huang, was an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security. Nvidia has said that it is conducting an internal investigation. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

“It is brazen, and yet I don’t think we should be surprised at all,” said Christopher K. Johnson, a former U. S. government intelligence officer who is now president of China Strategies Group, a risk consultancy. “Whenever the Chinese declare something a national strategic, whole-of-society priority, like they have done with chips and A. I., that implies they will use every tool available to them to work, buy or steal their way to that end.”

So far, the scandal has not apparently disrupted plans for Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi to meet next week in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. Mr. Trump said on Monday that he did not plan to bring the matter up with Mr. Xi. He has repeatedly downplayed reports of Chinese spying and cyberattacks on the United States, arguing that Washington does the same.

That is a contrast with the Biden administration, which confronted China in early 2023 about a spy balloon that was spotted drifting across the continental United States. Official relations between the countries froze for months.

Mr. Trump’s approach could embolden China to take bigger risks, said Dennis Wilder, a former U. S. intelligence analyst on China and a senior fellow at Georgetown University.

“The president’s whole laissez-faire attitude toward spying reassures Beijing that the political blowback from espionage operations will be very manageable,” he said.

Mr. Huang was until recently also expected to travel to Shenzhen. When Mr. Xi visited the United States in September, the tech executive was a guest at the White House state dinner. He had joined a presidential trip to Beijing in May at Mr. Trump’s invitation.

“The president has over and over dismissed Chinese spying by saying that everyone does it,” Mr. Wilder said. “The problem is that no one else does it to the very damaging effect that the Chinese can and do.”

In recent years, Chinese spies have been accused of targeting the phones of American presidential candidates, recruiting U. S. Navy sailors, cultivating political aides and planting malicious code in power grids and water systems that Americans rely on every day.

Beijing also a history of ruthless counterintelligence operations. From 2010 through 2012, the Chinese government killed or imprisoned 18 to 20 of the C. I. A.’s sources in China, crippling American spying there for years, The New York Times reported in 2017.

Espionage has repeatedly strained relations, at times erupting into diplomatic crises, as when a U. S. Navy surveillance plane collided with a Chinese fighter jet in 2001 near China’s Hainan Island, killing the Chinese pilot. Beijing condemned Washington for spying and held the 24 American crew members for 11 days.

China’s lead intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security, has transformed from a service that relied on gathering gossip at embassy dinner parties into a sophisticated spy shop that can go toe-to-toe with the C. I. A. with bigger budgets and modern tools like A. I.

Its political standing has risen as well. In 2022, Mr. Xi elevated the ministry’s then chief, Chen Wenqing, to the Communist Party’s Politburo, a council of the 24 most senior national leaders. He was the first spy chief in decades to ascend to that body.

The once-shadowy ministry has also stepped into public view, posting a stream of warnings on its WeChat social media account about foreign spies. It has publicized examples of Chinese nationals working for the government and a military contractor in Tokyo and Rome being recruited by C. I. A. officers to provide information about the government or the military.

At the same time, the United States has stepped up its intelligence gathering to include not just military and government targets, but also private Chinese companies, the deputy C. I. A. director, Michael Ellis, told a cybersecurity conference this year. Compared with past geopolitical rivals, China “poses a fundamentally different kind of threat to us because the competition is economic,” Mr. Ellis said.

The C. I. A. has also taken the unusual step of recruiting in public, producing a series of Mandarin-language videos urging disaffected Chinese officials to share secrets with the United States. (The Ministry of State Security’s WeChat account mocked the videos as “crude,” “farcical” and a sign of the C. I. A.’s “baffling incompetence.”)

In China, the case has drawn official denials and questions about what Beijing would stand to gain.

Ms. Huang had been an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that buys advanced Nvidia chips. The United States began restricting sales of advanced chips directly to China in late 2022, but Chinese companies can lease computing power from data centers that use those chips in Southeast Asia, like the ones Megaspeed operates.

At the same time, China has also encouraged domestic companies to make do with less powerful domestically produced chips to promote greater national self-reliance, leading some analysts to question the significance of the Nvidia case.

“China does not want to import so many Nvidia chips,” said Shen Dingli, an international relations scholar in Shanghai. “They are trying to force Chinese companies to use Chinese chips from Huawei.”

The Chinese Foreign Ministry has rejected the espionage allegations surrounding Ms. Huang as “nothing but a smear against China.” On Chinese social media platforms, which are heavily censored, comments about Mr. Huang have centered on his extramarital affair.

Nationalist commentators in China have described the scandal as an effort that brings together American opponents of China, Mr. Trump, and artificial intelligence.

Ren Yi, a Harvard-educated Chinese blogger who goes by the pen name “Chairman Rabbit,” wrote: “Once again, anti-China politics weaves America’s disparate political causes together.”

Berry Wang contributed research.

David Pierson covers Chinese foreign policy and China’s economic and cultural engagement with the world. He has been a journalist for more than two decades.

Jensen Huang’s Affair Puts His Wife in the Spotlight

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Lori Huang, who has been married to the Nvidia chief executive for more than 40 years, stands out among tech titan spouses for how private she has been.

By Erin Griffith and Don Clark

Reporting from San Francisco

In November 2021, Jensen Huang attended the annual dinner held by the Semiconductor Industry Association in San Jose, Calif. That night, the trade group gave Mr. Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, its highest honor, named for the Intel co-founder Robert Noyce.

Mr. Huang arrived early with his wife, Lori Huang, and quickly headed to the bar at the pre-dinner reception, saying the event was the first time he had been out of his house since the Covid lockdown began in March 2020. He introduced Ms. Huang to reporters who clustered nearby, but they mainly talked to him.

By the time Mr. Huang received the award, two hours had passed. The Nvidia leader walked onstage with a bottle of red wine and two glasses, sharing them with a moderator and taking the conversation into unexpected topics. Throughout, Ms. Huang remained in the background.

For more than 40 years, Ms. Huang has been by Mr. Huang’s side as he built his fledgling chip start-up into one of the most valuable companies in the world. Nvidia’s success turned Mr. Huang into an international business star. His face is on sweaters, his signature leather jackets have become collectors items, and his net worth has soared to nearly $150 billion.

By contrast, Ms. Huang stayed far from the spotlight.

That changed this week, when Mr. Huang, 63, revealed he had an affair with an executive identified by the U. S. government as a Chinese spy. In his admission, which he shared in a message to Nvidia employees, Mr. Huang apologized to his wife, as well as his two children, who both work at Nvidia, thrusting them into the limelight.

The bombshell news had implications for U. S. national security and the economy. Nvidia’s role as the A. I. industry’s main supplier of chips makes Mr. Huang a crucial linchpin for an industry that has come to dominate the stock market.

It also has ramifications for his personal life. Mr. Huang’s admission has fueled speculation about the fate of his 41-year marriage with Ms. Huang, 64. She is president of the Jen-Hsun Lori Huang Foundation, which had $9 billion in assets as of 2024, including $6 billion in fresh funding that year. Of Mr. Huang’s 922 million Nvidia shares, more than half belong to a trust where Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang are the co-trustees, according to financial filings. She is also the sole controller of a trust that owns around $5 billion worth of Nvidia shares.

Ms. Huang joins a small group of tech titan spouses who have had to grapple with public infidelity. The list includes MacKenzie Scott, the ex-wife of the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Melinda French Gates, ex-wife of the Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates. The billionaire ex-wife of a tech mogul has become such a fixture in American pop culture that it has inspired characters in “The Devil Wears Prada 2” and the Maya Rudolph comedy “Loot.”

Ms. Huang’s public profile stands out among the current and former spouses of powerful business leaders because of how private she has been. She has not promoted her philanthropic work in interviews or on the conference circuit.

“Lori is unusually modest by the standards of billionaire couples,” said George Rush, who formerly coauthored Rush & Molloy, a long-running gossip column at The Daily News.

That adds further intrigue to the political and economic consequences of the affair, Mr. Rush noted. “Bezos and Gates didn’t have this dynamic, where the relationship could move markets and have this global fallout,” he said. “It is one of a kind.”

Nvidia declined to comment and Ms. Huang did not respond to a request for comment. (China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)

Similar to other tech billionaire spouses like Ms. Scott, Ms. Huang was crucial to the start of her husband’s company.

She met Mr. Huang as one of a handful of women studying engineering at Oregon State University in the early 1980s. Mr. Huang was her lab partner in an electrical engineering fundamentals class, and he convinced her to join him for a weekly study date. He later called meeting her “the most important, single event of OSU, and of my life.”

After the pair graduated and married, they moved to Silicon Valley to work as microchip designers. Both were known as gifted engineers. Ms. Huang worked at Silicon Graphics, a hardware and software maker, where her salary was higher than Mr. Huang’s at LSI Logic, a semiconductor company, he said in a 2023 profile in The New Yorker.

But the couple struggled to find the right child care, according to “The Thinking Machine,” a biography of Mr. Huang. Just before he co-founded Nvidia in 1993, Ms. Huang gave up her career to raise their children, Spencer and Madison. While Mr. Huang missed their karate tournaments to build his company, Ms. Huang never complained, he recalled in May on the podcast How I Built This With Guy Raz. “That’s the gift that she gave me.”

Mr. Huang has frequently shared a warm reverence for Ms. Huang in interviews. “It’s good to have someone in your life who unconditionally believes in you, who believes you’re doing your best,” he said in an interview with a publication run by Oregon State University in 2014. “You need people like that, and Lori’s always been that person for me — ever since I was 18, she was there believing in me and knowing I could do it. Even when I had self-doubts, she didn’t.”

When Mr. Huang’s Nvidia shares made him wealthy, the family set up an endowment that ballooned alongside their net worth. The foundation has donated to the San Francisco Opera and acquired computing power to donate to universities and nonprofits. The Huangs have sidestepped political donations.

Through it all, Ms. Huang was a frequent presence at Mr. Huang’s public events, including state dinners, conference appearances and celebrations of the couple’s donations to Stanford University and Oregon State University. She generally stayed in the background while he gave speeches and hobnobbed with industry executives and reporters.

“She’s been to every conference, every speech, you know, and every moment of Nvidia, she was there,” he said in an interview this year with CNA, an Asian news network. “Lori’s been with me for a long time, our whole life.”

She even helped shape his public image. Along with her daughter Madison, she dressed Mr. Huang in a designer leather jacket that has become his trademark look. Madison joined Nvidia in 2020 and Spencer joined the company in 2022. Madison’s husband, Nico Caprez, also works there.

Mr. Huang ended his message to Nvidia employees about the affair with a request: “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.”

Georgia Gee contributed research.

Erin Griffith covers tech companies, start-ups and the culture of Silicon Valley from San Francisco.

The View From Space the U. S. Government Doesn’t Want You to See

The New York Times November 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Video

By Ollie Ballinger and Zach Toombs

Ollie Ballinger is an open-source researcher and lecturer in Geocomputation at the Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis at University College London. Zach Toombs is a journalist and founder of Evident, a nonprofit news organization for visual journalism.

The U. S. government is trying to censor your view from space.

Ollie Ballinger, an open-source researcher and lecturer, uses satellite imagery to monitor conflicts around the world. But he says pressure from the government has prompted private companies to restrict access to images of places it may not want the public to see.

Why would companies listen to these requests? “Any pressure from the U. S. government carries a lot of weight for these companies,” Mr. Ballinger says, “because the American government is their biggest customer.”

In the Opinion video above, he reveals how these restrictions are limiting a vital tool for accountability and public safety and warns of a future in which governments have the power to control what the public can see and, ultimately, what it can know.

Below is an edited transcript of this video. We recommend watching it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the video player above.

Ollie Ballinger: Let me show you something the U. S. government doesn’t want you to see. The aftermath of American missile strikes on schools and homes, revealed by satellite imagery.

This view from space has been used to uncover destruction in Gaza, mass graves in Ukraine, internment camps in China and the Minab school strike in Iran. Journalists, humanitarian groups and researchers like me rely on satellite imagery to monitor conflicts, natural disasters and atrocities around the world.

Several months ago, I could go to multiple companies based in the U. S. and buy high quality images of the Middle East. But for much of this year, here’s what we’ve seen: a blackout. The U. S. government is pressuring private companies to censor satellite imagery. And that limits the public’s view of what’s happening in some of the most critical parts of the world.

In the early days of the Iran war, satellite imagery showed us details of American missile strikes on civilian targets. And it revealed the extent of damage to U. S. bases beyond what the Trump administration was admitting. But there was also concern, from both the administration and from members of Congress, that commercially available satellite imagery had been used by Iran to target U. S. troops.

Clip of U. S. House Armed Services Committee, March 25:

Representative Seth Moulton of Massachusetts: What are you doing, between the D. O. D. and the intelligence community, to work with these providers — many of whom have contracts with the U. S. government — to make sure we have better control over this?

William Adkins, National Reconnaissance Office deputy director: We have a strong partnership with our commercial providers. Their C. E. O. s meet with our leadership quarterly. We have an ongoing dialogue.

This email landed shortly after this exchange: It’s from Planet Labs, one of the biggest satellite companies in the world. They made it clear to their customers: They were restricting satellite imagery at the request of the U. S. government.

The other big player in this space, Vantor, began rolling out restrictions even earlier. They told us that they are just following their own policies. But any pressure from the U. S. government carries a lot of weight for these companies — because the American government is their biggest customer.

The blackouts imposed by U. S. companies were sweeping. They don’t just cover U. S. bases and troop positions. They cover much of the Gulf region, including Gaza, Lebanon and other places with conflict but with no official U. S. military presence. In the last couple of decades, open access to satellite images has become the norm. But this kind of censorship takes us back to a time when we had to take our governments at their word.

Archival clip of then-Secretary of State Colin Powell at the U. N.: Let me say a word about satellite images before I show a couple.

In 2003, Colin Powell justified the U. S. invasion of Iraq in part through the use of satellite imagery. He claimed that they showed evidence of weapons of mass destruction. At that time, governments had a near-monopoly on the view from above.

Powell: “The photos that I am about to show you are sometimes hard for the average person to interpret. But as I show you these images, I will try to capture and explain what they mean — what they indicate to our imagery specialists.”

In the case of Iraq, the story the government told was completely false. The result was decades of war. And now, we’re losing the ability to independently verify these sorts of claims.

Satellites have shrunk from the size of school buses to shoeboxes and now there are thousands of them taking photos from orbit, operated by companies all over the world. That means, even with U. S. restrictions, Iran can still view the pictures that it wants by using Chinese satellites.

Clip of Kevin O’Connell, former director, Office of Space Commerce: It makes sense that governments will reserve the right to control the dissemination of imagery in a crisis. I think the problem that we see is that as soon as the U. S. companies stopped providing satellite imagery, competitors — and specifically our adversaries, and the Chinese — were able to provide imagery in very short order of the exact same scenarios. And so when you ask the companies to control the imagery, are you actually having the effect that you want to have?

Meanwhile, researchers like me don’t have reliable access to that data. The imagery that the U. S. government is restricting is exactly the kind of imagery that we’ve been relying on for years.

Back in 2023, I built this tool to detect damage in Gaza. It uses a combination of freely available imagery from the European Space Agency and higher resolution imagery from American commercial providers to reveal details of damaged buildings and people killed in bombings. But for much of the year, we’ve seen this: I couldn’t tell you much about the kind of building that’s been damaged or the kind of bomb that’s been dropped.

When governments pressure private companies to withhold this kind of data, it sets a dangerous precedent for researchers like me who are investigating possible war crimes, for journalists making independent assessments of Iran’s nuclear program and aid groups figuring out where help is needed.

Clip of Rhiannan Price, a founder of Common Space: Satellite imagery helps you understand how to get to affected populations. Are there ways in which we need to make sure that refugee and internally displaced person camps are safe, that they are receiving the adequate resources that they need? These are just some of the questions that humanitarians are using high resolution satellite imagery for. When they don’t have access, it’s a real gap in terms of the information at every moment of a crisis.

Even environmental watchdogs rely on this data to protect rainforests.

Clip of Mark Fahey, Environmental Investigation Agency-U. S.: There’s no hiding these things from space. We have these territories in the Amazon that we work with, and now we can just scan the entire area using machine learning, find places that have the start of a pit and then order the high definition image. It is crazy, the vast amount of land that you can monitor once you have access to these things.”

Government censorship makes all of this work difficult or even impossible. And there’s reason to worry that the U. S. government is going to double down on these blackouts.

The House Intelligence Committee has asked the Pentagon, and the director of national intelligence, to come up with a new plan to regulate satellite companies that do business with the government. This could give the government new levers of control over the satellite imagery that the public relies on.

O’Connell: The United States has always been the world leader in commercial satellite imagery. When restrictions are put in place, that potentially dampens interest in buying access to those capabilities from American companies.

More government control over this industry would be a bad thing, especially under an administration that has consistently misled the public.

Reporter, off camera: Did the United States bomb a girls’ elementary school in southern Iran on the first day of the war and kill 175 people?

President Trump: No, in my opinion, based on what I’ve seen, that was done by Iran.

There’s a lot to lose when our view from space is blocked. And the public has a right to see the earth without government censorship.

The U. S. Department of Defense and National Reconnaissance Office declined to answer questions about requests for restricting commercial satellite imagery. Planet Labs has partly lifted restrictions on its imagery across the Middle East. As of Nov. 1, multiple companies, including Planet Labs and Vantor, are still restricting imagery over Gaza and southern Lebanon, where bombings and demolitions continue.

This video was produced by Zach Toombs. It was edited by Jennifer Smart. The associate producers are Amanda Su and Rebecca Shaid. The creative director was Kevin Clancy. Fact-checking by Julie Beer. Cinematography by Niall Kenny. The field producer was Veronika Silchenko. Audio mixing by Efim Shapiro. The postproduction manager is Mike Puretz. Audience strategy by Kristina Samulewski. The executive producer of Opinion Video is Erica Berenstein. The director of Opinion Video is Jonah M. Kessel. The director of audio engineering is Isaac Jones. The deputy director of Opinion Shows is Alison Bruzek. The director of Opinion Shows is Annie-Rose Strasser. The head of Times Opinion is Kathleen Kingsbury. Special thanks to Evident.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Signals can be detected in the way people talk years before symptoms of cognitive decline emerge, researchers are finding.

Research is analyzing subtle aspects of how people talk and speech-related movements like chewing and swallowing to try to help predict the risk of developing dementia. Credit...

Supported by

By Pam Belluck

Visuals by Cassandra Klos for The New York Times

Pam Belluck covers neuroscience and brain health.

It’s not every day that a 76-year-old woman is asked to talk nonsense — repeating “ga ba da” and “ka pa ta” as fast as she can.

All with sensors affixed to her tongue, forehead, chin, jaw, upper and lower lip recording her tiniest muscle movements in the name of science.

The goal is to analyze changes in people’s speech to try to predict their likelihood of developing dementia and track shifts in their brain health.

“We are seeing differences that humans can’t see or can’t really detect by their ears, but it’s there years and years before cognitive decline,” said Marziye Eshghi, the researcher leading the effort at Mass General Brigham University of Health Professions in Boston.

Dr. Eshghi’s project measures about 130 different speech-related features in participants like the 76-year-old woman from suburban Boston, who asked to be identified by her first name, Deb, to protect her privacy. The data is run through artificial intelligence algorithms and compared with known biological risk factors for Alzheimer’s. In preliminary results, speech-related data was better than cognitive testing at identifying Alzheimer’s risk in cognitively unimpaired older people, Dr. Eshghi’s team reported.

“What we are doing is capturing individuals who are at higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, but they are still not showing any symptoms,” said Dr. Eshghi, who directs her institution’s speech, physiology and neurobiology of aging and dementia lab.

Increasingly, researchers are embracing what was once considered an intriguing but relatively fringe idea: that speech and how it changes over time can help predict and track cognitive decline. Technological advances are making it possible to collect and analyze many aspects of speech, including how fast people talk, how often they pause, the complexity and variety of their vocabulary, their pitch and cadence and the coordination of their vocal and facial muscles.

“It’s really a window into brain health,” said Dr. Marilu Gorno Tempini, director of the language neurobiology laboratory at the University of California, San Francisco. “The way we can analyze speech and language now,” she said, allows insight into “detailed brain function and cognition that was unheard of before.”

Researchers see a future in which everyday speech that people can easily record themselves could be analyzed for incremental indicators of brain health. That analysis, combined with other measures like brain imaging and blood tests, could be used to predict dementia risk and monitor progression of cognitive impairment.

Dr. Steven Arnold, an Alzheimer’s expert and professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School who collaborates on some of Dr. Eshghi’s studies, said more research and evidence are needed before speech analysis could play a part in diagnosing or monitoring neurological conditions. “I still consider it to be early stage,” he said of speech research, “but potentially very important for the field for early detection of dementia, for detecting progression of cognitive impairment and decline and for detecting response to treatment or interventions.”

He said he expected speech would be most useful in tracking changes over time, not as a single snapshot, and could be especially informative in monitoring clinical trial participants.

Speech analysis could also help researchers identify those at greater risk within a group of people who have tested positive for Alzheimer’s biomarkers, said Melissa Lee, who directs digital and A. I. at the nonprofit Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation. “If we have two people with positive blood tests, one shows decline and one won’t, and we’d use their speech to tell them apart,” she said.

Dr. Lee leads a large study, SpeechDX, that is collecting three years of speech data along with blood tests, brain scans and cognitive assessments for 2,000 people in the United States, Australia and Spain. The study, which includes speakers of English, Spanish and Catalan, will provide data “others can use to build models that use speech to predict someone’s cognitive state,” she said.

Dr. Eshghi’s research combines speech analysis with other assessments including brain imaging, blood biomarker measures and genetic tests.

How we choose health experts to talk to. Times reporters often spend weeks interviewing doctors, researchers and other health professionals to help report an article. We seek leaders in their fields, watch out for conflicts of interest and try to get a variety of viewpoints.

In one study Deb participated in, 49 people without cognitive impairment were classified as low-risk, moderate-risk or high-risk for Alzheimer’s based on levels of an Alzheimer’s-related protein in their blood and whether they had a genetic variant linked to increased risk. Then, without knowing participants’ risk categories, researchers analyzed speech recordings and tested whether a computer model could determine which participants were in which group.

In preliminary results, the speech-based analysis classified participants accurately up to 77 percent of the time, much better than the 47 percent accuracy of commonly used cognitive testing models. Deb is in the low-risk category, Dr. Eshghi said.

Participants are being reassessed multiple times to track how their speech changes, Dr. Eshghi said. One goal is to identify which specific aspects of speech are most informative in detecting early brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s and in predicting cognitive decline.

Speech offers a gold mine of information because it involves so many elements, including word-generation, memory, attention, expression, processing speed, context awareness and muscle movements. It’s also a widespread daily activity that doesn’t require time-consuming or costly tests like brain scans and spinal taps.

“Most people speak, and speaking is a very cognitively complex task,” said Rhoda Au, a professor of anatomy and neurobiology at Boston University. And voice recordings can be stored indefinitely and be reanalyzed as new information emerges, said Dr. Au, whose research includes showing that A. I. analysis of recordings from neuropsychological exams could help predict whether people with mild cognitive impairment would develop Alzheimer’s dementia in the next six years.

Dr. Au, a pioneer in studying speech as an indicator of cognitive change, said that years ago, “no one was listening to us,” but now, other researchers’ attitudes have shifted to “‘Wow, this is pretty interesting.’”

Deb’s speech was evaluated two years ago, and she returned over the summer for a second assessment. The intensive two-hour session included a series of timed tasks. She read increasingly complex sentences, rattled off words beginning with certain letters and counted backward from 620.

After Dr. Eshghi placed sensors on her face, she repeated tongue twisters four times, including “Clever Kim called the cat clinic” and “Take today’s tasty tea on the terrace.”

In free-form speaking segments, she was asked to describe her hobbies. Deb said she belongs to a mushroom foraging club, enjoys contra dancing and “I collect giant fruit.” The fruit is made of plastic, papiermâché and other materials, she clarified, adding: “I’m very proud of this strange activity.”

Later, she was given gum and then Cheerios to chew so sensors could measure tongue and jaw movements and coordination during chewing and swallowing.

Dr. Eshghi said an analysis of Deb’s results found that, compared with two years earlier, she paused somewhat more often and spent more time pausing. Her average pitch was slightly higher and the maximum speed of some speech-related movements decreased. She remained cognitively unimpaired.

“Those differences could relate to normal aging, changes in vocal or motor function or underlying biological processes,” Dr. Eshghi said. “This illustrates the potential of speech measurements to capture subtle differences that are not reflected in a change in overall cognitive status,” she added.

Speech and voice quality are also being analyzed for signs of other health conditions. Those include depression, which can be characterized by subtle changes in talking speed and pauses; Parkinson’s, in which speech may become softer or slurred; and diabetes, which can be accompanied by vocal hoarseness.

In studying the relationship of speech to cognitive impairment, some researchers have focused on linguistic aspects, such as vocabulary and sentence complexity. Decades ago, one part of a long-running research project called the Nun Study found that Catholic nuns who wrote more verbal and idea-rich essays as young women were less likely to develop Alzheimer’s later.

But such verbal attributes may not be broadly representative because they can be affected by socioeconomic conditions and education. Most researchers now include elements like speed, pauses and vocal tone.

Dr. Gorno Tempini said speech might even reflect changes in emotional perception and empathy that can occur with dementia. For example, she said, someone with encroaching cognitive impairment may look at a picture and say “there is a dog and there is a person and there is a car crash,” instead of “Oh my God, this dog died, it was just hit by a car, and the owner is there crying.”

Several companies have entered the speech analysis arena. One, Sonde, has an app that offers a general gauge of “cognitive fitness” by analyzing eight characteristics of short voice samples to assess if the speaker is exerting high, moderate or lower cognitive effort.

Dr. Au and other researchers said there’s not yet enough evidence for using commercial speech analysis tools as specific indicators of brain health. The field first needs to collect and analyze more data and learn which aspects of speech are significantly linked to cognitive changes, she said.

“I personally don’t think this is ready for prime time, not in the health care space,” Dr. Au said.

Experts said information privacy will also have to be addressed so patients’ results are not shared without their consent. Dr. Lee said the SpeechDX study deletes any identifying information participants provide and, to ensure that even the research staff cannot distinguish participants by their voices, recordings are analyzed by computer without being played aloud.

“Speech is extremely promising and it’s extremely powerful,” she said. “You only want to be able to use it in ways that people give you permission to use it for.”

Pam Belluck is a health and science reporter for The Times, covering a range of subjects, including reproductive health, long Covid, brain science, neurological disorders, mental health and genetics.

When Measles Came to an Amish Community, Many Suffered and One Died

The New York Times November 11, 2026

U. S. Health Policy

Advertisement

Supported by

In Lewis County, N. Y., the highly contagious virus has swept through Amish homes. Public health experts fear there’s no end in sight.

By Joseph Goldstein and David Andreatta

Joseph Goldstein reported from New York City, and David Andreatta from Lewis County, N. Y., where an infant died from measles.

On a recent Saturday morning in New York’s North Country, there were signs that work had fallen behind.

Standing on his porch in suspenders and shirtsleeves, 32-year-old David Stoltzfus pointed at a heap of logs, some thicker than telephone poles and stacked two stories high. He needed to saw them into lumber. But Mr. Stoltzfus was still playing catch-up after falling ill.

“You see the big pile of wood that all got piled up?” he asked, pointing to hundreds of logs. “That’s because of the measles.”

The viral illness ripped through his house five weeks ago, sickening him, his wife and their six children. “I was sick in bed for about four days,” he said. And it was weeks before he felt healed. Work lagged. “It was hard for a couple of weeks until I got energy,” he said.

All across Lewis County, N. Y., where the trees are already bare and stands selling maple syrup dot the roadside, Amish families — Mr. Stoltzfus’s included — have stories of measles sweeping through their homes in recent weeks, their community disproportionately affected by the virus. One man described how it had attacked nine of 10 people in his house. Another said it had infected eight of nine people.

“Right now, just about everybody” has recovered, said Samuel Stoltzfus, 23, a distant cousin of David’s who lives about eight miles away.

Except for a family living way down a private road, amid a fast-growing Amish settlement. There, on Nov. 1, an ambulance was summoned. Then the county coroner. A 7-month-old boy had died at home after contracting measles, according to the coroner.

It was the first death from the disease in New York in 30 years. On Tuesday, health officials reported that the state has recorded more than 235 measles cases since Aug. 1, with 16 in Lewis County. That is almost certainly an undercount, doctors and public health experts say. Families that have weathered infections without going to a doctor, opting for bed rest, aren’t typically included in official case counts.

“We’re only catching the tip of the iceberg,” said Dr. Jana Shaw, a pediatric infectious-disease specialist at SUNY Upstate Medical University in Syracuse who has treated Amish patients during this outbreak.

The outbreak, in its fourth month, does not appear to be subsiding. Only a few cases have been recorded in the counties with some of the largest Amish populations in New York, including St. Lawrence County, which neighbors Lewis County. In Seneca County, in the Finger Lakes region, the count of new infections is climbing rapidly, with health authorities having recorded 21 new cases in the first week of November.

Measles landed in the state after tearing through Amish settlements in Ohio and Pennsylvania. The Amish tend to have lower vaccination rates than the general population.

Dr. Shaw said she knew of five newborns who were infected with measles. Their mothers transmitted the infection during pregnancy or delivery — or shortly thereafter.

Lynne M. Brown, a nurse and the director of infection prevention at University of Rochester Medicine, said that nine children with complications related to measles had been admitted to Golisano Children’s Hospital in Rochester during this outbreak. Four were sick enough to be put on ventilators in the intensive care unit.

Doctors there have seen a worrisome pattern. Children, after being infected with measles, are prone to bacterial infections in the days or weeks after.

“We’ve seen some meningitis cases, and we’ve seen some pneumonias as well,” said Dr. Tyler Stephen, who specializes in pediatric infectious diseases at Golisano Children’s, part of the University of Rochester system.

Measles is among the most contagious diseases. If an infected person coughs or sneezes in a room, an infectious dose of the virus can linger in the air for up to two hours.

The virus was once all but vanquished in the United States. But cases have spiked in recent years, as more families forgo or delay vaccinating their children.

A number of insular communities — all with lower than average vaccination rates — have faced outbreaks. In 2018 and 2019, New York endured a significant outbreak among ultra-Orthodox Jewish communities in Brooklyn and elsewhere. Last year, measles rampaged through Colorado City, Ariz., and Hildale, Utah, adjoining cities that once were the stronghold of a polygamist offshoot of the Mormon Church. This year, a close-knit evangelical Slavic community in South Carolina bore the brunt of an outbreak that sickened nearly 1,000 people, mostly unvaccinated children.

In a court affidavit in 2023, Ezra Wengerd, an Amish leader who represents Amish schools in their dealings with state government, described his community’s approach to childhood illnesses.

“We have age-old practices for addressing when a child gets sick in our community including having them recover in bed, tended to by one parent, and not attending communal activities while sick,” he wrote.

Doctors and county health officials say that the outbreak in New York State remains largely confined to “Plain communities,” as Amish and Mennonite settlements are often called, referring to their unadorned clothes and way of living. That could change.

“Measles remains a threat to anyone who is unvaccinated,” the state Health Department said in a statement.

New York State has more than 25,000 Amish residents, according to the latest estimates by the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College in Pennsylvania. They are scattered across more than 50 settlements, from western New York to the North Country.

The population has grown substantially in New York, buoyed by Amish people who moved from Ohio and Pennsylvania, seeking cheaper farmland, or to form communities because of schisms and division within older communities.

“Coming here was a conservative decision, intended to establish new settlements and as much as possible to raise families who would farm,” said Karen Johnson-Weiner, a retired professor at SUNY Potsdam, who has written books about the Amish.

The outbreak in New York appears to have been seeded by measles infections picked up in Ohio and Pennsylvania, according to local news reports and county health officials.

Though most Amish people travel short distances by horse and buggy, they tend to travel longer distances by bus.

Under normal circumstances, the health authorities recommend that children receive their first dose of the M. M. R. vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — at about 12 months of age. But given the active risk, New York State health officials have encouraged families in affected counties to have infants as young as 6 months vaccinated.

By age 2, about 81 percent of children in the state have received a first dose of vaccine. By the start of kindergarten, more than 97 percent have been vaccinated, reflecting New York’s strict school vaccination requirements.

Rates are far lower among Amish New Yorkers. Several Amish communities are locked in a legal fight with the state Health Department over whether their children must be vaccinated to attend small private Amish schools.

Some Amish parents oppose vaccinating schoolchildren for religious reasons, saying they must put their faith in God, not vaccines or state health regulations. Many believe that salvation requires that they live in tightknit religious communities — and keep worldly influences at bay.

Attitudes toward vaccination vary widely among the Amish. In Lewis County, one 50-year-old man, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he wanted to maintain his privacy, said he had developed rheumatic fever as a boy, which left him frail. So his parents vaccinated him against measles and other diseases to give him more protection. But he had not vaccinated his seven children, he said, and they had all gotten measles in the last month.

Samuel Stoltzfus, the Amish man who said that most of the affected people in his community had recovered, paused on a walk home after a morning of hunting deer in nearby woods to describe his family’s experience with vaccines and the measles.

Wearing a tattered broad-brimmed straw hat and carrying a rifle in one hand and an orange hunting vest in the other, Mr. Stoltzfus said that only one of 10 people in his parents’ home had been spared the measles: his mother. She had been vaccinated as a young girl to protect a sibling with health issues.

In his own case, Mr. Stoltzfus was sick enough that he stayed in bed for two weeks last month.

“It’s miserable,” he said. “It starts in your head, and you get dots, like a red rash, around your eyes and it travels all the way down to your feet.”

Joseph Goldstein covers health care in New York for The Times, following years of criminal justice and police reporting.
